mini_conversation: Customer: Hi, I'm calling about my order. | Agent: Sure, I can help with that. Could you give me your order number and tell me what's happening? | Customer: It's SO37542, and it hasn't arrived. | Agent: Thank you. Let me check where it is.
source_rule: Listen fully and ask an open question before solving; do not assume the problem.
fill_blank: Sure, I can help with that. Could you give me your order number and ____ me what's happening?
mcq_question: A caller says only "I'm calling about my order." What should you do first?
mcq_options: A) Ask for the order number and what is happening with it. | B) Offer a discount on their next order, to keep them happy. | C) Transfer the call to a manager, in case it is serious. | D) Start the cancellation process, in case they want that.
mcq_why: They have only named the topic, so you need the order and the real problem first. B, C and D all guess at a request the caller has not made.
reorder_task: happening / tell / with / me / Could / what's / your / you / order
reorder_answer: Could you tell me what's happening with your order
hindi_to_english: Main apne order ke baare mein call kar raha hoon. Woh abhi tak nahin aaya.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm calling about my order. It hasn't arrived yet.
whats_next_customer: It was supposed to come yesterday.
whats_next_reply: I'm sorry it hasn't arrived. Could I have the order number so I can check where it is?
role_play: Partner A says only "I'm calling about my order" and waits. Partner B reassures A, asks for the order number and asks an open question to find the real problem (A wants to change the size).
record_task: Record your reply to "I'm calling about my order", including the open question you use to find the real problem.
self_check: Did you ask what is happening instead of guessing? · Did you ask for the order number? · Did your tone sound ready to help, not impatient?

sentence: I want to speak to your manager.
speaker: Customer
situation: A customer whose refund has been delayed twice interrupts you with this line.
recall_cue: An upset caller demands to talk to someone senior. What do they really want, and how do you answer?
linking: want_to → "wan-tuh" · speak_to → "spee-ktuh" · your_manager → "yor-man-uh-jer"
intonation: Usually firm and falling, sometimes loud. Answer more slowly and in a lower voice than the caller, without a rising "but…".
indian_pron_tip: In your reply, "manager" is MAN-uh-jer, with stress on the first part; avoid "ma-NAY-jar" with the stress in the middle.
customer_emotion: Frustrated, feels unheard, and doubts that you have the power to help.
memory_hook: "Manager" often means "Someone, please take me seriously"; answer the feeling before the job title.
hindi_meaning: मैं आपके मैनेजर से बात करना चाहता/चाहती हूँ।
hindi_roman: Main aapke manager se baat karna chahta/chahti hoon.
simple_meaning: The customer wants someone with more authority to handle their problem.
why_it_works: Usually the caller feels stuck and unheard, not angry at you personally. Acknowledge that, say what you can do now, and if they still ask, arrange it; Zendesk's chat-etiquette guidance is to transfer to a supervisor if the customer asks.
key_chunk: I want to speak to ___.
grammar_pattern: I + want + to + base verb
grammar_note: "Want to + verb" states a clear wish; on the phone it sounds stronger than "I'd like to".
tone_note: The caller sounds blunt because they are upset. Arguing ("There's no need for that") makes it worse; a calm, honest reply lowers the heat.
watch_out: ✗ Sir, calm down, manager is not available. → ✓ I can see why you'd want that. Let me arrange it for you.
dont_say: "My manager will only tell you what I told you." — it dismisses the request and makes the caller feel trapped.
positive_swap: Instead of "The manager is busy", say "I can see why you'd want that. Let me arrange it, and I'll explain what happens next."
alt_1: Can I talk to someone senior, please?
alt_2: Put me through to your supervisor.
more_formal: I would like to escalate this to your manager, please.
ask_next: I can see why you'd want that, after two delays. I'll arrange it. Can I first tell you what I can do for you right now?
replies_you_may_hear: Fine, go on. · No, I want the manager now. · I've already heard enough excuses.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "No, I want the manager now." → Agent: "Of course. I'll explain your case to my supervisor so you don't need to repeat it. It will take about three minutes. Could you hold, please?"
cultural_note: Agents sometimes try to avoid an escalation with lines like "No need for manager, I will help you". International callers see asking for a manager as a normal request, so blocking it tends to make them angrier.
channel_note: Chat version: "i want to talk to ur manager" — reply: "I understand. I'll pass this to my supervisor now. Could you stay in this chat for a few minutes?" Email: say who will reply and by when.
when_not_to_use: Do not keep offering your own fix after the caller has asked twice; arrange the escalation then.
mini_conversation: Customer: I want to speak to your manager. | Agent: I can see why you'd want that, after two delays. I'll arrange it. Can I first tell you what I can do right now? | Customer: Fine, go on. | Agent: I can mark your refund as urgent and call you back by 5 pm today.
source_rule: Pass to a supervisor if the customer asks (Zendesk chat etiquette); acknowledge the feeling first, never say "calm down".
fill_blank: I can see ____ you'd want that. I'll arrange it for you.
mcq_question: A caller says, "I want to speak to your manager." What is the best first reply?
mcq_options: A) I understand you are upset, but please calm down so that I can help you properly. | B) I'm sorry, but my manager is in meetings all day, so I can't arrange that today. | C) I can see why you'd want that. I'll arrange it. Can I first tell you what I can do right now? | D) There is no need for a manager. I can handle this myself, so please tell me the problem.
mcq_why: C acknowledges the feeling, agrees to the request and offers help now. A tells them how to feel, B blocks the request with an excuse, and D refuses what they asked for.
reorder_task: why / I / can / you'd / see / that / want
reorder_answer: I can see why you'd want that
hindi_to_english: Main samajh sakti hoon aap manager se baat kyun karna chahte hain. Main arrange karti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: I can see why you'd want to speak to my manager. I'll arrange it.
whats_next_customer: Fine. But I don't want to explain everything again.
whats_next_reply: You won't have to. I'll give my supervisor the details of your two delays before I connect you. Could you hold for about three minutes?
role_play: Partner A's refund has been delayed twice and A demands a manager. Partner B acknowledges the feeling, offers one concrete action, and when A insists, arranges a warm transfer with a time estimate.
record_task: Record your reply to "I want to speak to your manager", then your reply when the caller insists a second time.
self_check: Did you acknowledge the feeling first? · Did you avoid "calm down" and an outright refusal? · Did you give a time for the hold or callback?

sentence: My payment didn't go through.
speaker: Customer
situation: A customer calls while trying to pay for their phone plan online.
recall_cue: A customer says their money "didn't go through". What exactly might have happened, and what do you check?
linking: didn't_go → "didn-go" · go_through → "go-throo"
intonation: Usually falling, with the main stress on "through", and often worried. Reply calmly and clearly, with rising yes/no questions to check details.
indian_pron_tip: When you repeat "through", start with a voiceless "th" (tongue between the teeth, no voice) and say "throo"; it must not sound like "true".
customer_emotion: Worried about losing money or being charged twice.
memory_hook: The payment is a parcel stuck at the bank's gate: did it leave the house, or did it never start?
hindi_meaning: मेरा पेमेंट नहीं हो पाया।
hindi_roman: Mera payment nahin ho paaya.
simple_meaning: The customer tried to pay, but the payment failed or they are not sure it worked.
why_it_works: "Didn't go through" can mean declined with no money taken, or money taken with no confirmation. The real worry is often "Have I lost money?", so ask what they saw and whether money left their account.
key_chunk: ___ didn't go through.
grammar_pattern: Subject + didn't + go through (phrasal verb, past)
grammar_note: "Go through" here means "be accepted and completed".
tone_note: The customer is worried, not blaming you yet. A calm question shows you understand; "It must be your bank" brushes them off.
watch_out: ✗ I'm sorry your payment is not go through. Did you saw any error? → ✓ I'm sorry your payment didn't go through. Did you see an error message?
dont_say: "That's your bank's problem, not ours." — it may not be true, and it leaves a worried customer with nowhere to go.
positive_swap: Instead of "Payment failed, try again", say "I'm sorry the payment didn't go through. Let me check whether any money was taken."
alt_1: My card got declined.
alt_2: It took the money but says the payment failed.
more_formal: I attempted to make a payment, but the transaction was not completed.
ask_next: I'm sorry the payment didn't go through. Did you see an error message, and has any money left your account?
replies_you_may_hear: It just said "transaction failed". · The money's gone from my account though. · I've tried three times.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I've tried three times and you've taken my money!" → Agent: "I understand why that's worrying. Let me check right now whether any payment reached us, and I'll tell you exactly what I see."
cultural_note: Indian customers often say "payment is failed" or "amount got debited". International customers say "it didn't go through" or "it was declined"; in both cases, listen for whether money actually left the account.
channel_note: Chat version: "payment didnt go thru" — reply: "Sorry about that! Did you get an error message? Has any money left your account?" Email: ask for the date, the amount and any error text.
when_not_to_use: Do not assume no money was taken; always ask, because a failed payment can still show as pending on the customer's account.
mini_conversation: Customer: My payment didn't go through. | Agent: I'm sorry it didn't go through. Did you see an error message, and has any money left your account? | Customer: It said "declined", and nothing's gone. | Agent: Thank you. Let me check on my side that nothing was taken. Then we can try another way to pay.
source_rule: Listen and ask before you solve; check the facts, then explain the next step clearly.
fill_blank: I'm sorry the payment didn't go ____. Did you see an error message?
mcq_question: A customer says "My payment didn't go through." What are they most likely worried about?
mcq_options: A) Whether money has been taken without the order going through. | B) Whether the shop will give them a discount for the trouble. | C) Whether the agent can explain how card payments work. | D) Whether their order will be delivered to the right address.
mcq_why: A failed payment makes many people fear that money has gone without an order. B, C and D are not the first worry when a payment fails.
reorder_task: through / payment / the / sorry / didn't / I'm / go
reorder_answer: I'm sorry the payment didn't go through
hindi_to_english: Kya aapko koi error message dikha? Kya aapke account se paise kate?
hindi_to_english_answer: Did you see an error message? Has any money left your account?
whats_next_customer: It says "declined", but my card works everywhere else.
whats_next_reply: Thank you. Sometimes a bank stops one payment as a safety check, even when the card works elsewhere. Would you like to try once more, or pay with a different card?
role_play: Partner A's payment for a phone plan failed and A thinks money was taken. Partner B asks what A saw, checks whether money left the account, and explains the next step.
record_task: Record your reply to "My payment didn't go through", including both questions you ask to understand what happened.
self_check: Did you ask whether money was taken? · Did you avoid blaming the bank? · Did "through" start with a soft "th"?

sentence: Hang on a sec, let me find it.
speaker: Customer
situation: You asked for the order number, and the customer needs a moment to look for it.
recall_cue: The customer goes off to look for something you asked for. What do they mean, and what do you say?
linking: hang_on → "ha-ngon" (the ng slides into "on", no hard g) · let_me → "lem-mee" · find_it → "fine-dit"
intonation: Quick and casual, falling at the end; the customer is busy searching. Your reply should be short and relaxed, not hurried.
indian_pron_tip: Listen for the word after "hang": "hang ON" (short o) means wait, and "hang UP" (u as in cup) means end the call. Say the "ng" in "hang" as one nasal sound, with no hard "g".
customer_emotion: Cooperative but a little flustered while searching.
memory_hook: The customer is rummaging in a drawer; you just keep the light on and wait quietly.
hindi_meaning: एक सेकंड रुकिए, मैं ढूँढ़ता/ढूँढ़ती हूँ।
hindi_roman: Ek second rukiye, main dhoondhta/dhoondhti hoon.
simple_meaning: Please wait a short time while I look for it.
why_it_works: The customer is asking you to wait, the reverse of a hold. They may feel rushed, so a calm "Take your time" relaxes them, and a gentle check-in after a long silence shows you are still there.
key_chunk: Hang on a ___.
grammar_pattern: Hang on (informal phrasal verb) + a sec · Let me + base verb
grammar_note: "Hang on" means "wait"; "a sec" is short for "a second", but it often means a minute or more.
tone_note: It is informal but not rude. Do not copy it back; reply politely with "Of course, take your time."
watch_out: ✗ Okay, fast please, I have other calls. → ✓ Of course, take your time. I'm right here.
dont_say: "Hurry up, please." — it makes the customer feel rushed, and they may read out the wrong number.
positive_swap: Instead of "Okay, do it fast", say "Of course, take your time. I'm right here."
alt_1: Give me a minute, I'll grab it.
alt_2: One moment, it's in my emails somewhere.
more_formal: Could you give me a moment, please? I need to find the number.
ask_next: Of course, take your time. I'm right here.
replies_you_may_hear: Okay, found it. · Sorry, I can't find it anywhere. · Is it the long number or the short one?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I can't find it anywhere." → Agent: "That's okay, I can find it another way. Could you give me the email address you ordered with?"
cultural_note: Indian callers might say "One minute, please" or "Just wait". International callers often say "Hang on" or "Bear with me". All mean the same thing: wait, I am looking.
channel_note: Chat version: "hang on lemme check" — reply: "Sure, take your time." Email: not used; the customer simply replies later.
when_not_to_use: Do not stay silent for a long time after "Take your time"; if the silence goes on, check in gently: "Any luck finding it?"
mini_conversation: Customer: Hang on a sec, let me find it. | Agent: Of course, take your time. I'm right here. | Customer: Okay, here it is: SO48210. | Agent: Thank you. Let me pull that up.
source_rule: Fill silence gently: tell the caller you are there, and check in if the wait goes on.
fill_blank: Of course, take your ____. I'm right here.
mcq_question: The customer says "Hang on a sec, let me find it." What do they want?
mcq_options: A) They want you to wait on the line while they look for it. | B) They want to end the call and phone you back later. | C) They want you to search for it in your system instead. | D) They want to be passed to someone who can find it.
mcq_why: "Hang on" means wait, and "let me find it" means they are searching. B confuses "hang on" with "hang up", C swaps who does the searching, and D asks for a transfer nobody mentioned.
reorder_task: time / your / take / course / Of
reorder_answer: Of course take your time
hindi_to_english: Koi baat nahin, aap aaram se dhoondhiye. Main line par hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: Of course, take your time. I'm still on the line.
whats_next_customer: Is it the long number or the short one?
whats_next_reply: It's the longer one. It starts with the letters SO and it's in the subject line of your confirmation email.
role_play: Partner B asks for an order number. Partner A says "Hang on a sec, let me find it" and searches for a while. B reassures A, checks in once, and offers another way when A cannot find it.
record_task: Record your reply to "Hang on a sec, let me find it", then the gentle check-in you say if the silence goes on.
self_check: Did you sound relaxed, not rushed? · Did you understand "hang on" as "wait", not "hang up"? · Did you offer another way if they cannot find it?

sentence: You already asked me that.
speaker: Customer
situation: After a transfer, the customer is asked for their account number a second time.
recall_cue: An irritated caller says you are repeating a question. What are they feeling, and what do you say next?
linking: already_asked → "awl-red-ee-askt" · asked_me → "ask-mee"
intonation: Usually flat and falling, with stress on "already"; it signals irritation. Reply more slowly and softly, without defending yourself.
indian_pron_tip: "Asked" is one syllable, "askt", ending in s-k-t; avoid "ask" or "aas-ked". Hear it in the customer's line and say it right in yours.
customer_emotion: Irritated and tired of repeating themselves; feels the company is not listening.
memory_hook: Every repeated question is a stone in the customer's shoe; say sorry for the stone, then take it out.
hindi_meaning: आप यह मुझसे पहले ही पूछ चुके/चुकी हैं।
hindi_roman: Aap yeh mujhse pehle hi poochh chuke/chuki hain.
simple_meaning: You asked me this before, and I am annoyed to answer again.
why_it_works: The customer feels the company does not listen or share notes. CEB/Gartner's customer-effort research found that cutting customer effort predicts loyalty better than "delighting" customers, so apologise, use what they already gave, or give a one-line reason if you must ask again.
key_chunk: You already ___ that.
grammar_pattern: You + already + past simple (common in American English) / You have already + past participle (British)
grammar_note: "Already" means it happened before now; here it carries annoyance.
tone_note: The customer is blunt because they are frustrated. "It's the process" makes it worse; a short apology and a reason sound respectful.
watch_out: ✗ Sir, it is the process, you have to tell again. → ✓ You're right, I'm sorry. I can see it in the notes now.
dont_say: "It's our process to ask again." — it hides behind process and gives no reason the customer cares about.
positive_swap: Instead of "It's mandatory, please tell again", say "You're right, and I'm sorry you've had to repeat it. I'll use the details you gave earlier."
alt_1: I've already told the last person this.
alt_2: Why do I keep having to repeat myself?
more_formal: I believe I have already provided that information.
ask_next: You're right, and I'm sorry you've had to repeat it. I have your account number from earlier, so let's carry on.
replies_you_may_hear: Thank you. · This is the third time today! · Fine, it's 22019.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "This is the third time today!" → Agent: "I'm sorry, that's frustrating. I'll add everything to your account notes now so the next person can see it."
cultural_note: Agents sometimes answer "It's mandatory, please tell again" after a transfer. International customers may not expect this; they expect the details to travel with the transfer, or a reason in plain words if you must ask again.
channel_note: Chat version: "i already told u that" — reply: "You're right, sorry! I can see it above. Let me carry on." Email: quote what they sent instead of asking again.
when_not_to_use: Do not ignore it and simply repeat the question; if you truly must ask again for security, say why in one sentence.
mini_conversation: Customer: You already asked me that. | Agent: You're right, and I'm sorry you've had to repeat it. I have your account number from earlier. | Customer: Okay. So can you fix my bill? | Agent: I'll look at your bill now and tell you what I can do.
source_rule: Reduce customer effort: do not make the customer repeat themselves (CEB/Gartner effort research).
fill_blank: You're right, and I'm ____ you've had to repeat it.
mcq_question: After a transfer, the customer says "You already asked me that." What is the best response?
mcq_options: A) You're right, and I'm sorry you've had to repeat it. I have your details from earlier. | B) It is mandatory to ask again after every transfer, so please repeat it once more. | C) That was a different department, not me, so I have to ask you again myself now. | D) Please be patient, sir. I only need your account number one more time, then I can help.
mcq_why: A agrees, apologises and uses the details already given. B hides behind a rule, C blames another team, and D asks again with no reason.
reorder_task: right / You're / and / sorry / I'm
reorder_answer: You're right and I'm sorry
hindi_to_english: Aap sahi keh rahe hain, maaf kijiye. Mere paas aapka number pehle se hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: You're right, I'm sorry. I already have your number.
whats_next_customer: Good. So can you sort out my bill now?
whats_next_reply: I can see an extra charge from March. I'll look at it now and tell you what I can do.
role_play: Partner A was transferred and is asked for an account number again. A says "You already asked me that." Partner B apologises, uses the earlier details or gives a one-line security reason, and moves on.
record_task: Record your reply to "You already asked me that" in two versions: one when you have the details, one when you must ask again for security.
self_check: Did you agree and say sorry first? · Did you avoid "process" and "mandatory"? · Did "asked" end in a clear "kt"?

sentence: So, if I've understood correctly, your internet stopped working after last night's update. Is that right?
speaker: Agent
situation: The caller has spent a minute explaining that their internet died after an update, and you want to confirm the details before you troubleshoot.
recall_cue: The caller has just told you a long story about a fault. Before you try to fix anything, what do you say to check you heard it right?
linking: if_I've → "i-fyv" · stopped_working → "stopt-WUR-king" · last_night's → "las-NIGHTS" · is_that → "iz-that"
intonation: Short pause after "So," and after "correctly". Even, falling tone through the summary, then a clear rise on "Is that right?" because it is a real yes/no question. Medium pace.
indian_pron_tip: "Stopped" is one syllable, "stopt", ending in a clear /t/; do not say "stop-ped". "Working" starts with rounded lips for /w/, with no teeth on the lip as in "v".
customer_emotion: Annoyed, and hoping this agent has actually listened.
memory_hook: Think of a mirror: you hold the customer's own story up to them, and they nod or correct it before you touch a single wire.
hindi_meaning: तो अगर मैंने सही समझा है, तो कल रात के अपडेट के बाद से आपका इंटरनेट काम नहीं कर रहा है। क्या यह सही है?
hindi_roman: To agar maine sahi samjha hai, to kal raat ke update ke baad se aapka internet kaam nahin kar raha hai. Kya yeh sahi hai?
simple_meaning: Let me repeat your problem in my own words: your internet broke after the update. Did I get that right?
why_it_works: It proves you listened and gives the caller a chance to correct you before you start fixing the wrong thing, which saves time for both of you.
key_chunk: So, if I've understood correctly, ___. Is that right?
grammar_pattern: So, if + I've + past participle + adverb, + summary of the problem · Is that right?
grammar_note: "If I've understood" uses the present perfect because your understanding matters right now.
tone_note: It sounds careful and humble, as if any mistake would be yours. A flat "So you're saying the internet just died?" can sound as if you doubt the customer.
watch_out: ✗ If I understand correct, your internet is stopped after update. → ✓ If I've understood correctly, your internet stopped working after last night's update.
dont_say: "Okay, okay, I got it." It cuts the caller off and gives them no proof that you understood anything.
positive_swap: Instead of "What is your problem exactly?", say "So, if I've understood correctly, your internet stopped working after the update. Is that right?"
alt_1: So the internet dropped after last night's update, and it hasn't come back since. Have I got that right?
alt_2: Just to check I understand, the connection has been down since the update last night. Is that correct?
more_formal: To make sure I have understood you correctly, your internet service has not worked since last night's update. Is that accurate?
ask_next: Thanks for confirming. Have you restarted the router since then?
replies_you_may_hear: Yes, exactly. · Not quite, it was already slow before the update. · Yes, and the TV box isn't working either.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I just told you all that!" → Agent: "You did, and thank you. I just want to be sure of the details, because the fix depends on exactly when it stopped."
cultural_note: Many Indian agents end statements with "no?" or "isn't it?" as a check. International callers may not expect this; a clear "Is that right?" with a rising tone sounds more natural to them.
channel_note: Chat: "Just to check: your internet stopped after last night's update. Is that right?" Email: summarise the issue in the first line of your reply.
when_not_to_use: Do not paraphrase after every sentence of a long story; wait until the caller has finished, then sum up once.
mini_conversation: Customer: My internet hasn't worked since the update last night. | Agent: So, if I've understood correctly, your internet stopped working after last night's update. Is that right? | Customer: Yes, exactly. | Agent: Thanks for confirming. Let's start by checking the lights on your router.
source_rule: Paraphrase before solving ("If I've understood correctly, … Is that right?") so the customer can correct you early.
fill_blank: So, if I've ____ (understand) correctly, your internet stopped working after last night's update. Is that right?
mcq_question: The caller has finished describing a fault. Which line best checks your understanding before you start troubleshooting?
mcq_options: A) Okay, I've got the picture, so let me look at your account and fix it now. | B) Sorry, could you tell me again exactly what the problem is with your internet? | C) If I've understood correctly, your internet stopped after the update. Is that right? | D) I understand completely. There is no need to explain it again, I have noted everything.
mcq_why: C repeats the problem in your own words and asks a real yes/no question, so the caller can correct you. A and D claim to understand without checking, and B makes the caller start again.
reorder_task: correctly / I've / So / understood / if
reorder_answer: So if I've understood correctly
hindi_to_english: Agar maine sahi samjha hai, to aapka card kal se kaam nahin kar raha. Kya yeh sahi hai?
hindi_to_english_answer: If I've understood correctly, your card hasn't worked since yesterday. Is that right?
whats_next_customer: Not quite, it was slow even before the update.
whats_next_reply: Thank you for correcting me. So it was slow first, and it stopped completely after the update?
role_play: Partner A explains a broadband fault in three or four long sentences with one extra detail. Partner B listens without interrupting, then paraphrases the whole problem and asks "Is that right?"
record_task: Record yourself paraphrasing two different problems that a partner reads to you, each one ending with "Is that right?"
self_check: Did you wait until the caller had finished? · Did your voice rise on "Is that right?" · Did you say "stopped" as one syllable?

sentence: I can see why that's frustrating, especially after waiting all week. Let me sort this out for you right now.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer has waited a week for a technician who never came and is clearly fed up when they explain it.
recall_cue: A customer has waited a whole week for nothing and sounds fed up. What do you say to show you understand, and what do you do straight after?
linking: can_see → "kun-SEE" · that's_frustrating → "thats-frus-TRAY-ting" · sort_this_out → "sor-this-OUT" · right_now → "rye-NOW"
intonation: Slower, warm and level on the empathy part; do not sound cheerful. Falling tone on "week". Small pause, then a firmer, confident fall on "right now".
indian_pron_tip: Stress "frustrating" on the second syllable: frus-TRAY-ting, not FRUS-tra-ting. Say "that's" with the tongue lightly between the teeth for /ð/, not "dats".
customer_emotion: Fed up, let down and doubting anyone will help.
memory_hook: Picture a hand on the shoulder followed straight away by rolled-up sleeves: feel it with them, then get to work.
hindi_meaning: मैं समझ सकता/सकती हूँ कि यह कितना परेशान करने वाला है, ख़ासकर पूरे हफ़्ते इंतज़ार करने के बाद। मैं इसे अभी आपके लिए ठीक करता/करती हूँ।
hindi_roman: Main samajh sakta/sakti hoon ki yeh kitna pareshan karne wala hai, khaaskar poore hafte intezaar karne ke baad. Main ise abhi aapke liye theek karta/karti hoon.
simple_meaning: I understand why you are upset after waiting a whole week, and I am going to fix it now.
why_it_works: It names the feeling and the real reason for it (the long wait), then moves straight to action. Empathy without action sounds like a script.
key_chunk: I can see why that's ___. Let me ___ for you right now.
grammar_pattern: I can see why + clause · especially after + verb-ing · Let me + base verb
grammar_note: "Especially after waiting" uses verb-ing after a preposition, so it is not "after wait".
tone_note: Naming the customer's real reason makes it personal. "Sorry for the inconvenience" sounds scripted and does not show you heard what happened.
watch_out: ✗ I can understand why it is frustrating, specially after wait all week. → ✓ I can see why that's frustrating, especially after waiting all week.
dont_say: "These things happen." It brushes off a week of waiting and offers no fix.
positive_swap: Instead of "Sorry for the inconvenience, these things happen", say "I can see why that's frustrating. Let me sort this out for you right now."
alt_1: I completely understand why you're upset after a week of waiting. I'll book you a new visit now.
alt_2: That must be really frustrating after waiting all week. Let's get this sorted straight away.
more_formal: I fully understand your frustration after such a long wait, and I will arrange a new appointment for you straight away.
ask_next: I'm booking the first available technician now. Would tomorrow morning or tomorrow afternoon suit you better?
replies_you_may_hear: Thank you, finally someone gets it. · I've heard that before. · I don't want sympathy, I want it fixed.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Everyone says they understand." → Agent: "That's fair. So here is exactly what I'm doing: I'm booking a technician for tomorrow and I'll text you the time."
cultural_note: Indian agents often say "I understand, sir" quickly and repeatedly. International callers may hear that as a script; one specific empathy line, followed by action, sounds more sincere.
channel_note: Chat: "I can see why that's frustrating after a week of waiting. I'm on it now." Email: put the empathy line first, then the numbered steps you are taking.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it when the customer is only asking a neutral question, such as how to change a password; it sounds over-the-top.
mini_conversation: Customer: The engineer was supposed to come on Monday and nobody showed up all week! | Agent: I can see why that's frustrating, especially after waiting all week. Let me sort this out for you right now. | Customer: Okay. What can you do? | Agent: I'm booking the first slot tomorrow and I'll send you the time by text.
source_rule: Empathy line, then action: never an empathy line on its own ("I can see why that's frustrating. Here's what I'll do.").
fill_blank: I can see why that's ____ (frustrate), especially after waiting all week.
mcq_question: An upset customer has waited a week for a technician. Which reply best shows empathy and moves the call forward?
mcq_options: A) Sorry for the inconvenience caused. Your patience is much appreciated, sir. | B) I can see why that's frustrating. Let me sort this out for you right now. | C) I understand, sir. These delays happen sometimes, so please be patient. | D) I'm sorry to hear that. You can check the technician times on our website.
mcq_why: B names the feeling and starts the fix now. A and C are scripted and offer no action, and D sounds sympathetic but sends the customer away to do the work.
reorder_task: sort / out / Let / now / this / me / right / for / you
reorder_answer: Let me sort this out for you right now
hindi_to_english: Main samajh sakta hoon ki yeh kitna pareshan karne wala hai. Main abhi ise theek karta hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: I can see why that's upsetting. Let me fix this for you right now.
whats_next_customer: Fine, but I need it done this week.
whats_next_reply: Understood. I can see a slot tomorrow morning, between eight and twelve. Shall I book it for you?
role_play: Partner A is angry that a fridge repair visit was missed twice. Partner B gives one specific empathy line, then offers a new visit with a clear day and time.
record_task: Record the sentence, then record a version for a missed delivery, keeping the empathy line followed by an action.
self_check: Did you stress frus-TRAY-ting? · Did your empathy line name the real reason? · Did you follow it with a clear action?

sentence: I'll take care of this for you personally, so you won't need to explain it to anyone else.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer has already been passed between two departments and worries they will have to tell the story again.
recall_cue: The caller fears being passed around again. What do you say to show that you own the problem from now on?
linking: take_care_of → "tay-KEH-ruv" · care_of_this → "keh-ruv-THIS" · explain_it → "ex-PLAY-nit" · anyone_else → "en-ee-wun-ELSE"
intonation: Calm, steady and slightly slower than normal. Falling tone on "personally" and on "else", which makes it a firm promise, not a question.
indian_pron_tip: "Won't" starts with rounded lips for /w/ and has a long "oh": "wohnt", not "vont" and not "want". "This" needs /ð/ with the tongue between the teeth, not "dis".
customer_emotion: Tired of being transferred and afraid of starting over again.
memory_hook: Imagine taking a heavy bag from the customer's hands and saying "I've got it from here": they do not carry it to another desk.
hindi_meaning: मैं ख़ुद इसका ध्यान रखूँगा/रखूँगी, ताकि आपको किसी और को फिर से समझाना न पड़े।
hindi_roman: Main khud iska dhyaan rakhoonga/rakhoongi, taaki aapko kisi aur ko phir se samjhana na pade.
simple_meaning: I will handle this problem myself, so you do not have to tell your story again to another person.
why_it_works: It shows one person is now responsible and removes the customer's biggest worry, repeating the story. "I'll" is a promise; "we'll try" is not.
key_chunk: I'll take care of this for you, so you won't need to ___.
grammar_pattern: I'll + base verb · so + you won't need to + base verb
grammar_note: "I'll" here is a promise you make now; "so" shows the result for the customer.
tone_note: Saying "I" instead of "we" or "the team" sounds accountable. "Somebody will look into it" sounds like nobody owns it.
watch_out: ✗ I will take care for this, you need not explain again. → ✓ I'll take care of this for you personally, so you won't need to explain it to anyone else.
dont_say: "That's not my department." It passes the problem back to the customer and sounds like you do not care.
positive_swap: Instead of "We'll try to see what can be done", say "I'll take care of this for you personally, so you won't need to explain it to anyone else."
alt_1: I'm going to handle this myself from here, so you won't have to repeat any of it.
alt_2: Leave this with me. I'll look after it, and you won't need to go over it again.
more_formal: I will take personal responsibility for your case, so there is no need to explain the details to anyone else.
ask_next: I've got all the notes here. I'll call you by five o'clock today with an update.
replies_you_may_hear: Thank you, that's a relief. · That's what the last person said. · So you'll call me back yourself?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "The last agent promised that too." → Agent: "I understand why you doubt it. I've put my name on your case, and I'll call you myself by five today."
cultural_note: Indian agents often say "we will look into it" to sound polite and humble. International customers may hear "we" as vague; a clear "I'll" sounds more trustworthy.
channel_note: Chat: "I'll take care of this for you, so you won't need to explain it again." Email: add your name and a direct way to reach you.
when_not_to_use: Do not promise this if you know the case must go to another team; tell the customer honestly and do a warm transfer instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: I've already explained this to two people. | Agent: I'm sorry you've had to explain this twice. I'll take care of this for you personally, so you won't need to explain it to anyone else. | Customer: Okay, thank you. | Agent: I'll call you by five today with an update.
source_rule: Use "I will" plus a time, instead of "we'll try" or "hopefully soon"; take ownership of the case.
fill_blank: I'll take care ____ this for you personally, so you won't need to explain it to anyone else.
mcq_question: A customer has been passed between two teams. Which line takes ownership most clearly?
mcq_options: A) We'll try to see what can be done and let you know as soon as possible. | B) Somebody from the billing team will look into it and get back to you. | C) I've passed your details to the right team, so they will look into it. | D) I'll take care of this personally, so you won't need to explain it again.
mcq_why: D uses "I'll" and removes the need to repeat the story. A is tempting because it sounds helpful, but "try" promises nothing, and B and C hand the case to someone else.
reorder_task: of / care / take / I'll / for / this / you
reorder_answer: I'll take care of this for you
hindi_to_english: Main khud yeh dekh loonga, aapko kisi aur ko batana nahin padega.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'll look after this myself, so you won't need to tell anyone else.
whats_next_customer: How do I know you'll actually do it?
whats_next_reply: I've added my name to your case, and I'll call you myself by five o'clock today.
role_play: Partner A has been transferred twice about a wrong bill and is tired. Partner B takes ownership with one clear "I'll" sentence and gives a time for the next update.
record_task: Record the sentence, then add a follow-up promise with a specific time, as you would on a live call.
self_check: Did you say "I'll" and not "we'll try"? · Did you pronounce "won't" with rounded lips? · Did you give a time after the promise?

sentence: Here's what I'm going to do now: first I'll check your last payment, and then I'll reset your account.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer's account is locked after a payment issue, and you are about to start working on it while they stay on the line.
recall_cue: You are about to start fixing an account. How do you tell the caller the steps you will take, in order, before you go quiet?
linking: here's_what → "heerz-wut" · going_to → "gon-nuh" · check_your → "chek-yer" · last_payment → "las-PAY-ment"
intonation: A short pause after "now:" so the caller knows a list is coming. Slight rise on "payment" (more to come), then a clear fall on "account" (list finished). Unhurried pace.
indian_pron_tip: Stress "reset" on the second syllable as a verb: re-SET, not REE-set. Say "first" with a clean /st/ at the end and no extra vowel: not "firstu".
customer_emotion: Uncertain and a little anxious about what happens next.
memory_hook: Picture road signs on a highway: "First exit, then second exit". The caller always knows where the call is going.
hindi_meaning: अब मैं यह करूँगा/करूँगी: पहले आपका आख़िरी पेमेंट देखूँगा/देखूँगी, और फिर आपका अकाउंट रीसेट करूँगा/करूँगी।
hindi_roman: Ab main yeh karoonga/karoongi: pehle aapka aakhri payment dekhoonga/dekhoongi, aur phir aapka account reset karoonga/karoongi.
simple_meaning: I will tell you my plan: step one, check your payment; step two, reset your account.
why_it_works: Telling the caller the steps before you start explains any silence and makes the call feel controlled. People wait more patiently when they know the plan.
key_chunk: Here's what I'm going to do: first I'll ___, and then I'll ___.
grammar_pattern: Here's what + I'm going to + base verb · first + I'll + verb · then + I'll + verb
grammar_note: "Going to" shows a plan you have already made; "first" and "then" order the steps.
tone_note: It sounds organised and in control. Going silent while typing, or saying "just wait, I am doing", leaves the caller guessing.
watch_out: ✗ First I will check your last payment, then I will do reset of your account. → ✓ First I'll check your last payment, and then I'll reset your account.
dont_say: "Let me do something, hold on." It gives no plan, and the silence that follows feels like being ignored.
positive_swap: Instead of "Wait, I am checking something", say "Here's what I'm going to do now: first I'll check your last payment, and then I'll reset your account."
alt_1: Let me explain the next steps: I'll look at your last payment first, then reset the account.
alt_2: So the plan is this: I'll check the payment, and once that's done I'll reset your account.
more_formal: I will now take two steps: first, I will review your most recent payment, and then I will reset your account.
ask_next: It will take about a minute, and I'll tell you what I find as I go.
replies_you_may_hear: Okay, go ahead. · Will I lose any data? · How long will that take?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why do you need to check the payment?" → Agent: "The lock was caused by a failed payment, so checking it first helps make sure the lock doesn't come straight back."
cultural_note: Indian English often uses "firstly … secondly" in speech. International callers may not expect it on the phone; "first … then" sounds more natural and lighter.
channel_note: Chat: send each step as a short line. Email: number the steps: "1. I checked your last payment. 2. I reset your account."
when_not_to_use: Do not give a long plan when the fix is one quick step; just say "I'll reset that now."
mini_conversation: Customer: My account is locked and I can't pay my bill. | Agent: Here's what I'm going to do now: first I'll check your last payment, and then I'll reset your account. | Customer: Okay. | Agent: Your last payment failed because the card expired. I'm resetting the account now.
source_rule: Be specific about what will happen and when; tell the caller what you are doing so silence is never unexplained.
fill_blank: Here's what I'm going to do now: first I'll check your last payment, and ____ I'll reset your account.
mcq_question: You need to do two things on a customer's account. Which line prepares the caller best?
mcq_options: A) Here's what I'm going to do: first I'll check your last payment, then I'll reset your account. | B) Please hold the line, sir. I am checking a few things in the system for you. | C) I'll sort out your account now. It might take a little while, so thanks for your patience. | D) First checking your payment, second resetting the account, and later I will inform you.
mcq_why: A gives a clear plan in order. B and C give no steps, so the silence that follows feels unexplained. D has the right idea but drops its verbs and sounds like a list read from a screen.
reorder_task: then / reset / and / account / your / I'll
reorder_answer: and then I'll reset your account
hindi_to_english: Pehle main aapka order dekhunga, phir main refund shuru karunga.
hindi_to_english_answer: First I'll check your order, and then I'll start the refund.
whats_next_customer: Will I lose my saved settings?
whats_next_reply: As far as I can see, no. Your saved settings stay as they are, and I'll tell you before I change anything else.
role_play: Partner A calls because a streaming account is locked. Partner B explains two steps with "first" and "then", does them, and reports back after each step.
record_task: Record the sentence, then record a two-step plan for a different problem, such as a wrong address on an order.
self_check: Did you pause after "now"? · Did you stress re-SET? · Did your voice fall at the end of the list?

sentence: Thank you for holding, Mr Rao. I need about five more minutes. Would you like to stay on the line, or shall I call you back?
speaker: Agent
situation: You asked for two minutes on hold, but the check is taking longer, so you come back before the time is up.
recall_cue: Your check is taking longer than you promised. When you come back to the caller, what do you say first, and what choice do you offer?
linking: thank_you → "THANG-kyoo" · need_about → "nee-duh-BOUT" · stay_on → "stay-yon" · call_you_back → "kawl-yoo-BACK"
intonation: Warm fall on "holding". Clear, slower delivery of "five more minutes". On the choice, rise on "line" and fall on "back", which shows these are the only two options.
indian_pron_tip: "Five" ends in /v/: top teeth lightly on the lower lip, so it is not "faiw" with rounded lips. "Would" starts with /w/: rounded lips and no teeth on the lip, not "vould".
customer_emotion: Getting impatient and wondering if they have been forgotten.
memory_hook: Think of a cooking timer: you come back before it rings, say "Thank you", and ask if they want to wait or have the meal delivered later.
hindi_meaning: होल्ड करने के लिए धन्यवाद, मिस्टर राव। मुझे लगभग पाँच मिनट और चाहिए। क्या आप लाइन पर रहना चाहेंगे, या मैं आपको वापस कॉल करूँ?
hindi_roman: Hold karne ke liye dhanyavaad, Mister Rao. Mujhe lagbhag paanch minute aur chahiye. Kya aap line par rehna chahenge, ya main aapko wapas call karoon?
simple_meaning: Thanks for waiting. I need five more minutes. You can wait, or I can phone you later.
why_it_works: It thanks the caller first, gives an honest new time and hands them control with a real choice. Coming back early shows they were not forgotten.
key_chunk: I need about ___ more minutes. Would you like to ___, or shall I ___?
grammar_pattern: Would you like to + base verb, or shall I + base verb?
grammar_note: "Would you like to" offers a choice; "shall I" offers to do something for them.
tone_note: Giving a choice respects the caller's time. Leaving them on hold again without a word, or saying "one more minute" repeatedly, feels careless.
watch_out: ✗ Please be on hold, it will take some more time. → ✓ I need about five more minutes. Would you like to stay on the line, or shall I call you back?
dont_say: "Just one more minute." said again and again. Callers stop believing it after the first time.
positive_swap: Instead of "It is still taking time, please hold", say "Thank you for holding. I need about five more minutes. Would you like to stay on the line, or shall I call you back?"
alt_1: Thanks for waiting, Mr Rao. This needs about five more minutes. Are you happy to hold, or would a callback suit you better?
alt_2: Thanks for staying with me, Mr Rao, and I'm sorry it's taking longer. I need roughly five more minutes. I can keep you on hold or ring you back, whichever you prefer.
more_formal: Thank you for your patience, Mr Rao. I will need approximately five more minutes. Would you prefer to remain on the line, or may I call you back?
ask_next: Of course. Is this the best number to reach you on? I'll call by 3:20 at the latest.
replies_you_may_hear: I'll hold. · Call me back, please. · Five more? Why is it taking so long?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why is it taking so long?" → Agent: "I'm sorry it's taking longer than I said. The payment team's system is slow today, and I need their answer before I can confirm anything."
cultural_note: In India "call you back" is the usual phrase; British callers also say "ring you back". Both are fine on international calls, as long as you add a real time.
channel_note: Chat: "Thanks for waiting. I need about five more minutes. Is that okay, or shall I email you the answer?" Email: not needed; give a reply time instead.
when_not_to_use: Do not offer a callback if your team cannot call out; offer only choices you can really keep.
mini_conversation: Customer: Hello? Are you still there? | Agent: Thank you for holding, Mr Rao. I need about five more minutes. Would you like to stay on the line, or shall I call you back? | Customer: Call me back, please. | Agent: Of course. I'll call you on this number by 3:20.
source_rule: Long hold: check back before the promised time is up, thank the caller first, and offer a callback instead of a long wait.
fill_blank: Would you like ____ stay on the line, or shall I call you back?
mcq_question: Your two-minute hold is turning into seven. What is the best thing to do?
mcq_options: A) Say nothing and keep checking until you have the full answer. | B) Put the call on mute and keep checking until you have an answer. | C) Return, thank the caller, give a new time and offer a callback. | D) Return and say "just one more minute" so the caller keeps waiting.
mcq_why: C keeps the caller informed and gives them a choice. D is tempting because it keeps the call moving, but a repeated "one more minute" sounds untrue. A and B leave the caller in silence.
reorder_task: back / call / I / shall / you / or
reorder_answer: or shall I call you back
hindi_to_english: Intezaar ke liye dhanyavaad. Mujhe paanch minute aur chahiye. Aap hold karenge ya main call back karoon?
hindi_to_english_answer: Thank you for waiting. I need five more minutes. Would you like to hold, or shall I call you back?
whats_next_customer: Okay, call me back, but not after four.
whats_next_reply: Of course. I'll call you on this number by 3:20, well before four.
role_play: Partner A is on hold about a refund. Partner B returns just before the promised two minutes are up, thanks A, gives a new estimate and offers a choice; A picks a callback and B confirms the time.
record_task: Record yourself returning from a hold that is running late, with the thank-you, the new time and the choice.
self_check: Did you thank the caller before the update? · Did you give a real number of minutes? · Did your voice fall on "back" to close the choice?

sentence: I'll connect you to Anita in billing, because she can change your plan directly. I'll brief her first, so you won't need to repeat anything.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer wants a plan change that only the billing team can make, so you are about to do a warm transfer.
recall_cue: Only another team can fix this. Before you transfer the caller, what three things do you tell them?
linking: connect_you → "kuh-NEK-chuh" · brief_her → "BREE-fer" · won't_need → "wohn-NEED" · repeat_anything → "ri-PEE-ten-ee-thing"
intonation: Steady and reassuring. Fall on "directly" and on "anything". Pause briefly between the two sentences so the caller hears both the reason and the promise.
indian_pron_tip: "Connect" is stressed on the second syllable: con-NECT, not KON-nect. In "anything", the "th" is /θ/ with the tongue between the teeth, not "anyting".
customer_emotion: Worried about being lost in the system or starting again.
memory_hook: Picture a relay race where you run alongside and place the baton firmly in the next runner's hand, instead of throwing it over a wall.
hindi_meaning: मैं आपको बिलिंग टीम की अनीता से जोड़ रहा/रही हूँ, क्योंकि वे सीधे आपका प्लान बदल सकती हैं। मैं पहले उन्हें सब बता दूँगा/दूँगी, ताकि आपको कुछ दोहराना न पड़े।
hindi_roman: Main aapko billing team ki Anita se jod raha/rahi hoon, kyonki ve seedhe aapka plan badal sakti hain. Main pehle unhe sab bata doonga/doongi, taaki aapko kuch dohrana na pade.
simple_meaning: I am passing you to Anita because she can change your plan. I will tell her your problem first, so you do not have to say it again.
why_it_works: It tells the caller who, why and what happens next, and promises a briefing, which removes the fear of repeating everything to a stranger.
key_chunk: I'll connect you to ___, because ___. I'll brief her first, so ___.
grammar_pattern: I'll + verb + person + because + reason · I'll + verb + first, so + result
grammar_note: "Because" gives the reason for the transfer; "so" gives the result for the caller.
tone_note: Naming the person and the reason shows care. "I am transferring your call" with no reason feels like being passed on to get rid of you.
watch_out: ✗ I will brief to her first, so you will not need to repeat again. → ✓ I'll brief her first, so you won't need to repeat anything.
dont_say: "Please hold, I am transferring your call." It gives no name, no reason and no promise about repeating the story.
positive_swap: Instead of "This is not handled by me, I am transferring", say "I'll connect you to Anita in billing, because she can change your plan directly."
alt_1: The best person for this is Anita in our billing team. I'll explain your case to her before I put you through.
alt_2: Anita in billing can make this change for you. I'll give her all the details first, so you can carry on from where we are now.
more_formal: I will transfer you to my colleague Anita in Billing, who can amend your plan directly. I will brief her beforehand, so there is no need to repeat your details.
ask_next: Is it all right if I put you on a short hold of about a minute while I speak to her?
replies_you_may_hear: Okay, thank you. · Can't you do it yourself? · What if I get cut off?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "What if I get cut off?" → Agent: "I have your number, so if the call drops I'll call you straight back and connect you again."
cultural_note: "Concerned department" is common in Indian English. International callers may not expect this phrase; naming the team and the person ("Anita in billing") sounds clearer.
channel_note: Chat: "I'm passing this chat to Anita in billing. She'll see everything we've written, so you won't need to repeat it." Email: copy the colleague in and introduce them by name.
when_not_to_use: Do not promise a named person or a briefing if your system only allows a blind transfer to a queue; tell the caller honestly what will happen.
mini_conversation: Customer: I want to move to the cheaper plan. | Agent: I'll connect you to Anita in billing, because she can change your plan directly. I'll brief her first, so you won't need to repeat anything. | Customer: Great, thanks. | Agent: Is it all right if I put you on a short hold for about a minute while I speak to her?
source_rule: Transfer: prefer warm. Say who and why, brief the colleague, and introduce the caller and the issue so they do not repeat themselves.
fill_blank: I'll ____ (starts with b) her first, so you won't need to repeat anything.
mcq_question: You need to transfer a caller to the billing team. Which line is the best warm transfer?
mcq_options: A) Please hold the line, sir. I am transferring your call to the billing department now. | B) I'll connect you to Anita in billing, because she can change your plan. I'll brief her first. | C) I can't change plans myself, so you will need to call the billing team on their direct line. | D) Billing handles plan changes, so I'm passing you over now. They will ask for your details again.
mcq_why: B names the person, the reason and the briefing. D gives a reason but admits the caller will have to repeat everything. A gives no name and no reason, and C sends the caller away.
reorder_task: Anita / connect / I'll / in / you / billing / to
reorder_answer: I'll connect you to Anita in billing
hindi_to_english: Main aapko technical team ke Arjun se jodta hoon, kyonki woh yeh theek kar sakte hain.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'll connect you to Arjun in our technical team, because he can fix this for you.
whats_next_customer: Can't you just do it yourself?
whats_next_reply: I wish I could. Plan changes need billing access, and Anita can do it in a few minutes.
role_play: Partner A wants a refund that only the payments team can approve. Partner B explains who and why, says aloud the one-sentence briefing for the colleague, then hands A over by name.
record_task: Record the two transfer sentences, then the one-line briefing you would give Anita before connecting the caller.
self_check: Did you name the person and the team? · Did you give the reason? · Did you stress con-NECT on the second syllable?

sentence: Your refund will reach your account within five to seven working days, so by next Friday at the latest.
speaker: Agent
situation: It is Wednesday, and you have just processed a refund; your system shows the standard five to seven working days for it, and the customer wants to know when the money will arrive.
recall_cue: The refund is done and the caller asks when they will get the money. How do you give a timeline they can check on a calendar?
linking: refund_will → "REE-fun-wil" · reach_your → "ree-chyer" · five_to_seven → "FYV-tuh-SEV-en" · at_the_latest → "a-thuh-LAY-test"
intonation: Slow down on the numbers. Fall on "days". Small pause, then a firm fall on "at the latest", which marks the outside date.
indian_pron_tip: "Seven" has a /v/ in the middle: top teeth on the lower lip, not "sewen". "Within" has /ð/ with the tongue between the teeth, not "widin".
customer_emotion: Wanting certainty about when the money will arrive.
memory_hook: Picture circling next Friday on a wall calendar in red: the customer leaves the call with one date to watch.
hindi_meaning: आपका रिफ़ंड पाँच से सात कामकाजी दिनों में आपके खाते में आ जाएगा, यानी ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा अगले शुक्रवार तक।
hindi_roman: Aapka refund paanch se saat kaamkaaji dinon mein aapke khaate mein aa jaayega, yaani zyaada se zyaada agle Shukravaar tak.
simple_meaning: The money will be back in your account in five to seven working days, no later than next Friday.
why_it_works: It turns a vague range into one clear last date, so the customer knows exactly when to worry and when not to call again.
key_chunk: Your ___ will reach your account within ___, so by ___ at the latest.
grammar_pattern: Subject + will + verb + within + time period, + so by + day + at the latest
grammar_note: "Within" means inside that time; "at the latest" means no later than that day.
tone_note: A specific date sounds honest and in control. "It will come soon" or "hopefully next week" sounds like a guess.
watch_out: ✗ Your refund will reach to your account in five to seven working days, so by next Friday at latest. → ✓ Your refund will reach your account within five to seven working days, so by next Friday at the latest.
dont_say: "It will come soon, don't worry." It gives no date, so the customer will call again in two days.
positive_swap: Instead of "Hopefully you will get it soon", say "Your refund will reach your account within five to seven working days, so by next Friday at the latest."
alt_1: You should see the money in your account in five to seven working days, by next Friday at the latest.
alt_2: The refund takes five to seven working days, so please expect it no later than next Friday.
more_formal: The refund will be credited to your account within five to seven working days, and no later than next Friday.
ask_next: That's Friday the twenty-third. I'll also email you a confirmation now, with your refund reference number.
replies_you_may_hear: Okay, that's fine. · Can't it be faster? · What do I do if it hasn't come by then?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why does it take a whole week?" → Agent: "I know a week feels long. Your bank needs that time to process it, and if it hasn't arrived by Friday, call us with your reference and we'll trace it."
cultural_note: "Working days" is common in India and the UK; US customers often say "business days". Both are understood, but a named last day ("by next Friday") removes any doubt about weekends and holidays.
channel_note: Chat: "Your refund will reach your account in 5–7 working days, by Friday 23 October at the latest." Email: write the exact date, not just "next Friday".
when_not_to_use: Do not give a date you cannot check in the system; say what you know and promise to confirm.
mini_conversation: Customer: When will I get my money back? | Agent: Your refund will reach your account within five to seven working days, so by next Friday at the latest. | Customer: And if it doesn't? | Agent: I'm emailing you a reference number now. If the money hasn't arrived by then, call us with it and we'll trace it straight away.
source_rule: Replace vague promises with a clear timeline, a reference number and the next step.
fill_blank: Your refund will reach your account within five to seven working days, so by next Friday at the ____.
mcq_question: A caller asks when their refund will arrive. Which reply sets the clearest expectation?
mcq_options: A) It should come very soon, so please don't worry. I'll keep an eye on it. | B) Hopefully by early next week, but sometimes banks can be a little slow. | C) Within five to seven working days, so by next Friday at the latest. | D) It depends on your bank, so I can't give you an exact date, I'm afraid.
mcq_why: C gives a range and a final date. D may be true, but it gives the customer nothing to plan around, and A and B are guesses.
reorder_task: latest / by / at / Friday / the / next
reorder_answer: by next Friday at the latest
hindi_to_english: Aapka naya card das din ke andar aa jaayega, yaani zyaada se zyaada agle mahine ki paanch tareekh tak.
hindi_to_english_answer: Your new card will arrive within ten days, so by the fifth of next month at the latest.
whats_next_customer: What if it still hasn't come by then?
whats_next_reply: Then please call us with your reference number, and we'll trace the payment with the bank straight away.
role_play: Partner A has returned a jacket and asks about the money. Partner B gives a time range and a final date, then gives a reference number and says what to do if it is late.
record_task: Record the sentence, then record a version for a replacement parcel with a different range and a final day.
self_check: Did you give one final date? · Did you slow down on the numbers? · Did you say "seven" with a clear /v/?

sentence: The order has already shipped, so what I can do is arrange a free return as soon as it reaches you.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer wants to cancel an order, but it has already left the warehouse, so cancelling is no longer possible; your system shows it qualifies for a free return.
recall_cue: A caller wants to cancel an order that is already on the way. How do you say no without using "can't", and what do you offer?
linking: has_already → "ha-zawl-RED-ee" · what_I_can → "wuh-dye-CAN" · arrange_a → "uh-RAIN-juh" · as_soon_as → "uh-SOON-uz"
intonation: Neutral fall on "shipped", with no apology in the voice yet. Lift and stress "CAN" in "what I can do", then a positive, falling finish on "reaches you".
indian_pron_tip: "Shipped" is one syllable ending in /pt/: "shipt", not "ship-ped". Stress "arrange" on the second syllable: a-RANGE, and keep the /dʒ/ soft at the end.
customer_emotion: Disappointed and expecting to hear a flat no.
memory_hook: Picture a closed door with a bright arrow painted on it pointing to the open door next to it: the answer moves straight to the way through.
hindi_meaning: ऑर्डर पहले ही भेजा जा चुका है, इसलिए मैं यह कर सकता/सकती हूँ कि जैसे ही यह आप तक पहुँचे, मुफ़्त वापसी का इंतज़ाम कर दूँ।
hindi_roman: Order pehle hi bheja ja chuka hai, isliye main yeh kar sakta/sakti hoon ki jaise hi yeh aap tak pahunche, muft wapsi ka intezaam kar doon.
simple_meaning: I cannot cancel it because it is already on the way, but I can set up a free return when it arrives.
why_it_works: It gives the reason in plain words and moves straight to what is possible. The customer hears a solution, not a closed door.
key_chunk: ___, so what I can do is ___.
grammar_pattern: Reason clause, + so what I can do is + base verb + …
grammar_note: "What I can do is" puts the possible action at the end, where the listener remembers it.
tone_note: Leading with what you can do sounds helpful. "Sorry, we can't cancel it. That's the rule." sounds like you are hiding behind rules.
watch_out: ✗ Cancellation is not possible as order is dispatched. → ✓ The order has already shipped, so what I can do is arrange a free return.
dont_say: "No, that's not possible." A bare no ends the conversation and leaves the customer stuck.
positive_swap: Instead of "We can't cancel it now", say "The order has already shipped, so what I can do is arrange a free return as soon as it reaches you."
alt_1: It's already on its way to you, but I can set up a free return the day it arrives.
alt_2: Because it has shipped, the quickest option is a free return once it reaches you, and I can set that up now.
more_formal: As the order has already been dispatched, I am able to arrange a free return for you as soon as it is delivered.
ask_next: Would you like me to email you the return label now, so it's ready when the parcel arrives?
replies_you_may_hear: Okay, that works. · But I don't want it at all. · Will I get all my money back?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "But I cancelled within an hour!" → Agent: "I'm sorry, I can see you asked quickly. By then it had already been packed and handed to the courier. The return is free, and you'll get the full amount back."
cultural_note: "Dispatched" is the usual word in India and the UK; US customers more often say "shipped". Both are understood, so use the word that appears in the customer's order email.
channel_note: Chat: "Your order has already shipped, so what I can do is set up a free return." Email: give the reason, the alternative and the next step in separate lines.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it if the order can still be stopped; if cancelling is possible, just cancel it.
mini_conversation: Customer: I want to cancel my order. | Agent: The order has already shipped, so what I can do is arrange a free return as soon as it reaches you. | Customer: Will I get the full refund? | Agent: Yes, the full amount, once the item is back with us.
source_rule: Swap "can't" for "can": give the reason in plain words, then lead with what is possible ("What I can do is…").
fill_blank: The order has already shipped, so what I ____ (am able to) do is arrange a free return.
mcq_question: A customer asks to cancel an order that has already shipped. Which reply follows positive-language practice best?
mcq_options: A) I'm sorry, but the order has already shipped, so cancelling it is not possible now. | B) Unfortunately our system does not allow cancellation after dispatch. That is how it works. | C) Sorry, I can't help with that. Once an order has shipped, nobody here can stop it. | D) It has already shipped, so what I can do is arrange a free return when it arrives.
mcq_why: D explains why and offers a way forward. A is polite and gives a reason, but it ends on "not possible" with nothing for the customer to do. B hides behind the system, and C is a bare refusal.
reorder_task: is / can / what / do / I / a / arrange / return / free
reorder_answer: what I can do is arrange a free return
hindi_to_english: Aapki booking non-refundable hai, isliye main yeh kar sakta hoon ki aapki date badal doon.
hindi_to_english_answer: Your booking is non-refundable, so what I can do is change the date for you.
whats_next_customer: But I don't want to wait for it to arrive.
whats_next_reply: I understand. If you refuse the parcel at the door, it will come straight back to us, and I'll start your refund as soon as it arrives.
role_play: Partner A wants a hotel booking refunded after the free-cancellation period. Partner B gives the reason in one plain sentence and offers a date change instead, without saying "can't".
record_task: Record the sentence, then record a second refusal for a different request, again leading with "What I can do is…".
self_check: Did you avoid "can't" and "not possible"? · Did you stress "CAN" in "what I can do"? · Did you say "shipped" as one syllable?

sentence: The extra twelve dollars on this bill is a roaming charge for data you used abroad on the fourteenth of March.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer is calling because their monthly bill is higher than usual and they do not recognise one charge; you have their itemised bill open on your screen.
recall_cue: A caller does not recognise an extra amount on their bill. How do you explain exactly what it is and when it happened?
linking: extra_twelve → "ek-struh-TWELV" · charge_for → "charj-fer" · used_abroad → "yoo-zduh-BRAWD" · fourteenth_of → "four-teen-thuv"
intonation: Calm, matter-of-fact fall on "charge". Slow down for the amount and the date, which are the parts the caller is checking. No defensive rise.
indian_pron_tip: "Fourteenth" ends in /θ/: tongue between the teeth, "four-TEENTH", not "fourteent". Stress it on the second syllable. "Twelve" ends with a /lv/ cluster: keep the /v/ voiced.
customer_emotion: Suspicious and worried they are being overcharged.
memory_hook: Picture a shop receipt with one line circled: amount, what it was for and the date, the three things the caller needs.
hindi_meaning: इस बिल पर जो बारह डॉलर ज़्यादा हैं, वह चौदह मार्च को विदेश में इस्तेमाल किए गए डेटा का रोमिंग चार्ज है।
hindi_roman: Is bill par jo barah dollar zyaada hain, woh chaudah March ko videsh mein istemaal kiye gaye data ka roaming charge hai.
simple_meaning: The extra twelve dollars is because you used mobile data in another country on 14 March.
why_it_works: It names the amount, the reason and the date in one sentence, so the customer can match it to their own memory and stop worrying.
key_chunk: The extra ___ on this bill is a ___ charge for ___ on ___.
grammar_pattern: The extra + amount + on this bill + is + a/an + noun + charge + for + noun clause
grammar_note: "Data you used" is a short relative clause; "that" is left out, which sounds natural in speech.
tone_note: A neutral, factual tone sounds honest. "You only used it, that's why it came" sounds like you are blaming the customer.
watch_out: ✗ This twelve dollars has come because of roaming. → ✓ The extra twelve dollars on this bill is a roaming charge.
dont_say: "It's in the terms and conditions." It sounds defensive and does not explain the charge.
positive_swap: Instead of "You used it, so you have to pay", say "The extra twelve dollars on this bill is a roaming charge for data you used abroad on the fourteenth of March."
alt_1: I can see what that is: twelve dollars for mobile data you used while you were abroad on 14 March.
alt_2: That twelve-dollar charge is for roaming data, from the fourteenth of March when your phone was outside the country.
more_formal: The additional charge of twelve dollars relates to mobile data used abroad on 14 March.
ask_next: Does that match your trip? If you'd like, I can show you travel packs that may be cheaper for your next trip.
replies_you_may_hear: Oh, right, I was in Dubai that day. · I turned data off, though. · Nobody told me it would cost extra.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I turned roaming off!" → Agent: "Thanks for telling me. Could you stay on the line for about two minutes while I check the usage log for that day?"
cultural_note: Indian agents often explain bills with "the same has been charged". International customers may not expect that; naming the amount and the reason ("the twelve dollars is…") is clearer.
channel_note: Chat: "The extra $12 is a roaming charge for data used abroad on 14 March." Email: show the charge as a line with the date and amount.
when_not_to_use: Do not explain a charge as correct before you have checked it; if you are unsure, say you will check first.
mini_conversation: Customer: Why is my bill higher this month? | Agent: The extra twelve dollars on this bill is a roaming charge for data you used abroad on the fourteenth of March. | Customer: Oh, I was in Singapore then. | Agent: That explains it. If you travel again, I can tell you about our travel packs.
source_rule: Plain language: explain the charge in words the customer understands, with the amount, the reason and the date.
fill_blank: The extra twelve dollars on this bill is a roaming charge ____ data you used abroad on the fourteenth of March.
mcq_question: A caller asks about an unknown charge. Which explanation is clearest?
mcq_options: A) It is in the terms and conditions, and I can email you a copy if that helps. | B) The extra twelve dollars is a roaming charge for data you used abroad on 14 March. | C) That is an extra usage charge from this month, added automatically by our billing system. | D) You used mobile data in another country, so you were charged extra. That is normal.
mcq_why: B gives the amount, the reason and the date. C is tempting because it sounds official, but it does not say what was charged or when. A points to the rules and D blames the customer.
reorder_task: charge / a / is / roaming / it
reorder_answer: it is a roaming charge
hindi_to_english: Yeh extra paanch dollar late payment ka charge hai, jo das tareekh ke baad laga.
hindi_to_english_answer: The extra five dollars is a late payment charge, added after the tenth.
whats_next_customer: Nobody told me it would cost extra.
whats_next_reply: I'm sorry that wasn't clear. I can turn on roaming alerts, so you get a text before any charge starts.
role_play: Partner A sees an unexpected $8 charge on a streaming bill. Partner B explains it in one sentence with the amount, the reason and the date, then offers a way to avoid it next time.
record_task: Record the sentence, then record an explanation of a different charge, such as a late payment fee, with an amount and a date.
self_check: Did you say the amount, the reason and the date? · Did you pronounce the "th" in "fourteenth"? · Did you sound neutral, not defensive?

sentence: Could you unplug the router, wait ten seconds and plug it back in? Then tell me which lights you can see on the front.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer's Wi-Fi is down and you are guiding them through the first troubleshooting step while they stand at the router.
recall_cue: You want the caller to restart a device and report back. How do you give one clear step and ask what they see?
linking: unplug_the → "un-PLUG-thuh" · plug_it_back_in → "plu-git-ba-KIN" · tell_me → "TEL-mee" · lights_you → "lyts-yoo"
intonation: Rise on "back in?" as a request. Pause and let them do it. Then a falling tone on "front", because this is an instruction, not a yes/no question.
indian_pron_tip: "Seconds" ends in /ndz/: "SEK-undz", not "second" or "secon". "Lights" ends in /ts/; say both sounds clearly so it is not heard as "light".
customer_emotion: Impatient and a bit unsure about the technical steps.
memory_hook: Picture a doctor saying "Breathe in… now tell me what you feel": one action, then one observation, before the next step.
hindi_meaning: क्या आप राउटर का प्लग निकालकर दस सेकंड रुकेंगे और फिर लगा देंगे? फिर मुझे बताइए कि सामने कौन-सी लाइटें दिख रही हैं।
hindi_roman: Kya aap router ka plug nikaalkar das second rukenge aur phir laga denge? Phir mujhe bataiye ki saamne kaun-si lights dikh rahi hain.
simple_meaning: Please switch the router off at the plug, count to ten, switch it on again, and then tell me which lights are on.
why_it_works: It gives one clear action with a real time, then asks for a specific observation, so you can diagnose from facts instead of guessing.
key_chunk: Could you ___? Then tell me what you see on ___.
grammar_pattern: Could you + verb, + verb + and + verb? · Then tell me + which + noun + you can see
grammar_note: "Which lights you can see" is an embedded question, so the word order is "you can", not "can you".
tone_note: "Could you" makes the step a request. "Do this: unplug it" sounds like an order and can feel rude to a stressed caller.
watch_out: ✗ Then tell me which lights can you see. → ✓ Then tell me which lights you can see.
dont_say: "Just restart everything and call back." It sends the customer away without checking whether it worked.
positive_swap: Instead of "You have to restart the router first", say "Could you unplug the router, wait ten seconds and plug it back in?"
alt_1: Let's try a restart: unplug the router, count to ten and plug it in again. What lights do you see now?
alt_2: Please switch the router off at the wall for ten seconds, then switch it back on and tell me what the lights are doing.
more_formal: Would you please disconnect the router for ten seconds, reconnect it, and then describe the lights on the front panel?
ask_next: Is the light marked "Internet" green, orange or off?
replies_you_may_hear: Okay, done. They're all flashing. · There's a red light now. · Which one is the router?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I've already restarted it!" → Agent: "That's helpful, thank you, so we can skip that step. Could you tell me which lights you can see on the front right now?"
cultural_note: Indian agents often say "do one thing, unplug the router". International callers may not expect "do one thing" as a lead-in; a direct "Could you…?" request sounds more natural to them.
channel_note: Chat: send the step on one line and the question on the next. Email: number each step and ask for a photo of the lights.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask an older or very stressed caller to do several actions at once; give one step and wait.
mini_conversation: Customer: My Wi-Fi isn't working at all. | Agent: Could you unplug the router, wait ten seconds and plug it back in? Then tell me which lights you can see on the front. | Customer: Okay… the Internet light is still orange. | Agent: Thanks, that helps. An orange light usually means the router has no internet connection, so I'm going to check your line from my side.
source_rule: Swap "you have to" for guidance ("Could you…?"); give one clear step, then check the result.
fill_blank: Could you unplug the router, wait ten seconds and plug it back in? Then tell me which lights you ____ see.
mcq_question: You want the caller to restart the router and then describe what they see. Which line does this correctly and politely?
mcq_options: A) Could you unplug the router, wait ten seconds and plug it in? Then tell me which lights can you see. | B) You have to unplug the router for ten seconds. After that, tell me what are the lights doing. | C) Could you unplug the router, wait ten seconds and plug it in? Then call us back if it still fails. | D) Could you unplug the router, wait ten seconds and plug it in? Then tell me which lights you can see.
mcq_why: D is a polite request with correct embedded-question order ("which lights you can see"). A has the right idea but uses question order inside the sentence. B uses "you have to" and the same word-order mistake, and C never asks what the caller sees.
reorder_task: lights / which / me / see / tell / can / you
reorder_answer: tell me which lights you can see
hindi_to_english: Kya aap app band karke dobara khol sakte hain? Phir batayiye screen par kya dikh raha hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: Could you close the app and open it again? Then tell me what you can see on the screen.
whats_next_customer: All the lights are flashing now.
whats_next_reply: That's normal while it starts up. Let's give it one more minute, then tell me which ones stay on.
