role_play: Partner A has a TV box with a frozen screen. Partner B gives one restart step with a time, then asks a specific question about what A can see, and decides the next step from the answer.
record_task: Record yourself guiding a caller through a restart in two sentences, ending with a question about what they see.
self_check: Did you use "Could you"? · Did you say "which lights you can see" in that order? · Did you pronounce "seconds" with the final /dz/?

sentence: Let me read that back to you: ravi dot mehta at example dot com, with "Mehta" spelt M-E-H-T-A. Is that correct?
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer has just given their email address for an account update, and you need to confirm it before saving.
recall_cue: A caller has just told you their email address. What do you say before you save it, and how do you say the "@" sign?
linking: read_that_back → "ree-dthat-BACK" · at_example → "a-teg-ZAM-pul" · spelt_M → "spel-TEM" · is_that → "iz-that"
intonation: Slow and even. Pause slightly at each "dot" and "at". Read the spelling as two groups, M-E-H … T-A. Clear rise on "correct?" as a yes/no question.
indian_pron_tip: Say the /t/ in "dot" and "at" lightly, with the tongue tip just behind the top teeth and not curled back (retroflex "ḍoṭ"). Keep the final /lt/ of "spelt" crisp: "spelt", not "spell".
customer_emotion: Wanting it right, slightly impatient with the details.
memory_hook: Picture reading a phone number off a sticky note back to its owner, letter by letter, before you stick it on the fridge.
hindi_meaning: मैं इसे आपको दोबारा पढ़कर सुनाता/सुनाती हूँ: ravi.mehta@example.com, "Mehta" की स्पेलिंग M-E-H-T-A। क्या यह सही है?
hindi_roman: Main ise aapko dobara padhkar sunata/sunati hoon: ravi dot mehta at example dot com, "Mehta" ki spelling M-E-H-T-A. Kya yeh sahi hai?
simple_meaning: I will repeat your email address and spell the hard part. Please tell me if it is right.
why_it_works: Reading back catches typing mistakes before they cause lost emails and repeat calls. Spelling the tricky part shows exactly where errors usually happen.
key_chunk: Let me read that back to you: ___. Is that correct?
grammar_pattern: Let me + base verb + that back to you · Is that correct?
grammar_note: "Read that back" means repeat what you heard; "spelt" is the British past form of "spell".
tone_note: Reading back sounds careful and professional. Just saying "Okay, got it" without reading it back skips the check and sounds rushed.
watch_out: ✗ Let me to read back you the email: ravi dot mehta at example dot com. Is it correct? → ✓ Let me read that back to you: ravi dot mehta at example dot com. Is that correct?
dont_say: "I've noted it down, it should be fine." If one letter is wrong, the customer never gets the email and blames you.
positive_swap: Instead of "Email noted, sir", say "Let me read that back to you: ravi dot mehta at example dot com. Is that correct?"
alt_1: Just to confirm, that's ravi dot mehta at example dot com, M-E-H-T-A?
alt_2: I'll repeat that to make sure I have it: ravi, dot, mehta, at example dot com. Did I get it right?
more_formal: To confirm, I have your email address as ravi dot mehta at example dot com, spelt M-E-H-T-A. Could you tell me whether that is correct?
ask_next: Thank you. I've updated it, and you'll get a confirmation email there in a few minutes.
replies_you_may_hear: Yes, that's right. · No, it's mehta with a double t. · There's an underscore, not a dot.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I just told you, why repeat it?" → Agent: "Sorry, I know it's an extra step. One wrong letter would stop every email reaching you, so I'd like to be sure."
cultural_note: Many Indian speakers say "at the rate" for @. International customers may not expect it; "at" is the standard way to say it in an email address.
channel_note: Chat: no need to read back; ask them to check the address you typed. Email: reply to the address they gave, so it confirms itself.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it for a full card number or any password; you should not be taking those on a call at all.
mini_conversation: Customer: It's ravi dot mehta at example dot com. | Agent: Let me read that back to you: ravi dot mehta at example dot com, with "Mehta" spelt M-E-H-T-A. Is that correct? | Customer: Yes, that's right. | Agent: Thank you. I've updated your account.
source_rule: Verification: confirm details by repeating them back, and ask only for what you need.
fill_blank: Let me read that back to you: ravi dot mehta ____ example dot com. Is that correct?
mcq_question: How should you say the "@" sign when reading back an email address to an international caller?
mcq_options: A) "ravi at the rate example dot com" | B) "ravi at example dot com" | C) "ravi at the rate of example dot com" | D) "ravi at sign example dot com"
mcq_why: International callers say "at", as in "ravi at example dot com". A and C are common in India, so they are tempting, but callers abroad may not expect them. D is understood but sounds clumsy.
reorder_task: back / you / me / that / read / to / let
reorder_answer: let me read that back to you
hindi_to_english: Main aapka number dobara padhta hoon: nau-aath-saat-chhe. Kya yeh sahi hai?
hindi_to_english_answer: Let me read that back: nine-eight-seven-six. Is that correct?
whats_next_customer: No, it's mehta with an underscore, not a dot.
whats_next_reply: Thank you. So that's ravi underscore mehta at example dot com. Is that correct now?
role_play: Partner A gives an email address with a tricky surname and an underscore. Partner B reads it back with "at" and "dot", spells the hard part, and asks A to confirm.
record_task: Record yourself reading back three email addresses a partner gives you, spelling the hard part of each one.
self_check: Did you say "at" for the @ sign? · Did you spell the tricky part slowly? · Did your voice rise on "correct?"

sentence: I'll call you back by four o'clock tomorrow with an update, even if the issue isn't fully fixed by then.
speaker: Agent
situation: The fault needs a technical team to investigate overnight, so you cannot solve it on this call.
recall_cue: You cannot fix the problem on this call. What do you promise the caller about the next contact, and when?
linking: call_you_back → "kawl-yoo-BACK" · four_o'clock → "faw-ruh-CLOCK" · with_an_update → "wi-thuh-NUP-date" · fixed_by → "fiks-by"
intonation: Firm, steady fall on "tomorrow". Slight pause before "even if". Falling, honest tone at the end, not apologetic.
indian_pron_tip: "Fixed" is one syllable ending in /kst/: "fikst", not "fix-ed". "Then" starts with /ð/: tongue between the teeth, not "den".
customer_emotion: Frustrated that it is not fixed yet, but willing to wait.
memory_hook: Picture an alarm clock set for 4:00 with a note "call Mrs Shah": it rings whether the news is good or not yet.
hindi_meaning: मैं कल चार बजे तक आपको अपडेट के साथ वापस कॉल करूँगा/करूँगी, चाहे तब तक समस्या पूरी तरह ठीक न हुई हो।
hindi_roman: Main kal chaar baje tak aapko update ke saath wapas call karoonga/karoongi, chahe tab tak samasya poori tarah theek na hui ho.
simple_meaning: I will phone you tomorrow before four with news, even if the problem is not solved yet.
why_it_works: It gives a real time and promises contact whatever happens, so the customer does not sit wondering. "Even if" shows honesty about what may not be done.
key_chunk: I'll call you back by ___ with an update, even if ___.
grammar_pattern: I'll + verb + by + time + with + noun · even if + present simple (negative)
grammar_note: After "even if" we use the present simple for the future: "isn't fixed", not "won't be fixed".
tone_note: A fixed time and "even if" sound trustworthy. "We'll call you when it's done" leaves the customer waiting without a date.
watch_out: ✗ I will call you back tomorrow till four o'clock. → ✓ I'll call you back by four o'clock tomorrow with an update.
dont_say: "We'll call you once it's resolved." The customer has no idea when that is and may never hear back.
positive_swap: Instead of "Hopefully someone will call you", say "I'll call you back by four o'clock tomorrow with an update, even if the issue isn't fully fixed by then."
alt_1: I'll ring you tomorrow before four with an update, whether it's fixed or not.
alt_2: You'll hear from me by 4 p.m. tomorrow, with an update on where things stand.
more_formal: I will call you by 4 p.m. tomorrow with an update, even if the issue has not been fully resolved by that time.
ask_next: Shall I call you on this number, or is there a better one for tomorrow afternoon?
replies_you_may_hear: Okay, that's fine. · Can you make it earlier? · I'm in meetings until three.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why can't you fix it today?" → Agent: "I know you hoped it would be sorted today. The network team has to test the line overnight, so tomorrow I'll be able to tell you what they found."
cultural_note: "I will revert" is common in Indian English, and dictionaries list it. International customers may not expect it; "I'll call you back" or "I'll get back to you" sounds clearer to them.
channel_note: Chat: "I'll email you an update by 4 p.m. tomorrow, even if it isn't fixed yet." Email: put the update time in the last line, in bold.
when_not_to_use: Do not promise a callback if outbound calls are not allowed in your process; promise an email or SMS update instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: So you can't fix it today? | Agent: Not on this call. I'll call you back by four o'clock tomorrow with an update, even if the issue isn't fully fixed by then. | Customer: Okay, please do. | Agent: I will. Is this the best number for you?
source_rule: Use "I will" plus a time; offer a callback and keep it even when the fix is not finished.
fill_blank: I'll call you back by four o'clock tomorrow with an update, even ____ the issue isn't fully fixed by then.
mcq_question: You need more time to fix a fault. Which promise sets the best expectation?
mcq_options: A) We'll call you as soon as the technical team has finished their checks. | B) I'll call you back by four tomorrow with an update, even if it isn't fixed. | C) I'll get back to you soon with some news, either way, once I hear something. | D) Hopefully it will be fixed by tomorrow, and I'll call you if there is any news.
mcq_why: B has a time and a promise that does not depend on the fix. A and C sound positive but give no time, and D depends on a fix nobody can promise.
reorder_task: back / you / call / tomorrow / I'll
reorder_answer: I'll call you back tomorrow
hindi_to_english: Main aapko kal dopahar do baje tak call karke update doonga.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'll call you by two o'clock tomorrow afternoon with an update.
whats_next_customer: Can you make it earlier? I'm busy after lunch.
whats_next_reply: Of course. I'll call you by eleven tomorrow morning instead, with whatever news I have.
role_play: Partner A has a broken oven that needs a parts check. Partner B explains it cannot be solved today, promises a callback with a day and time, and confirms the phone number.
record_task: Record the sentence, then record a version with an email update instead of a call, with a day and a time.
self_check: Did you give a clear time? · Did you say "fixed" as one syllable? · Did you say "call you back" or "get back to you"?

sentence: So, to sum up: I've reset your password and unlocked your account, and a confirmation email is on its way. Does that sort everything out for you?
speaker: Agent
situation: You have fixed a locked account and are about to end the call, so you recap before checking the issue is resolved.
recall_cue: The fix is done and you are ready to close. What do you say to recap the call, and what do you ask before "anything else"?
linking: sum_up → "suh-MUP" · unlocked_your → "un-LOCK-chyer" · on_its_way → "on-its-WAY" · sort_everything_out → "sor-tev-ree-thing-OUT"
intonation: Pause after "sum up:". List the actions with a slight rise on "password" and a fall on "way". Rise on "for you?" as a real yes/no question.
indian_pron_tip: "Unlocked" ends in /kt/: "un-LOCKT", one beat at the end, not "un-lock-ed". "Everything" has /θ/: tongue between the teeth, not "every-ting".
customer_emotion: Pleased the account works again, and keen to get on with their day.
memory_hook: Picture a waiter reading the bill aloud before you pay: everything you got, and a pause for you to say "yes, that's right".
hindi_meaning: तो, संक्षेप में: मैंने आपका पासवर्ड रीसेट कर दिया है और अकाउंट अनलॉक कर दिया है, और कन्फ़र्मेशन ईमेल आ रहा है। क्या इससे आपकी समस्या पूरी तरह हल हो गई?
hindi_roman: To, sankshep mein: maine aapka password reset kar diya hai aur account unlock kar diya hai, aur confirmation email aa raha hai. Kya isse aapki samasya poori tarah hal ho gayi?
simple_meaning: Here is what I did: new password, account open, email coming. Is your problem fully solved now?
why_it_works: The recap shows the customer exactly what changed, and the check question confirms the issue is really solved before you move to "anything else".
key_chunk: So, to sum up: I've ___. Does that sort everything out for you?
grammar_pattern: So, to sum up: + I've + past participle … · Does that + verb + for you?
grammar_note: "I've reset" uses the present perfect because the result matters now.
tone_note: Asking if it is solved respects the customer's view. Jumping straight to "Anything else?" assumes it is fixed, which may not be true.
watch_out: ✗ I have done reset of your password and account is unlocked. → ✓ I've reset your password and unlocked your account.
dont_say: "Okay, done. Anything else?" It skips the recap and assumes the customer is happy.
positive_swap: Instead of "That's all, anything else?", say "So, to sum up: I've reset your password and unlocked your account. Does that sort everything out for you?"
alt_1: Just to recap, your password is reset, the account is unlocked and a confirmation email is coming. Is everything working now?
alt_2: So that's your password reset and your account unlocked, with an email on the way. Has that solved it for you?
more_formal: To summarise, I have reset your password and unlocked your account, and a confirmation email has been sent. Has this fully resolved the issue?
ask_next: Great. Is there anything else I can help you with today?
replies_you_may_hear: Yes, all good, thanks. · I haven't got the email yet. · Will I need to reset it again?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I haven't got the email." → Agent: "It can take a few minutes. Could you check your spam folder? If it's not there in ten minutes, I'll send it again."
cultural_note: Indian agents often close with "anything else, sir?" straight away. International callers may expect a short recap first; it sounds more complete and caring.
channel_note: Chat: list the actions as short lines, then ask "Is everything working now?" Email: put the summary in numbered points at the top.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask "Does that sort everything out?" when you know the issue is still open; give the next steps instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: Okay, I can log in now. | Agent: So, to sum up: I've reset your password and unlocked your account, and a confirmation email is on its way. Does that sort everything out for you? | Customer: Yes, thanks. | Agent: Great. Is there anything else I can help you with today?
source_rule: Close the call by summarising the next steps, checking the issue is resolved, then "Is there anything else…?"
fill_blank: So, to sum up: I've reset your password and unlocked your account. Does that ____ everything out for you?
mcq_question: You have fixed the customer's issue. What is the best order for the close?
mcq_options: A) Recap what you did, check it is solved, then ask if there is anything else. | B) Ask if there is anything else, then recap what you did and say goodbye. | C) Say goodbye warmly, then send the customer a summary email after the call. | D) Ask for a rating first, then recap what you did and say goodbye.
mcq_why: A recaps, checks the fix and only then asks about more help. B asks "anything else" before the fix is confirmed, C never checks the result, and D puts the rating before the recap.
reorder_task: sort / out / that / Does / everything
reorder_answer: Does that sort everything out
hindi_to_english: Toh, sankshep mein: maine aapka address badal diya hai aur order dobara bhej diya hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: So, to sum up: I've changed your address and sent the order again.
whats_next_customer: Not quite, I still can't log in on my phone.
whats_next_reply: Thank you for telling me. Let's sort that out before we finish. Which app are you using on your phone?
role_play: Partner A called to change a delivery address and add a phone number. Partner B recaps both changes, asks if that solves everything, then asks "anything else" and closes warmly.
record_task: Record the recap and the check question, then record a second recap for a call where you changed a delivery date.
self_check: Did you list what you did? · Did you check it was solved before "anything else"? · Did you say "unlocked" with a clean /kt/?

sentence: I have a reference number for your complaint. Do you have something to write it down with? I'll say it slowly.
speaker: Agent
situation: You have logged a complaint and need the customer to note the reference number for any future call.
recall_cue: You have just created a case. Before you read out its number, what do you check, and how do you say it?
linking: reference_number → "REF-rens-NUM-ber" · have_something → "ha-vsum-thing" · write_it_down → "ry-dit-DOWN" · say_it → "SAY-yit"
intonation: Fall on "complaint". Rise on "write it down with?" because it is a yes/no question, then stop and wait for the answer. Calm, falling "I'll say it slowly." When you read the code, use short groups with a pause: "C-K … 4-7 … 2-9".
indian_pron_tip: Stress "reference" on the first syllable: REF-rence, two beats, not re-FER-ence. In "something", say /θ/ with the tongue between the teeth, not "sumting".
customer_emotion: Mildly rushed, may be looking for a pen.
memory_hook: Picture a teacher dictating: "Pens ready?", then reading each part slowly and waiting for the class to catch up.
hindi_meaning: आपकी शिकायत के लिए मेरे पास एक रेफ़रेंस नंबर है। क्या आपके पास इसे लिखने के लिए कुछ है? मैं इसे धीरे-धीरे बोलूँगा/बोलूँगी।
hindi_roman: Aapki shikayat ke liye mere paas ek reference number hai. Kya aapke paas ise likhne ke liye kuch hai? Main ise dheere-dheere boloonga/boloongi.
simple_meaning: I have a case number for you. Please get something to write with, and I will say it slowly.
why_it_works: Checking that they can write first stops the number being lost. With a reference, the next agent can find the case quickly and the customer does not have to explain again.
key_chunk: I have a reference number for ___. Do you have something to write it down with?
grammar_pattern: Do you have + something + to-infinitive + with?
grammar_note: "Something to write it down with" ends in "with" because you write with a pen.
tone_note: Checking for a pen shows patience. Rattling off "CK4729, okay?" fast makes the customer ask again or give up.
watch_out: ✗ Note down your reference number, it is CK4729. → ✓ I have a reference number for your complaint. Do you have something to write it down with?
dont_say: "Note it down: CK4729." said at full speed. The customer hears a blur of letters and numbers.
positive_swap: Instead of "Note down quickly", say "Do you have something to write it down with? I'll say it slowly."
alt_1: I'll give you a reference number for this. Have you got a pen handy?
alt_2: I've got a case number for you. Just tell me when you're ready, and I'll read it out slowly.
more_formal: I have a reference number for your complaint. Would you like a moment to find something to note it down with? I will read it slowly.
ask_next: Thank you. The number is C-K … 4-7 … 2-9. Could you read it back to me, just to make sure I said it clearly?
replies_you_may_hear: Hang on, let me get a pen. · Okay, go ahead. · Can you text it to me instead?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Can't you just text it to me?" → Agent: "Of course. I'll send it by SMS now, and I'll still say it once so you have it straight away."
cultural_note: "Double seven" and "triple two" are common in India and the UK, but some callers, especially in the US, may not expect them. In a reference code, saying each digit separately is clearest.
channel_note: Chat: paste the reference on its own line so it can be copied. Email: put it in the subject line and the first sentence.
when_not_to_use: Do not read the number while the customer is driving or clearly cannot write; offer to text or email it instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: Do I get a reference for this? | Agent: Yes. I have a reference number for your complaint. Do you have something to write it down with? I'll say it slowly. | Customer: Okay, I'm ready. | Agent: C-K … 4-7 … 2-9. Could you read it back to me?
source_rule: Give a reference the customer can quote next time, and check they have noted it correctly.
fill_blank: Do you have something to ____ (starts with w) it down with? I'll say it slowly.
mcq_question: What is the best way to give a caller a reference number?
mcq_options: A) Say it once at normal speed, then ask if they have any other questions. | B) Tell them it will arrive in an email later, so there is no need to write it. | C) Say it slowly with "double" and "triple" for repeated digits, then move on. | D) Check they can write, say it slowly in groups, then ask them to read it back.
mcq_why: D checks the caller can write, uses slow groups and ends with a read-back. C is slow but skips the pen check and the read-back, and A and B leave the caller to remember or hunt for the number.
reorder_task: something / you / Do / have / to / write / with / it / down
reorder_answer: Do you have something to write it down with
hindi_to_english: Mere paas aapke liye ek ticket number hai. Kya aapke paas pen hai?
hindi_to_english_answer: I have a ticket number for you. Do you have a pen handy?
whats_next_customer: Hang on, let me find a pen.
whats_next_reply: No rush, take your time. Just tell me when you're ready.
role_play: Partner A has reported a lost card. Partner B checks A can write, then gives a reference number in groups and asks A to read it back; A makes one mistake to correct.
record_task: Record yourself giving two reference numbers in groups, with the pen check and the read-back request.
self_check: Did you check they could write it down? · Did you read it in short groups? · Did you stress REF-rence on the first syllable?

sentence: I've been charged twice for the same thing.
speaker: Customer
situation: A customer calls after checking their bank app and seeing two payments for one order.
recall_cue: A caller says they paid two times for one purchase. What do they want, and what do you need to find out first?
linking: I've_been → "aiv-bin" · charged_twice → "charj-TWICE" · same_thing → "SAYM-thing"
intonation: The customer usually stresses "twice" hard and falls on "thing". A rising, sharp tone means they are angry; a flat tone means they are tired or worried.
indian_pron_tip: When you repeat it back, say "charged" as one syllable, "charjd", not "char-ged". Say "thing" with /θ/, tongue between the teeth, not "ting".
customer_emotion: Worried about losing money and annoyed at the mistake.
memory_hook: Picture a shop till ringing up the same item twice while the customer watches: they want the second ring taken off, fast.
hindi_meaning: एक ही चीज़ के लिए मेरे खाते से दो बार पैसे काट लिए गए हैं।
hindi_roman: Ek hi cheez ke liye mere khaate se do baar paise kaat liye gaye hain.
simple_meaning: The customer paid two times for one product or service and wants one payment back.
why_it_works: The real need is reassurance that the money is safe and will come back. They may also suspect fraud, so a calm, quick check matters more than a long apology.
key_chunk: I've been charged ___ for ___.
grammar_pattern: I've been + past participle (passive present perfect) + for + noun
grammar_note: "I've been charged" is passive: someone charged the customer, and the result matters now.
tone_note: The customer is not blaming you personally. Reply calmly and with a specific apology; "This is not possible, our system doesn't do that" sounds defensive.
watch_out: ✗ (Agent) Sir, you might have paid two times yourself. → ✓ I'm sorry you've been charged twice. Let me check both payments for you now.
dont_say: "Our system can't charge twice." It contradicts the customer before you have checked and makes them angrier.
positive_swap: Instead of "That is not possible", say "I'm sorry you've been charged twice. Let me check both payments for you now."
alt_1: You've taken the money twice for one order.
alt_2: I can see two payments for the same order on my statement.
more_formal: I would like to report a duplicate charge for a single purchase.
ask_next: I'm sorry you've been charged twice. In your bank app, do both payments say "completed", or is one still "pending"?
replies_you_may_hear: Both were on Monday, 40 dollars each. · I don't know, I just saw it on my app. · Is my card hacked?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I want my money back right now!" → Agent: "I understand, it's your money and you want it back. I'm checking both payments now, and once I find the duplicate I'll start the refund on this call."
cultural_note: Indian agents may reply "the same will be refunded". International customers may not expect "the same" used this way; naming it ("the second payment will be refunded") is clearer.
channel_note: Chat: customers often write "charged 2x!!" or "double charged". Email: they may attach a screenshot of the statement, so check it before asking for details.
when_not_to_use: Do not treat this as fraud straight away; first check whether it is a duplicate charge or a temporary hold that will disappear.
mini_conversation: Customer: I've been charged twice for the same thing. | Agent: I'm sorry you've been charged twice. In your bank app, do both payments say "completed", or is one still "pending"? | Customer: Both say completed, 40 dollars each, on Monday. | Agent: Thank you. I can see both on my side too, so I'm refunding the second one now.
source_rule: Paraphrase before solving and apologise specifically; take responsibility, then offer a fix.
fill_blank: I've ____ charged twice for the same thing.
mcq_question: A customer says "I've been charged twice for the same thing." What do they most likely want?
mcq_options: A) They want the duplicate checked and the extra money returned. | B) They want to cancel the whole order and close their account. | C) They want a discount on their next order as an apology. | D) They want you to explain how the payment system works.
mcq_why: They paid twice for one thing, so they want the duplicate checked and the extra money returned. B is tempting, but nothing in the sentence suggests they dislike the order; only the double payment is the problem.
reorder_task: both / Let / check / payments / me / now
reorder_answer: Let me check both payments now
hindi_to_english: Customer keh raha hai ki ek order ke liye do baar paisa kata. Aap maafi maangiye aur kahiye ki aap dono payment abhi check karte hain.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry you've been charged twice. Let me check both payments for you right now.
whats_next_customer: Is my card hacked or something?
whats_next_reply: I can see both payments came from our checkout, so it looks like a duplicate, not fraud. I'll start the refund for the second one now.
role_play: Partner A was charged twice for a 30-dollar phone case. Partner B apologises, asks for the date and amounts, confirms the duplicate and explains when the refund will arrive.
record_task: Record your reply to this customer: a short apology, the question you need answered, and what you will do next.
self_check: Did you apologise before asking for details? · Did you avoid saying "not possible"? · Did you tell the customer what happens next?

sentence: This is the third time I'm calling about this.
speaker: Customer
situation: A customer rings again about a broken washing machine that two earlier calls failed to fix.
recall_cue: A caller says they have rung several times about one problem. What are they really feeling, and what must you do first?
linking: this_is → "thi-siz" · third_time → "thurd-TIME" · calling_about → "kaw-lin-guh-BOUT"
intonation: The customer often stresses "third" and slows down on it. A sharp fall at the end shows anger; a tired, low voice shows they have almost given up.
indian_pron_tip: When you repeat "third", start with /θ/, tongue between the teeth, and keep the "r" light: "thurd", not "tird" or "tard". "This" needs /ð/, not "dis".
customer_emotion: Fed up, ignored and close to giving up on the company.
memory_hook: Picture someone knocking on the same door for the third time, louder each time: the knock is not about the door, it is about being ignored.
hindi_meaning: इसके बारे में मैं तीसरी बार कॉल कर रहा/रही हूँ।
hindi_roman: Iske baare mein main teesri baar call kar raha/rahi hoon.
simple_meaning: I have already called two times about this problem, and it is still not fixed.
why_it_works: The customer is saying "nobody has taken responsibility". They need acknowledgement of the repeat calls, proof you know the history, and one person who will own it.
key_chunk: This is the ___ time I'm calling about ___.
grammar_pattern: This is the + ordinal + time + I'm + verb-ing + about + noun
grammar_note: After "This is the third time", you will hear both "I'm calling" and "I've called"; both are natural on the phone.
tone_note: It is a complaint, not a question. Replying "Okay, what is the issue?" ignores the history and sounds as if you have not listened at all.
watch_out: ✗ (Agent) Sorry for the inconvenience. Please give me your complaint details. → ✓ I'm sorry you've had to call three times. I can see the notes from your earlier calls.
dont_say: "Please explain the problem from the beginning." It proves the customer's fear that nobody remembers them.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please tell me your problem again", say "I'm sorry you've had to call three times. I can see the earlier notes, so let's fix it now."
alt_1: I've rung you three times now about this.
alt_2: I keep calling and nothing gets done.
more_formal: This is my third call regarding this matter, and it is still unresolved.
ask_next: I'm sorry you've had to call three times. I can see the notes from your earlier calls, and I'll take care of it personally now.
replies_you_may_hear: I hope so, because I'm tired of this. · Every time someone says that. · Then why hasn't anyone fixed it?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Everyone says they'll fix it!" → Agent: "After two calls, I don't blame you for doubting it. I'm booking the engineer now, and I'll call you tomorrow to confirm the visit."
cultural_note: Indian agents may say "sorry, sir, I will check" and start the script again. International customers may not expect a fresh start; they expect you to know the history and say so.
channel_note: Chat: often "3rd time contacting u about this!!!" Email: subject lines may say "THIRD REQUEST"; reply with the case history in the first line.
when_not_to_use: Do not claim you can see the history if you cannot; say honestly that the notes are missing and apologise for that too.
mini_conversation: Customer: This is the third time I'm calling about this. | Agent: I'm sorry you've had to call three times. I can see the notes from your earlier calls, and I'll take care of it personally now. | Customer: Fine, but I want it fixed this week. | Agent: I'm booking the engineer for Thursday and I'll call you on Wednesday to confirm.
source_rule: HEARD (often credited to Disney): hear, empathise, apologise, resolve; take ownership so the customer does not repeat the story.
fill_blank: This is the third ____ I'm calling about this.
mcq_question: A customer says "This is the third time I'm calling about this." What is the best first reply?
mcq_options: A) Thank you for calling. Could you please start from the beginning and tell me what happened? | B) I'm sorry for the inconvenience. Please bear with me while I open your account. | C) I'm sorry you've had to call three times. I can see your notes, so I'll take care of it. | D) I understand, sir. Please be patient, and I will send this to the right team.
mcq_why: C acknowledges the repeat calls, shows you know the history and takes ownership. A and B make the customer start again or wait, and D passes the problem on to someone else.
reorder_task: earlier / see / notes / I / your / can
reorder_answer: I can see your earlier notes
hindi_to_english: Customer teesri baar call kar raha hai. Pehle maafi maangiye, phir boliye ki aapke paas pichli calls ke notes hain, taaki unhe kuch dohrana na pade.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry you've had to call again. I have the notes from your earlier calls, so you won't need to repeat anything.
whats_next_customer: Then why hasn't anyone fixed it?
whats_next_reply: That's a fair question, and I'm sorry it has taken three calls. The part was never ordered. I've ordered it now, and I'll call you on Wednesday with the delivery date.
role_play: Partner A is calling for the third time about a router that keeps dropping. Partner B acknowledges the repeat calls, mentions the earlier notes, takes ownership and gives a date.
record_task: Record your full reply to this customer, including the acknowledgement, the ownership line and a clear next step with a time.
self_check: Did you acknowledge the repeat calls? · Did you avoid asking them to start again? · Did you give a clear next step?

sentence: It keeps freezing whenever I open it.
speaker: Customer
situation: A customer calls about the company's banking app on their phone, which stops responding each time it starts.
recall_cue: A caller says something "keeps freezing". What exactly is happening, and what two questions do you ask next?
linking: keeps_freezing → "keep-SFREE-zing" · whenever_I → "wen-ev-ruh-RYE" · open_it → "OH-puh-nit"
intonation: The customer often stresses "keeps" to show it happens again and again. A falling end shows frustration; a rising end may mean they are unsure what is wrong.
indian_pron_tip: When you repeat it, say "freezing" with a buzzing /z/ in the middle: "FREE-zing", not "free-sing". "Whenever" starts with /w/, rounded lips, not "venever".
customer_emotion: Irritated and unable to do what they need on the app.
memory_hook: Picture a video call where the other person's face freezes mid-word, every single time you dial: that is "keeps freezing".
hindi_meaning: जब भी मैं इसे खोलता/खोलती हूँ, यह बार-बार अटक जाता है।
hindi_roman: Jab bhi main ise kholta/kholti hoon, yeh baar-baar atak jaata hai.
simple_meaning: Every time I start the app, the screen stops moving and I cannot use it.
why_it_works: "Keeps" means it happens again and again, and "freezing" means the screen stops responding. The customer needs a fix, but first you need the device and the exact moment it stops.
key_chunk: It keeps ___ whenever I ___.
grammar_pattern: keep + verb-ing (repeated action) · whenever + present simple
grammar_note: "Keeps freezing" means it freezes again and again; "whenever" means every time.
tone_note: The customer is frustrated with the app, not with you. "Your phone may be old" sounds like you are blaming them before checking anything.
watch_out: ✗ (Agent) So your app is stopped working every time? → ✓ So the app stops responding every time you open it. Is that right?
dont_say: "Uninstall and install it again." said as the first reply. It skips the questions and may lose the customer's saved data.
positive_swap: Instead of "Your phone is the problem", say "Let's find out what's causing it. What phone are you using?"
alt_1: It hangs every time I start it.
alt_2: The app gets stuck as soon as I open it.
more_formal: The application becomes unresponsive each time I launch it.
ask_next: That sounds annoying. Does it freeze straight away, or after you log in? And what phone are you using?
replies_you_may_hear: Straight away, on the first screen. · After I put in my PIN. · It's an older Android phone.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Just fix it, I don't know the technical stuff!" → Agent: "That's fine, you don't need to. Just tell me what you see on the screen, and I'll guide you step by step."
cultural_note: In Indian English, "it is hanging" is common, and "hung" is the standard past form ("it hung"). Many international customers say "freeze", "crash" or "get stuck" instead.
channel_note: Chat: often "app keeps freezing wen i open it". Email: ask for a screenshot and the phone model in your first reply.
when_not_to_use: Do not treat "freezing" as "crashing" without checking; freezing means it stays open but stops, crashing means it closes by itself.
mini_conversation: Customer: It keeps freezing whenever I open it. | Agent: That sounds annoying. Does it freeze straight away, or after you log in? | Customer: Straight away, on the first screen. | Agent: Thanks. So the app freezes on the first screen every time. Let's try updating it first. Could you open your app store?
source_rule: Paraphrase before solving and ask clarifying questions, so you fix the right problem.
fill_blank: It keeps ____ (freeze) whenever I open it.
mcq_question: A customer says their app "keeps freezing". What does this mean?
mcq_options: A) The app closes by itself a few seconds after the customer opens it. | B) The app will not install on the customer's phone at all. | C) The app opens, but it is very slow to load the first screen. | D) The app opens, but the screen stops responding again and again.
mcq_why: Freezing means the screen stops responding but the app stays open. A is tempting, but that is crashing, which needs different questions. C is slowness, not a complete stop.
reorder_task: open / I / freezing / whenever / it / keeps / It
reorder_answer: It keeps freezing whenever I open it
hindi_to_english: Customer bol raha hai app baar-baar atak jaata hai. Pehle afsos jataiye, phir poochhiye ki kab atakta hai aur kaun-sa phone hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry the app keeps freezing. When does it freeze, and what phone are you using?
whats_next_customer: It's an old Android phone, about four years old.
whats_next_reply: Thanks. Let's check for an app update first, because updates often fix freezing.
role_play: Partner A's food-delivery app freezes on the payment screen. Partner B asks when it freezes and which phone A uses, paraphrases the answer, and gives one first step.
record_task: Record your reply to this customer with a short empathy line and your two clarifying questions.
self_check: Did you ask when it freezes? · Did you ask which device they use? · Did you avoid blaming the customer's phone?

sentence: Can you just tell me when it'll arrive?
speaker: Customer
situation: The agent has been explaining the courier process for a while, and the customer interrupts because they only want the delivery date, which you can see on the tracking screen.
recall_cue: A caller interrupts with "can you just tell me…". What is the word "just" telling you, and how should your reply begin?
linking: can_you → "kuh-nyoo" · tell_me → "TEL-mee" · when_it'll → "we-NIT-ul" · it'll_arrive → "it-luh-RIVE"
intonation: Heavy stress on "just" and "when", often with a sharp, falling end. That fall signals impatience, not a real yes/no question.
indian_pron_tip: When you answer, say "arrive" with stress on the second syllable, a-RIVE, and a clear /v/ at the end with teeth on the lip. Do not let "it'll" become "it will" with full stress; keep it short.
customer_emotion: Impatient and tired of hearing about the process.
memory_hook: Picture someone at a bus stop who does not want the route map, only the time the bus comes. Give them the time first.
hindi_meaning: क्या आप बस इतना बता सकते/सकती हैं कि यह कब पहुँचेगा?
hindi_roman: Kya aap bas itna bata sakte/sakti hain ki yeh kab pahunchega?
simple_meaning: Stop explaining the process; I only want to know the delivery day.
why_it_works: "Just" shows the customer feels the agent is talking too much. They need the answer first, in one short sentence, and details only if they ask.
key_chunk: Can you just tell me ___?
grammar_pattern: Can you just + verb + me + wh- clause (when + subject + will + verb)
grammar_note: "Just" here means "only" or "simply"; it shows impatience, not rudeness.
tone_note: The customer sounds blunt but is not being rude. Giving more explanation after this sounds like you are not listening.
watch_out: ✗ (Agent) Sir, first let me explain the process. → ✓ Yes, it's due on Thursday, between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m.
dont_say: "As I was saying, the courier partner will…" It ignores the request and makes the customer angrier.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please listen, I am explaining", say "Of course. It's due to arrive on Thursday, between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m."
alt_1: When is it actually coming?
alt_2: I just need a date, please.
more_formal: Could you please confirm the expected delivery date?
ask_next: Of course. It's due to arrive on Thursday, between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m.
replies_you_may_hear: Thursday? Not before? · Okay, thank you. · Will someone call before they come?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Thursday? That's too late!" → Agent: "I understand, you were hoping for sooner. Could you hold for about a minute while I check whether a faster delivery is possible for this parcel?"
cultural_note: Some agents explain the whole process first to be thorough. International customers may not expect that; many prefer the answer first and the reason only if they ask.
channel_note: Chat: often "just tell me when it's coming" or "ETA??". Reply with the date in the first line. Email: put the date in the first sentence.
when_not_to_use: Do not give a date you are unsure of just to please the customer; say what the system shows and that you will confirm.
mini_conversation: Customer: Can you just tell me when it'll arrive? | Agent: Of course. It's due to arrive on Thursday, between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. | Customer: Okay, good. | Agent: You'll also get a text on Thursday morning with a tracking link.
source_rule: Reduce customer effort: give a clear timeline first; be specific about what will happen and when.
fill_blank: Can you ____ (only, simply) tell me when it'll arrive?
mcq_question: In "Can you just tell me when it'll arrive?", what does the word "just" show?
mcq_options: A) The customer is relaxed and would like to chat about the delivery. | B) The customer is asking politely and has plenty of time to listen. | C) The customer is impatient and wants only the date, not an explanation. | D) The customer is unsure about the date and wants to cancel the order.
mcq_why: "Just" means "only" here and signals impatience with long explanations. D is tempting because the customer sounds annoyed, but they are asking for a date, not cancelling. A and B ignore the tone.
reorder_task: Thursday / arrive / It's / on / to / due
reorder_answer: It's due to arrive on Thursday
hindi_to_english: Customer sirf delivery ki date jaanna chahta hai. Seedha date aur time batayiye.
hindi_to_english_answer: Of course. It's due on Thursday, between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m.
whats_next_customer: Thursday? Not before?
whats_next_reply: I've checked, and Thursday is the earliest. I'll ask the courier to call you an hour before.
role_play: Partner B starts explaining the warehouse process; Partner A interrupts with "Can you just tell me when it'll arrive?" Partner B stops, gives the date and time window in one sentence, and offers a tracking text.
record_task: Record your reply to this customer: the date and time window first, then one helpful extra detail.
self_check: Did you give the date in your first sentence? · Did you stop explaining the process? · Did you keep your reply short?

sentence: I never signed up for this.
speaker: Customer
situation: A customer has noticed a monthly subscription charge on their card and calls to dispute it.
recall_cue: A caller says they never agreed to a subscription they are paying for. What might really have happened, and how do you start?
linking: never_signed → "NEV-er-SYND" · signed_up → "syn-DUP" · up_for → "up-fer"
intonation: Heavy stress on "never" and often on "this", with a sharp fall. It can sound accusing; the customer may feel tricked.
indian_pron_tip: When you repeat it, say "signed" as "synd", one syllable with a soft final /d/; the "g" is silent. "Never" needs a /v/ with teeth on the lip, not "newer".
customer_emotion: Feeling cheated, suspicious and worried about more charges.
memory_hook: Picture finding a gym card in your wallet that you never asked for: you want to know how it got there, and you want it gone.
hindi_meaning: मैंने इसके लिए कभी साइन अप नहीं किया।
hindi_roman: Maine iske liye kabhi sign up nahin kiya.
simple_meaning: I did not agree to join this service, so I should not be paying for it.
why_it_works: The customer feels tricked and fears more money will go. They need you to take it seriously, find out how it started without blaming them, and stop or refund it.
key_chunk: I never ___ for this.
grammar_pattern: I + never + past simple verb + up + for + noun
grammar_note: "Sign up for" is a phrasal verb meaning "join" or "register for".
tone_note: The customer may sound accusing. Saying "You must have clicked on it" blames them and turns the call into an argument.
watch_out: ✗ (Agent) You must have done it by mistake. → ✓ I understand. Let's find out how this started, and I'll stop it if it shouldn't be there.
dont_say: "You must have subscribed yourself." It blames the customer before you have checked anything.
positive_swap: Instead of "It shows you subscribed", say "Let's find out how this started. I can see it began on 3 May. Does that date mean anything to you?"
alt_1: I didn't agree to this at all.
alt_2: I don't remember joining anything like this.
more_formal: I have no record of subscribing to this service.
ask_next: I understand, and I'll look into it now. I can see it started on 3 May after a free trial. Does that ring a bell?
replies_you_may_hear: No, never. · Oh, maybe that free trial? · Just cancel it and give me my money back.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I want all my money back!" → Agent: "I understand. I'll cancel it now so nothing more is taken, and I'll check what I can refund for the past months."
cultural_note: Indian agents may say "as per our records, you have subscribed". International customers may not expect that phrase and may hear it as "you are lying"; describing what you see and asking is calmer.
channel_note: Chat: often "i never signed up for this??" or "didnt sign up for anything". Email: may include the bank statement; quote the date and amount back to them.
when_not_to_use: Do not say "I can see you signed up" as your first line, even if it is true; it sounds like an argument before you have listened.
mini_conversation: Customer: I never signed up for this. | Agent: I understand, and I'll look into it now. I can see it started on 3 May after a free trial. Does that ring a bell? | Customer: Oh, maybe. But I don't want it. | Agent: Of course. I'll cancel it now, so there are no more charges.
source_rule: Don't hide behind records or policy: listen without blaming, give the facts in plain words, then offer what you can do.
fill_blank: I never ____ (sign) up for this.
mcq_question: A customer says "I never signed up for this." What is the best first reply?
mcq_options: A) Let's find out how this started, and I'll stop it if it shouldn't be there. | B) I can see that you subscribed on 3 May, so the charge is correct, I'm afraid. | C) I'm sorry about that. Could you check whether someone else in your home signed up? | D) Our system shows your consent, so I can't cancel it without a good reason.
mcq_why: A takes the customer seriously and moves to a fix without blame. B is tempting because it is factual, but it sounds like calling the customer a liar. C hands the investigation to the customer, and D hides behind the system.
reorder_task: started / out / this / find / how / Let's
reorder_answer: Let's find out how this started
hindi_to_english: Customer keh raha hai usne kabhi join nahin kiya. Uski baat sun kar boliye ki aap check karenge kaise shuru hua, aur agar yeh nahin hona chahiye tha to ise band kar denge.
hindi_to_english_answer: I understand. Let me check how this started, and I'll stop it if it shouldn't be there.
whats_next_customer: Oh, maybe it was that free trial.
whats_next_reply: That's likely. The trial turned into a paid plan when it ended. I can cancel it now, so nothing more is charged.
role_play: Partner A sees a 9-dollar monthly music charge they do not recognise. Partner B listens, checks the start date without blaming A, explains the free trial and cancels it.
record_task: Record your reply to this customer: an acknowledgement, what you can see, and a question that helps them remember, all without blame.
self_check: Did you avoid blaming the customer? · Did you give a fact, such as the start date? · Did you offer to stop further charges?

sentence: I'll think about it and get back to you.
speaker: Customer
situation: You have offered the customer an upgrade to a faster broadband plan, and they answer at the end of the call.
recall_cue: At the end of an offer, a caller says they will think about it. What might they really mean, and how do you close well?
linking: think_about_it → "thing-kuh-BOU-tit" · get_back → "geh-BACK" · back_to_you → "BAK-tuh-yoo"
intonation: A light, falling tone often means a polite "no for now". A slower, thoughtful tone means they are really considering it. Listen to the pace, not only the words.
indian_pron_tip: When you reply, say "think" with /θ/, tongue between the teeth, not "tink". In "about it", link the /t/ into "it": "a-bou-tit", not two separate words.
customer_emotion: Unsure, slightly pressured, wanting space to decide.
memory_hook: Picture a shopper putting a shirt back on the rail and saying "maybe later": push and they walk out; hand them the tag and they may come back.
hindi_meaning: मैं इसके बारे में सोचूँगा/सोचूँगी और फिर आपको बताऊँगा/बताऊँगी।
hindi_roman: Main iske baare mein sochoonga/sochoongi aur phir aapko bataoonga/bataoongi.
simple_meaning: I am not ready to decide now; maybe I will contact you later.
why_it_works: It is often a polite way to say "not now" without saying no. The customer wants no pressure; making it easy to decide later keeps their trust and the chance of a yes.
key_chunk: I'll think about it and ___.
grammar_pattern: I'll + think about + it + and + get back to + person
grammar_note: "Get back to you" means contact you again later; it is the common international form.
tone_note: The customer is polite but closing the topic. Pushing with "But this offer ends today!" sounds pushy and can damage trust.
watch_out: ✗ (Agent) Okay, then you call back to us. → ✓ Of course, take your time. Shall I email you the details so you can compare?
dont_say: "But sir, this is the best offer, you should take it now." It ignores the customer's answer and feels like pressure.
positive_swap: Instead of "Why don't you decide now?", say "Of course, take your time. Shall I email you the details so you can compare?"
alt_1: Let me think it over and I'll let you know.
alt_2: I'm not sure yet. I'll call you back if I decide to go ahead.
more_formal: I would like some time to consider it, and I will contact you once I have decided.
ask_next: Of course, take your time. Would it help if I emailed you the details so you can compare?
replies_you_may_hear: Yes, please email it. · No, I'll look on the website. · Okay, but I probably won't change.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I said I'll think about it!" → Agent: "Absolutely, no pressure at all. The details will be in your email whenever you're ready."
cultural_note: Indian customers often say "I will let you know" or "Let me discuss with family and revert". International customers more often say "I'll get back to you" or "Let me think it over". All of them usually mean "not yet", so answer them the same way: no pressure.
channel_note: Chat: often "ok will think n let u know". Email: "I'll consider it and come back to you." Reply with a short, no-pressure summary.
when_not_to_use: Do not offer to call them back about it unless they agree; an unwanted sales call feels like pressure.
mini_conversation: Customer: I'll think about it and get back to you. | Agent: Of course, take your time. Would it help if I emailed you the details so you can compare? | Customer: Yes, please. | Agent: Done. It's in your inbox now. Is there anything else I can help you with today?
source_rule: Respect the customer's decision: avoid pressure, and leave one clear, easy next step.
fill_blank: I'll think about it and get ____ to you.
mcq_question: After an upgrade offer, a customer says "I'll think about it and get back to you." What is the best reply?
mcq_options: A) Of course, take your time. Shall I email you the details so you can compare? | B) I understand, but this offer ends today, so it would be best to decide now. | C) Okay. Please remember that prices can change, so don't wait too long. | D) Of course. May I ask what is stopping you from deciding today?
mcq_why: A respects the decision and makes it easy to come back. B is tempting because it creates urgency, but it ignores what the customer said. C and D add pressure.
reorder_task: details / so / Shall / you / email / compare / I / can / the / you
reorder_answer: Shall I email you the details so you can compare
hindi_to_english: Customer sochna chahta hai. Usse boliye aaram se sochiye, aur details email karne ka offer kariye.
hindi_to_english_answer: Of course, take your time. Shall I email you the details so you can compare?
whats_next_customer: Yes, email it, but please don't call me about it.
whats_next_reply: Of course. I'll just send the email, and I'll note on your account that you don't want a call about it.
role_play: Partner B offers Partner A an annual plan that saves money. Partner A says "I'll think about it and get back to you." Partner B accepts without pressure, offers an email summary and closes the call.
record_task: Record your reply to this customer, then the closing line of the call, without any pressure to decide now.
self_check: Did you accept the answer without pushing? · Did you offer something useful, like an email? · Did you close the call warmly?

sentence: I can hear how frustrating this has been, and you have every right to be upset. Let me find out what went wrong and put it right.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer's internet has been down for three days, and they open the call by shouting at you.
recall_cue: The caller is shouting about a problem that has gone on for days. How do you name their feeling and move to action without arguing back?
stress: i can HEAR how frus-TRAY-ting this has BEEN · you have EV-ery RIGHT to be up-SET · let me FIND out what went WRONG · and PUT it RIGHT
linking: has_been → "hez-bin" · and_you → "an-joo" · find_out → "fine-dout" · put_it → "pu-tit"
intonation: Low, slow and steady; do not match the caller's volume. Falling tone on "upset", a short pause, then a firmer falling tone on "put it right" to show action is starting.
indian_pron_tip: "Frustrating" is stressed on the second syllable, frus-TRAY-ting, not with equal beats. Make the "tr" with the tongue just behind the top teeth, not a heavy retroflex ṭ.
customer_emotion: Angry, exhausted and expecting to be brushed off again.
memory_hook: Think of a fire: you do not throw words at it; first you name the heat, then you pick up the hose.
hindi_meaning: मैं समझ सकता/सकती हूँ कि यह कितना परेशान करने वाला रहा है, और आपका नाराज़ होना बिल्कुल जायज़ है। मुझे पता लगाने दीजिए कि क्या गड़बड़ हुई, और मैं उसे ठीक करूँगा/करूँगी।
hindi_roman: Main samajh sakta/sakti hoon ki yeh kitna pareshaan karne wala raha hai, aur aapka naraaz hona bilkul jaayaz hai. Mujhe pata lagane dijiye ki kya gadbad hui, aur main use theek karoonga/karoongi.
simple_meaning: I understand you are very annoyed, and you are right to feel that way. I will find the problem and fix it.
why_it_works: It names the feeling instead of arguing with it, agrees the anger is fair, and moves straight to action. The caller hears that you are on their side and that something will now happen.
key_chunk: I can hear how ___ this has been. Let me ___.
grammar_pattern: I can hear + how + adjective + this has been · Let me + base verb
grammar_note: "Has been" (present perfect) shows the problem started in the past and is still going on.
tone_note: Agreeing that the anger is fair lowers it. "There's no need to shout" or "Please calm down" tells the caller they are wrong to feel angry and usually makes them louder.
watch_out: ✗ Sir, please calm down, I am understanding your problem. → ✓ I can hear how frustrating this has been. Let me put it right.
dont_say: "Please calm down, sir." — it tells an angry person their feeling is wrong and usually makes them angrier.
positive_swap: Instead of "Calm down, there's no need to shout", say "I can hear how frustrating this has been. Let me find out what went wrong."
alt_1: Three days without internet is a long time, and I'd be annoyed too. Let me look at your line right now.
alt_2: I completely understand why you're upset. Let me see exactly what has happened and fix it.
more_formal: I fully appreciate how frustrating this has been, and your concern is entirely justified. Allow me to investigate and resolve it for you.
ask_next: So I can fix this properly, could you tell me when the connection first stopped working?
replies_you_may_hear: You're the third person I've told this to. · I don't want sympathy, I want it fixed. · Fine. What are you going to do?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I don't need you to understand, I need it fixed!" → Agent: "You're right. I'm checking your line now, and I'll tell you exactly what I find in two minutes."
cultural_note: Some agents answer an angry caller with "Sir, please listen to me first" or "Sir, sir, sir". International callers may hear this as talking over them; a short, specific acknowledgement before any explanation works better.
channel_note: Chat: "I can see why this is frustrating. Let me check your line now." Email: name the problem specifically in the first line, then list what you have already done.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it when the caller is calm and asking a small question; strong empathy for a small issue sounds fake.
mini_conversation: Customer: Three days! Three days without internet, and nobody does anything! | Agent: I can hear how frustrating this has been, and you have every right to be upset. Let me find out what went wrong and put it right. | Customer: Fine, but hurry. | Agent: I'm running a line test now; it takes about a minute.
source_rule: Empathy line, then action; never say "calm down", name the feeling instead.
fill_blank: I can hear how frustrating this has been. Let me find out what went wrong and put it ____.
mcq_question: A caller shouts that their internet has been down for three days. Which opening response is most likely to lower the tension?
mcq_options: A) Please calm down, sir. Shouting will not help me fix your problem any faster. | B) I can hear how frustrating this has been. Let me find out what went wrong. | C) I'm sorry for the inconvenience, sir. Many customers are facing this problem. | D) I understand, sir. Our engineers are very busy this week, so repairs are slow.
mcq_why: B names the feeling and moves to action. A tells the caller their anger is wrong, C is a script that treats the problem as ordinary, and D is an excuse that offers no help.
reorder_task: what / find / Let / went / out / wrong / me
reorder_answer: Let me find out what went wrong
hindi_to_english: Teen din se internet nahin hai, to aapka naraaz hona bilkul jaayaz hai. Main abhi aapki line check karta/karti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: You've had no internet for three days, so you have every right to be upset. I'll check your line right now.
whats_next_customer: You people always say that and nothing happens.
whats_next_reply: I can see why it feels that way after three days. This time I'm staying on the call until the line test is done, and I'll give you a ticket number.
role_play: Partner A is a customer whose internet has been down for three days and is shouting. Partner B acknowledges the anger without arguing, agrees it is fair, and moves to a line test.
record_task: Record yourself saying the sentence twice, once at normal speed and once slower and lower, then keep the version that sounds calmer.
self_check: Did you keep your voice low and steady? · Did you avoid "calm down" and "sorry for the inconvenience"? · Did you move to an action in the second sentence?

sentence: Please go on, I'm listening. I'd like to hear everything before I suggest anything.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer explaining a complicated billing mix-up stops mid-story, expecting you to interrupt like the last agent did.
recall_cue: The caller pauses halfway through a long complaint and says, "Sorry, I'll let you talk." How do you invite them to finish?
stress: PLEASE go ON · i'm LIS-ning · i'd LIKE to HEAR EV-ery-thing · be-FORE i sug-GEST AN-y-thing
linking: go_on → "go-won" · I'm_listening → "aim-LIS-ning" · hear_everything → "hee-REV-ree-thing" · suggest_anything → "sug-jes-TEN-ee-thing"
intonation: Warm and unhurried, falling tone on "listening". Leave a clear pause after the first sentence so the caller can start again; keep the second sentence soft.
indian_pron_tip: "Listening" has a silent t: LIS-ning, not "lis-ten-ing" with a hard t. In "everything" and "anything" put the tongue tip between the teeth for th; avoid "ev-ry-ting".
customer_emotion: Frustrated and unsure anyone will hear the whole story.
memory_hook: Picture handing the caller the microphone and sitting back with a notebook; your job right now is the pen, not the voice.
hindi_meaning: आप बोलते रहिए, मैं सुन रहा/रही हूँ। कोई सुझाव देने से पहले मैं पूरी बात सुनना चाहता/चाहती हूँ।
hindi_roman: Aap bolte rahiye, main sun raha/rahi hoon. Koi sujhaav dene se pehle main poori baat sunna chahta/chahti hoon.
simple_meaning: Keep talking; I am paying attention. I want the full story before I give you an answer.
why_it_works: It hands control back to the caller and promises you will not jump in with a quick fix. Customers who feel fully heard usually argue less and give you the details you need.
key_chunk: Please go on, I'm listening. I'd like to ___ before I ___.
grammar_pattern: Please + go on · I'd like to + base verb + before + I + present verb
grammar_note: After "before", use the present tense ("before I suggest") even when you mean the future.
tone_note: It sounds patient because it asks for more. Cutting in with "Yes, yes, I know, sir" sounds as if you stopped listening.
watch_out: ✗ Yes yes, I am getting it, tell fast. → ✓ Please go on, I'm listening.
dont_say: "Okay, okay, I got it." while the caller is mid-sentence — it tells them you have stopped listening and want to move on.
positive_swap: Instead of "Yes, yes, I know, let me tell you the solution", say "Please go on, I'm listening. I'd like to hear everything first."
alt_1: Take your time, I'm with you. Tell me the rest.
alt_2: No, please carry on. I want the full picture before I check anything.
more_formal: Please continue; I'd like to understand the full situation before I propose a solution.
ask_next: Thank you. So you moved in March, the bills kept going to your old address, and now there's a late fee. Have I got that right?
replies_you_may_hear: Okay, so then in April… · That's basically it. · Sorry, it's a long story.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why aren't you saying anything? Are you even there?" → Agent: "Yes, I'm here and I'm taking notes. Please go on; I don't want to miss anything."
cultural_note: Some agents fill every pause with "yes sir, yes sir" or jump in with a solution to show speed. International callers often read this as impatience; short signals like "I see" and "Mm-hm" are enough.
channel_note: Chat: "Please go on, I'm reading every message." Email: not needed; instead, answer every point the customer raised.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it when the caller has clearly finished and is waiting for your answer; then you must summarise and act.
mini_conversation: Customer: So I told you I'd moved, but the bills kept going to my old flat, and then… sorry, I'll let you talk. | Agent: Please go on, I'm listening. I'd like to hear everything before I suggest anything. | Customer: Then this month I got a late fee for a bill I never saw. | Agent: I see. So the bills went to your old address, and now there's a late fee on top. Is that right?
source_rule: Interrupting frustrates customers: let them finish, take notes, then paraphrase.
fill_blank: Please go on, I'm ____. I'd like to hear everything before I suggest anything.
mcq_question: A caller stops in the middle of a long complaint and apologises for talking so much. What is the best response?
mcq_options: A) Okay, okay, I understand, sir. Let me tell you what we can do for you. | B) Please go on, I'm listening. I'd like to hear everything first. | C) That's fine, but could you give me only the main points, please? | D) Don't worry, sir. This is a common problem and the solution is simple.
mcq_why: B invites the caller to finish. D sounds reassuring but jumps to a fix before you have the full story; A cuts the caller off and C asks for a shorter version, so both make the caller feel rushed.
reorder_task: I'm / on / go / listening / Please
reorder_answer: Please go on, I'm listening
hindi_to_english: Aap boliye, main sun raha/rahi hoon. Pehle main poori baat samajhna chahta/chahti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: Please go on, I'm listening. I'd like to understand everything first.
whats_next_customer: That's all, really. Can you fix it?
whats_next_reply: Thank you for explaining. Let me repeat it to make sure I have it right, and then I'll check your account.
role_play: Partner A tells a long, messy story about bills going to an old address and a late fee, and keeps stopping. Partner B uses only short listening signals and "Please go on" until A finishes, then paraphrases.
record_task: Record the sentence, then record a 30-second role-play where you use only "I see", "Mm-hm" and this line while your partner talks.
self_check: Did you leave a pause after "listening"? · Did you say "listening" as two syllables, LIS-ning? · Did you avoid offering a solution in this turn?

sentence: I'm afraid I'm not able to refund this order, as the thirty-day return period ended last week. What I can do is give you store credit for the full amount.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer wants a cash refund for shoes delivered five weeks ago, but refunds are only possible within thirty days of delivery; your system shows that full store credit is still available.
recall_cue: The customer asks for a refund you are not allowed to give. What three things must your answer contain?
stress: i'm a-FRAID i'm NOT A-ble to re-FUND this OR-der · as the THIR-ty-day re-TURN PE-ri-od END-ed LAST week · what i CAN do · is GIVE you STORE CRED-it for the FULL a-MOUNT
linking: afraid_I'm → "a-FRAY-dime" · not_able → "no-TAY-bul" · full_amount → "fu-la-MOUNT" · What_I → "wha-dai"
intonation: A soft, slightly lower tone on "I'm afraid", then a steady, falling tone on "last week" so the reason sounds final, not over-apologetic. Short pause, then a brighter, slightly higher start on "What I can do" to signal the good news.
indian_pron_tip: "Refund" as a verb is stressed re-FUND; the noun is RE-fund. Many speakers use RE-fund for both. Also say the "-ed" in "ended" as a full extra syllable: EN-did.
customer_emotion: Disappointed and ready to argue that they deserve their money back.
memory_hook: A closed door with a lit window beside it: you point at the door only once, then spend your words on the window.
hindi_meaning: मुझे अफ़सोस है, मैं इस ऑर्डर का रिफ़ंड नहीं कर सकता/सकती, क्योंकि रिटर्न की तीस दिन की अवधि पिछले हफ़्ते ख़त्म हो गई। लेकिन मैं आपको पूरी रकम का स्टोर क्रेडिट दे सकता/सकती हूँ।
hindi_roman: Mujhe afsos hai, main is order ka refund nahin kar sakta/sakti, kyunki return ki tees din ki avadhi pichhle hafte khatam ho gayi. Lekin main aapko poori rakam ka store credit de sakta/sakti hoon.
simple_meaning: I'm sorry, but I cannot give your money back because the time limit for returns is over. I can give you the full value to spend with us.
why_it_works: It gives the real reason in plain words, so the refusal does not sound random, and then moves straight to something the customer can actually have. The customer leaves with an option, not just a "no".
key_chunk: I'm afraid I'm not able to ___, as ___. What I can do is ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm afraid + I'm not able to + base verb · as + reason clause · What I can do is + base verb
grammar_note: "I'm not able to" is softer than "I can't", and "as" gives the reason, like "because".
tone_note: "I'm afraid" shows regret before the bad news, the reason makes it fair, and "What I can do" makes it helpful. "That's not possible, it's company policy" sounds like a wall and invites an argument.
watch_out: ✗ I am not able to refund this order because return period is finished last week. → ✓ I'm afraid I'm not able to refund this order, as the return period ended last week.
dont_say: "Sorry, as per policy, no refund." — it hides behind a rule, gives no reason and offers nothing.
positive_swap: Instead of "We can't refund it, it's policy", say "What I can do is give you store credit for the full amount."
alt_1: Refunds are available for thirty days after delivery, so I can't refund this one, but I can offer you full store credit today.
alt_2: The refund window closed last week, unfortunately. The good news is I can add the full amount to your account as store credit.
more_formal: I regret that a refund is no longer available, as the thirty-day return period has ended. However, I would be glad to issue store credit for the full value.
ask_next: Would you like me to add the store credit to your account now, or send you a credit code by email?
replies_you_may_hear: But I was travelling, I couldn't return it earlier. · I don't want credit, I want my money. · Okay, how do I use the credit?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "That's unfair, I was away for work!" → Agent: "I understand, and I'm sorry the timing worked out badly. Let me ask my team leader whether we can make an exception; if not, the store credit is still available."
cultural_note: Many agents say "As per policy" to sound official. International customers may not expect it and often hear it as hiding behind rules; a plain reason plus an alternative sounds more honest.
channel_note: Chat: split it into two messages, the reason first, then "What I can do is…". Email: reason, empathy, alternative, then a clear next step.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it when a refund might still be possible through an exception you have not checked; check first, then refuse.
mini_conversation: Customer: I want a refund for these shoes. | Agent: I'm afraid I'm not able to refund this order, as the thirty-day return period ended last week. What I can do is give you store credit for the full amount. | Customer: Hmm, can I use it on anything? | Agent: Yes, on anything on our site, and I'll email you the credit code now.
source_rule: Don't hide behind policy: give the reason in plain words, then an alternative (derived advice).
fill_blank: I'm afraid I'm not able to refund this order. What I can ____ is give you store credit for the full amount.
mcq_question: A customer wants a refund after the return period has ended. Which reply refuses in the most helpful way?
mcq_options: A) I'm sorry, sir, but our policy does not allow refunds after thirty days. | B) I understand, but that is not possible now. Is there anything else I can help you with? | C) I'm afraid the return period has ended, so I can't refund it, but I can offer store credit. | D) I will do my best to get you a refund. Please give me a few days to arrange it.
mcq_why: C gives a reason, shows regret and offers an alternative. D sounds kind but promises something you cannot deliver, A hides behind policy and offers nothing, and B is a bare no.
reorder_task: do / can / What / is / I / store / you / give / credit
reorder_answer: What I can do is give you store credit
hindi_to_english: Mujhe afsos hai, main aapko refund nahin de sakta/sakti, kyunki return ka time khatam ho gaya hai. Lekin main aapko poori rakam store credit mein de sakta/sakti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm afraid I'm not able to give you a refund, as the return period has ended. What I can do is give you the full amount as store credit.
whats_next_customer: I don't want store credit. I want my money back.
whats_next_reply: I understand you'd prefer your money back. I'm not able to refund it myself, but I can ask my team leader to review your case, and I'll call you back by 5 pm today with the answer.
role_play: Partner A wants a refund for shoes delivered five weeks ago. Partner B refuses with the reason, offers store credit, and handles one push-back calmly.
record_task: Record the sentence, then record your answer when the customer says "I don't want credit, I want my money."
self_check: Did you give a real reason, not "policy"? · Did your voice brighten on "What I can do"? · Did you stress the verb as re-FUND?

sentence: I want to help you with this, but I'm not able to continue if the personal insults go on. If we can keep it respectful, I'll look into your booking straight away.
speaker: Agent
situation: A caller whose flight booking failed has started swearing at you personally and calling you names.
recall_cue: A caller keeps insulting you personally. How do you set a clear limit while still offering help?
stress: i WANT to HELP you with THIS · but i'm NOT A-ble to con-TIN-ue · if the PER-son-al IN-sults go ON · if we can KEEP it re-SPECT-ful · i'll LOOK in-to your BOOK-ing straight a-WAY
linking: want_to → "won-tuh" · help_you → "hel-pyoo" · go_on → "go-won" · look_into → "loo-kin-too"
intonation: Slow, level and firm; avoid a rising tone, which sounds like pleading. Pause after "go on" so the caller hears the limit, then a slightly warmer fall on "straight away".
indian_pron_tip: The noun "insults" is stressed on the first syllable, IN-sults; the verb is in-SULT. Keep the final cluster "-lts" clear; do not drop it to "insul".
customer_emotion: Furious, feeling powerless, and taking it out on the agent.
memory_hook: A fence with an open gate: the fence marks the line, and the gate shows the way to help is still open.
hindi_meaning: मैं इसमें आपकी मदद करना चाहता/चाहती हूँ, लेकिन अगर व्यक्तिगत अपमान जारी रहा तो मैं बात आगे नहीं बढ़ा पाऊँगा/पाऊँगी। अगर हम सम्मान से बात करें, तो मैं अभी आपकी बुकिंग देखता/देखती हूँ।
hindi_roman: Main ismein aapki madad karna chahta/chahti hoon, lekin agar vyaktigat apmaan jaari raha to main baat aage nahin badha paaunga/paaungi. Agar hum sammaan se baat karein, to main abhi aapki booking dekhta/dekhti hoon.
simple_meaning: I still want to help, but I will stop the call if you keep insulting me. Talk politely and I will check your booking right away.
why_it_works: It separates the caller's anger, which is allowed, from personal abuse, which is not. Starting with "I want to help" shows the limit is about behaviour, not a refusal of service, and the last sentence shows the way forward.
key_chunk: I want to help you with ___, but I'm not able to continue if ___.
grammar_pattern: I want to + base verb, but + I'm not able to + base verb + if + present clause
grammar_note: First conditional: "if" + present tense, then "I'll" + verb for the result.
tone_note: It is firm without insulting back. "Don't talk to me like that!" or "You are being rude" attacks the caller and starts a fight.
watch_out: ✗ Mind your language, otherwise I will disconnect. → ✓ I want to help you with this, but I'm not able to continue if the personal insults go on.
dont_say: "If you shout at me, I will cut the call." — it sounds like a threat and gives no route back to help.
positive_swap: Instead of "Stop abusing me or I'll hang up", say "If we can keep it respectful, I'll look into your booking straight away."
alt_1: I understand you're angry, and I'm here to help, but I need us to keep this respectful so I can fix your booking.
alt_2: I'd really like to solve this for you. To do that, I need the personal comments to stop.
more_formal: I am keen to resolve this for you; however, I am unable to continue the call if the personal remarks persist.
ask_next: Thank you. Now, could you give me the booking reference so I can see why the payment failed?
replies_you_may_hear: Fine. Just fix it. · Sorry, I'm just really stressed. · Don't tell me how to talk!
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Don't tell me how to talk!" → Agent: "I'm not trying to stop you being angry; you have every reason to be. I just need the personal insults to stop so I can help you."
cultural_note: Some agents keep saying "sorry, sir" and absorb the abuse in silence. A clear, polite boundary is a normal part of customer service; follow your company's process for warnings and for ending abusive calls.
channel_note: Chat: "I'm here to help, but I need us to keep this respectful." Email: ignore the insults and answer the problem; mention conduct only if it repeats.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it when the caller is angry at the situation but not attacking you personally; then empathy, not a boundary, is needed.
mini_conversation: Customer: You people are useless idiots! | Agent: I want to help you with this, but I'm not able to continue if the personal insults go on. If we can keep it respectful, I'll look into your booking straight away. | Customer: Okay… sorry. My payment failed twice. | Agent: Thank you. Let me look at the booking now.
source_rule: Never say "calm down"; acknowledge the feeling and limit the behaviour, not the help (derived advice).
fill_blank: I want to help you with this, ____ I'm not able to continue if the personal insults go on.
mcq_question: A caller has started calling you personal names. Which reply sets a limit without making things worse?
mcq_options: A) Mind your language, sir, otherwise I will disconnect the call right now. | B) Please calm down, sir. I am also a human being and I am trying to help. | C) I want to help, but I'm not able to continue if the personal insults go on. | D) I'm very sorry, sir. Please tell me what the problem is and I will check.
mcq_why: C sets a clear limit and keeps help on offer. D seems patient but sets no limit, so the abuse continues; A is a threat, and B tells the caller to calm down.
reorder_task: it / keep / can / we / If / respectful
reorder_answer: If we can keep it respectful
hindi_to_english: Main aapki madad karna chahta/chahti hoon, lekin agar gaali-galauj hoti rahi to main call aage jaari nahin rakh paunga/paungi.
hindi_to_english_answer: I want to help you, but I'm not able to continue the call if the swearing goes on.
whats_next_customer: Whatever. Just fix my booking.
whats_next_reply: Thank you. Could you give me your booking reference, please? I'll check why the payment failed.
role_play: Partner A's flight booking failed and they start insulting Partner B personally. Partner B sets the boundary once, calmly, and moves back to the booking when A stops.
record_task: Record the sentence in a slow, level voice, then record it again and check that your voice does not rise or shake.
self_check: Did you start with "I want to help"? · Did you keep a level, non-pleading tone? · Did you say the final "-lts" in "insults"?
