hindi_to_english_answer: I understand. I can send a new machine by 5 pm today.
whats_next_customer: What do I do until then?
whats_next_reply: I can switch on payment links for you now, so you can send customers a link and still get paid until the machine arrives.
role_play: Partner A runs a café whose card machine stopped this morning and demands a same-day fix with no excuses. Partner B gives the earliest real time and a workaround without explaining or blaming.
record_task: Record your reply to the customer's line: one short empathy phrase, what you can do today, and by when.
self_check: Did you avoid starting with "actually" or a reason? · Did you give a specific time? · Did you offer a workaround in case the time is not soon enough?

sentence: Don't read me a script.
speaker: Customer
situation: You have just said "I apologise for the inconvenience caused, your concern is valuable to us" for the second time in the call.
recall_cue: A customer accuses you of sounding like a robot reading lines. What are they asking for, and how do you change your style?
linking: Don't_read → "dohn-REED" (the t almost disappears) · me_a → "mee-uh" · a_script → "uh-SKRIPT" (weak a, then the s-cluster)
intonation: Usually sharp and falling, often with every word stressed, and sometimes after a sigh. Hear it as "talk to me like a person".
indian_pron_tip: "Script" begins with an s-cluster: say it straight, skript, without an added vowel ("is-kript"). Listen for the strong stress on "SCRIPT", the key word.
customer_emotion: Annoyed and feeling they are talking to a machine, not a person.
memory_hook: Put the script down and look up from the page: the customer wants to see your face, even on the phone.
hindi_meaning: मुझे रटी-रटाई लाइनें मत सुनाइए। (मतलब: मुझसे इंसान की तरह सीधे बात कीजिए।)
hindi_roman: Mujhe rati-rataayi lines mat sunaaiye. (Matlab: mujhse insaan ki tarah seedhe baat kijiye.)
simple_meaning: The customer means: "Stop repeating fixed company phrases. Talk to me normally and answer my real question."
why_it_works: Repeated formal phrases make customers feel processed rather than helped. They want plain, personal language and a direct answer; changing your style at once shows you were listening.
key_chunk: Don't ___ me a ___.
grammar_pattern: Don't + base verb + me + noun (negative imperative)
grammar_note: "Don't + verb" is a direct instruction; here it is a complaint about how you are speaking.
tone_note: It is blunt but fair feedback. Defending the script ("Sir, this is the standard process") proves the customer's point.
watch_out: ✗ Agent: Sir, I am not reading, your concern is valuable to us. → ✓ Agent: Fair enough. Let me tell you straight what's happening.
dont_say: "I apologise for the inconvenience caused, your concern is very valuable to us." — repeating it after this complaint confirms you are reading a script.
positive_swap: Instead of "I apologise for the inconvenience caused", say "Fair enough. Here's exactly what's happening with your order."
alt_1: You're right, that sounded rehearsed. Here's the straight answer: your order is stuck at customs.
alt_2: Sorry, let me put it simply. Your order is held at customs, and I'll chase it today.
more_formal: That's a fair point, and I apologise. To be direct: your order is currently held at customs, and I will follow it up today.
ask_next: Fair enough. Let me tell you straight: your order is held at customs, and I'll chase it today.
replies_you_may_hear: Thank you. That's all I wanted. · So when will it arrive? · Better.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "And stop saying 'I understand'." → Agent: "Okay. Simply put: it's stuck at customs, I'm calling them today, and I'll text you by 6 pm."
cultural_note: Some centres require agents to use fixed phrases word for word. International customers often find over-scripted service annoying; keep the meaning of the script but use your own natural words.
channel_note: Chat: often "stop sending me copy paste replies"; answer with one personal, specific line. Email: "please don't send me a template"; write a short reply that mentions their exact order and problem.
when_not_to_use: Do not drop required wording such as legal or security statements; say them in a natural voice instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: Don't read me a script. Just tell me where my parcel is. | Agent: Fair enough. Let me tell you straight: your order is held at customs, and I'll chase it today. | Customer: Okay. When will I know more? | Agent: I'll text you by 6 pm with what customs say.
source_rule: Over-scripting backfires: use canned wording only when it fully fits, and personalise it.
fill_blank: Fair enough. Let me ____ you straight: your order is held at customs.
mcq_question: A customer says, "Don't read me a script." What is the best change to make?
mcq_options: A) Use plain, personal words and answer their actual question directly. | B) Read the same script more slowly and clearly so that they understand it. | C) Tell them politely that you are not reading a script and it is just the process. | D) Transfer the call to a supervisor who can speak without a script.
mcq_why: A gives the customer what they asked for: a real, direct answer. C sounds honest but argues and keeps the same style, B changes nothing, and D avoids the issue.
reorder_task: tell / Let / straight / me / you
reorder_answer: Let me tell you straight
hindi_to_english: Theek hai, main seedhi baat bataata/bataati hoon: aapka parcel customs mein ruka hua hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: Fair enough, let me tell you straight: your parcel is held at customs.
whats_next_customer: So when will it actually arrive?
whats_next_reply: I'll have a firm date once customs reply. I'm calling them today, and I'll text you by 6 pm with what they say.
role_play: Partner B answers with formal script phrases until Partner A says "Don't read me a script." Partner B then switches to plain, personal language and gives a direct answer about the parcel.
record_task: Record your reply to the customer's line in a natural, conversational voice, as if you were talking to a neighbour.
self_check: Did you avoid repeating any script phrase? · Did you answer the actual question? · Did you sound like yourself, not a recording?

sentence: Oh great, another hold.
speaker: Customer
situation: You have just asked the customer to hold for the third time in one call while you check with another team.
recall_cue: The customer says "great" but means the opposite. What are they telling you about the call so far, and what should you offer?
linking: great_another → "gray-tuh-NUH-ther" · another_hold → "uh-NUH-ther HOLD" (no link, keep the h clear)
intonation: Flat or falling, slow and heavy on "great", often with a sigh. That flat tone is what turns "great" into sarcasm; a real "Great!" rises and sounds bright.
indian_pron_tip: The sarcasm is in the tone, not the words: a low, flat "great" means the opposite. "Another" has a voiced /ð/ in the middle, uh-NUH-ther; if you repeat it, avoid "a-no-dar".
customer_emotion: Tired, annoyed and feeling their time is being wasted.
memory_hook: Imagine the word "great" said with an eye-roll: same letters, opposite meaning. Listen to the face, not the word.
hindi_meaning: वाह, बहुत बढ़िया, फिर से होल्ड। (व्यंग्य है; मतलब: मैं इंतज़ार करके तंग आ गया/गई हूँ।)
hindi_roman: Waah, bahut badhiya, phir se hold. (Vyangya hai; matlab: main intezaar karke tang aa gaya/gayi hoon.)
simple_meaning: The customer does not think it is great. They mean: "I am tired of being put on hold again and again."
why_it_works: Sarcasm hides real frustration about lost time. The customer needs you to notice it, apologise for the repeated waits, and either avoid the hold or offer a callback with a time.
key_chunk: Oh great, another ___.
grammar_pattern: Oh great + another + noun (sarcastic complaint)
grammar_note: "Another" means "one more"; with sarcasm it means "one more bad thing".
tone_note: It is sarcastic, not happy. Answering "Thank you, sir!" as if they agreed sounds as if you did not listen.
watch_out: ✗ Agent: Thank you so much, sir, please hold. → ✓ Agent: I know, that's the third time, and I'm sorry. Would a callback in 15 minutes be easier?
dont_say: "Great, thank you for holding!" — it takes the sarcasm literally and makes the customer feel unheard.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please hold the line again", say "I know you've waited a lot today. Would a callback in 15 minutes be easier?"
alt_1: I'm sorry, I know you've already held twice. Instead of another hold, can I call you back within 15 minutes?
alt_2: I'm sorry, you've waited long enough already. Let me message the team instead, so you don't need to hold again.
more_formal: I apologise for the repeated holds. Rather than ask you to wait again, may I call you back within 15 minutes with an update?
ask_next: I know, that's the third time, and I'm sorry. Would it be easier if I called you back within 15 minutes instead?
replies_you_may_hear: Yes, call me back. · No, I'll hold, just be quick. · Why does everything need a hold?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why does everything need a hold?" → Agent: "Fair question. The billing team has to approve this. A callback means you won't have to sit on hold."
cultural_note: Sarcasm is hard to catch on the phone, so learners may hear only the words and miss the tone. In British English especially, a flat "Oh great" or "Brilliant" usually means the opposite.
channel_note: Chat: often written as "oh great another wait" or with an eye-roll emoji; reply with an apology and a time. Email: rare; written sarcasm often appears as "Thanks for nothing".
when_not_to_use: If the customer says "Great!" in a bright, rising tone after good news, it is genuine; do not treat it as sarcasm.
mini_conversation: Customer: Oh great, another hold. | Agent: I know, that's the third time, and I'm sorry. Would it be easier if I called you back within 15 minutes instead? | Customer: Yes, please. | Agent: I'll call you on this number by 3:45 with an update from the billing team.
source_rule: Offer a callback instead of another long hold, and listen to the tone, not just the words, to notice frustration.
fill_blank: I know, that's the third time, and I'm ____. Would a callback in 15 minutes be easier?
mcq_question: After a third hold request, a customer says in a flat, tired voice: "Oh great, another hold." What do they mean?
mcq_options: A) They are fed up with waiting and would like a quicker solution this time. | B) They are pleased that you are checking carefully and are happy to wait again. | C) They are asking you to hold the call yourself while they find some information. | D) They are thanking you for finding a team that can answer the question.
mcq_why: A is right: the flat tone makes "great" sarcastic. B is tempting because "great" is a positive word, but here the tone reverses its meaning; C and D read the words too literally.
reorder_task: callback / easier / a / Would / in / minutes / 15 / be
reorder_answer: Would a callback in 15 minutes be easier
hindi_to_english: Main samajhta/samajhti hoon aap teesri baar wait kar rahe hain. Kya main aapko pandrah minute mein call back kar doon?
hindi_to_english_answer: I know this is the third time you've waited. Could I call you back in 15 minutes instead?
whats_next_customer: No, I'll hold. Just be quick.
whats_next_reply: Thank you. I'll be back within two minutes, with an answer or an update.
role_play: Partner A has already been asked to hold twice and replies "Oh great, another hold" in a flat voice. Partner B recognises the sarcasm, apologises and offers a callback with a time.
record_task: Record the customer line twice, once sarcastic and once genuinely happy, then record your reply to the sarcastic version.
self_check: Did you notice the flat, sarcastic tone? · Did you apologise for the repeated holds? · Did you offer a callback with a specific time?

sentence: I'll take my business elsewhere.
speaker: Customer
situation: A customer of six years is upset that their insurance premium rose without warning and says they will move to a competitor.
recall_cue: A loyal customer says they will move to a competitor. What are they really telling you, and what is your first move?
linking: take_my → "tay-kmy" (no gap between k and m) · my_business → "mai-BIZ-nis" · business_elsewhere → "biz-ni-sels-WAIR" (the s joins the e)
intonation: Usually calm, slow and final, falling on "elsewhere"; a quiet delivery can mean the decision is close. A loud one may be a bargaining move.
indian_pron_tip: "Business" has two syllables, BIZ-nis, with a z sound, not "bi-zi-ness" in three beats. Listen for "elsewhere": British speakers stress the second part, els-WHERE (American speakers often say ELS-wair).
customer_emotion: Disappointed, feeling unvalued after years of loyalty.
memory_hook: A customer with one foot out of the door: you don't block the door, you ask what made them stand up.
hindi_meaning: मैं किसी और कंपनी के पास चला/चली जाऊँगा/जाऊँगी। (मतलब: मुझे लगता है यहाँ मेरी कद्र नहीं है।)
hindi_roman: Main kisi aur company ke paas chala/chali jaaunga/jaaungi. (Matlab: mujhe lagta hai yahaan meri kadar nahin hai.)
simple_meaning: The customer means: "I will stop buying from you and use another company instead."
why_it_works: It often signals that a loyal customer feels taken for granted and may still stay if someone listens. They need you to acknowledge their loyalty, ask what went wrong, and offer something real, without pressure.
key_chunk: I'll take my ___ elsewhere.
grammar_pattern: I'll + take + my business + elsewhere (a decision made now)
grammar_note: "Business" here means "the money I spend with you", not a company the customer owns.
tone_note: It is a serious warning, not an insult. Replying "Okay, that's your choice" sounds as if the customer does not matter.
watch_out: ✗ Agent: Okay sir, it is your wish. → ✓ Agent: I'd be sorry to lose you after six years. Could you tell me what's changed?
dont_say: "Okay, that's your decision, sir." — it lets a loyal customer walk away without even asking why.
positive_swap: Instead of "If you want to go, you can go", say "I'd be sorry to lose you. Could you tell me what's made you feel this way?"
alt_1: You've been with us for six years, and I'd hate to lose you. Can you tell me what went wrong with the renewal?
alt_2: I understand, and I'd like to see if I can fix this first. What would make you want to stay?
more_formal: We greatly value your six years with us, and I would be sorry to lose you as a customer. Could you tell me what prompted this?
ask_next: I'd be sorry to lose you after six years. Could you tell me what's changed, so I can see what I can do?
replies_you_may_hear: My premium went up by 3,000 rupees with no warning. · Nothing you say will change my mind. · Another company has offered me a better price.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Nothing you say will change my mind." → Agent: "That's completely your choice, and I'll help either way. If you're happy for me to, I can check whether the increase was a mistake; it will take two minutes."
cultural_note: Some learners may hear "business" and think the customer owns a company. In this phrase it simply means "my custom", and it is a common way to threaten to switch providers.
channel_note: Chat: often "ill go to another company" or "switching provider"; acknowledge, then ask one question. Email: often the last line of a complaint; answer the complaint fully and mention their loyalty.
when_not_to_use: Do not keep trying to hold on to a customer who has clearly confirmed they want to leave; respect the decision and make leaving easy.
mini_conversation: Customer: My premium's gone up again. I'll take my business elsewhere. | Agent: I'd be sorry to lose you after six years. Could you tell me what's changed, so I can see what I can do? | Customer: It went up by 3,000 rupees without any warning. | Agent: I'm sorry you weren't told in advance. Let me review the renewal now and see if a better plan fits you.
source_rule: Listen, acknowledge, then act: one common version is LATTE (credited to Starbucks).
fill_blank: I'd be sorry to ____ you after six years. Could you tell me what's changed?
mcq_question: A long-time customer says, "I'll take my business elsewhere." What do they mean?
mcq_options: A) They are planning to open their own company somewhere else in the city. | B) They want to move their registered business address to another place. | C) They want to be transferred to the business team in another department. | D) They plan to stop using your company and buy from a competitor instead.
mcq_why: D is right: "take my business elsewhere" means spend money with another company. A and B are tempting because "business" often means a company, but here it means the customer's custom; C confuses it with a department.
reorder_task: what's / me / you / Could / changed / tell
reorder_answer: Could you tell me what's changed
hindi_to_english: Aap chhe saal se hamare saath hain, mujhe aapko khona achha nahin lagega. Kya aap bata sakte hain kya badla?
hindi_to_english_answer: You've been with us for six years, and I'd be sorry to lose you. Could you tell me what's changed?
whats_next_customer: Another company has offered me a cheaper price.
whats_next_reply: Thank you for telling me. Let me review your plan now; if I can match that cover for less, I'll tell you before you decide.
role_play: Partner A, a customer for six years, is angry about a surprise premium increase and says they will switch. Partner B acknowledges their loyalty, asks what changed, and offers one real option without pressure.
record_task: Record your reply to the customer's line in a sincere voice, then record what you would say if they answer "Nothing will change my mind."
self_check: Did you understand "business" as the customer's custom? · Did you mention their loyalty? · Did you ask a question before offering anything?

sentence: Hi, thanks for contacting [Company]. I'm Ananya. How can I help you today?
speaker: Agent
situation: A new chat window opens on the website and you send the first message to the customer.
recall_cue: A customer has just opened a chat with your company. What three things does your first message give them?
linking: If read aloud: thanks_for → "thanks-fer" · help_you → "hel-pyoo" · I'm_Ananya → "ai-ma-NAN-ya" (the "m" joins the next vowel)
intonation: If read aloud: a friendly lift on "Hi", a short pause after the company name, and a falling tone on "How can I help you today?" because it is a wh- question.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "thanks" starts with a soft "th" (tongue lightly between the teeth), not a hard "t" as in "tanks". Keep the final "s".
customer_emotion: Hopeful but unsure whether a real person is on the other side.
memory_hook: Think of a shop door bell: hello, the shop's name, your name tag and "how can I help?", all in one ring.
hindi_meaning: नमस्ते, [Company] से संपर्क करने के लिए धन्यवाद। मैं अनन्या हूँ। आज मैं आपकी कैसे मदद कर सकता/सकती हूँ?
hindi_roman: Namaste, [Company] se sampark karne ke liye dhanyavaad. Main Ananya hoon. Aaj main aapki kaise madad kar sakta/sakti hoon?
simple_meaning: Hello, thank you for writing to us. My name is Ananya. What do you need help with?
why_it_works: It tells the customer a real person has joined, gives a name they can use, and ends with an open question so they can explain the problem in their own words.
key_chunk: Hi, thanks for contacting ___. I'm ___.
grammar_pattern: Thanks + for + verb-ing · How + can + I + base verb + you …?
grammar_note: After "thanks for", use the -ing form: "thanks for contacting", not "thanks for contact".
tone_note: "Hi" and "thanks" sound human and friendly. "Dear Customer, state your query" sounds like a robot and makes the customer write back coldly.
watch_out: ✗ Hi, thanks for contact [Company]. How I can help you? → ✓ Hi, thanks for contacting [Company]. How can I help you today?
dont_say: "Hello Dear Customer, please state your query." — it is cold, sounds automated and gives no name.
positive_swap: Instead of "State your query", say "How can I help you today?"
alt_1: Hello and welcome to [Company]. My name's Ananya. What can I help you with?
alt_2: Hi there, you're chatting with Ananya from [Company]. How can I help?
more_formal: Good morning, and thank you for contacting [Company]. My name is Ananya. How may I help you today?
ask_next: Thanks, Sarah. Could you share your order number so I can take a look?
replies_you_may_hear: Hi, my parcel hasn't arrived. · I want to change my delivery address. · is this a bot?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Is this a bot?" → Agent: "No, I'm Ananya, a real person on the [Company] support team. How can I help you today?"
cultural_note: Many Indian agents introduce themselves with "Myself Ananya"; international customers may not expect this, so switch to "I'm Ananya" or "My name's Ananya" in chat.
channel_note: Voice: "Thank you for calling [Company]. This is Ananya." Email: "Hi Sarah, thanks for getting in touch," with your name in the sign-off.
when_not_to_use: Do not send the full greeting if a colleague has already greeted the customer and passed the chat to you; write "Hi Sarah, I'm Ananya from billing" instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: hello | Agent: Hi, thanks for contacting [Company]. I'm Ananya. How can I help you today? | Customer: my parcel is late | Agent: I'm sorry it's late. Could you share your order number so I can check?
source_rule: Chat: greet with your name, as you would on a call, and ask an open question.
fill_blank: Hi, thanks for ____ [Company]. I'm Ananya. How can I help you today? (Hint: the verb "contact")
mcq_question: Which first chat message sounds the most natural to an international customer?
mcq_options: A) Hello. What is your problem? Please tell me your order number first. | B) Dear Customer, welcome to [Company]. Please state your query so we can help. | C) Hi, thanks for contacting [Company]. I'm Ananya. How can I help you today? | D) HELLO!! WELCOME TO [Company]!! HOW CAN I HELP YOU TODAY?? 😊
mcq_why: C gives thanks, a name and an open question in plain English. A is blunt and asks for a number before offering help, B reads like a robot template, and D shouts in capitals.
reorder_task: help / today / can / How / you / I
reorder_answer: How can I help you today
hindi_to_english: Namaste, main Ananya hoon. Bataiye, aaj main aapki kya madad kar sakti hoon?
hindi_to_english_answer: Hi, I'm Ananya. How can I help you today?
whats_next_customer: hi, my refund hasn't come yet
whats_next_reply: I'm sorry your refund hasn't arrived yet. Could you share your order number so I can check it for you?
role_play: Partner A opens a chat about a late parcel. Partner B sends the greeting with their own name and an open question, then asks for the order number in the next message.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud the opening message you would send, with your own name, and then your reply when the customer writes "my parcel is late".
self_check: Did you say your own name with "I'm"? · Did you end with an open question? · Did you thank the customer for contacting you?

sentence: Could you type your order number here, please? It's in your confirmation email.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer says there is a problem with an order, and you need the number to find it.
recall_cue: You need to find the customer's purchase in the system. What do you ask for, and where do you tell them to look?
linking: If read aloud: could_you → "cud-joo" · it's_in → "it-sin" · confirmation_email → "con-fir-MAY-shu-nee-mail"
intonation: If read aloud: rise on "please?" because it is a yes/no request, then a falling, helpful tone on the second sentence.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: say "order" as OR-der with the tongue just behind the top teeth for "d", not curled back; "confirmation" is con-fir-MA-tion, with the stress on MA.
customer_emotion: Wants a quick answer and may feel slightly impatient at being asked for details.
memory_hook: The order number is the key to the locker; tell the customer which pocket the key is in: the confirmation email.
hindi_meaning: क्या आप अपना ऑर्डर नंबर यहाँ टाइप कर सकते हैं? यह आपके कन्फ़र्मेशन ईमेल में है।
hindi_roman: Kya aap apna order number yahan type kar sakte hain? Yeh aapke confirmation email mein hai.
simple_meaning: Please write your order number in the chat. You can find it in the email we sent when you ordered.
why_it_works: It asks politely and tells the customer exactly where to find the number, so they do not have to search or send another message asking where it is.
key_chunk: Could you type your ___ here, please?
grammar_pattern: Could + you + base verb + object + here, please? · It's + in + place
grammar_note: "Could you…?" makes a soft request; "It's in…" tells someone where something is.
tone_note: The question form and "please" make it a request. "Send order no." sounds like an order and uses shorthand, which looks careless in chat.
watch_out: ✗ Could you type here your order number, please? → ✓ Could you type your order number here, please?
dont_say: "Order ID?" — a two-word demand with no "please" feels cold and rushed in writing.
positive_swap: Instead of "You have to give the order number first", say "Could you type your order number here, please? It's in your confirmation email."
alt_1: Could you share your order number, please? You'll see it in your confirmation email.
alt_2: Could I have your order number, please? It starts with "ORD" and it's in the email we sent you.
more_formal: Could you please provide your order number so that I can locate your order? You will find it in your order confirmation email.
ask_next: Thank you. Let me look up order ORD-36571 now.
replies_you_may_hear: ORD-36571 · where do i find it? · i deleted the email
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "i deleted the email" → Agent: "That's fine. Could you give me the email address you ordered with instead? I can find the order that way."
cultural_note: "Please share me your order number" is common in Indian English; international customers may not expect "share me", so write "share your order number" or "send me your order number".
channel_note: Voice: "Could you read me your order number?" Email: "Could you reply with your order number? It's in your confirmation email."
when_not_to_use: Do not ask for it if the customer has already typed it earlier in the chat; scroll up and use it.
mini_conversation: Customer: my order hasn't come | Agent: I'm sorry about that. Could you type your order number here, please? It's in your confirmation email. | Customer: ORD-36571 | Agent: Thank you. Let me look that up now.
source_rule: Verification: ask only for what you need, and make it easy for the customer to find.
fill_blank: Could you type your order number here, please? It's in your confirmation ____. (Hint: starts with "e")
mcq_question: Which message asks for the order number in the clearest, most polite way?
mcq_options: A) You have to give me your order number first, then I can check your problem. | B) Order no. pls. It's in the confirmation email we sent you. | C) Could you type your order number here, please? It's in your confirmation email. | D) PLEASE TYPE YOUR ORDER NUMBER HERE. IT IS IN YOUR CONFIRMATION EMAIL.
mcq_why: C is polite and says where to look. A is an order ("You have to"), B uses shorthand ("no.", "pls"), and D is all capitals, which reads as shouting.
reorder_task: your / Could / here / type / number / you / order / please
reorder_answer: Could you type your order number here please
hindi_to_english: Kya aap apna order number yahan likh sakte hain? Woh aapke email mein milega.
hindi_to_english_answer: Could you type your order number here, please? You'll find it in your email.
whats_next_customer: where do i find it?
whats_next_reply: It's in the email we sent when you placed the order. It starts with "ORD".
role_play: Partner A says their parcel has not arrived but gives no details. Partner B asks politely for the order number, says where to find it, and helps when A says they deleted the email.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud the message you would send to ask for an order number, plus your reply when the customer cannot find it.
self_check: Did you use "Could you … please?" · Did you say where to find the number? · Did you avoid shorthand like "no." and "pls"?

sentence: Let me check that for you. One moment, please.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer has given their order number and you need a few seconds to look it up.
recall_cue: You are about to look something up, and the customer will see no reply for a short time. What do you send first?
linking: If read aloud: let_me → "let-mee" (very light "t") · check_that → "chek-that" (touch the "k", then "th") · for_you → "fer-yoo"
intonation: If read aloud: a falling, confident tone on "for you", a short pause, then a soft fall on "please".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "that" starts with a voiced "th" (tongue lightly between the teeth), not "dat". "Moment" is MO-ment, with a clear final "t".
customer_emotion: Waiting and watching the screen, wondering whether anyone is working on it.
memory_hook: A silent chat looks like an empty chair; this line puts a "back in a moment" sign on the chair.
hindi_meaning: मैं आपके लिए यह चेक करता/करती हूँ। कृपया एक पल रुकिए।
hindi_roman: Main aapke liye yeh check karta/karti hoon. Kripya ek pal rukiye.
simple_meaning: I'm going to look at this for you now. Please wait a few seconds.
why_it_works: In chat the customer cannot hear you typing, so silence looks like nobody is there. This tells them you are working on it and that the wait will be short.
key_chunk: Let me ___ that for you.
grammar_pattern: Let + me + base verb + that + for you
grammar_note: "Let me…" offers to do something now; it sounds softer than "I will…".
tone_note: "Let me" sounds helpful and active. "Wait" or "Hold" on its own sounds like an order and gives no reason.
watch_out: ✗ Let me to check that for you, wait one minute. → ✓ Let me check that for you. One moment, please.
dont_say: "Wait." — one word with no reason feels rude, and the customer does not know how long to wait.
positive_swap: Instead of "Wait, checking", say "Let me check that for you. One moment, please."
alt_1: I'll look into that for you now. It'll take just a moment.
alt_2: Thanks, Tom. Let me take a quick look at your order.
more_formal: Thank you. Please allow me a moment while I check your order details.
ask_next: Thanks for waiting. I can see your order, and it's out for delivery today.
replies_you_may_hear: ok · sure · how long will it take?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "how long will it take?" → Agent: "About a minute. I'll update you as soon as I have the details."
cultural_note: "I am checking the same" is common in Indian English; international customers may not expect "the same" used this way, so name the thing ("your order") or say "that".
channel_note: Voice: ask permission and give a real time: "Could you hold for about two minutes?" Email: not needed; say when you will reply instead.
when_not_to_use: Do not write "one moment" if the check will take more than a minute; give a real time instead, such as "about three minutes".
mini_conversation: Customer: my order number is ORD-50927 | Agent: Thanks, Tom. Let me check that for you. One moment, please. | Customer: ok | Agent: Thanks for waiting. Your order is out for delivery today.
source_rule: Chat: reply fast and never go silent; for a longer check, give a real time, not "a moment".
fill_blank: ____ me check that for you. One moment, please.
mcq_question: Your check will take a few minutes. Which message is best?
mcq_options: A) Let me check that for you. It'll only take a moment. | B) Let me check that for you. It'll take about three minutes. | C) Please wait. I'm checking your order now. Thank you. | D) Give me some time, please. I'll reply when I have it.
mcq_why: B gives a real time, which is right when the check will take a few minutes. A promises "a moment", which is misleading, and C and D give no time at all.
reorder_task: that / me / for / check / Let / you
reorder_answer: Let me check that for you
hindi_to_english: Ek minute, main aapka order check karti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: One moment, please. Let me check your order.
whats_next_customer: ok thanks, waiting
whats_next_reply: Thank you, Tom. I'm still checking the delivery details, and I'll have your answer in about a minute.
role_play: Partner A asks where their order is. Partner B sends the "let me check" message, waits 30 seconds, then thanks A for waiting and gives the update.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud the message you send before checking and the message you send when you come back with the answer.
self_check: Did you send a message before going quiet? · Did you give a real time if the check is long? · Did you thank the customer when you came back?

sentence: Thanks for waiting, James. Your parcel left our warehouse this morning.
speaker: Agent
situation: You told the customer you would check, and you are now back with the answer after a short wait.
recall_cue: You have just finished checking something while the customer waited. What do you write before you give the answer?
linking: If read aloud: thanks_for → "thanks-fer" · left_our → "lef-tower" · this_morning → "this-MOR-ning"
intonation: If read aloud: a warm fall on "James", a tiny pause, then a clear, falling statement for the news.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "warehouse" starts with a "w" (round the lips, no teeth on the lip) as in "west", not a "v" as in "vest".
customer_emotion: A little impatient after waiting and keen to hear the answer.
memory_hook: Like a waiter coming back to the table: say "thanks for waiting" before you put the plate down.
hindi_meaning: इंतज़ार करने के लिए धन्यवाद, जेम्स। आपका पार्सल आज सुबह हमारे गोदाम से निकल गया है।
hindi_roman: Intezaar karne ke liye dhanyavaad, James. Aapka parcel aaj subah hamare godaam se nikal gaya hai.
simple_meaning: Thank you for waiting. Your parcel was sent from our storage building this morning.
why_it_works: Thanking first shows you noticed their time; then the news comes straight away in one clear line, so the customer does not have to wait or ask again.
key_chunk: Thanks for waiting, ___. + the news
grammar_pattern: Thanks + for + verb-ing, name. · Subject + past simple + finished time
grammar_note: Use the past simple ("left") with a finished time like "this morning" or "yesterday".
tone_note: Thanking sounds respectful. Jumping straight to the news with no thanks feels a little cold, and answering only "Yes, I checked" leaves the customer still waiting.
watch_out: ✗ Thanks for waiting. Your parcel has left yesterday. → ✓ Thanks for waiting, James. Your parcel left our warehouse this morning.
dont_say: "Yes, I checked." — it makes the customer ask again for the actual answer.
positive_swap: Instead of "Sorry for delay, I was busy", say "Thanks for waiting, James. Your parcel left our warehouse this morning."
alt_1: Thanks for bearing with me, James. Your parcel was sent this morning.
alt_2: Thanks for waiting! Good news: your order is on its way.
more_formal: Thank you for waiting, Mr Brown. Your parcel was dispatched from our warehouse this morning.
ask_next: Would you like me to send you the tracking link, so you can follow it?
replies_you_may_hear: great, when will it arrive? · ok thanks · why so late?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "why so late?" → Agent: "I'm sorry it's taken longer than you expected. It's on its way now and should reach you by Thursday."
cultural_note: Indian-English scripts often say "Kindly bear with us" or "Thanks for being on hold" in chat; international customers may not expect these there, so switch to "Thanks for waiting" or "Thanks for bearing with me".
channel_note: Voice: "Thank you for holding, James." Email: "Thanks for waiting while we looked into this," at the start of the reply.
when_not_to_use: Do not use a thank-you alone after a very long wait; add an apology, such as "Thanks for waiting, and I'm sorry that took so long."
mini_conversation: Customer: where is my parcel? | Agent: Let me check that for you. One moment, please. | Customer: ok | Agent: Thanks for waiting, James. Your parcel left our warehouse this morning.
source_rule: Thank the customer first when you return, then give the information.
fill_blank: ____ for waiting, James. Your parcel left our warehouse this morning.
mcq_question: You come back to the chat after checking. What should your first words be?
mcq_options: A) Thanks for waiting, James. Here's what I found. | B) Yes, I checked it. Do you need anything else? | C) Sorry, I was busy with another chat just now. | D) Your parcel left our warehouse this morning.
mcq_why: A thanks the customer first and then moves to the news. D gives the news but skips the thank-you, which feels cold. B gives no answer, and C makes the wait about you instead of the customer.
reorder_task: warehouse / Your / this / left / parcel / morning / our
reorder_answer: Your parcel left our warehouse this morning
hindi_to_english: Intezaar ke liye shukriya. Aapka order kal bhej diya gaya tha.
hindi_to_english_answer: Thanks for waiting. Your order was sent yesterday.
whats_next_customer: great, when will it arrive?
whats_next_reply: It should reach you by Thursday. I'll send you the tracking link now.
role_play: Partner A asks about a parcel. Partner B says they will check, waits 20 seconds, then thanks A for waiting and gives the update with a delivery day.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your "thanks for waiting" message with the update, then your reply when the customer asks "why so late?".
self_check: Did you thank the customer before the news? · Did you give the actual answer in the same message? · Did you use the past simple with "this morning"?

sentence: I'm sorry your order arrived damaged. I'll send you a replacement today.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer writes that her new lamp arrived broken, and your system shows a free replacement can go out today with no need to return the broken one.
recall_cue: The customer's item came broken. What two things does a good short apology in chat contain?
linking: If read aloud: order_arrived → "or-de-ra-rived" · arrived_damaged → "a-rive-DAM-ijd" (the two "d" sounds join into one) · send_you → "sen-joo"
intonation: If read aloud: a sincere, slightly slower fall on "damaged"; a firm, confident fall on "today".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: say the final sounds in "arrived" ("-vd") and "damaged" ("-jd") clearly; do not drop them to "arrive damage".
customer_emotion: Disappointed and annoyed that they paid for something broken.
memory_hook: Sorry is the bandage and the replacement is the medicine: one without the other heals nothing.
hindi_meaning: मुझे खेद है कि आपका ऑर्डर टूटा हुआ पहुँचा। मैं आज ही आपको नया सामान भेज दूँगा/दूँगी।
hindi_roman: Mujhe khed hai ki aapka order toota hua pahuncha. Main aaj hi aapko naya saamaan bhej doonga/doongi.
simple_meaning: I apologise that your item came broken. I will send you a new one today.
why_it_works: It names the exact problem, so the customer knows you read their message, and the second line offers a fix with a time, which matters more to them than the apology words.
key_chunk: I'm sorry your ___. I'll ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm sorry + (that) + clause · I'll + base verb + time
grammar_note: After "I'm sorry" you can add a full sentence: "I'm sorry your order arrived damaged."
tone_note: A specific apology sounds sincere. A vague "Sorry for the inconvenience" sounds copied and pasted, and with an upset customer it can feel cold.
watch_out: ✗ I'm sorry for your order arrived damaged. → ✓ I'm sorry your order arrived damaged. I'll send you a replacement today.
dont_say: "These things happen during delivery." — it sounds like an excuse and does not say what you will do.
positive_swap: Instead of "Sorry for the inconvenience caused", say "I'm sorry your order arrived damaged. I'll send you a replacement today."
alt_1: I'm really sorry it reached you broken. I'll arrange a new one for you right away.
alt_2: Sorry about the damaged item, Grace. I'm sending a replacement today.
more_formal: I apologise that your order arrived damaged. I will arrange for a replacement to be dispatched today.
ask_next: Could you send a photo of the damage? It helps our warehouse team stop this happening again.
replies_you_may_hear: thank you · do i need to send it back? · i need it by friday
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "this is the second time!" → Agent: "I'm sorry it has happened twice. I'll send the replacement today and add a note asking for extra packing."
cultural_note: "Sorry for the inconvenience caused" is very common in Indian support scripts; international customers often read it as a template, so name the actual problem instead.
channel_note: Voice: the same words, said slowly and sincerely. Email: add the case number and the expected delivery date of the replacement.
when_not_to_use: Do not promise "today" if the replacement cannot go out today; give the real day instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: my lamp came broken | Agent: I'm sorry your order arrived damaged. I'll send you a replacement today. | Customer: ok, when will it get here? | Agent: It should arrive by Saturday. I'll email you the tracking link today.
source_rule: Apologise specifically, take responsibility and offer a fix; no emoji with a complaint.
fill_blank: I'm ____ your order arrived damaged. I'll send you a replacement today.
mcq_question: Which apology works best in chat for a broken item?
mcq_options: A) Sorry for the inconvenience. We hope to see you again soon. | B) I'm sorry your order arrived damaged. I'll send you a replacement today. | C) I'm so sorry your order arrived damaged 😔 Please let me know how I can help. | D) Parcels sometimes get damaged in delivery, but I'll look into it for you.
mcq_why: B names the problem and gives a fix with a time. A is a vague template, C uses an emoji with a complaint and offers no fix, and D sounds like an excuse.
reorder_task: replacement / send / I'll / today / a / you
reorder_answer: I'll send you a replacement today
hindi_to_english: Mujhe afsos hai ki aapka order toota hua aaya. Main aaj hi naya bhej deti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry your order arrived broken. I'll send you a new one today.
whats_next_customer: do i need to send the broken one back?
whats_next_reply: No, you don't need to send it back. You can keep it or recycle it.
role_play: Partner A writes that their new headphones arrived with a cracked case. Partner B apologises for that exact problem, offers a replacement with a time, and answers A's question about returning the broken pair.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your short apology message and the next message, where you ask for a photo of the damage.
self_check: Did you name the exact problem? · Did you offer a fix with a time? · Did you avoid a vague "sorry for the inconvenience" and emoji?

sentence: Could you send me a screenshot of the error message? It'll help me see exactly what's happening.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer says the app shows an error when they try to pay, but they cannot describe it clearly.
recall_cue: The customer says "it shows some error" but cannot describe it. What do you ask them to send, and how do you explain why?
linking: If read aloud: send_me → "sen-mee" · of_the_error → "uv-thee-ER-ror" · what's_happening → "wots-HAP-ning"
intonation: If read aloud: rise on "message?" because it is a yes/no request; fall on "happening".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "message" is MES-ij, two syllables with a soft "-ij" ending, not "mes-SAGE" with the stress at the end.
customer_emotion: Frustrated and a little confused by a technical problem.
memory_hook: A screenshot is the patient's X-ray: the doctor sees in one look what ten lines of words cannot describe.
hindi_meaning: क्या आप मुझे एरर मैसेज का स्क्रीनशॉट भेज सकते हैं? इससे मैं ठीक-ठीक देख पाऊँगा/पाऊँगी कि क्या हो रहा है।
hindi_roman: Kya aap mujhe error message ka screenshot bhej sakte hain? Isse main theek-theek dekh paoonga/paoongi ki kya ho raha hai.
simple_meaning: Please take a picture of your screen showing the error and send it to me, so I can understand the problem.
why_it_works: It asks politely and gives the reason, so the customer sees the extra step helps them and is not just more work.
key_chunk: Could you send me a ___ of ___? It'll help me ___.
grammar_pattern: Could + you + send + me + a + noun · It'll + help + me + base verb
grammar_note: After "help me", use the base verb: "help me see", not "help me seeing".
tone_note: Giving a reason makes it a shared task. "Send screenshot" on its own sounds like a demand and can suggest you do not believe the customer.
watch_out: ✗ Could you send me screenshot of error message? → ✓ Could you send me a screenshot of the error message?
dont_say: "I can't help without a screenshot." — it puts the blame on the customer and sounds like a refusal.
positive_swap: Instead of "I can't help without a screenshot", say "Could you send me a screenshot of the error message? It'll help me see exactly what's happening."
alt_1: Could you take a screenshot of what you see on the screen and send it here?
alt_2: If you can, please send a screenshot of the error. That way I can find the cause faster.
more_formal: Would you be able to send a screenshot of the error message? It will help me identify the problem more quickly.
ask_next: Thank you, that helps. I can see the card was declined, so let's try another payment method.
replies_you_may_hear: how do i take a screenshot? · sent · it says payment failed
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "i already told you what it says, why a screenshot?" → Agent: "Thank you, and I'm sorry for the extra step. The screenshot shows me the exact wording, so I don't have to guess. It only takes a few seconds."
cultural_note: "Kindly share the screenshot of the same" is common in Indian English; international customers may not expect "of the same", so name the thing: "a screenshot of the error".
channel_note: Voice: ask the caller to read the error message aloud, or offer to email them so they can reply with the screenshot. Email: "Could you reply with a screenshot of the error message?"
when_not_to_use: Do not ask for a screenshot of a screen that shows a full card number or password; ask the customer to describe it or cover those parts.
mini_conversation: Customer: payment not working, some error | Agent: Could you send me a screenshot of the error message? It'll help me see exactly what's happening. | Customer: sent | Agent: Thank you. I can see the card was declined, so let's try another card.
source_rule: Chat: ask with "Could you…?", give the reason for the extra step, and keep the message short.
fill_blank: Could you send me a ____ of the error message? It'll help me see exactly what's happening. (Hint: one word for a picture of your screen)
mcq_question: Why does the agent add "It'll help me see exactly what's happening"?
mcq_options: A) To make the message longer and sound more formal. | B) To give a reason, so the customer sees why the extra step helps. | C) To suggest that the customer caused the error themselves. | D) To promise the customer that the error will be fixed today.
mcq_why: B is right: a reason turns a demand into teamwork. C is the tempting wrong idea, because the line blames no one; A adds nothing for the customer, and D promises something the line never says.
reorder_task: screenshot / you / me / send / a / Could
reorder_answer: Could you send me a screenshot
hindi_to_english: Kya aap error ka screenshot bhej sakte hain? Isse mujhe problem samajhne mein madad milegi.
hindi_to_english_answer: Could you send me a screenshot of the error? It'll help me understand the problem.
whats_next_customer: how do i take a screenshot?
whats_next_reply: On most phones, press the power and volume-down buttons together. If that doesn't work, tell me which phone you have, and I'll walk you through it. Then send the picture here.
role_play: Partner A says the app shows "some error" when they log in. Partner B asks for a screenshot with a reason, explains how to take one, and responds once A describes what the error says.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your screenshot request and the message explaining how to take a screenshot on a phone.
self_check: Did you say why you need the screenshot? · Did you name exactly what to send (the error message)? · Did your request start with "Could you"?

sentence: You can reset your password here: [Company].com/reset. Just open it and enter your email address.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer cannot log in, and you send them the password reset page.
recall_cue: You are sending the customer a page where they can fix a login problem. What do you add so they know what to do on it?
linking: If read aloud: reset_your → "ree-set-cher" · open_it → "oh-pe-nit" · and_enter → "an-den-ter"
intonation: If read aloud: steady and falling; pause briefly before and after the link, so each part is clear.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: in "password" the "w" is a rounded-lip sound, PASS-wurd, not "pass-vord" with teeth on the lip.
customer_emotion: Locked out and slightly stressed about getting back into the account.
memory_hook: A link without an instruction is a door with no handle; give one handle: "open it and enter your email".
hindi_meaning: आप यहाँ अपना पासवर्ड रीसेट कर सकते हैं: [Company].com/reset। बस इसे खोलिए और अपना ईमेल पता डालिए।
hindi_roman: Aap yahan apna password reset kar sakte hain: [Company].com/reset. Bas ise kholiye aur apna email address daaliye.
simple_meaning: Here is the page to make a new password. Open it and type your email address.
why_it_works: One link with one action is easy to follow on a phone. The customer knows exactly what to do next and does not need to come back and ask.
key_chunk: You can ___ here: ___. Just ___.
grammar_pattern: You + can + base verb + here · Just + imperative + and + imperative
grammar_note: "Just" before a verb makes an instruction sound easy and friendly, not bossy.
tone_note: "You can… here" sounds like help on offer. "You have to go through the link and do the process" sounds like a rule and does not say what the process is.
watch_out: ✗ You can reset your password in this link. Just open and fill your email. → ✓ You can reset your password here: [Company].com/reset. Just open it and enter your email address.
dont_say: "Go through the link." — it gives no instruction, so the customer opens the page and does not know what to do.
positive_swap: Instead of "You have to go through the below link", say "You can reset your password here: [Company].com/reset. Just open it and enter your email address."
alt_1: Here's the reset page: [Company].com/reset. Enter your email address there, and we'll email you a link to choose a new password.
alt_2: This link lets you set a new password: [Company].com/reset. Tap it and type your email address.
more_formal: You can reset your password using this link: [Company].com/reset. Please open it and enter the email address linked to your account.
ask_next: Let me know once you've done that, and I'll check that you can log in.
replies_you_may_hear: done · the link isn't opening · i didn't get any email
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "the link isn't opening" → Agent: "I'm sorry the link isn't opening. Could you copy it into your browser? If it still doesn't open, I'll send the reset email to you directly."
cultural_note: "Go through the below link and do the needful" is common in Indian business English; international customers may not expect it and find it vague, so say the one action they should take.
channel_note: Voice: the caller cannot click anything on a call, so offer to send the link by SMS or email. Email: number the steps if there is more than one.
when_not_to_use: Do not send a link alone when the task has several steps; split it into short, numbered messages instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: i forgot my password | Agent: You can reset your password here: [Company].com/reset. Just open it and enter your email address. | Customer: done, got the email | Agent: Great. Open that email and choose a new password, and you'll be able to log in.
source_rule: Chat: short messages, one clear step at a time; number multi-step instructions.
fill_blank: You can reset your password here: [Company].com/reset. Just open it and ____ your email address. (Hint: starts with "e")
mcq_question: What makes a good chat message when you share a link?
mcq_options: A) The link on its own, so the message is as short as possible. | B) The link plus one clear action the customer should take. | C) The link plus a long explanation of how the system works. | D) The link plus five steps in one long paragraph of text.
mcq_why: B is right: one link with one clear action is easy to follow on a phone. A is tempting because it is short, but the customer may not know what to do; C and D bury the action in too much text.
reorder_task: email / your / open / enter / Just / address / and / it
reorder_answer: Just open it and enter your email address
hindi_to_english: Bas is link ko kholiye aur apna email address daaliye.
hindi_to_english_answer: Just open this link and enter your email address.
whats_next_customer: i didn't get any email
whats_next_reply: Could you check your spam folder? If it isn't there, I'll send it again now.
role_play: Partner A cannot log in. Partner B sends the reset link with one clear instruction, then helps when A says the email has not arrived.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud the link message you would send and your next message when the customer says no email arrived.
self_check: Did you give exactly one clear action with the link? · Did you say what the link is for ("reset your password")? · Is the message short enough to read on a phone?

sentence: Just to confirm, you'd like to change the delivery address to 14 Park Road, Pune?
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer asked to change where their parcel goes, and you check the new address before you update it.
recall_cue: Before you change an important detail, how do you check in one short message that you have understood it correctly?
linking: If read aloud: just_to → "jus-tuh" · you'd_like → "yood-like" · change_the → "chainj-the"
intonation: If read aloud: a rising tone at the end, because it is a yes/no check, even though the words look like a statement.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "fourteen" is four-TEEN, with the stress at the end; "forty" is FOR-ty. Mixing them up changes the address.
customer_emotion: Wants the change done quickly and correctly, and is a little anxious about mistakes.
memory_hook: Measure twice, cut once: read the address back before you press save.
hindi_meaning: बस पक्का करने के लिए, आप डिलीवरी का पता बदलकर 14 पार्क रोड, पुणे करना चाहते हैं?
hindi_roman: Bas pakka karne ke liye, aap delivery ka pata badalkar 14 Park Road, Pune karna chahte hain?
simple_meaning: I want to check: is the new delivery address 14 Park Road, Pune?
why_it_works: Repeating the exact detail lets the customer catch a mistake before it costs them a lost parcel, and it shows you read their message carefully.
key_chunk: Just to confirm, you'd like to ___?
grammar_pattern: Just to confirm, + you'd like + to + base verb …?
grammar_note: A statement with a question mark asks "Is this right?"; "you'd like" is a polite form of "you want".
tone_note: "Just to confirm" sounds careful, not doubtful. "Are you sure?" can sound as if you think the customer is wrong.
watch_out: ✗ Just to confirm, you want that I change the address? → ✓ Just to confirm, you'd like to change the delivery address to 14 Park Road, Pune?
dont_say: "Are you sure about the address?" — it sounds as if you doubt the customer instead of checking your own understanding.
positive_swap: Instead of "Are you sure it's correct?", say "Just to confirm, you'd like to change the delivery address to 14 Park Road, Pune?"
alt_1: Can I check: the new address is 14 Park Road, Pune. Is that right?
alt_2: So the parcel should now go to 14 Park Road, Pune. Have I got that right?
more_formal: Could you confirm that you would like the delivery address changed to 14 Park Road, Pune?
ask_next: Thanks. Should I add a flat number or landmark to help the courier find it?
replies_you_may_hear: yes thats right · no, it's 41 not 14 · yes, and add flat 2B
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "yes, I already said that!" → Agent: "Sorry to double-check, Imran. I just wanted to be sure your parcel goes to the right place. It's updated now."
cultural_note: "You want that I change…" copies the Hindi "chahte hain ki…" pattern; international customers may not expect it, so write "you'd like me to change…" or "you'd like to change…".
channel_note: Voice: say numbers slowly, digit by digit: "one-four Park Road". Email: put the new address on its own line so it is easy to check.
when_not_to_use: Do not confirm every small detail in a short chat; save it for things that are costly to get wrong, such as addresses, amounts and dates.
mini_conversation: Customer: can you send it to 14 Park Road, Pune instead | Agent: Just to confirm, you'd like to change the delivery address to 14 Park Road, Pune? | Customer: yes | Agent: Thanks. I've updated it, and you'll get a confirmation email shortly.
source_rule: Paraphrase before acting: repeat the key detail so the customer can correct you.
fill_blank: Just to confirm, you'd like to change the delivery ____ to 14 Park Road, Pune?
mcq_question: The customer writes "please send it to 14 Park Road, Pune instead". What is the best next message?
mcq_options: A) Done! I've changed your delivery address to 14 Park Road, Pune. | B) Are you sure that is the right address? 14 Park Road, Pune? | C) Just to confirm, you'd like the parcel sent to 14 Park Road, Pune? | D) Could you type the whole address again from the beginning, please?
mcq_why: C repeats the detail so the customer can catch an error. B is tempting as a check, but it sounds as if you doubt them. A changes the address without checking, and D makes the customer do the work again.
reorder_task: confirm / like / Just / you'd / to / change / to / the / address
reorder_answer: Just to confirm you'd like to change the address
hindi_to_english: Bas confirm karne ke liye, aap payment ki date badalkar 5 March karna chahte hain?
hindi_to_english_answer: Just to confirm, you'd like to change the payment date to 5 March?
whats_next_customer: no, it's 41 not 14
whats_next_reply: Thanks for catching that. So it's 41 Park Road, Pune. Is that right?
role_play: Partner A asks to change the delivery address and types it with one digit unclear. Partner B confirms the detail, A corrects it, and B confirms the corrected address before updating it.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your confirm message with a full address, using a rising tone at the end.
self_check: Did you repeat the exact detail? · Did you use "you'd like to" instead of "you want that"? · Did you wait for a yes before changing it?

sentence: Are you still there, Sarah? I'm here whenever you're ready.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer has not replied for a few minutes after you asked them a question.
recall_cue: The customer has gone quiet for several minutes. What friendly message do you send before you think about closing the chat?
linking: If read aloud: are_you → "ar-yoo" · still_there → "stil-there" · whenever_you're → "wen-ev-er-yor"
intonation: If read aloud: rise on "there?" because it is a yes/no question, then a soft, warm fall on "ready".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "there" starts with a voiced "th" (tongue between the teeth), not "dare"; "whenever" begins with a rounded-lip "w", not a "v".
customer_emotion: Probably busy or distracted, perhaps looking for a document, and not annoyed.
memory_hook: A gentle knock on the door, not a bang: "Still there? I'm here when you're ready."
hindi_meaning: सारा, क्या आप अभी भी चैट पर हैं? जब भी आप तैयार हों, मैं यहीं हूँ।
hindi_roman: Sarah, kya aap abhi bhi chat par hain? Jab bhi aap taiyaar hon, main yahin hoon.
simple_meaning: Are you still in the chat? Take your time; I'm waiting for you.
why_it_works: It checks politely without pressure and tells the customer they have not lost their place, so they can come back without starting again.
key_chunk: Are you still there, ___? I'm here whenever ___.
grammar_pattern: Are + you + still + there? · whenever + you're + adjective
grammar_note: "Still" means "continuing from before"; "whenever" means "at any time that".
tone_note: The second sentence removes pressure. "Hello?? Are you there??" with many question marks sounds impatient.
watch_out: ✗ Hello? Are you there or not? → ✓ Are you still there, Sarah? I'm here whenever you're ready.
dont_say: "If you don't reply, I will close the chat." as the first check-in — it sounds like a threat; warn only after a friendly check-in.
positive_swap: Instead of "No response from your side", say "Are you still there, Sarah? I'm here whenever you're ready."
alt_1: Just checking in, Sarah. Take your time; I'm still here.
alt_2: Hi Sarah, are you still with me? There's no rush.
more_formal: I just wanted to check whether you are still there. I'm happy to wait while you find the details.
ask_next: I haven't heard back, so I'll close this chat in two minutes. If you still need help, just reply here and I'll keep it open.
replies_you_may_hear: sorry, here · yes, looking for the receipt · 2 min
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "stop rushing me" → Agent: "Sorry, Sarah, I didn't mean to rush you. Take all the time you need; I'll wait."
cultural_note: "No response from your side" is common in Indian support scripts; international customers may read it as blame, so a friendly question works better.
channel_note: Voice: "Hello, are you still there?" after a few seconds of silence. Email: not used; send a follow-up email later instead.
when_not_to_use: Do not send it seconds after your own message; give the customer a real gap first, as they may be typing or looking something up.
mini_conversation: Customer: one sec, finding my receipt | Agent: (four minutes later) Are you still there, Sarah? I'm here whenever you're ready. | Customer: sorry, here it is: ORD-55102 | Agent: Thanks, Sarah. Let me check that now.
source_rule: Ending a chat: if the customer goes silent, check in, then warn, then close politely.
fill_blank: Are you ____ there, Sarah? I'm here whenever you're ready.
mcq_question: A customer has not replied for four minutes. What is the best first step?
mcq_options: A) Close the chat now, because the customer has probably left. | B) Send a friendly check-in and say you are still there. | C) Send "Hello?? Are you there??" so the customer sees it quickly. | D) Write "If you don't reply, the chat will close" straight away.
mcq_why: B follows best practice: check in first, then warn, then close. D is tempting, but it skips the friendly check-in and sounds like a threat; A closes too early and C sounds impatient.
reorder_task: ready / here / you're / I'm / whenever
reorder_answer: I'm here whenever you're ready
hindi_to_english: Kya aap abhi bhi chat par hain? Koi jaldi nahin hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: Are you still there? There's no rush.
whats_next_customer: sorry, my phone rang. here now
whats_next_reply: No worries, Sarah. Could you send me the order number when you have it?
role_play: Partner B asks for an order number, and Partner A goes silent. B sends a friendly check-in, then a polite warning, and A comes back just before the chat closes.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your check-in message, then the polite warning you would send two minutes later if there is still no reply.
self_check: Did you check in before warning? · Did you remove pressure with "whenever you're ready"? · Did you avoid capitals and extra question marks?

sentence: You're welcome, Sarah. Thanks for chatting with us, and have a great evening!
speaker: Agent
situation: The issue is solved, and the customer has written "thanks, bye".
recall_cue: The customer thanks you and says goodbye after the problem is fixed. How do you return the goodbye in one message?
linking: If read aloud: thanks_for → "thanks-fer" · with_us → "wi-thus" · have_a → "ha-vuh"
intonation: If read aloud: a warm fall on "Sarah", then a bright, slightly higher pitch on "great evening" before the final fall.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "with" ends in a soft "th", not a "t" ("wit"); "evening" is EEV-ning, two syllables, not "ee-ve-ning".
customer_emotion: Relieved and satisfied, and ready to leave the chat.
memory_hook: The customer waved goodbye; wave back with three fingers: "you're welcome", "thanks", "have a great evening".
hindi_meaning: धन्यवाद की कोई बात नहीं, सारा। हमसे चैट करने के लिए धन्यवाद, आपकी शाम अच्छी हो!
hindi_roman: Dhanyavaad ki koi baat nahin, Sarah. Humse chat karne ke liye dhanyavaad, aapki shaam acchi ho!
simple_meaning: No need to thank me. Thank you for talking to us. Enjoy your evening!
why_it_works: It answers the customer's thanks, thanks them back and says goodbye, so the chat ends warmly instead of stopping suddenly.
key_chunk: You're welcome, ___. Thanks for ___, and have a great ___!
grammar_pattern: You're welcome · Thanks + for + verb-ing · Have + a + adjective + noun
grammar_note: "Have a great evening" is a wish, not an order, even though it starts with a verb.
tone_note: "You're welcome" is the safe, polite reply to thanks. Saying nothing and closing the window feels cold after a good chat.
watch_out: ✗ You welcome, Sarah. Thanks for chat with us. → ✓ You're welcome, Sarah. Thanks for chatting with us.
dont_say: "Chat is being closed." — it is a system message, not a goodbye, and ends a good chat coldly.
positive_swap: Instead of "Closing the chat now", say "You're welcome, Sarah. Thanks for chatting with us, and have a great evening!"
alt_1: My pleasure, Sarah! Thanks for getting in touch, and have a lovely evening.
alt_2: Glad I could help! Take care, Sarah.
more_formal: You're very welcome. Thank you for contacting [Company], and have a pleasant evening.
ask_next: If anything else comes up, just message us again any time. Take care, Sarah!
replies_you_may_hear: bye · thanks again · you too
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "actually, one more thing" → Agent: "Of course, Sarah. What else can I help with?"
cultural_note: Many Indian English speakers reply to "thank you" with "Welcome"; international customers may not expect this and usually hear "You're welcome" or "My pleasure".
channel_note: Voice: "You're welcome, Mr Lee. Have a great evening." Email: end with "Best regards" and your name.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it while the issue is still open; first tell the customer the next step and when they will hear from you.
mini_conversation: Customer: that worked, thanks! bye | Agent: You're welcome, Sarah. Thanks for chatting with us, and have a great evening! | Customer: you too | Agent: Thank you, Sarah. Take care!
source_rule: Ending a chat: return the customer's goodbye; "You're welcome" is the safe default reply to thanks.
fill_blank: You're ____, Sarah. Thanks for chatting with us, and have a great evening!
mcq_question: The customer writes "thanks so much, bye!" Which reply is the most natural for an international customer?
mcq_options: A) This chat is now closed. Please rate your experience with us in the survey. | B) YOU'RE WELCOME!! THANKS FOR CHATTING WITH US. HAVE A GREAT EVENING!! | C) No problem, Sarah! Is there anything else I can help you with before I close the chat? | D) You're welcome, Sarah. Thanks for chatting with us, and have a great evening!
mcq_why: D returns the thanks and the goodbye. A sounds like a system message, B shouts in capitals, and C asks a new question when the customer is already leaving.
reorder_task: chatting / us / Thanks / with / for

sentence: I'm glad that's sorted. Is there anything else I can help you with today?
speaker: Agent
situation: You have fixed the customer's problem, and they have confirmed that it works.
recall_cue: The customer confirms the fix worked. What do you say about the fix, and what do you ask before you close?
linking: If read aloud: that's_sorted → "that-SORT-ed" (the two "s" sounds join) · anything_else → "en-ee-thing-els" (the "ng" flows into "else", with no hard g) · help_you → "hel-pyoo"
intonation: If read aloud: a warm fall on "sorted"; a rise on "today?" because it is a yes/no question.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "anything" ends in "-thing" with the tongue between the teeth, not "any-ting"; "else" ends in a clear "s", not "el-se".
customer_emotion: Pleased the problem is fixed and perhaps ready to leave.
memory_hook: Close the first door ("glad that's sorted") before you open the next one ("anything else?").
hindi_meaning: मुझे खुशी है कि यह ठीक हो गया। क्या आज मैं आपकी किसी और चीज़ में मदद कर सकता/सकती हूँ?
hindi_roman: Mujhe khushi hai ki yeh theek ho gaya. Kya aaj main aapki kisi aur cheez mein madad kar sakta/sakti hoon?
simple_meaning: Good, the problem is fixed. Do you need help with something else?
why_it_works: It first confirms the problem is solved, then gives the customer a clear chance to raise another issue before the chat ends.
key_chunk: Is there anything else I can help you with ___?
grammar_pattern: Is + there + anything + else + (that) + I + can + base verb …?
grammar_note: Use "anything" in questions ("anything else?") and "something" in offers ("something to drink?").
tone_note: Asking after the fix sounds caring. Asking it before the problem is solved sounds as if you want to end the chat.
watch_out: ✗ Is there anything else I can help you today? → ✓ Is there anything else I can help you with today?
dont_say: "Anything else?" while the problem is still open — it suggests the issue is finished when it is not.
positive_swap: Instead of "Any other query?", say "I'm glad that's sorted. Is there anything else I can help you with today?"
alt_1: Great, that's working now. Can I help with anything else?
alt_2: Happy to hear that's fixed! Is there anything else you need today?
more_formal: I'm pleased the issue is resolved. Is there anything else I can assist you with today?
ask_next: If it stops working again, Kiran, just message us here and we'll pick it up.
replies_you_may_hear: no that's all, thanks · yes, one more thing · nope
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "yes, actually, my last bill looks wrong too" → Agent: "Of course. Could you tell me which amount looks wrong? I'll check it now."
cultural_note: "Any other query?" is common in Indian support chats; international customers may find "query" formal and a little cold, so ask "anything else I can help you with?".
channel_note: Voice: the same line, said warmly and not rushed. Email: "If there's anything else I can help with, just reply to this email."
when_not_to_use: Do not ask it on an unresolved case; tell the customer the next step and when they will hear back instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: it's working now | Agent: I'm glad that's sorted. Is there anything else I can help you with today? | Customer: no that's all, thanks | Agent: You're welcome, Kiran. Have a great day!
source_rule: Check the issue is resolved first, then ask "Is there anything else…?"; never ask it on an unresolved case.
fill_blank: I'm glad that's sorted. Is there anything else I can help you ____ today?

mcq_why: The question assumes the issue is finished, so ask it only after the customer confirms. B is tempting, but it makes the customer feel rushed.

sentence: I'm transferring you to our billing team now, because they can change your plan. I'll share our chat with them, so you won't need to repeat anything.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer wants to change their plan, which only the billing team can do.
recall_cue: Another team must handle this request. What three things do you tell the customer before you pass the chat on?
linking: If read aloud: transferring_you → "trans-fer-ing-yoo" · share_our → "shair-rour" · need_to → "nee-tuh"
intonation: If read aloud: steady and reassuring; fall on "plan" and on "anything", with a short pause between the two sentences.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: the verb "transfer" is trans-FER, with the stress at the end (the noun is TRANS-fer). Say "won't" with a long "oh" (like "own" + t), so it is not heard as "want".
customer_emotion: Worried about being passed around and having to explain everything again.
memory_hook: Hand over the baton with the notes taped to it: the next runner already knows the race.
hindi_meaning: मैं अभी आपको हमारी बिलिंग टीम के पास ट्रांसफ़र कर रहा/रही हूँ, क्योंकि वे आपका प्लान बदल सकते हैं। मैं हमारी चैट उनके साथ शेयर करूँगा/करूँगी, ताकि आपको कुछ दोहराना न पड़े।
hindi_roman: Main abhi aapko hamari billing team ke paas transfer kar raha/rahi hoon, kyunki woh aapka plan badal sakte hain. Main hamari chat unke saath share karoonga/karoongi, taaki aapko kuch dohraana na pade.
simple_meaning: Another team will take over because they can make this change. They will see what we wrote, so you don't need to explain again.
why_it_works: It says who, why and what happens to the information, so the customer does not feel dropped and will not have to type the problem again.
key_chunk: I'm transferring you to ___, because ___. I'll share ___, so you won't need to ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm + verb-ing + now · so + you + won't + need to + base verb
grammar_note: "So" here gives the result: because I share the chat, you won't need to repeat anything.
tone_note: Giving the reason makes the transfer feel like help. "Transferring" on its own feels as if the agent is getting rid of the customer.
watch_out: ✗ I'm transferring you to the billing team because they can to change your plan. → ✓ I'm transferring you to our billing team now, because they can change your plan.
dont_say: "That's not my department." — it sounds as if you do not care, and it gives no next step.
positive_swap: Instead of "I can't do plan changes", say "I'm transferring you to our billing team now, because they can change your plan."
alt_1: Our billing team can make that change for you, so I'll connect you with them now. They'll see our chat, so there's no need to explain again.
alt_2: I'll pass you to a colleague in billing who can update your plan. I've added a note with all the details.
more_formal: I will now transfer you to our billing team, who can change your plan. I have shared our conversation with them, so you will not need to repeat any details.
ask_next: Is that all right with you? I'll stay in the chat until they join.
replies_you_may_hear: ok · how long will it take? · can't you just do it?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "can't you just do it?" → Agent: "I'd like to, but plan changes are handled by billing. I'll stay here until they join, so you're not left waiting alone."
cultural_note: "Concerned team" and "concerned department" are common in Indian English; international customers may not expect them and want the team's real name ("our billing team").
channel_note: Voice: ask permission and brief your colleague before connecting (a warm transfer). Email: "I've passed your request to our billing team, and they will reply by tomorrow."
when_not_to_use: Do not transfer if you can solve the problem yourself; every transfer costs the customer time.
mini_conversation: Customer: I want to change to the cheaper plan | Agent: I'm transferring you to our billing team now, because they can change your plan. I'll share our chat with them, so you won't need to repeat anything. | Customer: ok thanks | Agent: You're welcome. Ravi from billing will join you in about a minute.
source_rule: Transfer warm: say who and why, and pass on the details so the customer does not repeat themselves.
fill_blank: I'll share our chat with them, so you won't need to ____ anything. (Hint: starts with "r")
mcq_question: The customer needs the billing team. Which transfer message is best?
mcq_options: A) I can't change plans, sorry. I'm transferring you to another team now, so please wait a moment. | B) That's not my department, sorry. Please contact our billing team yourself through the website. | C) I'm transferring you to our billing team, because they can change your plan. I'll share our chat with them. | D) Billing handles plans, not me. I'm passing you to them now, but you may need to explain it all again.
mcq_why: C names the team, gives the reason and saves the customer from repeating the story. A does not say which team or why, B sends the customer away, and D admits the customer will have to explain everything again.
reorder_task: repeat / won't / anything / You / need / to
reorder_answer: You won't need to repeat anything
