sentence: Could you tell me a bit more about what happened? For example, when did you first notice the problem?
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer wrote only "app not working", and you need more information before you can help.
recall_cue: The customer's first message is very short and vague. How do you ask for more information and make it easy to answer?
linking: If read aloud: tell_me → "tel-mee" · what_happened → "wot-HAP-nd" (keep the "h") · first_notice → "firs-NO-tis" (the "t" of "first" is very light)
intonation: If read aloud: rise on "happened?" (a yes/no request); fall on "problem?" (a wh- question).
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "happened" ends in "-nd" and has two syllables, HAP-pnd, not "hap-pen-ed". Say the "st" in "first" clearly; do not drop the "t".
customer_emotion: Frustrated, and maybe not sure how to describe the problem.
memory_hook: Give the customer a handle to hold: "For example, when…?" is easier to answer than an empty "please explain".
hindi_meaning: क्या आप मुझे थोड़ा और बता सकते हैं कि क्या हुआ? जैसे, आपने यह समस्या पहली बार कब देखी?
hindi_roman: Kya aap mujhe thoda aur bata sakte hain ki kya hua? Jaise, aapne yeh problem pehli baar kab dekhi?
simple_meaning: Please explain a little more. When did the problem start?
why_it_works: An open request plus one example question helps customers who do not know which details matter, so you get useful facts in one reply.
key_chunk: Could you tell me a bit more about ___? For example, ___?
grammar_pattern: Could + you + tell + me + about + what + happened? · When + did + you + first + base verb …?
grammar_note: Inside a request, keep normal word order: "tell me what happened", not "tell me what did happen".
tone_note: "A bit more" sounds gentle. "Your message is not clear" blames the customer for the problem.
watch_out: ✗ Could you tell me a bit more about what did happen? → ✓ Could you tell me a bit more about what happened?
dont_say: "Your message is not clear." — it blames the customer instead of helping them explain.
positive_swap: Instead of "I don't understand your problem", say "Could you tell me a bit more about what happened? For example, when did you first notice the problem?"
alt_1: I'm sorry the app isn't working. What happens when you open it?
alt_2: Could you describe what you see on the screen? For example, is there an error message?
more_formal: Could you please give me a few more details about the issue, such as when it started?
ask_next: Thanks, that helps. Have you tried closing the app and opening it again?
replies_you_may_hear: since yesterday · it just shows a white screen · after the update
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "i already told you it's not working!" → Agent: "I know that's frustrating, and I want to fix it quickly. Knowing when it started helps me find the cause faster."
cultural_note: "Please elaborate your issue" is common in Indian business English; international customers may find it formal and cold, so ask one simple, specific question.
channel_note: Voice: ask one question at a time and wait for the answer. Email: list two or three short, numbered questions.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask for more details if the customer has already explained clearly; repeat back what you understood and act instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: app not working | Agent: I'm sorry the app isn't working. Could you tell me a bit more about what happened? For example, when did you first notice the problem? | Customer: since the update yesterday | Agent: Thanks, that helps. Let me check what changed in that update.
source_rule: If you are unsure, ask a clarifying question first instead of guessing or sending a canned reply.
fill_blank: Could you tell me a bit more about what ____? For example, when did you first notice the problem? (Hint: the past tense of "happen")
mcq_question: Which follow-up question is easiest for a customer to answer?
mcq_options: A) Can you explain the whole problem again in more detail? | B) What exactly is wrong with your app? Please be specific. | C) When did you first notice the problem? Was it today or earlier? | D) Why did you only write three words? Please write more.
mcq_why: C asks one specific question the customer can answer quickly. A and B ask for everything at once, and D blames the customer for writing a short message.
reorder_task: happened / about / tell / a / Could / what / bit / more / me / you
reorder_answer: Could you tell me a bit more about what happened
hindi_to_english: Kya aap thoda aur bata sakte hain? Yeh kab se ho raha hai?
hindi_to_english_answer: Could you tell me a bit more? When did this start?
whats_next_customer: it just shows a white screen
whats_next_reply: Thanks, that helps. Does the white screen appear straight away, or after you log in?
role_play: Partner A writes only "card not working". Partner B asks for more detail with one example question and keeps asking short questions until they know when and where the card fails.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your request for more details and your next message after the customer answers.
self_check: Did you give an example question? · Did you avoid blaming the customer? · Did you write "what happened", not "what did happen"?

sentence: Thank you for your patience today, Fatima. Your new card will arrive by Friday.
speaker: Agent
situation: The chat took a long time because of several checks; you can now see the new card has been posted with delivery booked for Friday, and you are closing the chat.
recall_cue: The chat was long and the customer waited a lot. What do you thank them for at the end, and what do you remind them of?
linking: If read aloud: thank_you → "thang-kyoo" · for_your → "fer-yor" · card_will → "car-dwil"
intonation: If read aloud: a warm fall on "Fatima"; a clear, falling statement for the next step, with stress on "Friday".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "patience" is PAY-shuns, two syllables, the same sound as "patients"; do not say "pa-ti-ence".
customer_emotion: Tired after a long chat but relieved the problem is handled.
memory_hook: Patience is a gift the customer gave you: say thank you for the gift, then tell them when their card arrives.
hindi_meaning: आज धैर्य रखने के लिए धन्यवाद, फ़ातिमा। आपका नया कार्ड शुक्रवार तक पहुँच जाएगा।
hindi_roman: Aaj dhairya rakhne ke liye dhanyavaad, Fatima. Aapka naya card Shukravaar tak pahunch jayega.
simple_meaning: Thanks for waiting so long today. You will get your new card on or before Friday.
why_it_works: It recognises the effort the customer made and ends with a clear next step and date, so they leave knowing exactly what will happen.
key_chunk: Thank you for your patience, ___. + next step with a date
grammar_pattern: Thank you + for + your + noun · Subject + will + base verb + by + day
grammar_note: "By Friday" means "on or before Friday"; "till Friday" means "continuing up to Friday".
tone_note: Thanking for patience sounds respectful. "Sorry for wasting your time" sounds negative and puts the focus back on the problem.
watch_out: ✗ Your new card will reach till Friday. → ✓ Your new card will arrive by Friday.
dont_say: "Thanks for your patience." with no next step — it sounds like a script, and the customer still does not know what happens now.
positive_swap: Instead of "Sorry for wasting your time", say "Thank you for your patience today, Fatima. Your new card will arrive by Friday."
alt_1: Thanks so much for bearing with me, Fatima. Your new card is on its way and should arrive by Friday.
alt_2: I really appreciate your patience today. Your replacement card will be with you by Friday.
more_formal: Thank you for your patience throughout this chat, Ms Khan. Your new card will be delivered by Friday.
ask_next: Is there anything else I can help you with today?
replies_you_may_hear: thanks for your help · great, thanks · what if it doesn't come?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "this took over an hour, why so long?" → Agent: "I'm sorry the chat took so long. Several checks were needed on your account, and I wanted to get it right. Your card will arrive by Friday."
cultural_note: "Will reach till Friday" mixes up "till" and "by"; international customers expect "by Friday" for a deadline.
channel_note: Voice: "Thank you for your patience, Fatima," said slowly and warmly. Email: "Thank you for your patience while we sorted this out."
when_not_to_use: Do not use it after a very short wait, because it can sound scripted; write "Thanks for waiting" instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: so is it done now? | Agent: Yes. Thank you for your patience today, Fatima. Your new card will arrive by Friday. | Customer: great, thanks for your help | Agent: You're welcome. Have a lovely evening!
source_rule: Close by summarising the next step with a clear time.
fill_blank: Thank you for your ____ today, Fatima. Your new card will arrive by Friday. (Hint: the noun for waiting calmly)
mcq_question: The new card will come on Thursday or Friday. Which sentence is correct?
mcq_options: A) It will arrive till Friday. | B) It will arrive until Friday. | C) It will arrive up to Friday. | D) It will arrive by Friday.
mcq_why: D is right: "by Friday" means on or before Friday. "Till" and "until" mean an action continues up to that time, so they do not fit "arrive", and "up to Friday" is not used for a deadline.
reorder_task: patience / you / your / Thank / for
reorder_answer: Thank you for your patience
hindi_to_english: Aapke dhairya ke liye shukriya. Aapka refund Somvaar tak aa jayega.
hindi_to_english_answer: Thank you for your patience. Your refund will arrive by Monday.

self_check: Did you thank the customer for their patience? · Did you give a clear next step with a day? · Did you write "by Friday", not "till Friday"?

sentence: hi good morning
speaker: Customer
situation: A customer opens the chat with only a greeting and does not mention a problem yet.
recall_cue: A customer sends only a greeting and nothing else. What do they want, and how fast should you reply?
linking: If read aloud: good_morning → "gud-MOR-ning" · hi_good → "high-gud"
intonation: If read aloud: friendly and slightly rising; the customer is opening the door, not complaining.
indian_pron_tip: If you read your reply aloud, "morning" ends in a clean "ng"; do not add a hard "g" after it ("mor-ning-guh").
customer_emotion: Unsure whether a real person is there, and waiting to see if anyone answers.
memory_hook: "Hi" is a knock on the door: open it fast, smile, and ask how you can help.
hindi_meaning: हाय, आपको सुप्रभात।
hindi_roman: Hi, aapko suprabhaat.
simple_meaning: The customer is saying hello and checking that someone is there before explaining the problem.
why_it_works: Many customers send a greeting first to see whether a person will answer. A quick, warm reply with your name and an open question invites them to explain the problem.
key_chunk: hi + a greeting, with no problem yet
grammar_pattern: Greeting only: hi + time-of-day greeting
grammar_note: Customers often skip capitals and commas in chat; this is normal and not rude.
tone_note: The customer is being polite. A slow reply or a long script can turn a polite start into a frustrated one.
watch_out: ✗ Good morning! I am Kabir, how can I help to you today? → ✓ Good morning! I'm Kabir from [Company]. How can I help you today?
dont_say: "Please state your issue." — it is cold and robotic after a friendly greeting.
positive_swap: Instead of "State your query", say "Good morning! I'm Kabir. How can I help you today?"
alt_1: hello good afternoon
alt_2: hi, hello sir
more_formal: Good morning, I hope you can help me.
ask_next: Good morning! I'm Kabir from [Company]. How can I help you today?
replies_you_may_hear: my order is late · i need to change my address · i have a question about my bill
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "hello?? anyone?" → Agent: "Yes, I'm here! Sorry for the wait. I'm Kabir. How can I help you today?"
cultural_note: Agents in India often reply "Good morning, sir" or "madam" to every customer; international customers may not expect this, so use "Good morning!" and the customer's name if you have it, then move to the problem quickly.
channel_note: Voice: the caller usually says hello after your greeting. Email: customers rarely send a greeting alone, so this is mostly a chat habit.
when_not_to_use: Do not reply with only "hi" back; that wastes a turn. Add your name and an open question.
mini_conversation: Customer: hi good morning | Agent: Good morning! I'm Kabir from [Company]. How can I help you today? | Customer: my parcel hasn't come | Agent: I'm sorry your parcel hasn't arrived. Could you share your order number so I can check?
source_rule: Chat: reply fast, greet with your name, and ask an open question.
fill_blank: Good ____! I'm Kabir from [Company]. How can I help you today? (Hint: return the customer's greeting)

mcq_options: A) Good morning! I'm Kabir from [Company]. How can I help you today? | B) Good morning. Please type your order number so I can start. | C) Hello. What is your problem? Please write it clearly in one message. | D) Wait until the customer types the problem, then answer with a greeting.
mcq_why: A replies quickly with a name and an open question. D is tempting, but the customer may be waiting to see whether anyone is there; B asks for details before knowing the problem, and C sounds blunt.

sentence: need help with my order
speaker: Customer
situation: The customer's first real message names their order but not the problem.
recall_cue: The customer names their order but not what is wrong. What two things do you need from them?
linking: If read aloud: need_help → "nee-dhelp" · with_my → "wi-my"
intonation: If read aloud: flat and falling; it may hide worry or frustration, so read the next messages carefully.
indian_pron_tip: If you read your reply aloud, say "order" as OR-der: put the tongue just behind the top teeth for the "d" (not curled back) and end with a soft "uh", not a full "ar".
customer_emotion: Possibly worried or irritated, and wants to get to the point quickly.
memory_hook: The customer handed you a closed box labelled "order"; your open question is the key that opens it.
hindi_meaning: मुझे अपने ऑर्डर के बारे में मदद चाहिए।
hindi_roman: Mujhe apne order ke baare mein madad chahiye.
simple_meaning: I have a problem or a question about something I bought.
why_it_works: The customer has named the topic, not the problem. It could be tracking, a change, a return or a complaint, so ask for the order number and one open question before you guess.
key_chunk: need help with ___
grammar_pattern: (I) + need + help + with + my + noun

whats_next_reply: Thanks, Ananya. I'm checking the courier update now, and I'll tell you where it is within two minutes.
role_play: Partner A opens a chat as "Ananya" with an order number and a one-line complaint. Partner B types an opening that uses her name, their own name, the order number and a next step.
record_task: Record yourself reading your typed opening aloud, then say in one sentence why you used the customer's name and order number.
self_check: Did you use the customer's first name once? · Did you give your own name? · Did you mention her issue and a next step?

sentence: Here's how to reset your password: 1. Tap Log in. 2. Tap Forgot password. 3. Type your email address. Let me know when you reach step 3.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer in the mobile app cannot log in and needs to reset the password by following a few taps.
recall_cue: The customer needs to follow three short steps in the app. How do you lay out the instructions so nothing gets missed?
stress: HERE'S how to re-SET your PASS-word · TAP log-IN · TAP for-GOT PASS-word · TYPE your E-mail ad-DRESS · let me KNOW when you REACH step THREE
linking: If read aloud: log_in → "lo-gin" · email_address → "ee-may-la-DRESS" · let_me → "let-mee" (very light "t")
intonation: If read aloud: pause briefly after each number, fall on every step, and lift slightly on "let me know" to invite a reply.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: say the "w" in "password" with rounded lips ("PASS-wurd"), not with teeth on the lower lip ("PASS-vurd"). Practise the pair "west / vest".
customer_emotion: Frustrated at being locked out and worried about doing it wrong.
memory_hook: Think of a recipe card: numbered steps, one action each, and the cook tells you when the dish reaches the oven.
hindi_meaning: पासवर्ड रीसेट करने का तरीका यह है: 1. Log in पर टैप करें। 2. Forgot password पर टैप करें। 3. अपना ईमेल पता टाइप करें। जब आप स्टेप 3 पर पहुँच जाएँ, तो मुझे बता दीजिए।
hindi_roman: Password reset karne ka tareeka yeh hai: 1. Log in par tap karein. 2. Forgot password par tap karein. 3. Apna email pata type karein. Jab aap step 3 par pahunch jaayein, to mujhe bata deejiye.
simple_meaning: Do these three things in order, one at a time, and send me a message when you get to the third one.
why_it_works: Numbered steps with one action each are easy to follow on a small screen and cut down follow-up questions. Asking the customer to report back keeps you in step with them.
key_chunk: Here's how to ___: 1. ___ 2. ___ 3. ___ Let me know when you reach step ___.
grammar_pattern: Here's how + to + base verb · Imperative (Tap + noun) · Let me know when + you + present simple
grammar_note: Each step starts with a command verb like "Tap"; in instructions this is polite and clear, not rude.
tone_note: Short commands are normal in instructions. A long paragraph with "you need to first go to the login screen and then…" feels heavy and is easy to misread.
watch_out: ✗ You have to go login then forgot password then type email. → ✓ 1. Tap Log in. 2. Tap Forgot password. 3. Type your email address.
dont_say: "Just follow the steps on the website." It sends the customer away with no help and feels dismissive.
positive_swap: Instead of "You have to go to the login page, click forgot password and type your email", say "Here's how to reset your password: 1. Tap Log in. 2. Tap Forgot password. 3. Type your email address."
alt_1: Let's reset it together. 1. Open the login screen. 2. Choose Forgot password. 3. Type your email address. Tell me what you see.
alt_2: Three quick steps: 1. Login screen. 2. Forgot password. 3. Your email address. Let me know once you're there.
more_formal: To reset your password, please follow these steps: 1. Open the login screen. 2. Select Forgot password. 3. Enter your email address.
ask_next: Can you see the "Send reset link" button under the email box?
replies_you_may_hear: Done, I'm on step 3. · I can't see Forgot password. · Should I do this on the app or the website?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I don't have time for all this." → Agent: "I know you're in a hurry. It takes about a minute, and I'll stay with you at each step."
cultural_note: Indian agents often write the whole process as one long sentence joined by "then". International customers expect numbered, one-action steps they can scan quickly.
channel_note: Voice: give one step, wait for "done", then the next. Email: number the steps on separate lines and add a screenshot if possible.
when_not_to_use: Do not send a numbered list before you know which device or app version the customer uses; ask first.
mini_conversation: Customer: I can't log in to the app. | Agent: Here's how to reset your password: 1. Tap Log in. 2. Tap Forgot password. 3. Type your email address. Let me know when you reach step 3. | Customer: Okay, I'm there. | Agent: Great. Now tap "Send reset link". The email usually arrives within a minute.
source_rule: Number multi-step instructions, one action per step, to cut follow-up questions.
fill_blank: Here's ____ to reset your password: 1. Tap Log in. 2. Tap Forgot password. 3. Type your email address.
mcq_question: Which chat message gives password-reset instructions in the clearest way?
mcq_options: A) First go to the login screen, then tap Forgot password, then type your email. | B) Please see the help page on our website, which explains how to reset it. | C) Here's how: 1. Tap Log in. 2. Tap Forgot password. 3. Type your email address. | D) 1. Open the app, go to the login screen, tap Forgot password and type your email.
mcq_why: C gives one action per numbered step, so the customer can follow it and report back. D is numbered, but it packs four actions into one step, A is one long line, and B sends the customer away without help.
reorder_task: know / me / step / when / Let / reach / you / 3
reorder_answer: Let me know when you reach step 3
hindi_to_english: Order cancel karne ka tareeka: 1. My Orders kholiye. 2. Order chuniye. 3. Cancel par tap kijiye.
hindi_to_english_answer: Here's how to cancel your order: 1. Open My Orders. 2. Choose the order. 3. Tap Cancel.
whats_next_customer: I can't find Forgot password anywhere.
whats_next_reply: Don't worry, it's easy to miss. It's a small link just under the password box. Could you scroll down a little?
role_play: Partner A is locked out of an app and types short, confused replies. Partner B gives three numbered steps and checks progress after each one until A reaches the reset screen.
record_task: Record yourself reading your numbered instructions aloud with a clear pause after each step number.
self_check: Did each step have only one action? · Did you number the steps? · Did you ask the customer to report back?

sentence: I've processed your refund of ₹1,499 today. It should reach your original payment method within 5 to 7 working days.
speaker: Agent
situation: You have just processed a refund for a returned item, and the customer wants to know when the money will come back.
recall_cue: The refund is done on your side. What three facts does the customer need from you before the chat ends?
stress: i've PRO-cessed your RE-fund of one-THOU-sand four-HUN-dred and NINE-ty-NINE ru-PEES to-DAY · it should REACH your o-RI-gi-nal PAY-ment METH-od · with-IN FIVE to SEV-en WORK-ing DAYS
linking: If read aloud: refund_of → "REE-fun-duv" · hundred_and → "hun-dred-n" · reach_your → "ree-chyer"
intonation: If read aloud: fall firmly on "today", pause, then say the number range slowly with a fall on "days".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "processed" ends in "st" ("PRO-sest"), not "PRO-ses-sed". Stress RE-fund as a noun, and keep the "v" in "I've" with top teeth on the lower lip.
customer_emotion: Anxious about whether and when the money will come back.
memory_hook: Think of a courier receipt: what was sent, where it is going and when it will arrive. A refund message needs all three.
hindi_meaning: मैंने आज आपका ₹1,499 का रिफ़ंड प्रोसेस कर दिया है। यह 5 से 7 कामकाजी दिनों में आपके मूल पेमेंट तरीके में आ जाना चाहिए।
hindi_roman: Maine aaj aapka ₹1,499 ka refund process kar diya hai. Yeh 5 se 7 kaamkaaji dinon mein aapke original payment method mein aa jaana chahiye.
simple_meaning: I have sent your money back today. You should see it on the card or account you paid with in about one week.
why_it_works: It says the action is done, the exact amount, where the money goes and a time range. A clear timeline stops the customer chasing you every day.
key_chunk: I've processed your ___ today. It should reach ___ within ___.
grammar_pattern: I've + past participle (done now) · It should + base verb + within + time
grammar_note: "I've processed" shows the action is finished; "should reach" is a careful prediction, not a guarantee.
tone_note: Specific facts sound trustworthy. "Your refund will come soon" sounds vague and makes the customer wonder if anything happened.
watch_out: ✗ It should reach to your original payment method within 5 to 7 working days. → ✓ It should reach your original payment method within 5 to 7 working days.
dont_say: "Refund will reflect soon." It gives no amount, no date and no place to look.
positive_swap: Instead of "It will take time, nothing can be done", say "It should reach your original payment method within 5 to 7 working days."
alt_1: Your refund of ₹1,499 is on its way. Please allow 5 to 7 working days for it to appear in your account.
alt_2: Good news: I've sent back ₹1,499 today. You should see it on the card or account you paid with within 5 to 7 working days.
more_formal: I can confirm that a refund of ₹1,499 was issued today. It should appear in your account within 5 to 7 working days, depending on your bank.
ask_next: You'll also get a confirmation email in the next few minutes. Is there anything else I can help with?
replies_you_may_hear: Why does it take so long? · Can it go to my wallet instead? · OK, thanks.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why 7 days? You took my money in seconds." → Agent: "I can see why that feels unfair. We sent the refund today, and from here the timing depends on your bank."
cultural_note: Indian support teams often say a refund is "raised" or "initiated". That is clear inside India; international customers more often expect "processed" or "issued", plus a date range.
channel_note: Voice: say the amount and days slowly and offer to repeat. Email: put the amount and timeline on their own line and mention the confirmation email.
when_not_to_use: Do not say "I've processed" if the refund still needs approval from another team; say it has been requested and when they will decide.
mini_conversation: Customer: I returned the shoes. When do I get my money? | Agent: I've processed your refund of ₹1,499 today. It should reach your original payment method within 5 to 7 working days. | Customer: Will I get any message? | Agent: Yes, you'll get a confirmation email within a few minutes.
source_rule: Replace vague promises with a clear timeline and the next step.
fill_blank: I've processed your refund of ₹1,499 today. It should reach your original payment method within 5 to 7 working ____.
mcq_question: Which message sets the clearest expectation for a refund?
mcq_options: A) Your refund of ₹1,499 is being processed. Please wait for it to appear. | B) I've processed your ₹1,499 refund today. It should arrive within 5 to 7 working days. | C) We will try to refund your ₹1,499 quickly, so please keep checking your account. | D) Your refund is being handled and will show in your account soon, so please wait.
mcq_why: B is the only option that says the refund is done and gives a time range. A and D say "being processed" or "soon", which tells the customer nothing about when, and C only says you will try.
reorder_task: refund / processed / today / I've / your
reorder_answer: I've processed your refund today
hindi_to_english: Maine aaj aapka refund process kar diya hai. Yeh paisa 5 se 7 working days mein aapke account mein aa jaana chahiye.
hindi_to_english_answer: I've processed your refund today. It should reach your account within 5 to 7 working days.
whats_next_customer: What if I don't see it after 7 days?
whats_next_reply: If it hasn't arrived by then, message us with your order number, and we'll check it with our payments team straight away.
role_play: Partner A returned a ₹1,499 item and asks when the money will come. Partner B confirms the refund in one message with the amount, where it goes and the time range, then handles one follow-up question.
record_task: Record yourself reading the refund message aloud, saying the amount and the number range slowly and clearly.
self_check: Did you give the exact amount? · Did you say where the money will go? · Did you give a time range?

sentence: Your payment didn't go through because the one-time password expired before it was entered. That's why the order wasn't placed.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer tried to pay, got an error and now wants to know why the order is missing from their account.
recall_cue: You have found the real cause of a failed payment. How do you explain it in two short sentences without blaming the customer?
stress: your PAY-ment DID-n't go THROUGH · be-CAUSE the one-time PASS-word ex-PIRED · THAT'S why the OR-der WAS-n't PLACED
linking: If read aloud: didn't_go → "did-n-go" · before_it_was → "bi-for-it-wuz" · that's_why → "thats-why"
intonation: If read aloud: fall on "through", slight pause before "because", then fall again on "placed" to close the explanation.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "through" starts with "th" (tongue lightly between the teeth), not "t"; "thru" versus "true" is the pair to practise.
customer_emotion: Confused and suspicious that money may have gone missing.
memory_hook: Think of a door with a timer lock: the code was right, but the door closed before it was typed. Explain the timer, not the person.
hindi_meaning: आपका पेमेंट नहीं हुआ क्योंकि OTP डालने से पहले ही उसकी समय-सीमा खत्म हो गई थी। इसी वजह से ऑर्डर प्लेस नहीं हुआ।
hindi_roman: Aapka payment nahin hua kyunki OTP daalne se pehle hi uski samay-seema khatm ho gayi thi. Isi wajah se order place nahin hua.
simple_meaning: The code from the bank stopped working before it was typed in, so the payment failed and there is no order.
why_it_works: It gives the real reason in plain words and links it to what the customer saw. Saying "the password expired" describes the system, not the customer's mistake, so nobody feels blamed.
key_chunk: Your ___ didn't go through because ___. That's why ___.
grammar_pattern: Result + because + past simple/passive · That's why + past simple
grammar_note: "because" gives the reason; "that's why" links the reason to what the customer noticed.
tone_note: Neutral, factual wording keeps it calm. "You didn't enter the OTP in time" points a finger and sounds like a telling-off.
watch_out: ✗ Payment is failed due to OTP is expired. → ✓ Your payment didn't go through because the one-time password expired.
dont_say: "It's a technical issue from your side." It is vague and sounds like blame.
positive_swap: Instead of "You entered the OTP late", say "The one-time password expired before it was entered."
alt_1: The payment failed because the bank's code timed out before it was entered, so no order was created.
alt_2: The one-time password expired before it was typed in, which stopped the payment. That's why you can't see the order.
more_formal: The payment was not completed because the one-time password expired before it was entered. As a result, the order was not placed.
ask_next: Would you like to try again now? I'll stay in the chat while you pay.
replies_you_may_hear: But was money taken from my account? · Oh, I see. · The code came really late.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "The OTP came late, it's not my fault!" → Agent: "I'm sorry, that's frustrating. If the code arrives late, the timer can run out before you can type it. Let's try again, and if it's slow, tap Resend."
cultural_note: "Due to" plus a full clause ("due to OTP is expired") is a common learner habit. International customers expect "because" + clause, or "due to" + a noun ("due to an expired code").
channel_note: Voice: say "one-time password" in full once before using "OTP". Email: add one line on what to do next.
when_not_to_use: Do not give a cause you have not checked; if you are not sure yet, say what you are checking instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: I paid but there's no order! | Agent: Your payment didn't go through because the one-time password expired before it was entered. That's why the order wasn't placed. | Customer: Was money taken? | Agent: I can see no completed payment on our side. If your bank shows a hold, it's normally released automatically.
source_rule: Use plain language: explain the reason simply, without jargon or blame.
fill_blank: Your payment didn't go through because the one-time password expired before it was entered. That's ____ the order wasn't placed.
mcq_question: Which message gives the real reason for a failed payment in correct English, without blaming the customer?
mcq_options: A) The payment failed because you did not enter the one-time password in time. | B) There was a technical problem with the payment, so please try again later. | C) Your payment failed because the one-time password expired before it was entered. | D) Payment is failed due to OTP is expired, so the order is not placed.
mcq_why: C gives the real cause in correct English and describes the system, not the person. A points at the customer, B gives no real reason, and D has the grammar error "due to OTP is expired".
reorder_task: placed / That's / order / why / wasn't / the
reorder_answer: That's why the order wasn't placed
hindi_to_english: Aapka payment isliye fail hua kyunki card ki expiry date nikal chuki hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: Your payment didn't go through because the card has expired.
whats_next_customer: Was any money taken from my account?
whats_next_reply: I can't see a completed payment on our side. If your bank shows a temporary hold, it should be released automatically. If it's still there after 5 working days, message us and we'll check it.
role_play: Partner A says "I paid but there's no order" and is getting worried. Partner B explains the expired-code cause in two sentences, without blame, and offers to stay while A pays again.
record_task: Record yourself reading the explanation aloud, with a clear "th" in "through" and a short pause before "because".
self_check: Did you give the real cause? · Did you avoid blaming the customer? · Did you link the cause to what they saw?

sentence: I've passed this to our billing team. They'll email you by 6 pm tomorrow, so you don't need to stay in this chat.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer's billing question needs the billing team, who you cannot reach during this chat; you have checked that they reply to such cases by 6 pm the next day.
recall_cue: Another team will answer later, not you. What three things does the customer need to hear before they leave the chat?
stress: i've PASSED this to our BILL-ing TEAM · they'll E-mail you by SIX pee-EM to-MOR-row · you DON'T need to STAY
linking: If read aloud: passed_this → "pas-this" · they'll_email → "thay-lee-mail" · don't_need → "dohn-need"
intonation: If read aloud: fall on "team", say "by 6 pm tomorrow" slowly as the key fact, then a gentle fall on "chat".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "passed" sounds like "past", one syllable, not "pas-sed"; and "they'll" starts with a soft "th" (tongue touching the teeth), not a "d".
customer_emotion: Worried they will be forgotten once the chat closes.
memory_hook: Think of a token at a bakery counter: who has your order, when it will be ready, and that you are free to walk away meanwhile.
hindi_meaning: मैंने यह हमारी बिलिंग टीम को भेज दिया है। वे कल शाम 6 बजे तक आपको ईमेल करेंगे, इसलिए आपको इस चैट में रुकने की ज़रूरत नहीं है।
hindi_roman: Maine yeh hamari billing team ko bhej diya hai. Ve kal shaam 6 baje tak aapko email karenge, isliye aapko is chat mein rukne ki zaroorat nahin hai.
simple_meaning: Another team now has your question. They will write to you by email before 6 pm tomorrow, so you can close this chat.
why_it_works: It names who has the issue, how they will reply and by when. Telling the customer they can leave saves their time and stops them waiting in an empty chat.
key_chunk: I've passed this to ___. They'll ___ by ___, so you don't need to ___.
grammar_pattern: I've + past participle · They'll + verb + by + time · so + you don't need to + verb
grammar_note: "by 6 pm" means at or before 6 pm; it is a deadline, not an exact time.
tone_note: A real deadline sounds trustworthy. "Someone will get back to you" sounds like it may never happen.
watch_out: ✗ They'll email you by tomorrow 6 pm, so you need not to stay in this chat. → ✓ They'll email you by 6 pm tomorrow, so you don't need to stay in this chat.
dont_say: "Team will revert soon." "Revert" means "go back" to many international customers, and "soon" gives no time.
positive_swap: Instead of "I can't do anything about billing", say "I've passed this to our billing team. They'll email you by 6 pm tomorrow."
alt_1: Our billing team has your question now, and they'll reply by email before 6 pm tomorrow. You're free to close this chat.
alt_2: I've sent this to billing. Expect an email from them by 6 pm tomorrow; there's no need to wait here.
more_formal: I have forwarded your query to our billing team, who will reply by email no later than 6 pm tomorrow.
ask_next: Is the email address on your account the best one for them to use?
replies_you_may_hear: OK, which email will they use? · Can't you do it now? · What if they don't reply?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "What if nobody emails me?" → Agent: "Your case number is CS-31852. If you don't hear by 6 pm tomorrow, message us with it and we'll follow up straight away."
cultural_note: "Will revert" is common in Indian business English and is listed as Indian English in Oxford's learner's dictionary. For international customers, switch to "will reply" or "will get back to you".
channel_note: Voice: give the time and confirm the email address aloud. Email: put the deadline in its own sentence near the top.
when_not_to_use: Do not promise a deadline the other team has not agreed to; check their usual reply time first.
mini_conversation: Customer: Why was I charged twice? | Agent: I'm sorry to hear you were charged twice. I've passed this to our billing team. They'll email you by 6 pm tomorrow, so you don't need to stay in this chat. | Customer: Which email address will they use? | Agent: The one saved on your account. Could you check that it's still correct?
source_rule: State a real reply time and the next step; never leave the timing vague.
fill_blank: They'll email you by 6 pm tomorrow, so you don't need ____ stay in this chat.
mcq_question: Which message best tells the customer when to expect a reply from another team?
mcq_options: A) Our billing team will get back to you soon, so please wait for their reply. | B) Someone from our team will contact you about this as soon as possible. | C) They'll email you by 6 pm tomorrow, so you don't need to stay in this chat. | D) Please stay in this chat while the billing team looks at your question.
mcq_why: C is the only option with a real time (6 pm tomorrow) and the channel (email), and it tells the customer they can leave. A and B say "soon" or "as soon as possible", and D keeps them in the chat with no time given.
reorder_task: email / They'll / tomorrow / by / you / 6 / pm
reorder_answer: They'll email you by 6 pm tomorrow
hindi_to_english: Maine yeh technical team ko bhej diya hai. Ve aapko kal dopahar 12 baje tak call karenge.
hindi_to_english_answer: I've passed this to our technical team. They'll call you by 12 noon tomorrow.
whats_next_customer: Can't you just fix it yourself now?
whats_next_reply: I'd like to fix it now, but only our billing team can change a charge. I've marked your case as urgent for them.
role_play: Partner A has a billing question you cannot answer in chat. Partner B passes it on and tells A who will reply, how, by when, and that A can leave the chat.
record_task: Record yourself reading the message aloud, slowing down on the time and the team name.
self_check: Did you name the team? · Did you give a clear deadline? · Did you tell the customer they can leave the chat?

sentence: I'm really sorry the gift didn't arrive in time for your daughter's birthday, Vikram. I can see why that's upsetting, and I've refunded the express delivery charge.
speaker: Agent
situation: Vikram paid for express delivery so a gift would reach his daughter on her birthday, but it arrived a day late; you have checked the order and refunded the delivery charge.
recall_cue: A customer's gift arrived a day after a family birthday, even though he paid extra for speed. What three things should your written reply contain?
stress: i'm REAL-ly SOR-ry · the GIFT DID-n't ar-RIVE in TIME · for your DAUGH-ter's BIRTH-day, VIK-ram · i can SEE why that's up-SET-ting · and i've re-FUND-ed the ex-PRESS de-LIV-er-y CHARGE
linking: If read aloud: arrive_in_time → "a-rai-vin-TIME" · that's_upsetting → "that-sup-SET-ing" · refunded_the → "ri-FUN-did-the"
intonation: If read aloud: soft and slower on "really sorry", a falling tone on "birthday" and "upsetting", then a firmer, confident fall on "charge".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "daughter's" has no "g" sound (DAW-terz), and "birthday" has a soft "th" with the tongue between the teeth (BURTH-day), not "bur-day" or "birt-day".
customer_emotion: Hurt and angry that a birthday surprise was spoiled after paying extra for speed.
memory_hook: Think of a friend who hears the cake reached the party late, says "Oh no, on her birthday too", and quietly hands back the money you paid for fast delivery.
hindi_meaning: विक्रम, मुझे सच में अफ़सोस है कि तोहफ़ा आपकी बेटी के जन्मदिन तक नहीं पहुँचा। मैं समझ सकता/सकती हूँ कि यह क्यों परेशान करने वाला है, और मैंने एक्सप्रेस डिलीवरी का चार्ज वापस कर दिया है।
hindi_roman: Vikram, mujhe sach mein afsos hai ki tohfa aapki beti ke janmdin tak nahin pahuncha. Main samajh sakta/sakti hoon ki yeh kyon pareshaan karne wala hai, aur maine express delivery ka charge wapas kar diya hai.
simple_meaning: I am very sorry the present came after your daughter's birthday. I understand why you feel bad, and I have given back the extra money you paid for fast delivery.
why_it_works: It names exactly what went wrong and why it mattered, accepts the feeling, and shows a fix that is already done. In writing the customer cannot hear your voice, so the words must carry the warmth.
key_chunk: I'm really sorry ___. I can see why that's ___, and I've ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm sorry + (that) + clause · I can see why + clause · I've + past participle (already done)
grammar_note: "I can see why" shows you understand the reason for the feeling; "I've refunded" shows the fix is already done, not just promised.
tone_note: A specific apology that names what mattered (the birthday) feels real. "Sorry for the inconvenience caused" sounds copied and pasted, and stops at words.
watch_out: ✗ I'm really sorry the gift didn't arrived in time. → ✓ I'm really sorry the gift didn't arrive in time.
dont_say: "We regret the inconvenience caused." It is vague, scripted and offers no fix.
positive_swap: Instead of "Delays can happen at busy times", say "I'm really sorry the gift didn't arrive in time for your daughter's birthday. I've refunded the express delivery charge."
alt_1: That must have been so disappointing on her birthday, Vikram, and I'm sorry. As it didn't arrive when we promised, I've refunded the express charge.
alt_2: I'm so sorry it missed the birthday, Vikram. You paid for it to arrive on time, so I've given you back the express delivery charge.
more_formal: I sincerely apologise that your gift did not arrive in time for your daughter's birthday. I completely understand your disappointment, and I have refunded the express delivery charge.
ask_next: You'll get an email confirming the refund in the next few minutes. Did the gift itself arrive in good condition?
replies_you_may_hear: Thanks, but that doesn't fix her birthday. · Is the gift at least OK? · How did you miss the date?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "A refund doesn't fix her birthday!" → Agent: "You're right, it doesn't, and I'm sorry. The refund is the part I can put right now, and I've reported the delay to our delivery team today."
cultural_note: "Sorry for the inconvenience caused" is a standard line in many Indian support scripts. International customers often read it as copied text; a named problem and an action feel more sincere.
channel_note: Voice: slow down and lower your pitch slightly on "really sorry". Email: put the apology and the fix in the first two lines.
when_not_to_use: Do not say "I've refunded" until the refund has actually gone through; if it still needs approval, say you have requested it and when the customer will hear.
mini_conversation: Customer: The gift came a day late. Her birthday was yesterday, and I paid for express! | Agent: I'm really sorry the gift didn't arrive in time for your daughter's birthday, Vikram. I can see why that's upsetting, and I've refunded the express delivery charge. | Customer: Is the gift at least OK? | Agent: The courier marked it as delivered undamaged. If anything is wrong, send me a photo and I'll sort it out today.
source_rule: Apologise specifically, take responsibility, then offer a fix; never an empathy line on its own.
fill_blank: I'm really sorry the gift didn't arrive in time for your daughter's birthday, Vikram. I can see ____ (starts with w) that's upsetting, and I've refunded the express delivery charge.
mcq_question: A birthday gift arrived a day late, although the customer paid for express delivery. Which written reply shows empathy best?
mcq_options: A) We sincerely regret the inconvenience caused and thank you for your patience. | B) I'm really sorry it missed your daughter's birthday. I've refunded the express charge. | C) I understand you're upset. Deliveries can be delayed at busy times of the year. | D) I'm sorry to hear that. Please raise a refund request for the delivery charge online.
mcq_why: B names what went wrong and why it mattered, then shows a fix already done. A is vague and scripted, C follows the empathy line with an excuse, and D pushes the work onto the customer.
reorder_task: I've / the / charge / delivery / refunded / express
reorder_answer: I've refunded the express delivery charge
hindi_to_english: Mujhe sach mein afsos hai ki aapka order shaadi se pehle nahin pahuncha. Main samajh sakta/sakti hoon ki yeh kyon pareshaan karne wala hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm really sorry your order didn't arrive before the wedding. I can see why that's upsetting.
whats_next_customer: How did you miss the date when I paid for express?
whats_next_reply: I can see the parcel was held at the courier's local hub for a day, and I'm sorry we didn't warn you. I've reported it to our delivery team so they can look into it.
role_play: Partner A writes that an anniversary cake arrived the day after the party, even though they paid for express delivery. Partner B writes one reply that names the problem, shows understanding and states the fix already made.
record_task: Record yourself reading your apology aloud, sounding sincere and slowing down on "really sorry".
self_check: Did you name the exact problem and why it mattered? · Did you avoid "sorry for the inconvenience"? · Did you state the fix in the same message?

sentence: Thanks for waiting, Meera. I'm still checking with the warehouse, and it's taking a bit longer than I expected. I'll update you within 3 minutes.
speaker: Agent
situation: You told the customer you would check stock, but the warehouse has not replied yet and she has heard nothing for a while.
recall_cue: Your check is taking longer than you said and the chat has gone quiet. What do you send before the customer starts to worry?
stress: THANKS for WAIT-ing MEE-ra · i'm STILL CHECK-ing with the WARE-house · it's TAK-ing a bit LONG-er than i ex-PECT-ed · i'll up-DATE you with-IN THREE MIN-utes
linking: If read aloud: than_I → "tha-nai" · taking_a_bit → "tay-king-a-bit" · update_you → "up-DAY-choo"
intonation: If read aloud: fall on "warehouse", say "a bit longer" honestly with no rush, then fall clearly on "three minutes".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "expected" ends with "kt-id" ("ik-SPEK-tid"); do not drop the "k". And "warehouse" starts with rounded lips for "w", not teeth on lip.
customer_emotion: Starting to wonder whether the agent has gone away.
memory_hook: Think of a pizza tracker that pings "Still in the oven" before you even ask; silence is what makes people angry.
hindi_meaning: इंतज़ार करने के लिए धन्यवाद, मीरा। मैं अभी भी वेयरहाउस से जाँच कर रहा/रही हूँ, और इसमें मेरी उम्मीद से थोड़ा ज़्यादा समय लग रहा है। मैं 3 मिनट के अंदर आपको अपडेट दूँगा/दूँगी।
hindi_roman: Intezaar karne ke liye dhanyavaad, Meera. Main abhi bhi warehouse se jaanch kar raha/rahi hoon, aur ismein meri ummeed se thoda zyaada samay lag raha hai. Main 3 minute ke andar aapko update doonga/doongi.
simple_meaning: I am still working on your question. It is slower than I thought, and I will write again in three minutes or less.
why_it_works: It breaks the silence before the customer has to ask, admits the delay honestly and sets a new short deadline. Long gaps between replies are what make chat customers unhappy.
key_chunk: I'm still ___, and it's taking a bit longer than I expected. I'll update you within ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm still + verb-ing · it's taking + longer than + I expected · I'll + verb + within + time
grammar_note: "still" shows the work has not stopped; "within 3 minutes" means "in 3 minutes or less".
tone_note: Admitting the delay builds trust. Saying nothing, or sending only "please wait", makes the customer feel forgotten.
watch_out: ✗ I am still checking with warehouse, it is taking more longer than I expected. → ✓ I'm still checking with the warehouse, and it's taking a bit longer than I expected.
dont_say: "Please wait." on its own, again and again. It gives no news and no time.
positive_swap: Instead of "It is taking time, please wait", say "It's taking a bit longer than I expected. I'll update you within 3 minutes."
alt_1: Just a quick update, Meera: I'm still waiting to hear from the warehouse. I'll be back with you in 3 minutes at most.
alt_2: Still on it, Meera. The warehouse check is slower than usual, so give me up to 3 more minutes.
more_formal: Thank you for your patience. I am still waiting for confirmation from our warehouse and will update you within three minutes.
ask_next: Thanks for waiting, Meera. The warehouse has confirmed the blue one is in stock and can ship today.
replies_you_may_hear: OK, no problem. · How much longer? · Can you just email me instead?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I've already waited 10 minutes!" → Agent: "I'm sorry you've waited so long. If you'd prefer, I'll email you the answer within 15 minutes, so you don't need to wait here."
cultural_note: Agents often go silent while checking, as they might on a call. In chat, the customer cannot hear you working, so international customers expect a short update during long checks.
channel_note: Voice: return to the caller before the promised hold time ends. Email: send a short "still working on it" note if the promised time will pass.
when_not_to_use: Do not keep sending new 3-minute promises; after one update, offer to email or call back instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: Any news? | Agent: Thanks for waiting, Meera. I'm still checking with the warehouse, and it's taking a bit longer than I expected. I'll update you within 3 minutes. | Customer: OK. | Agent: Good news, Meera: the blue one is in stock and can ship today.
source_rule: Long gaps between chat replies hurt satisfaction (Zendesk); update before the customer has to ask.
fill_blank: I'm still checking with the warehouse, and it's taking a bit ____ than I expected.
mcq_question: Your stock check is slow and the customer has heard nothing for a while. What should you send?
mcq_options: A) Please wait while I check this. I will reply as soon as I have an answer. | B) Thanks for waiting. I'm still checking and will update you within 3 minutes. | C) Sorry for the delay. The warehouse is very busy today, so I can't say when I'll reply. | D) I know this is taking long. It's the warehouse's delay, not mine, so please be patient.
mcq_why: B gives an honest status and a new short deadline. A and C give no time, and D blames the warehouse instead of helping the customer.
reorder_task: update / I'll / within / you / minutes / 3
reorder_answer: I'll update you within 3 minutes
hindi_to_english: Main abhi bhi courier company se pata kar raha/rahi hoon. Main 5 minute ke andar aapko update doonga/doongi.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm still checking with the courier company. I'll update you within 5 minutes.
whats_next_customer: How much longer will this take?
whats_next_reply: Up to 3 more minutes. If I don't have an answer by then, I'll email it to you within the hour, so you're free to go.
role_play: Partner A asks if a product is in stock and then waits. Partner B sends one honest progress update with a new deadline, then the final answer.
record_task: Record yourself reading the update aloud, sounding calm and honest, with a clear fall on "three minutes".
self_check: Did you thank the customer for waiting? · Did you say honestly that it is taking longer? · Did you give a new, short deadline?

sentence: I'm sorry, the address is locked once an order ships, but I can send it to a nearby pickup point or arrange a free return. Which would you prefer?
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer wants to change the delivery address, but the parcel has already left the warehouse; your system shows a pickup point near the new address and a free return are both available.
recall_cue: The customer's request is not possible any more. How do you say so in one message and still give them a choice?
stress: i'm SOR-ry · the ad-DRESS is LOCKED · once an OR-der SHIPS · but i CAN · send it to a NEAR-by PICK-up POINT · or ar-RANGE a FREE re-TURN · WHICH would you pre-FER
linking: If read aloud: send_it → "sen-dit" · arrange_a → "a-RAIN-ja" · an_order → "a-NOR-der"
intonation: If read aloud: fall on "ships", lift slightly on "pickup point", then fall on "free return" to present a choice; fall again on "prefer".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "locked" and "ships" end in clear "kt" and "ps" sounds; do not add a vowel ("lock-ed", "ship-su"). Stress pre-FER on the second syllable.
customer_emotion: Anxious that the parcel will go to the wrong place.
memory_hook: Think of a closed door with two open windows beside it: show the closed door briefly, then point to the windows.
hindi_meaning: माफ़ कीजिए, ऑर्डर शिप होने के बाद पता बदला नहीं जा सकता, लेकिन मैं इसे पास के पिकअप पॉइंट पर भिजवा सकता/सकती हूँ या फ़्री रिटर्न करवा सकता/सकती हूँ। आप क्या पसंद करेंगे?
hindi_roman: Maaf kijiye, order ship hone ke baad pata badla nahin ja sakta, lekin main ise paas ke pickup point par bhijwa sakta/sakti hoon ya free return karwa sakta/sakti hoon. Aap kya pasand karenge?
simple_meaning: Sorry, we cannot change the address now because the parcel has left, but you can choose: collect it nearby, or send it back for free.
why_it_works: It says sorry, gives the reason in a few words, moves straight to what is possible and lets the customer choose. A choice gives back some control after hearing "no".
key_chunk: I'm sorry, ___ once ___, but I can ___ or ___. Which would you prefer?
grammar_pattern: Reason + but + I can + verb + or + verb · Which would you prefer?
grammar_note: "but I can" turns the sentence from the limit to the solution; "Which would you prefer?" offers a choice.
tone_note: Giving options straight after the reason sounds helpful. "Not possible, it's our policy" sounds like a wall and gives the customer nowhere to go.
watch_out: ✗ I'm sorry, the address is locked once an order ship, but I can send it to nearby pickup point. → ✓ I'm sorry, the address is locked once an order ships, but I can send it to a nearby pickup point.
dont_say: "It is not possible as per company policy." It hides behind policy and offers nothing.
positive_swap: Instead of "We can't change the address", say "I can send it to a nearby pickup point or arrange a free return."
alt_1: As the parcel is already on its way, the address is fixed, but I can redirect it to a pickup point near you. Would that work?
alt_2: Once it ships, the address is fixed. What I can do is arrange a free return or redirect it to a pickup point near you. Which suits you better?
more_formal: Unfortunately, the delivery address cannot be changed after dispatch. However, I would be happy to redirect the parcel to a pickup point or arrange a free return.
ask_next: Great. Which area would you like to collect it from? A postal code is fine.
replies_you_may_hear: The pickup point, please. · Why can't you just call the courier? · I'll take the return.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Just call the courier and change it!" → Agent: "I understand you want it to reach your new address. Once it ships, the courier only accepts changes to a pickup point, so that's the closest option I can arrange."
cultural_note: "As per policy" is common in Indian service writing. International customers often hear it as a refusal to help; give the plain reason, then what you can do.
channel_note: Voice: pause after the reason, then offer the two choices slowly. Email: put each option on its own line.
when_not_to_use: Do not offer options you have not checked are available, such as a pickup point in that area.
mini_conversation: Customer: Can I change the address? I moved. | Agent: I'm sorry, the address is locked once an order ships, but I can send it to a nearby pickup point or arrange a free return. Which would you prefer? | Customer: Pickup point, please. | Agent: Great. Could you share the postal code of the area where you'd like to collect it?
source_rule: Don't hide behind "policy": give the reason in plain words, then an alternative (derived advice).
fill_blank: I'm sorry, the address is locked once an order ships, ____ I can send it to a nearby pickup point or arrange a free return.
mcq_question: The parcel has shipped and the customer wants a new address. Which reply is best?
mcq_options: A) I'm sorry, but our rules do not allow an address change after dispatch, so it is not possible. | B) I'm sorry, the parcel has shipped, but I can send it to a pickup point or arrange a free return. | C) You can only change the address before an order ships, so please check it carefully next time. | D) I'm sorry, the parcel has already shipped, so there is nothing more that I can do for you now.
mcq_why: B says sorry, gives a short reason and offers two real options. A hides behind a rule, C blames the customer, and D leaves them with nothing to do.
reorder_task: locked / order / The / ships / is / address / once / an
reorder_answer: The address is locked once an order ships
hindi_to_english: Maaf kijiye, order pack hone ke baad size badla nahin ja sakta, lekin main aapke liye exchange karwa sakta/sakti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry, the size is locked once the order is packed, but I can arrange an exchange for you.
whats_next_customer: Is the free return really free? Do I pay for anything?
whats_next_reply: Yes, there is nothing to pay. I'll email you a prepaid return label as soon as you confirm.
role_play: Partner A asks to change the delivery address of a shipped parcel and gets a little annoyed. Partner B explains briefly and offers two clear options, then completes A's choice.
record_task: Record yourself reading the message aloud with a falling tone on "free return" to make it sound like a choice.
self_check: Did you say sorry and give a short, plain reason? · Did you move straight to what you can do? · Did you let the customer choose?

sentence: Could you try logging in again now and let me know if it works? I'll stay in the chat until you're in.
speaker: Agent
situation: You have unlocked the customer's account and need to know if the fix really worked before you close the chat.
recall_cue: You think you have fixed the login problem. What do you ask before you say goodbye, and what do you promise?
stress: could you TRY LOG-ging in a-GAIN NOW · let me KNOW if it WORKS · i'll STAY in the CHAT un-TIL you're IN
linking: If read aloud: could_you → "cud-joo" · if_it → "i-fit" · let_me → "let-mee" (very light "t")
intonation: If read aloud: rise on "works?" because it is a yes/no question, then a calm fall on "you're in".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "works" needs rounded lips for "w" (not teeth on lip, like "v") and a clear "ks" at the end: practise "worse / verse".
customer_emotion: Hopeful the problem is fixed, but not sure yet.
memory_hook: Think of a mechanic who hands back the keys and says "Start it while I'm here", not "Bye, it should be fine".
hindi_meaning: क्या आप अभी फिर से लॉग इन करके देख सकते हैं और बता सकते हैं कि यह काम कर रहा है या नहीं? जब तक आप लॉग इन नहीं हो जाते, मैं चैट में रहूँगा/रहूँगी।
hindi_roman: Kya aap abhi phir se log in karke dekh sakte hain aur bata sakte hain ki yeh kaam kar raha hai ya nahin? Jab tak aap log in nahin ho jaate, main chat mein rahoonga/rahoongi.
simple_meaning: Please try to log in now and tell me if it works. I will wait here until you are inside your account.
why_it_works: It checks that the problem is really solved before closing, so the customer does not need to come back. Staying in the chat removes the fear of being left alone if it fails.
key_chunk: Could you try ___ and let me know if it works? I'll stay ___ until ___.
grammar_pattern: Could you + try + verb-ing · let me know if + present simple · I'll + verb + until + clause
grammar_note: "try logging in" means "do it to test it"; "until you're in" means "up to the moment you are logged in".
tone_note: Checking before closing shows care. "Your issue is resolved, is there anything else?" assumes it worked, which may not be true.
watch_out: ✗ Could you try to login again now and tell me it is working or not? → ✓ Could you try logging in again now and let me know if it works?
dont_say: "It should work now. Thanks for contacting us." It closes before checking and leaves the customer alone if it fails.
positive_swap: Instead of "Your issue is resolved", say "Could you try logging in again now and let me know if it works?"
alt_1: I've unlocked your account. Could you log in now and tell me if you get through? I'll wait here.
alt_2: Please give it a try now; I'll stay with you until you're logged in.
more_formal: Your account has now been unlocked. Could you please try to log in and confirm whether it works? I will remain in the chat until you have access.
ask_next: Great, I'm glad you're in. To sum up, your account is unlocked and working again. Is there anything else I can help with today?
replies_you_may_hear: Yes, it works now! · Still the same error. · One sec, trying.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Can't you just check from your side?" → Agent: "I can see the account is unlocked, but your device may still have old details saved, so a quick try from your side is the only sure check."
cultural_note: Many scripts close with "Is there anything else?" straight after a fix. International best practice is to confirm the issue is resolved first, then ask about anything else.
channel_note: Voice: "Could you try now while I'm on the line?" Email: ask the customer to reply and say whether it worked.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask the customer to test when the fix needs hours to take effect; give the time and follow up instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: OK, you said it's unlocked? | Agent: Yes. Could you try logging in again now and let me know if it works? I'll stay in the chat until you're in. | Customer: I'm in, thanks! | Agent: Great, I'm glad it's working. Is there anything else I can help with today?
source_rule: Check the issue is resolved before asking "Is there anything else…?" (SQM).
fill_blank: Could you ____ logging in again now and let me know if it works?
mcq_question: You have just unlocked an account. What should you send before closing the chat?
mcq_options: A) Could you try logging in now and let me know if it works? I'll stay here. | B) Your issue is resolved now. Is there anything else I can help you with today? | C) Thanks for contacting us today. Have a nice day, and please rate this chat. | D) Please check again later and contact us if it still doesn't work for you.
mcq_why: A is the only reply that checks the fix before closing. B assumes it worked, C closes without checking, and D leaves the customer to test it alone later.
reorder_task: stay / chat / I'll / the / in
reorder_answer: I'll stay in the chat
hindi_to_english: Kya aap abhi ek baar phir payment karke dekh sakte hain? Jab tak payment ho nahin jaata, main chat mein hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: Could you try the payment again now? I'll stay in the chat until it goes through.
whats_next_customer: It's still showing an error.
whats_next_reply: Thanks for trying. What does the error say, word for word? Then I'll know if it's the same problem or a new one.
role_play: Partner A could not log in; Partner B has just unlocked the account. B asks A to test it and stays until A confirms, then closes properly. Repeat once with A saying it still fails.
record_task: Record yourself reading the message aloud, with a rising tone on "works?" and a calm finish.
self_check: Did you ask the customer to test the fix? · Did your question rise at the end? · Did you promise to stay until it works?

sentence: Thanks, Arjun. You've asked about three things, so let's take them one at a time, starting with your missing refund.
speaker: Agent
situation: Arjun has sent one long message about a missing refund, a wrong bill and a change of phone number.
recall_cue: A customer sends one long message with several different problems. How do you organise the chat without ignoring any of them?
stress: THANKS AR-jun · you've ASKED a-BOUT THREE THINGS · let's TAKE them ONE at a TIME · START-ing with your MISS-ing RE-fund
linking: If read aloud: asked_about → "ask-ta-bout" · take_them → "tay-kem" · one_at_a → "wun-a-ta"
intonation: If read aloud: fall on "three things", a steady rhythm on "one at a time", then fall on "refund" to show where you start.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "asked" is one syllable ending in "skt" ("askt"), not "ask-ed" or "ass"; and "three things" needs the tongue between the teeth for both "th" sounds.
customer_emotion: Overwhelmed and worried that some issues will be forgotten.
memory_hook: Think of a doctor with three complaints on one form: she numbers them and treats the most painful one first.
hindi_meaning: धन्यवाद, अर्जुन। आपने तीन बातें पूछी हैं, तो चलिए इन्हें एक-एक करके देखते हैं, पहले उस रिफ़ंड से शुरू करते हैं जो आपको अभी तक नहीं मिला।
hindi_roman: Dhanyavaad, Arjun. Aapne teen baatein poochi hain, to chaliye inhein ek-ek karke dekhte hain, pehle us refund se shuru karte hain jo aapko abhi tak nahin mila.
simple_meaning: You have three questions. I will answer them one by one, and I will begin with your refund that has not arrived.
why_it_works: Counting the questions shows you read all of them, and choosing one to start with gives the chat a clear order. A missing refund is a sensible first choice, and the customer can still change the order.
key_chunk: You've asked about ___ things, so let's take them one at a time, starting with ___.
grammar_pattern: You've + past participle · so + let's + base verb · starting with + noun
grammar_note: "let's take them one at a time" suggests a plan you do together; "starting with" names the first step.
tone_note: "Let's" makes it teamwork. "Please ask one question at a time" puts the work on the customer and sounds like a rule.
watch_out: ✗ You've asked about three things, so let's take them one after one. → ✓ You've asked about three things, so let's take them one at a time.
dont_say: "Please raise separate tickets for each issue." It pushes extra work onto the customer.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please ask one question at a time", say "Let's take them one at a time, starting with your missing refund."
alt_1: I can see three questions here, Arjun. I'll answer each one, beginning with the refund.
alt_2: Thanks for the details. Let's go through your three points in order; first, the refund.
more_formal: Thank you for your message. I will address each of your three questions in turn, beginning with the missing refund.
ask_next: Could you tell me the date you returned the item?
replies_you_may_hear: OK, the refund first. · Actually, the bill is more urgent. · Fine, but don't forget the phone number.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Can't you do them all at once?" → Agent: "I'm working on all three, and I'll answer each one fully. Going in order makes sure nothing is missed."
cultural_note: Agents sometimes answer only the first question in a long message. International customers notice the others being skipped; naming the number of questions shows nothing was ignored.
channel_note: Voice: "You've mentioned three things; let me note them down." Email: answer each question under a number or a short heading.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it when two of the questions are really one issue; answer them together instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: My refund hasn't come, my bill is wrong, and I've changed my number. | Agent: Thanks, Arjun. You've asked about three things, so let's take them one at a time, starting with your missing refund. | Customer: OK. | Agent: Thank you. To check your refund, could you tell me which day you returned the item?
source_rule: Keep chat replies short but answer every question the customer asked.
fill_blank: You've asked about three things, so let's take them one at a ____.
mcq_question: A customer asks about three different problems in one long chat message. What is the best reply?
mcq_options: A) Thanks. That's a lot to cover, so please send me one question at a time. | B) Thanks, Arjun. I'm checking your refund now and will come back to you shortly. | C) Thanks. Please raise three separate tickets so each team can deal with its own issue. | D) Thanks, Arjun. You've asked about three things, so let's take them one at a time.
mcq_why: D shows you saw all three and sets a clear order. B starts helping but ignores two of the questions, while A and C push the work onto the customer.
reorder_task: one / take / let's / at / time / them / a
reorder_answer: let's take them one at a time
hindi_to_english: Aapne do baatein poochi hain, to chaliye unhein ek-ek karke dekhte hain, pehle delivery se shuru karte hain.
hindi_to_english_answer: You've asked about two things, so let's take them one at a time, starting with the delivery.
whats_next_customer: Actually, the wrong bill is more urgent for me.
whats_next_reply: Of course, let's start with the bill, then come back to the refund.
role_play: Partner A sends one long message with three problems. Partner B counts them, suggests an order and answers the first one, then moves to the next.
record_task: Record yourself reading the reply aloud, with clear "th" sounds in "three things".
self_check: Did you say how many questions there were? · Did you choose a starting point? · Did you avoid asking the customer to split their message?

sentence: Are you still there, Sana? If I don't hear back in the next 5 minutes, I'll close this chat. You can message us again anytime.
speaker: Agent
situation: Sana stopped replying in the middle of the chat and has not answered your friendly check-in, and other customers are waiting in the queue.
recall_cue: The customer has gone silent. What do you send before you end the chat, and what do you tell them about coming back?
stress: are you STILL THERE SA-na · if i DON'T hear BACK · in the NEXT FIVE MIN-utes · i'll CLOSE this CHAT · MES-sage us a-GAIN AN-y-time
linking: If read aloud: if_I → "i-fai" · message_us → "MES-i-jus" · again_anytime → "a-GEN-ee-time"
intonation: If read aloud: rise on "Sana?" as a real question, then a neutral, even tone for the warning and a warm fall on "anytime".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "there" starts with a voiced "th" (tongue between teeth), not "dare"; and "close" here ends in a "z" sound ("kloze"), not "s".
customer_emotion: Probably distracted or busy, not upset.
memory_hook: Think of a shopkeeper who calls "Still looking?" before pulling down the shutter, and adds "Come back tomorrow".
hindi_meaning: सना, क्या आप अभी भी यहाँ हैं? अगर अगले 5 मिनट में आपका जवाब नहीं आया, तो मैं यह चैट बंद कर दूँगा/दूँगी। आप कभी भी हमें दोबारा मैसेज कर सकती हैं।
hindi_roman: Sana, kya aap abhi bhi yahan hain? Agar agle 5 minute mein aapka jawaab nahin aaya, to main yeh chat band kar doonga/doongi. Aap kabhi bhi humein dobaara message kar sakti hain.
simple_meaning: Are you still here? If you do not reply in five minutes, I will end the chat, but you can write to us again later.
why_it_works: It checks in, gives a fair warning with a real time and keeps the door open. The customer is not surprised by a closed chat and knows they can return.
key_chunk: If I don't hear back in ___, I'll close this chat. You can ___ anytime.
grammar_pattern: If + present simple (negative), + I'll + base verb · You can + verb + again anytime
grammar_note: This is a first conditional: "If I don't hear back, I'll close" talks about a real possible future.
tone_note: A warning plus an open door sounds fair. Closing a chat with no warning feels like a door slammed in the customer's face.
watch_out: ✗ Due to no response, this chat is being closed. → ✓ If I don't hear back in the next 5 minutes, I'll close this chat.
dont_say: "Since there is no response from your end, closing the chat." It sounds like blame and gives no way back.
positive_swap: Instead of "Due to no response, chat is closed", say "If I don't hear back in the next 5 minutes, I'll close this chat. You can message us again anytime."
alt_1: Just checking you're still with me, Sana. I'll close the chat in 5 minutes if I don't hear from you, but you're welcome back anytime.
alt_2: Hi Sana, are you still there? I'll keep this chat open for 5 more minutes; after that, feel free to start a new one.
more_formal: As I haven't heard from you for a little while, I will close this chat in five minutes. Please feel free to contact us again at any time.
ask_next: I haven't heard back, so I'm closing this chat now. Your case number is CS-40275 if you need us again.
replies_you_may_hear: Sorry, I'm here! · Yes, one minute please. · (no reply)
if_customer_pushes: Customer (later): "Why did you close my chat?" → Agent: "I'm sorry, I didn't hear back for a while. I'm here now; let's carry on from where we stopped."
cultural_note: Some scripts close silent chats with "Due to no response from your end". International customers expect a friendly check-in, a warning and an easy way back.
channel_note: Voice: "Hello, are you still there?" twice, then explain you'll end the call and they can call back. Email: not needed; the ticket stays open for a set time.
when_not_to_use: Do not send it when you were the one who kept the customer waiting; apologise for the wait instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: (no reply to your check-in for 4 minutes) | Agent: Are you still there, Sana? If I don't hear back in the next 5 minutes, I'll close this chat. You can message us again anytime. | Customer: Sorry, I'm here! | Agent: No worries, welcome back. Let's carry on with your exchange.
source_rule: Ending a chat: if the customer goes silent, check in, warn, then close politely.
fill_blank: If I don't ____ back in the next 5 minutes, I'll close this chat.
mcq_question: A customer has been silent for several minutes, and your friendly check-in got no reply. What should you send now?
mcq_options: A) Are you still there? If I don't hear back in 5 minutes, I'll close this chat. | B) Since I haven't received a reply from your end, this chat is now being closed. | C) Hello? Hello? Are you there? Please reply now, as other customers are waiting. | D) Reply within 5 minutes or this chat will be closed and your request cancelled.
mcq_why: A checks in politely and gives a fair warning with a real time. B closes without warning, C sounds impatient and gives no information, and D threatens to cancel the request.
reorder_task: message / can / again / You / anytime / us
reorder_answer: You can message us again anytime
hindi_to_english: Kya aap abhi bhi yahan hain? Agar 5 minute mein jawaab nahin aaya, to main chat band kar doonga/doongi.
hindi_to_english_answer: Are you still there? If I don't hear back in 5 minutes, I'll close this chat.
whats_next_customer: Sorry, I was on another call! I'm back.
whats_next_reply: Welcome back, Sana. I was about to confirm the size for your exchange, so let's pick it up from there.
role_play: Partner A stops replying in the middle of a chat. Partner B sends a check-in with a 5-minute warning, then either continues when A returns or sends a polite closing message.
record_task: Record yourself reading the message aloud with a real rising question on "Sana?" and a warm finish.
self_check: Did you check if the customer is still there? · Did you give a clear time before closing? · Did you tell them they can come back?

sentence: I'm glad that's sorted, Neha. You'll see a short survey after this chat, and if you have a moment, I'd really value your feedback.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer's problem is fixed and the system will show a rating survey when the chat ends.
recall_cue: The issue is fixed and a survey will pop up after the chat. How do you mention it without begging for a good score?
stress: i'm GLAD that's SORT-ed · you'll SEE a SHORT SUR-vey · if you HAVE a MO-ment · i'd REAL-ly VAL-ue your FEED-back
linking: If read aloud: that's_sorted → "thats-SOR-tid" · if_you_have_a → "if-yoo-ha-va" · value_your → "VAL-yoo-yor"
intonation: If read aloud: warm fall on "sorted", lighter and quicker for the survey part, a soft fall on "feedback" with no pleading tone.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "survey" as a noun is SUR-vey, stress on the first part; and "value" needs top teeth on the lower lip for "v", not a "w".
customer_emotion: Relieved and ready to leave.
memory_hook: Think of a waiter who leaves the comment card on the table and walks away, rather than standing over you while you fill it in.
hindi_meaning: नेहा, ख़ुशी है कि यह ठीक हो गया। चैट के बाद आपको एक छोटा सर्वे दिखेगा, अगर आपके पास समय हो तो मुझे आपकी राय जानकर अच्छा लगेगा।
hindi_roman: Neha, khushi hai ki yeh theek ho gaya. Chat ke baad aapko ek chhota survey dikhega, agar aapke paas samay ho to mujhe aapki raay jaankar achchha lagega.
simple_meaning: I am happy your problem is fixed. A short form will appear after the chat; please fill it in if you have time.
why_it_works: It asks only after the problem is solved, tells the customer what to expect and leaves the choice to them. Asking for "feedback", not "5 stars", keeps it honest.
key_chunk: You'll see a short ___ after this chat, and if you have a moment, I'd really value ___.
grammar_pattern: You'll + see + noun · if you have a moment · I'd + really + value + noun
grammar_note: "I'd really value" is a soft, polite way to say "I would like"; "if you have a moment" makes it optional.
tone_note: It is a light invitation, not a demand. "Please give 5 stars" or "my job depends on it" pressures the customer and can break company rules.
watch_out: ✗ If you will have a moment, I'd really value your feedback. → ✓ If you have a moment, I'd really value your feedback.
dont_say: "Please give me 5 stars, it's important for me." It pressures the customer and makes the rating meaningless.
positive_swap: Instead of "Kindly do rate us 10 out of 10", say "If you have a moment, I'd really value your feedback."
alt_1: Glad we got that fixed, Neha. A quick survey will appear when the chat ends, and your feedback helps us improve.
alt_2: That's all sorted. If you have a minute, the short survey after this chat helps us learn what went well.
more_formal: I'm pleased the issue has been resolved. You will receive a brief survey after this chat, and we would appreciate any feedback you are able to share.
ask_next: Is there anything else I can help with before you go?
replies_you_may_hear: Sure, will do. · Thanks for your help! · I don't usually do surveys.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I don't have time for surveys." → Agent: "That's completely fine. Thanks for chatting with us, and have a good day."
cultural_note: Some teams ask agents to request "10 out of 10" or "5 stars". International customers often find this uncomfortable; a neutral request for feedback is more widely accepted.
channel_note: Voice: "You may get a short survey after the call; I'd value your feedback." Email: add one line above your sign-off.
when_not_to_use: Do not mention the survey when the issue is still unresolved or the customer is upset; fix the problem first.
