mini_conversation: Customer: It's working now, thank you! | Agent: I'm glad that's sorted, Neha. You'll see a short survey after this chat, and if you have a moment, I'd really value your feedback. | Customer: Sure. | Agent: Thanks, Neha. Have a lovely evening.
source_rule: Close only after the issue is resolved; keep it short, honest and free of pressure.
fill_blank: You'll see a short survey after this chat, and if you ____ (starts with h) a moment, I'd really value your feedback.
mcq_question: The problem is solved and a survey will follow. Which message is most appropriate?
mcq_options: A) I'm so glad that's sorted. Please give me 5 stars, because my job depends on this rating. | B) Glad that's sorted. Please complete the feedback form before you leave this chat today. | C) Glad that's sorted. A short survey follows, and I'd value your feedback if you have a moment. | D) Your issue is solved now. Please rate this chat 10 out of 10 on the survey that follows.
mcq_why: C invites feedback and leaves the choice to the customer. A, B and D all pressure the customer, either for a high score or to fill in the form.
reorder_task: your / I'd / feedback / value / really
reorder_answer: I'd really value your feedback
hindi_to_english: Khushi hai ki problem solve ho gayi. Chat ke baad ek chhota survey aayega.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm glad that's sorted. You'll see a short survey after this chat.
whats_next_customer: Sure, I'll fill it in. Thanks for your help!
whats_next_reply: You're welcome, Neha. Take care, and enjoy the rest of your day.
role_play: Partner A says the problem is fixed and thanks the agent. Partner B mentions the survey politely, without asking for a score, and closes the chat.
record_task: Record yourself reading the message aloud in a light, warm tone with no pleading.
self_check: Was the issue fully solved before you asked? · Did you avoid asking for a specific score? · Did you make it optional?

sentence: Your case number is CS-20417. If you contact us again, just share this number and we'll pick up where we left off.
speaker: Agent
situation: The issue needs more work after this chat, and you have created a case the customer may need later.
recall_cue: The customer may need to come back about this issue. What do you give them so they don't start from the beginning next time?
stress: your CASE NUM-ber is C-S two-oh-four-one-SEV-en · if you CON-tact us a-GAIN · just SHARE this NUM-ber · we'll PICK UP where we LEFT OFF
linking: If read aloud: contact_us → "CON-tak-tus" · pick_up → "pi-kup" · left_off → "lef-toff"
intonation: If read aloud: say the case number slowly in small groups (C-S · 2-0 · 4-1-7) with a fall at the end, then a relaxed, friendly fall on "left off".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "left off" keeps the "f-t" cluster ("left", not "lef") before linking into "off"; and say "seven" with top teeth on the lower lip for "v".
customer_emotion: Worried about explaining everything again next time.
memory_hook: Think of a bookmark: the case number marks the exact page, so nobody starts the story again from chapter one.
hindi_meaning: आपका केस नंबर CS-20417 है। अगर आप फिर से संपर्क करें, तो बस यह नंबर बताइए और हम वहीं से आगे बढ़ेंगे जहाँ हमने छोड़ा था।
hindi_roman: Aapka case number CS-20417 hai. Agar aap phir se sampark karein, to bas yeh number bataiye aur hum wahin se aage badhenge jahaan humne chhoda tha.
simple_meaning: Here is the number for your problem. If you write to us again, give this number and we will continue without starting again.
why_it_works: It gives the number and tells the customer exactly why it matters. They know they will not need to repeat the whole story, which saves effort.
key_chunk: Your case number is ___. If you contact us again, just share this number and we'll ___.
grammar_pattern: If + present simple, + (just) imperative + and + we'll + verb · pick up where we left off
grammar_note: "pick up where we left off" is a fixed phrase meaning "continue from the point where we stopped".
tone_note: Explaining how to use the number is helpful. Just "Ticket no. CS-20417" with nothing else feels like an admin form.
watch_out: ✗ If you contact us again, just share this number and we'll pick up from where we left. → ✓ If you contact us again, just share this number and we'll pick up where we left off.
dont_say: "Note the ticket number for future reference." It sounds like a form letter and does not explain the benefit.
positive_swap: Instead of "Without the ticket number we cannot help you", say "Just share this number and we'll pick up where we left off."
alt_1: I've created case CS-20417 for you. Mention it if you get in touch again, and we'll see the full history straight away.
alt_2: For next time, your case number is CS-20417. Quote it and you won't need to explain everything again.
more_formal: Your case reference is CS-20417. Please quote this number in any future contact so that we can continue from where we left off.
ask_next: I'll also email it to you now so you have it saved.
replies_you_may_hear: Can you email it to me? · Got it, thanks. · Do I need it to get my refund?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why should I keep a number? You have my details." → Agent: "You're right, we can find you by your phone number too. The case number just takes us straight to this conversation."
cultural_note: "Please note down the same" is common in Indian service writing. International customers expect the thing named ("this number") and a reason to keep it.
channel_note: Voice: read it slowly in groups and ask them to read it back. Email: put the case number in the subject line and near the top.
when_not_to_use: Do not give a case number for a question you fully answered and closed; it suggests the issue is still open.
mini_conversation: Customer: So someone will check the faulty charger? | Agent: Yes. Your case number is CS-20417. If you contact us again, just share this number and we'll pick up where we left off. | Customer: Can you email it to me? | Agent: Of course. I've just sent it to the email on your account.
source_rule: Replace vague promises with a clear timeline, a ticket number and the next step.
fill_blank: If you contact us again, just share this number and we'll pick up where we left ____.
mcq_question: How do you share a case number most helpfully in chat?
mcq_options: A) Ticket no. CS-20417 has been created. Please note it down for future reference. | B) Please note down your ticket number for future reference and quote it when required. | C) Your case number is CS-20417. Share it if you write again and we'll pick up from there. | D) Your case number is CS-20417. Without it we cannot help you if you contact us again.
mcq_why: C gives the number and says how it helps. A and B read like form letters, and D turns the number into a threat instead of a benefit.
reorder_task: up / pick / where / we'll / off / left / we
reorder_answer: we'll pick up where we left off
hindi_to_english: Aapka complaint number CS-55902 hai. Agli baar bas yeh number bataiye, hum wahin se aage badhenge.
hindi_to_english_answer: Your complaint number is CS-55902. Next time, just share this number and we'll pick up from there.
whats_next_customer: Where do I type this number when I come back?
whats_next_reply: Just type it into the chat as your first message. Whoever answers can open your case straight away.
role_play: Partner A has a faulty charger that needs a technician's check. Partner B shares the case number, explains why to keep it, and offers to email it.
record_task: Record yourself reading the case number slowly in groups, then the rest of the message in a natural, friendly tone.
self_check: Did you give the full case number? · Did you explain why it is useful? · Did you offer to send it by email?

sentence: I think there's been a small mix-up. The ₹99 is a one-time delivery charge, not a monthly fee, so it won't be charged again next month.
speaker: Agent
situation: The customer thinks they have been signed up for a monthly fee, but the ₹99 was only a single delivery charge.
recall_cue: The customer has misread their bill and is a little angry about it. How do you correct them without making them feel silly?
stress: i THINK there's been a SMALL MIX-up · the NINE-ty-NINE ru-PEES is a ONE-time de-LIV-er-y CHARGE · NOT a MONTH-ly FEE · so it WON'T be CHARGED a-GAIN NEXT MONTH
linking: If read aloud: there's_been → "thairz-bin" · mix_up → "mik-sup" · charged_again → "charj-da-gen"
intonation: If read aloud: a soft, low start on "small mix-up", contrast stress on "ONE-time" and "MONTH-ly", then a reassuring fall on "again".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "monthly" has "nth" in the middle; put the tongue between the teeth ("munth-lee"), not "mun-tly". And "delivery" needs a "v" with teeth on lip.
customer_emotion: Annoyed and suspicious, ready to complain about a hidden fee.
memory_hook: Think of gently turning a map the right way up for a friend: you do not say "you're holding it wrong", you just turn it.
hindi_meaning: मुझे लगता है थोड़ी ग़लतफ़हमी हो गई है। ₹99 एक बार का डिलीवरी चार्ज है, मासिक फ़ीस नहीं, इसलिए यह अगले महीने दोबारा नहीं लगेगा।
hindi_roman: Mujhe lagta hai thodi galatfehmi ho gayi hai. ₹99 ek baar ka delivery charge hai, maasik fees nahin, isliye yeh agle mahine dobaara nahin lagega.
simple_meaning: You may have misunderstood the bill. The ₹99 was paid only once for delivery; it will not come every month.
why_it_works: "There's been a mix-up" blames nobody, so the customer can accept the correction without losing face. The clear contrast ("one-time, not monthly") and the reassurance answer the real worry.
key_chunk: I think there's been a small mix-up. The ___ is ___, not ___, so ___.
grammar_pattern: There's been + noun · X is A, not B · so + it won't + be + past participle
grammar_note: "A, not B" puts the right meaning next to the wrong one so the difference is clear.
tone_note: "Small mix-up" keeps it light and shared. "You have misunderstood" or "You are wrong" makes the customer defensive.
watch_out: ✗ You have misunderstood, it is not monthly. → ✓ I think there's been a small mix-up. The ₹99 is a one-time delivery charge, not a monthly fee.
dont_say: "You have read the bill wrongly." It blames the customer and starts an argument.
positive_swap: Instead of "You are wrong, it's not a subscription", say "I think there's been a small mix-up. The ₹99 is a one-time delivery charge."
alt_1: I can see why that might look like a monthly fee. It's actually a one-time ₹99 delivery charge, so it won't repeat next month.
alt_2: Thanks for checking. That ₹99 was charged once for delivery; it isn't a subscription, so there's nothing to cancel.
more_formal: I believe there may have been a misunderstanding. The ₹99 is a one-time delivery charge rather than a monthly fee, so it will not be charged again next month.
ask_next: Would you like me to send you a copy of the invoice so you can see the breakdown?
replies_you_may_hear: Oh, OK, that makes sense. · Are you sure? It says "plan". · Then why does it say "renewal"?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "But the bill says 'plan'!" → Agent: "I can see that word there, and it is confusing. It's the name of the delivery option. I'll send you the invoice breakdown now so you can check."
cultural_note: Direct corrections like "You are wrong" or "You have not understood" can sound rude to international customers. Shared wording such as "a mix-up" saves face for everyone.
channel_note: Voice: stress "ONE-time" and "MONTH-ly" to make the contrast heard. Email: show the charge line from the bill with a short note beside it.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it until you have checked the bill; if the customer is right, apologise and fix it instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: Why am I paying ₹99 every month?? | Agent: I think there's been a small mix-up. The ₹99 is a one-time delivery charge, not a monthly fee, so it won't be charged again next month. | Customer: Oh, OK. Are you sure? | Agent: Yes, I've checked your account. I'll email you the invoice breakdown now so you can see it too.
source_rule: Plain language: explain clearly without blame; customers are not experts in your product.
fill_blank: The ₹99 is a one-time delivery charge, ____ a monthly fee.
mcq_question: A customer wrongly thinks a one-time charge is monthly. Which reply corrects them most gently?
mcq_options: A) I think there's been a small mix-up. The ₹99 is a one-time charge, not a monthly fee. | B) I'm afraid you have misunderstood the bill. The ₹99 is not a monthly fee. | C) Please read the bill properly. It clearly says the ₹99 is charged only once. | D) That is not correct. The ₹99 is a one-time delivery charge, and it is not monthly.
mcq_why: A corrects the facts and blames nobody. B, C and D all put the mistake on the customer, even though B and D are factually right.
reorder_task: mix-up / there's / a / small / think / been / I
reorder_answer: I think there's been a small mix-up
hindi_to_english: Mujhe lagta hai thodi galatfehmi ho gayi hai. Yeh ek baar ka setup charge hai, har mahine ka nahin.
hindi_to_english_answer: I think there's been a small mix-up. This is a one-time setup charge, not a monthly one.
whats_next_customer: So will I pay ₹99 again on my next order?
whats_next_reply: It depends on the delivery option you choose at checkout, and the page shows the exact charge before you pay. There is no monthly renewal.
role_play: Partner A is upset about a "monthly ₹99 fee" on their bill. Partner B checks, then corrects the misunderstanding gently without blame and offers proof.
record_task: Record yourself reading the message aloud with contrast stress on "ONE-time" and "MONTH-ly".
self_check: Did you avoid saying the customer was wrong? · Did you put the right meaning next to the wrong one? · Did you reassure them about what happens next?

sentence: still not working
speaker: Customer
situation: You gave the customer a fix a few minutes ago, and this is their whole reply.
recall_cue: A customer replies with three short words after trying your fix. What do they feel, and what is the worst thing you could send back?
linking: If read aloud: still_not → "stil-not" · not_working → "nod-WUR-king" (fast, flat)
intonation: If read aloud: flat and falling, with no question tone; it sounds tired and fed up, not curious.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "working" starts with rounded lips for "w", not teeth on lip; "wur-king", not "vur-king".
customer_emotion: Frustrated and losing patience; the fix did not help.
memory_hook: Think of a patient who comes back to the clinic holding the same bandage: the doctor must look again, not hand over another one.
hindi_meaning: अभी भी काम नहीं कर रहा।
hindi_roman: Abhi bhi kaam nahin kar raha.
simple_meaning: I tried what you said, but the problem is the same as before.
why_it_works: The short reply shows the customer is tired and starting to lose trust. They need you to own the next step and ask for new information, not repeat the same fix or send a long script.
key_chunk: I'm sorry it's still not working. Could you tell me ___?
grammar_pattern: (It is) still not + verb-ing (subject and verb dropped in chat) · Reply: I'm sorry + it's still not + verb-ing
grammar_note: In chat, people drop "it is"; "still" means the problem has not changed since last time.
tone_note: Reply short and specific to match their mood. A long, cheerful message or the same steps again feels like you are not listening.
watch_out: ✗ Please restart your device and try again. (the fix they already tried) → ✓ I'm sorry it's still not working. What do you see on the screen now?
dont_say: "Have you followed the steps correctly?" It suggests the customer made the mistake and makes them more frustrated.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please try the steps again properly", say "I'm sorry it's still not working. Could you send me a screenshot of what you see now?"
alt_1: Thanks for trying that. Let's look at it another way. What message do you see now?
alt_2: I'm sorry that didn't fix it. Could you tell me exactly what happens when you try it again?
more_formal: I apologise that the issue has not been resolved. Could you please describe what you see now, or share a screenshot, so that I can investigate further?
ask_next: I'm sorry it's still not working. What exactly do you see on the screen now? A screenshot would help.
replies_you_may_hear: still not working · same error · nothing happens
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I've tried everything, this is useless." → Agent: "I understand, and I'm sorry this has taken so long. Let me try one different step with you now. If that doesn't work, I'll hand it to our technical team within 10 minutes."
cultural_note: Agents sometimes reply with a long, formal script to a short message. In international chat, a short, specific and personal reply feels more like real help.
channel_note: Voice: the caller may sigh or speak slowly; acknowledge it ("I can hear this has been tiring"). Email: the subject may just say "Still not working"; reply with new steps, not the old ones.
when_not_to_use: Do not reply with the full troubleshooting list again; that is the right move only if you have not sent it before.
mini_conversation: Agent: Could you clear the app cache and try again? | Customer: still not working | Agent: I'm sorry it's still not working. Could you send me a screenshot of what you see now? | Customer: here | Agent: Thanks. That error is on our side, so I'm sending it to our technical team now.
source_rule: Empathy line, then action: acknowledge the frustration and take a new step.
fill_blank: I'm sorry it's ____ not working. Could you send me a screenshot?
mcq_question: A customer replies "still not working" after trying your fix. What does this message mostly tell you?
mcq_options: A) The fix did not help, and the customer is getting frustrated. | B) The customer has a new problem that needs different steps. | C) The customer did not follow the steps you sent them properly. | D) The customer wants to end the chat and is just being brief.
mcq_why: A: "still" means the problem has not changed, and the short reply shows frustration. C is tempting, but nothing says they skipped the steps; B and D read in things the message does not say.
reorder_task: still / I'm / sorry / it's / not / working
reorder_answer: I'm sorry it's still not working
hindi_to_english: Mujhe afsos hai ki yeh ab bhi kaam nahin kar raha. Kya aap mujhe screenshot bhej sakte hain?
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry it's still not working. Could you send me a screenshot?
whats_next_customer: same error as before
whats_next_reply: Thanks for checking. Since the same error keeps coming back, I'm sending it to our technical team now and will email you an update by 5 pm.
role_play: Partner B gives a fix; Partner A replies only "still not working". B replies with a short apology and a new, specific question, without repeating the old fix.
record_task: Record your typed reply to "still not working" read aloud, then explain in one sentence what the customer is feeling.
self_check: Did you acknowledge the fix did not work? · Did you avoid repeating the same steps? · Did you ask for new, specific information?

sentence: y is this taking so long
speaker: Customer
situation: The customer has been waiting in the chat while you check their delivery, and the last reply was a few minutes ago.
recall_cue: A customer types a short "why" question about the wait with no question mark. Is this really a question, and what do they need from you?
stress: WHY is THIS TAK-ing SO LONG
linking: If read aloud: why_is → "wai-yiz" · taking_so → "tay-king-so" · so_long → "so-long" (drawn out)
intonation: If read aloud: falling, not rising; it is a complaint shaped like a question, with stress on "so long".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "long" ends in a soft "ng" with no hard "g" ("lawng", not "long-g"); and "this" begins with a soft "th", not "dis".
customer_emotion: Impatient and feeling ignored during the wait.
memory_hook: Think of someone tapping their watch in a queue: they do not want a lecture on queues, just to know when it is their turn.
hindi_meaning: इसमें इतना समय क्यों लग रहा है?
hindi_roman: Ismein itna samay kyun lag raha hai?
simple_meaning: I have waited too long and I am annoyed. Tell me what is happening and when it will be done.
why_it_works: "y" for "why" and no question mark show a fast, annoyed message. It is more a complaint than a real question: the customer feels ignored and wants an apology, a reason in a few words and a time.
key_chunk: I'm sorry for the wait. I'm ___ now, and I'll ___ within ___.
grammar_pattern: Why + is + this + verb-ing + so long? (chat: "y", no capital, no "?") · Reply: I'm sorry for + noun
grammar_note: "so long" here means "such a long time"; "y" is chat shorthand for "why" that customers use, but agents should not.
tone_note: Answer with a short apology and a time, not excuses. "We have high volumes today" sounds like an excuse and makes it about you.
watch_out: ✗ Sir, please have patience, we are checking. → ✓ I'm sorry for the wait. I'm checking with the courier now and will update you within 2 minutes.
dont_say: "Please be patient." It tells the customer how to feel and gives no information.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please have patience, it takes time", say "I'm sorry for the wait. I'll have an answer for you within 2 minutes."
alt_1: You're right, it's taking a while, and I'm sorry. The courier hasn't replied yet; I'll update you in 2 minutes.
alt_2: Sorry for the delay. I'm still waiting on the courier, and I'll be back with you within 2 minutes.
more_formal: I apologise for the delay. I am waiting for an update from the courier and will reply within two minutes.
ask_next: I'm sorry for the wait. I'm checking with the courier now and will update you within 2 minutes.
replies_you_may_hear: ok · u said that before · fine but hurry pls
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "u said that 10 mins ago" → Agent: "You're right, and I'm sorry I haven't had an answer for you yet. If you'd rather not wait, I'll email you the answer within 30 minutes."
cultural_note: Agents may reply to an angry "y" message with "Sir, please have patience". International customers often hear "be patient" as a telling-off; an apology plus a time works better.
channel_note: Voice: "I know you've been waiting, and I'm sorry." Email: the subject might be "Still waiting!!"; reply with the reason and a firm date.
when_not_to_use: Do not reply with a long explanation of why the system is slow; one short reason is enough.
mini_conversation: Customer: y is this taking so long | Agent: I'm sorry for the wait. The courier hasn't replied yet, so I'll update you within 2 minutes. | Customer: ok hurry pls | Agent: Thanks for waiting. Your parcel is at the local hub and will be delivered tomorrow.
source_rule: Chat: reply fast, no excuses for delays, and give a real time.
fill_blank: I'm ____ for the wait. I'm checking with the courier now and will update you within 2 minutes.
mcq_question: A customer types "y is this taking so long". What do they most need from you?
mcq_options: A) A detailed technical explanation of why the system is slow today. | B) A polite reminder that good service takes a little patience. | C) A request to close this chat and start a new one with a fresh agent. | D) A short apology and a clear time for when you will reply next.
mcq_why: D: the message is a complaint more than a question, so an apology and a time answer the real need. A seems logical, but a long reason feels like an excuse; B tells them how to feel, and C sends them away.
reorder_task: the / for / sorry / wait / I'm
reorder_answer: I'm sorry for the wait
hindi_to_english: Intezaar karwane ke liye mujhe afsos hai. Main courier se check kar raha/rahi hoon aur 2 minute ke andar aapko update doonga/doongi.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry for the wait. I'm checking with the courier and will update you within 2 minutes.
whats_next_customer: just tell me when it will arrive
whats_next_reply: I want to give you the right date, and the courier's update will give me that. I'll message you within 2 minutes.
role_play: Partner A waits in a chat and then sends "y is this taking so long". Partner B replies within a few seconds with a short apology, a reason in a few words and a time.
record_task: Record yourself reading the customer's line in an annoyed tone, then reading your reply in a calm, sorry tone.
self_check: Did you apologise for the wait? · Did you give a clear time? · Did you avoid telling the customer to be patient?

sentence: ur website is broken
speaker: Customer
situation: A customer opens a chat with this line and gives no other detail about what they were trying to do.
recall_cue: A customer says the whole website is broken but gives no details. What do you need to find out before you can help?
linking: If read aloud: website_is → "WEB-sai-tiz" · is_broken → "iz-BRO-kn"
intonation: If read aloud: flat and falling; it is an angry statement, with heavy stress on "BRO-ken".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "website" begins with rounded lips for "w", not teeth on lip ("web", not "veb"); practise "west / vest".
customer_emotion: Annoyed and stuck; something they needed to do has failed.
memory_hook: Think of a patient saying "everything hurts": the doctor's first job is to ask "Where exactly?"
hindi_meaning: आपकी वेबसाइट ख़राब है।
hindi_roman: Aapki website kharaab hai.
simple_meaning: Something on your website is not working for me, and I cannot do what I wanted to do.
why_it_works: "Broken" is a feeling, not a diagnosis: usually one page or one button failed. The customer needs you to accept the problem and ask one clear question to find out where and what happened.
key_chunk: I'm sorry the site isn't working for you. Could you tell me which page ___ and what happens when ___?
grammar_pattern: Your + website + is + adjective ("ur" = "your" in chat) · Reply: Could you tell me + wh-clause
grammar_note: "Could you tell me which page you're on?" uses statement word order after "tell me", not "which page are you on".
tone_note: Accept the problem first, then ask. "Our website is working fine" argues with the customer and ends any trust.
watch_out: ✗ Our website is working fine from our side. → ✓ I'm sorry the site isn't working for you. Could you tell me which page you're on?
dont_say: "There is no issue with our website." It calls the customer wrong before you know anything.
positive_swap: Instead of "Website is working from our end", say "I'm sorry the site isn't working for you. Could you tell me which page you're on and what happens?"
alt_1: Sorry about that. Which page were you on, and what happened when you tried?
alt_2: I'm sorry you've hit a problem. Could you tell me what you were trying to do, and what you see on the screen?
more_formal: I'm sorry you're having trouble with the website. Could you tell me which page you were using and what happened, so I can look into it?
ask_next: I'm sorry the site isn't working for you. Could you tell me which page you're on and what happens when you try?
replies_you_may_hear: checkout page, it just keeps loading · cant login · the pay button does nothing
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "everything is broken just fix it" → Agent: "I'm sorry this is getting in your way, and I want to fix it quickly. If you tell me the last thing you clicked, I can find the problem much faster."
cultural_note: Some agents reply "Website is working fine from our end". Even if true, international customers hear it as "you are wrong"; accept their experience first.
channel_note: Voice: "I'm sorry about that. Which page are you on right now?" Email: ask for the page, the device and a screenshot in one short numbered list.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask for details when there is a known outage on your status page; tell the customer about it and when it should be fixed.
mini_conversation: Customer: ur website is broken | Agent: I'm sorry you're having trouble. Could you tell me which page you're on and what you see? | Customer: checkout, it keeps loading | Agent: Thanks, that helps. Could you tell me if you're paying by card or UPI?
source_rule: Paraphrase and clarify before solving; ask a clarifying question instead of a canned reply.
fill_blank: I'm sorry the site isn't working for you. Could you tell me which page ____ on?
mcq_question: A customer writes "ur website is broken". What is the best first reply?
mcq_options: A) Our website is working fine from our side, so the problem may be with your device. | B) I'm sorry about that. Please clear your cache and cookies, then try the site again. | C) I'm sorry about that. Please use our mobile app instead while we look into the site. | D) I'm sorry the site isn't working for you. Which page are you on and what happens?
mcq_why: D accepts the problem and asks for the facts you need. B and C offer a fix before you know what is wrong, which is a guess, and A tells the customer the problem is on their side.
reorder_task: page / Could / me / tell / you're / you / which / on
reorder_answer: Could you tell me which page you're on
hindi_to_english: Mujhe afsos hai ki aapke liye website kaam nahin kar rahi. Kya aap bata sakte hain ki aap kaunse page par hain?
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry the site isn't working for you. Could you tell me which page you're on?
whats_next_customer: i cant login at all
whats_next_reply: Thanks, that helps. Do you see an error message when you try, or does nothing happen?
role_play: Partner A writes only "ur website is broken" and gives details only when asked clearly. Partner B accepts the problem and asks short, clear questions until they know the page and the error.
record_task: Record yourself reading your reply aloud, then say in one sentence what you still need to find out.
self_check: Did you accept the customer's problem first? · Did you ask which page and what happened? · Did you avoid saying the website is fine?

sentence: i was promised a callback yesterday
speaker: Customer
situation: Another agent told this customer they would get a call yesterday, but no call came, and now they have opened a chat.
recall_cue: A customer says a promised call never came. What has gone wrong for them, and what must your reply include?
stress: i was PROM-ist a CALL-back YES-ter-day
linking: If read aloud: promised_a → "PROM-is-ta" · callback_yesterday → "KOL-bak-YES-ter-day"
intonation: If read aloud: steady and falling, with heavy stress on "PROM-ised" and "YES-ter-day"; it is disappointed, not shouting.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "promised" ends in "st" ("PROM-ist"), not "prom-ised"; and "yesterday" stresses the first syllable, YES-ter-day.
customer_emotion: Let down and losing trust because a promise was broken.
memory_hook: Think of a friend who waited all evening for your call: say sorry for the missed call itself, then fix a new time you will keep.
hindi_meaning: मुझसे कल कॉल बैक का वादा किया गया था।
hindi_roman: Mujhse kal callback ka vaada kiya gaya tha.
simple_meaning: Someone said you would call me yesterday, but nobody called. I am disappointed.
why_it_works: The customer is reporting a broken promise, so trust is low. They need a specific apology for the missed call, ownership from you now, and a new commitment with a time that you will keep.
key_chunk: I'm sorry you didn't get the callback you were promised. I'll ___ now. What time ___?
grammar_pattern: I + was + promised + noun (passive: someone promised me) · Reply: I'm sorry + you didn't get + noun
grammar_note: "I was promised a callback" is passive: it means "someone promised to call me".
tone_note: Own it as the company, even if another agent made the promise. "That was a different agent" pushes the blame away and makes it worse.
watch_out: ✗ That agent is not available, I can't say why. → ✓ I'm sorry you didn't get the callback you were promised yesterday. I'll arrange it now.
dont_say: "There is no note of a callback in the system." It suggests the customer is lying.
positive_swap: Instead of "I don't know why that agent didn't call", say "I'm sorry you didn't get the callback you were promised. I'll arrange it now; what time suits you today?"
alt_1: I'm really sorry nobody called you yesterday. I'll book the call myself now. When is a good time today?
alt_2: That shouldn't have happened, and I'm sorry. Let me set up the call now; what time works for you?
more_formal: I apologise that you did not receive the callback you were promised yesterday. I will arrange it now; what time would suit you today?
ask_next: I'm sorry you didn't get the callback you were promised yesterday. I'll arrange it now. What time suits you today?
replies_you_may_hear: anytime before 6 · why should I believe it this time · can't you just solve it here
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "why should I believe you this time" → Agent: "That's fair. I'll book it under my name for 4 pm and send you a confirmation now, so you have it in writing."
cultural_note: Agents sometimes explain internal reasons ("the team was busy"). International customers usually want a direct apology, ownership and a new time, not internal details.
channel_note: Voice: say the new time twice and confirm the number to call. Email: put the apology and the new time in the first two lines.
when_not_to_use: Do not offer another callback if you can solve the issue right now in the chat; offer to help immediately instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: i was promised a callback yesterday | Agent: I'm sorry you were left waiting for that call. I'll arrange it now. What time today suits you? | Customer: before 6 | Agent: I've booked a call for 4 pm today under my name, and you'll get a confirmation text now.
source_rule: Apologise specifically and take responsibility, then commit with "I will" plus a time.
fill_blank: I'm sorry you didn't get the callback you were ____ (starts with p) yesterday.
mcq_question: A customer writes "i was promised a callback yesterday". What are they mainly telling you?
mcq_options: A) They want to cancel their order because the delivery was late. | B) They want to know the name of the agent who made the promise. | C) They would prefer to talk on chat instead of on the phone. | D) A promise to call them back was broken, and they feel let down.
mcq_why: D: the passive "I was promised" plus "yesterday" means a commitment was not kept. B is tempting, but the name of the agent does not fix the problem; A and C add things the message does not say.
reorder_task: callback / get / I'm / the / didn't / sorry / you
reorder_answer: I'm sorry you didn't get the callback
hindi_to_english: Mujhe afsos hai ki kal aapko call nahin aaya. Main abhi call arrange karta/karti hoon. Aapko kaunsa time theek rahega?
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry you didn't get the call yesterday. I'll arrange it now. What time suits you?
whats_next_customer: can't you just solve it here in the chat?
whats_next_reply: Let me try. Tell me briefly what the call was about, and I'll work on it right now. If I can't solve it here, I'll book the call for you.
role_play: Partner A was promised a callback yesterday and is disappointed. Partner B apologises for the missed call, owns it and books a new call with a time and a confirmation.
record_task: Record yourself reading the customer's line with a let-down tone, then your reply with a sincere, firm tone.
self_check: Did you apologise for the missed callback itself? · Did you avoid blaming the other agent? · Did you give a new time you can keep?

sentence: can u do it or not?
speaker: Customer
situation: You have explained the exchange process in two long messages, and the customer still does not know if the exchange will happen.
recall_cue: A customer asks for a straight yes or no after your long explanations. What went wrong, and how should your next message start?
stress: CAN you DO it OR NOT
linking: If read aloud: can_you → "kan-yoo" · do_it → "doo-wit" · or_not → "or-not" (sharp)
intonation: If read aloud: rise on "do it", then a sharp fall on "or not"; it is a challenge, not a polite question.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: keep "not" short with a clear final "t" and a light English "t" (tongue behind the top teeth), not a heavy retroflex one.
customer_emotion: Impatient and confused by too much explanation.
memory_hook: Think of a traffic light: the driver only wants red or green, not a talk on how the signal works.
hindi_meaning: आप यह कर सकते हैं या नहीं?
hindi_roman: Aap yeh kar sakte hain ya nahin?
simple_meaning: Stop explaining and tell me clearly: yes or no, will you do this for me?
why_it_works: The customer is overloaded with detail and wants a clear decision. Start with "Yes" or a clear "No" plus what you can do, then give one next step; the explanation can follow only if they ask.
key_chunk: Yes, I can. I'll ___ now, and you'll ___.
grammar_pattern: Can + you + verb + or not? (chat: "u" = "you") · Reply: Yes, I can. · I'll + verb + now
grammar_note: "or not" at the end demands a yes/no answer; a short answer "Yes, I can" matches it exactly.
tone_note: A clear first word shows respect for their time. Another long paragraph before the answer feels like avoiding the question.
watch_out: ✗ Yes, I can do. I'll set the exchange now. → ✓ Yes, I can. I'll set up the exchange now.
dont_say: "As I mentioned earlier..." It sounds like the customer did not read properly.
positive_swap: Instead of "As I already explained, the process is...", say "Yes, I can. I'll set up the exchange now, and the pickup will be tomorrow."
alt_1: Yes. I'm booking the exchange now, and the courier will collect the old one tomorrow.
alt_2: Yes, I can do that. The exchange is booked, and you'll get a confirmation email in a few minutes.
more_formal: Yes, I can arrange that for you. I am setting up the exchange now, and you will receive a confirmation shortly.
ask_next: Yes, I can. I'll set up the exchange now, and the courier will collect the old one tomorrow.
replies_you_may_hear: ok good · finally · what time tomorrow
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "so why all those long messages?" → Agent: "You're right, and I'm sorry. I should have led with the answer. It's booked, and I'll keep the rest short."
cultural_note: Many agents explain the whole process before giving the answer, to be thorough. International customers usually expect the answer first and the details after, only if needed.
channel_note: Voice: say "Yes" clearly first, then one sentence. Email: put the answer in the first line, details below.
when_not_to_use: Do not say "Yes" if the answer is really no; say "I can offer a refund instead, because this item can't be exchanged" in one clear line.
mini_conversation: Customer: can u do it or not? | Agent: Yes, I can. I'm setting up the exchange now, and the old one will be collected tomorrow. | Customer: ok what time | Agent: Between 10 am and 2 pm. You'll get a text when the courier is on the way.
source_rule: Keep chat replies short and answer the question asked; give one clear next step.
fill_blank: Yes, I can. I'll set ____ the exchange now.
mcq_question: After two long explanations, the customer writes "can u do it or not?". How should your reply start?
mcq_options: A) As I mentioned earlier, the process is... | B) Sir, please read my previous message. | C) It depends on many factors. | D) Yes, I can. I'll set up the exchange now.
mcq_why: D answers the yes/no question first and gives one action. A is accurate, but repeating the process is exactly what frustrated the customer.
reorder_task: the / I'll / up / exchange / set / now
reorder_answer: I'll set up the exchange now
hindi_to_english: Haan, main kar sakta/sakti hoon. Main abhi aapka refund process karta/karti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: Yes, I can. I'll process your refund now.
whats_next_customer: do I need to pack the old one myself?
whats_next_reply: Yes, please put it in a sealed box or bag before the courier arrives. I'll email you the packing steps now.
role_play: Partner B gives a long explanation; Partner A replies "can u do it or not?". B answers in the first word ("Yes" or a clear "No" with an option) and gives one next step.
record_task: Record yourself reading the customer's line with an impatient tone, then your reply starting with a clear "Yes".
self_check: Did your first word answer the question? · Did you keep the reply to two short sentences at most? · Did you give one clear next step?

sentence: never mind then
speaker: Customer
situation: You asked the customer for their order number a second time, and they reply with just these three words.
recall_cue: A customer suddenly writes a short phrase that sounds like they are giving up. What could they mean, and what should you not do next?
linking: If read aloud: never_mind → "nev-er-maind" · mind_then → "main-then" (flat, quick)
intonation: If read aloud: a flat, falling tone; it can sound tired or annoyed, not relaxed.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "never" needs top teeth on the lower lip for "v" ("NEV-er", not "NEH-wer"), and "mind" ends with a clear "nd".
customer_emotion: Possibly frustrated and giving up, or the problem may have solved itself.
memory_hook: Think of a guest who walks away from the counter saying "Forget it": a good host asks "Wait, can I still help?" before they reach the door.
hindi_meaning: रहने दीजिए फिर / कोई बात नहीं।
hindi_roman: Rehne dijiye phir / koi baat nahin.
simple_meaning: Forget it. I do not want to continue this, or it does not matter any more.
why_it_works: "Never mind" can mean the problem is solved, or that the customer has given up because the chat feels like too much work. Do not just close: check gently which it is and make it easy to carry on.
key_chunk: Before you go, is ___ sorted, or would you like me to ___?
grammar_pattern: never mind = fixed phrase ("forget it") · Reply: Before you go, + yes/no question + or + would you like me to + verb?
grammar_note: "Never mind" is a fixed phrase meaning "forget it" or "it doesn't matter"; it has nothing to do with the word "mind" as in brain.
tone_note: A short, gentle check keeps the door open without pressure. "OK, closing the chat" accepts a possible failure as if it were a success.
watch_out: ✗ OK, thank you for contacting us, closing the chat. → ✓ Before you go, is the issue sorted, or would you like me to keep helping?
dont_say: "Okay, thank you for contacting us. Have a nice day." It ends the chat when the customer may still have the problem.
positive_swap: Instead of "OK, closing this chat", say "Before you go, is the issue sorted, or would you like me to keep helping?"
alt_1: I'm sorry if this has felt like hard work. If you'd still like help, I can find your order using your email instead.
alt_2: Sorry for the extra step. Just to check, has it been sorted, or can I still help? I can look it up by your phone number.
more_formal: I understand. Before we close, could I check whether the issue has been resolved, or would you like me to continue helping?
ask_next: Before you go, is the issue sorted, or would you like me to keep helping? I can look up your order with your email instead.
replies_you_may_hear: its fine i found it · forget it, too much hassle · ok use my email then
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "no just forget it" → Agent: "Of course. I'm sorry it was hard work today. If you need us later, just message us again and we'll pick it up."
cultural_note: Agents may read "never mind" as a polite goodbye and close at once. International customers often use it when they feel the help is too slow; one gentle check can save the contact.
channel_note: Voice: the caller may sigh and say "never mind"; ask "Before you go, can I try one more way to help?" Email: rarely seen; reply with one simple next step.
when_not_to_use: Do not push again if the customer has clearly said the issue is solved; thank them and close.
mini_conversation: Agent: Could you share your order number once more? | Customer: never mind then | Agent: Before you go, is the issue sorted? If not, I can look up your order with your email instead. | Customer: ok use my email then
source_rule: Check the issue is resolved before closing; don't treat silence or giving up as success.
fill_blank: Before you go, is the issue sorted, ____ would you like me to keep helping?
mcq_question: After you ask for the order number again, the customer writes "never mind then". What is the best reply?
mcq_options: A) Before you go, is the issue sorted? If not, I can use your email instead. | B) OK, no problem. Thank you for contacting us, and have a nice day. | C) I need the order number to continue, so please share it when you can. | D) Why do you not want help? I only need your order number to carry on.
mcq_why: A checks gently and removes the effort that made them give up. B sounds polite, but it may close a chat with the problem still unsolved; C repeats the demand that caused the problem, and D sounds like an accusation.
reorder_task: go / you / Before / sorted / the / is / issue
reorder_answer: Before you go is the issue sorted
hindi_to_english: Jaane se pehle, kya aapki problem solve ho gayi hai, ya main aur madad karoon?
hindi_to_english_answer: Before you go, is the issue sorted, or would you like me to keep helping?
whats_next_customer: its fine now, i sorted it out myself
whats_next_reply: Great, I'm glad it's sorted. If you need anything else, just message us again.
role_play: Partner B asks for an order number twice; Partner A replies "never mind then". B checks gently whether it is solved and offers an easier way, then closes or continues depending on A's answer.
record_task: Record yourself reading "never mind then" in two ways (relieved and fed up), then your reply that works for both.
self_check: Did you avoid closing the chat straight away? · Did you ask if the issue is sorted? · Did you offer an easier way to continue?

sentence: I can see this has been really frustrating, Daniel, and I'm taking it over now. I'll check your account and update you in two minutes.
speaker: Agent
situation: Daniel has sent three angry messages about a subscription that renewed after he cancelled it, and you have just picked up the chat.
recall_cue: An angry customer has sent several heated messages in a row. What three things should your first written reply do?
stress: i can SEE this has been REAL-ly FRUS-trat-ing · i'm TAK-ing it O-ver NOW · i'll CHECK your ac-COUNT · up-DATE you in TWO MIN-utes
linking: If read aloud: taking_it_over → "tay-king-i-to-ver" · check_your → "chek-yer" · update_you → "up-day-choo"
intonation: If read aloud: steady and low, falling on "frustrating" and on "now". Pause briefly before "I'll check" so the promise stands out. Do not sound cheerful.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "frustrating" is FRUS-tray-ting, stress on the first syllable. Make each "t" with the tongue tip on the bump just behind the top teeth, not curled back, so the word sounds light, not heavy.
customer_emotion: Angry and tired of repeating himself, expecting another useless answer.
memory_hook: Think of a firefighter arriving: "I see the fire", then "I'm in charge now", then "water in two minutes".
hindi_meaning: मैं समझ सकता/सकती हूँ कि यह सच में बहुत परेशान करने वाला रहा है, डैनियल, और अब इसे मैं संभाल रहा/रही हूँ। मैं आपका अकाउंट देखता/देखती हूँ और दो मिनट में आपको बताता/बताती हूँ।
hindi_roman: Main samajh sakta/sakti hoon ki yeh sach mein bahut pareshaan karne wala raha hai, Daniel, aur ab ise main sambhaal raha/rahi hoon. Main aapka account dekhta/dekhti hoon aur do minute mein aapko batata/batati hoon.
simple_meaning: I understand you are very annoyed. I am now responsible for this problem. I will look at your account and write back in two minutes.
why_it_works: It names the feeling without arguing, shows that one person now owns the problem, and gives a short, real time, so the customer has a reason to stop typing and wait.
key_chunk: I can see this has been ___, and I'm taking it over now.
grammar_pattern: I can see + (that) + present perfect · I'll + base verb + in + time
grammar_note: "Has been" (present perfect) shows the frustration started earlier and is still going on now.
tone_note: Naming the feeling and then acting sounds calm and in control. "Please don't be angry" or "There is no need to shout" tells the customer how to feel and makes things worse.
watch_out: ✗ I am understanding your frustration, I will check. → ✓ I can see this has been really frustrating. I'll check your account now.
dont_say: "Please calm down, sir, I am checking." — "calm down" adds fuel to the fire, and the line gives no time and no owner.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please don't get angry", say "I can see this has been really frustrating, and I'm taking it over now."
alt_1: I'm sorry this has dragged on, Daniel. I'm on it now and will update you within two minutes.
alt_2: That sounds really frustrating, and I want to fix it today. Give me two minutes to look at your account.
more_formal: I understand how frustrating this has been, Mr Hughes. I am taking personal responsibility for your case and will update you within two minutes.
ask_next: Thanks for waiting, Daniel. I've found the renewal, and I've started a full refund for it.
replies_you_may_hear: finally someone who listens · two minutes, not twenty · I've heard that before
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I've heard that before." → Agent: "I understand why you'd doubt it. I'm checking now, and I'll write back by 10:32 with whatever I find."
cultural_note: Many Indian agents open with "Sorry for the inconvenience caused"; international customers may hear it as scripted, so name the feeling and say what you are doing instead.
channel_note: Voice: say it slowly and drop your pitch a little. Email: add one line on what went wrong and a time for the next update.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it when the customer is only mildly confused and not upset; "Let me check that for you" is enough there.
mini_conversation: Customer: third time asking, why was I charged again?? | Agent: I can see this has been really frustrating, Daniel, and I'm taking it over now. I'll check your account and update you in two minutes. | Customer: fine | Agent: Thanks for waiting. The renewal was our error, and I've started a full refund.
source_rule: Empathy line, then action: name the feeling, never say "calm down", and give a real time.
fill_blank: I can see this has been really frustrating, Daniel, and I'm ____ it over now.
mcq_question: A customer has sent three angry messages in a row, some in capital letters. Which reply de-escalates best in writing?
mcq_options: A) Please calm down, sir, and give me a little time so that I can try to help you with this. | B) I'm sorry for the inconvenience caused to you. Your query is very important to us. | C) I can see how frustrating this is. I'm taking over now and will update you in two minutes. | D) There is no need to use capital letters. Please write politely so that I can help you.
mcq_why: C names the feeling, takes ownership and gives a time. B is polite but vague and scripted; A and D tell the customer how to behave, which usually makes them angrier.
reorder_task: over / I'm / it / now / taking
reorder_answer: I'm taking it over now
hindi_to_english: Main samajh sakti hoon ki aap bahut pareshaan hain. Ab yeh main sambhaalungi aur do minute mein update dungi.
hindi_to_english_answer: I can see you're really frustrated. I'm taking this over now, and I'll update you in two minutes.
whats_next_customer: two minutes, not twenty
whats_next_reply: Two minutes, I promise. I'll write back even if I'm still checking.
role_play: Partner A sends three angry chat messages about being charged after cancelling. Partner B replies once to name the feeling, take ownership and give a time, then comes back with a refund update.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your first reply to the angry customer and your follow-up message two minutes later.
self_check: Did you name the feeling without saying "calm down"? · Did you say you are taking it over? · Did you give a real time?

sentence: I'm sorry, Olivia. I'm not able to extend your free trial, because each account can have just one. What I can do is pause your plan for a month, free.
speaker: Agent
situation: Olivia asks in chat for a second free trial because she was travelling during her first one; your system allows only one trial per account but lets you offer a free one-month pause.
recall_cue: A customer asks for something the rules do not allow. In what order do you give the refusal, the reason and the option?
stress: i'm SOR-ry o-LIV-i-a · i'm NOT AB-le to ex-TEND your free TRI-al · each ac-COUNT can have just ONE · what i CAN do · is PAUSE your PLAN for a MONTH · FREE
linking: If read aloud: not_able → "no-tay-bul" · what_I_can → "wo-tai-kan" · pause_your → "paw-zyer"
intonation: If read aloud: a soft, falling tone on "I'm sorry, Olivia." Then fall gently on "one" to close the refusal, and lift your voice slightly on "What I can do" because the good news starts there.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "extend" ends in a "-nd" cluster; say both sounds (ex-TEND), not "exten". "Month" has a soft "th" with the tongue between the teeth, not "mont".
customer_emotion: Disappointed and a bit embarrassed to ask, hoping for an exception.
memory_hook: A closed door with a sign pointing to the open door next to it: "This one's locked; walk through here."
hindi_meaning: मुझे अफ़सोस है, ओलिविया। मैं आपका फ़्री ट्रायल नहीं बढ़ा सकता/सकती, क्योंकि हर अकाउंट को सिर्फ़ एक ट्रायल मिलता है। मैं यह कर सकता/सकती हूँ कि आपका प्लान एक महीने के लिए मुफ़्त में रोक दूँ।
hindi_roman: Mujhe afsos hai, Olivia. Main aapka free trial nahin badha sakta/sakti, kyunki har account ko sirf ek trial milta hai. Main yeh kar sakta/sakti hoon ki aapka plan ek mahine ke liye muft mein rok doon.
simple_meaning: I am sorry. I can't give you more free days, because every account gets only one trial. But I can stop your plan for one month without charging you.
why_it_works: The refusal comes once, with a plain reason, and the sentence ends on something the customer can actually have. The customer leaves with an option, not a closed door.
key_chunk: I'm sorry. I'm not able to ___, because ___. What I can do is ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm not able to + base verb + because + reason · What I can do is + base verb
grammar_note: "What I can do is…" moves the focus from the refusal to the option, so the customer reads the option last.
tone_note: The reason makes the refusal feel fair, not personal. A bare "Not possible" or "Our system doesn't allow it" sounds like a wall and invites an argument.
watch_out: ✗ It is not possible, that is our policy. → ✓ I'm sorry, Olivia. I'm not able to extend your free trial, because each account can have just one. What I can do is pause your plan for a month, free.
dont_say: "Sorry, that is not possible as per our policy." — it hides behind a rule, gives no real reason and offers nothing.
positive_swap: Instead of "We can't give a second trial", say "What I can do is pause your plan for a month, free."
alt_1: A second trial isn't something I can set up, as it's one per account. I can pause your plan for a month at no cost, though.
alt_2: I can't add more trial days, because the trial is one per account. Would a free one-month pause help instead?
more_formal: I'm afraid I'm unable to extend the free trial, as it is limited to one per account. However, I would be happy to pause your plan for one month at no charge.
ask_next: Would you like me to set up the pause now, starting today?
replies_you_may_hear: ok, pause it then · but I didn't even use it · can't you make one exception?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Can't you make one exception?" → Agent: "I understand why you're asking, and I'd like to help. The trial is one per account for everyone, but the free pause gives you a month to decide."
cultural_note: Indian agents often write "As per policy, it is not possible"; international customers may read that as hiding behind rules. Give the reason in plain words, then the option.
channel_note: Voice: say "I'm afraid" first to soften it. Email: give the reason, empathy, the option and a follow-up step, in separate short lines.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it if there is an exception process you have not checked; ask a supervisor before you refuse.
mini_conversation: Customer: can I get another free trial? I was travelling | Agent: I'm sorry, Olivia. I'm not able to extend your free trial, because each account can have just one. What I can do is pause your plan for a month, free. | Customer: ok, do that | Agent: Done. Your plan is paused until 14 November, and you won't be charged.
source_rule: Saying no: reason, then empathy, then an alternative. Don't hide behind "policy" (derived advice).
fill_blank: I'm sorry, Olivia. I'm not able to extend your free trial, because each account can have just one. What I can ____ is pause your plan for a month, free.
mcq_question: Which chat reply refuses a second free trial in the most customer-friendly way?
mcq_options: A) Not possible, ma'am. A second free trial is not available for any account, I'm afraid. | B) It is our policy that a second free trial is not allowed, so no exceptions can be made for you. | C) I'm sorry. Each account gets just one trial. What I can do is pause your plan for a month, free. | D) The system will not allow a second trial on this account, so you will need to buy a paid plan.
mcq_why: C shows regret, gives a real reason and ends with a real option. D blames the system and only pushes a sale; A is a bare refusal, and B hides behind policy instead of explaining.
reorder_task: do / What / is / can / I / pause / plan / your
reorder_answer: What I can do is pause your plan
hindi_to_english: Main trial nahin badha sakta, kyunki har account ko ek hi milta hai. Lekin main aapka plan ek mahine ke liye free mein rok sakta hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm not able to extend the trial, because each account gets just one. What I can do is pause your plan for a month, free.
whats_next_customer: but I didn't even use it
whats_next_reply: I understand, and I'm sorry you couldn't use it. The pause means you won't pay anything for a month.
role_play: Partner A asks for a second free trial after a holiday. Partner B refuses once with a clear reason, offers the free pause, and handles one "can't you make an exception?" message.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your refusal message and your reply to "can't you make one exception?".
self_check: Did you give a real reason, not "policy"? · Did you show regret before the refusal? · Did you end on what you can do?

sentence: I'm sorry you had to wait so long to reach us, Emma. That isn't the service we aim for. I'm here now, so let's sort out your refund.
speaker: Agent
situation: Emma waited about forty minutes in the chat queue to ask about a refund, and her first message to you says "finally".
recall_cue: A customer waited a long time in the queue and opens with "finally". What should your apology include, and how should it end?
stress: i'm SOR-ry you had to WAIT so LONG to REACH us, EM-ma · that IS-n't the SER-vice we AIM for · i'm HERE NOW · let's SORT OUT your RE-fund
linking: If read aloud: had_to → "hat-tuh" · isn't_the → "iz-n-the" · sort_out → "sor-tout"
intonation: If read aloud: sincere and slower on the apology, falling on "aim for", then a brighter, forward-moving tone on "I'm here now".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: keep the w in "wait" (rounded lips, no teeth on the lip) different from the v in "service" (top teeth on the lower lip), as in west and vest. Do not use one sound for both.
customer_emotion: Irritated and impatient after a long wait, ready to complain.
memory_hook: Picture a waiter who comes to a table that waited too long: "Sorry, that's not how we work. I'm here now — what can I bring you?"
hindi_meaning: मुझे अफ़सोस है कि हम तक पहुँचने के लिए आपको इतना लंबा इंतज़ार करना पड़ा, एमा। हम ऐसी सर्विस नहीं देना चाहते। अब मैं यहाँ हूँ, चलिए आपका रिफ़ंड ठीक करते हैं।
hindi_roman: Mujhe afsos hai ki hum tak pahunchne ke liye aapko itna lamba intezaar karna pada, Emma. Hum aisi service nahin dena chahte. Ab main yahan hoon, chaliye aapka refund theek karte hain.
simple_meaning: Sorry you waited so long. We should do better. I'm ready now, so let's fix your refund.
why_it_works: It apologises for the specific thing (the wait), admits it was not good enough, and turns at once to the customer's real problem, so the apology does not slow the chat down further.
key_chunk: I'm sorry you had to ___. That isn't ___. I'm here now, so let's ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm sorry (that) + you + had to + base verb · let's + base verb
grammar_note: "Had to wait" is past, because the wait is over; "let's" invites the customer to work with you.
tone_note: A specific apology plus a move to action feels honest. A long, repeated apology or "Due to high volume…" sounds like an excuse and wastes more of their time.
watch_out: ✗ Sorry for the delay caused due to high volume. → ✓ I'm sorry you had to wait so long to reach us.
dont_say: "We are experiencing high chat volumes, thank you for your patience." — it is an excuse, and it thanks them for patience they did not have.
positive_swap: Instead of "Sorry for the delay due to heavy traffic", say "I'm sorry you had to wait so long. I'm here now, so let's sort out your refund."
alt_1: Thanks for holding on, Emma, and I'm sorry it took so long. Let's get your refund sorted now.
alt_2: I'm really sorry about the long wait. You have my full attention now, so let's fix this refund.
more_formal: Please accept my apologies for the long wait, Ms Clarke. That is not the standard we aim for. I will now look into your refund.
ask_next: Could you share the order number for the refund so I can check it straight away?
replies_you_may_hear: 40 minutes!! · ok, at least you're here now · I almost gave up
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "40 minutes is ridiculous." → Agent: "You're right, that is far too long, and I'm sorry. Let me start on your refund straight away."
cultural_note: Indian agents often write "Sorry for the delay caused"; international customers may find it vague. Say what the delay was and move on to the fix.
channel_note: Voice: "I'm sorry you were on hold so long." Email: "I'm sorry it has taken us three days to reply," with the answer in the same email.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it if the customer reached you quickly; an unneeded apology sounds scripted.
mini_conversation: Customer: finally!! been waiting forever | Agent: I'm sorry you had to wait so long to reach us, Emma. That isn't the service we aim for. I'm here now, so let's sort out your refund. | Customer: ok it's order 58213 | Agent: Thank you. I can see it now, and I'm checking the refund status.
source_rule: Apologise specifically and take responsibility, then offer a fix; no excuses for delays.
fill_blank: I'm sorry you had to ____ so long to reach us, Emma. That isn't the service we aim for.
mcq_question: A customer has waited 40 minutes in the chat queue to ask about a refund. Which first message is best?
mcq_options: A) Due to high chat volumes there was a delay in connecting you, and we are working hard to improve it. | B) I'm sorry you had to wait so long to reach us. I'm here now, so let's sort out your refund. | C) Sorry for the inconvenience caused. Please tell me your query and I will assist you with it. | D) Thank you so much for your patience, we really do appreciate you waiting for us today!
mcq_why: B apologises for the specific wait and moves straight to the fix. D thanks an angry customer for "patience", which can feel sarcastic; A is an excuse, and C is a scripted, vague apology.
reorder_task: sort / let's / refund / your / out
reorder_answer: let's sort out your refund
hindi_to_english: Mujhe afsos hai ki aapko itna lamba intezaar karna pada. Ab main yahan hoon, chaliye aapka order check karte hain.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry you had to wait so long. I'm here now, so let's check your order.
whats_next_customer: I almost gave up
whats_next_reply: I'm glad you stayed, and I'm sorry it came to that. Your refund is the first thing I'll look at.
role_play: Partner A has waited in a chat queue for 40 minutes about a missing refund. Partner B apologises for the wait in one message and then moves straight to the refund.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your apology for the long wait and your next message asking for the order number.
self_check: Did you apologise for the wait itself, not "the inconvenience"? · Did you avoid excuses? · Did you move to the fix in the same message?

sentence: I want to sort this out for you, but I can only continue if we keep the language respectful. Shall we look at your booking together?
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer angry about a cancelled flight booking has started swearing at you personally in the chat.
recall_cue: A customer starts insulting you personally in chat. How do you set a limit without sounding angry or giving up on them?
stress: i WANT to SORT this OUT for you · but i can ON-ly con-TIN-ue · if we KEEP the LAN-guage re-SPECT-ful · shall we LOOK at your BOOK-ing to-GE-ther
linking: If read aloud: sort_this_out → "sort-thi-sout" · look_at_your → "loo-ka-cher" · want_to → "won-tuh"
intonation: If read aloud: even and low all through, with no rise of anger. Fall on "respectful", then rise on "together?" because it is a real yes/no question.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "together" has a soft voiced "th" (tongue between the teeth) — to-GE-ther, not "to-ge-dar". Stress the middle syllable.
customer_emotion: Furious and venting at the nearest person, feeling powerless about the booking.
memory_hook: A referee shows a yellow card, not a red one: "One warning, and the game goes on."
hindi_meaning: मैं आपकी यह समस्या सुलझाना चाहता/चाहती हूँ, लेकिन मैं तभी आगे बढ़ सकता/सकती हूँ जब हम भाषा सम्मानजनक रखें। क्या हम साथ में आपकी बुकिंग देखें?
hindi_roman: Main aapki yeh samasya suljhana chahta/chahti hoon, lekin main tabhi aage badh sakta/sakti hoon jab hum bhasha sammanjanak rakhein. Kya hum saath mein aapki booking dekhein?
simple_meaning: I want to help you, but I can only keep going if we both use respectful words. Let's look at your booking together.
why_it_works: It states the limit once, as a condition rather than a threat, and keeps the offer of help in the same message, so the customer can step back without losing face.
key_chunk: I want to ___, but I can only continue if ___.
grammar_pattern: I want to + verb, but + I can only + verb + if + present simple · Shall we + base verb …?
grammar_note: "If we keep…" uses the present simple for a real condition about what happens next.
tone_note: "We" and "together" make it a shared rule, not a punishment. "Mind your language" or "I will end this chat" sounds like a threat and escalates.
watch_out: ✗ Don't use bad words or I will close the chat. → ✓ I can only continue if we keep the language respectful.
dont_say: "Sir, you are being abusive, mind your language." — it labels and lectures the customer instead of setting a calm limit.
positive_swap: Instead of "Stop abusing me", say "I can only continue if we keep the language respectful."
alt_1: I'm here to help with your booking, and I'd like to keep going. Could we keep the conversation respectful?
alt_2: I can see you're really upset, and I want to help. I'll need us to keep the language respectful so we can fix this.
more_formal: I would like to resolve this for you, Mr Grant; however, I can only continue the conversation if it remains respectful.
ask_next: Thank you. I can see the cancelled flight now. Here are the two options I can offer you.
replies_you_may_hear: ok sorry, I'm just so angry · whatever, just fix it · don't tell me how to talk
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Don't tell me how to talk." → Agent: "I understand you're angry, and you have every reason to be. If the insults continue, I'll have to end this chat, but I'd much rather fix your booking."
cultural_note: Some Indian-English support scripts say "Kindly refrain from using abusive language"; international customers may hear it as a scolding. Use "we", state the limit once and keep the offer of help.
channel_note: Voice: say it slowly at a low pitch, with no raised voice. Email: rarely needed; reply only to the facts and leave out any insults.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it when the customer is angry but not insulting you; a customer who swears about the situation needs empathy, not a warning.
mini_conversation: Customer: you people are useless idiots | Agent: I want to sort this out for you, but I can only continue if we keep the language respectful. Shall we look at your booking together? | Customer: fine. just fix it | Agent: Thank you. I can see the cancelled flight now, and I have two options for you.
source_rule: Set the limit once, calmly and as a condition, then return to the solution (derived advice).
fill_blank: I want to sort this out for you, but I can only continue if we ____ the language respectful.
mcq_question: A customer starts insulting you personally. Which reply sets a limit best?
mcq_options: A) Mind your language, sir. I am only here to help you, and I will not be spoken to like this. | B) I want to sort this out for you, but I can only continue if we keep the language respectful. | C) I will not tolerate this behaviour. This chat is now closed, and I am ending it right away. | D) Please calm down and stop using that language so that we can continue with your booking.
mcq_why: B sets the limit as a condition and keeps the offer of help. D sounds gentle, but "calm down" usually makes angry customers angrier; A lectures and C ends the chat without a warning.
reorder_task: we / Shall / booking / look / your / at / together
reorder_answer: Shall we look at your booking together
hindi_to_english: Main aapki madad karna chahti hoon, lekin hum tabhi aage badh sakte hain jab baat izzat se ho.
hindi_to_english_answer: I want to help you, but I can only continue if we keep the conversation respectful.
whats_next_customer: ok sorry, I'm just so angry
whats_next_reply: That's completely understandable. Let's fix it: I can see your booking now.
role_play: Partner A is angry about a cancelled booking and sends one insult. Partner B sets a calm limit, then returns straight to the booking when Partner A apologises.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud the limit-setting message and your reply when the customer says "ok sorry".
self_check: Did you set the limit only once? · Did you keep an offer of help in the same message? · Did you avoid labels like "abusive" or "rude"?

sentence: Your notes stopped syncing because the latest update signed you out in the background. Once you sign in again, they'll all reappear.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer thinks a note-taking app deleted all her notes after an update; in fact the update signed her out without telling her.
recall_cue: A worried customer thinks her data is gone, but it is only a sign-in problem. How do you explain the cause and the fix in plain words?
stress: your NOTES stopped SYNC-ing · be-CAUSE the LAT-est UP-date · signed you OUT in the BACK-ground · once you SIGN IN a-GAIN · they'll ALL re-ap-PEAR
linking: If read aloud: signed_you_out → "sain-joo-out" · sign_in_again → "sai-ni-na-gen" · they'll_all → "thay-lawl"
intonation: If read aloud: falling on "background" to finish the cause, short pause, then a reassuring fall on "reappear".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: finish the clusters at the ends of "stopped" (-pt), "signed" (-nd) and "notes" (-ts); do not drop the last sound. "Syncing" is SINK-ing, with the c said as k.
customer_emotion: Panicked, afraid months of work have been lost.
memory_hook: The notes are not lost; the door just locked itself. Give the customer the key: sign in again.
hindi_meaning: आपके नोट्स का सिंक होना इसलिए बंद हो गया क्योंकि नए अपडेट ने बैकग्राउंड में आपको साइन आउट कर दिया। दोबारा साइन इन करते ही वे सब वापस दिखने लगेंगे।
hindi_roman: Aapke notes ka sync hona isliye band ho gaya kyunki naye update ne background mein aapko sign out kar diya. Dobara sign in karte hi ve sab wapas dikhne lagenge.
simple_meaning: Your notes are safe. The new update logged you out without showing it. Log in again and you will see them all.
why_it_works: It gives the cause in one short line, with no jargon, and ends with one action and a clear result. Plain language means easy to read and use, not dumbed down.
key_chunk: Your ___ stopped ___ because ___. Once you ___, ___.
grammar_pattern: Subject + past simple + because + clause · Once + present simple, + will + verb
grammar_note: "Once you sign in" means "as soon as you sign in"; use the present simple after "once", not "will".
tone_note: Cause, then action, then result calms a panicking customer. Words like "authentication token expired" or "user error" confuse or blame them.
watch_out: ✗ Once you will sign in, the notes will come. → ✓ Once you sign in again, they'll all reappear.
dont_say: "Your session token was invalidated during the client update." — it is jargon the customer cannot act on.
positive_swap: Instead of "You were logged out because you didn't update properly", say "The latest update signed you out in the background. Once you sign in again, they'll all reappear."
alt_1: Your notes are safe. The last update logged you out without warning, so signing in again will bring them back.
alt_2: Good news: nothing has been deleted. The update signed you out, and your notes will return as soon as you sign in.
more_formal: Your notes have not been deleted. The latest update signed you out in the background, so they will reappear as soon as you sign in again.
ask_next: Could you try signing in now and tell me if your notes are back?
replies_you_may_hear: oh thank god · I'm signed in but still nothing · why did it do that?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I'm signed in but still nothing." → Agent: "Thanks for trying. Could you pull down on the notes list to refresh it? If they're still missing, I'll check your account from here."
cultural_note: Indian-English support writing sometimes uses "re-login" or "login" as a verb; international customers may expect "sign in again" or "log in again" (the verb is two words), and everyday words rather than system terms.
channel_note: Voice: pause after the cause and check: "Does that make sense?" Email: number the steps if there are more than one.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it before you have checked that the data really is safe; never promise it will "reappear" if you are guessing.
mini_conversation: Customer: all my notes are GONE after the update | Agent: Your notes stopped syncing because the latest update signed you out in the background. Once you sign in again, they'll all reappear. | Customer: ok signing in... yes they're back! | Agent: I'm so glad. Is there anything else I can help with today?
source_rule: Plain language: explain the cause without jargon, then give one clear next step.
fill_blank: Your notes stopped syncing because the latest update signed you out in the ____. Once you sign in again, they'll all reappear.
mcq_question: Which explanation is clearest for a non-technical customer who thinks her notes were deleted?
mcq_options: A) Your authentication token expired after the client patch, so the app can no longer reach your data. | B) The latest update signed you out in the background. Once you sign in again, your notes will reappear. | C) This is a known issue with the latest release, and our engineers are looking into it for you now. | D) You did not sign in properly after updating, so the app has not loaded any of your notes yet.
mcq_why: B gives the cause in plain words and one clear action. A is accurate but full of jargon; D blames the customer, and C gives no action.
reorder_task: sign / Once / again / you / in
reorder_answer: Once you sign in again
hindi_to_english: Update ki wajah se aap sign out ho gaye the. Dobara sign in kijiye, aapke saare notes wapas aa jayenge.
hindi_to_english_answer: The update signed you out. Once you sign in again, all your notes will come back.
whats_next_customer: why did it do that?
whats_next_reply: I'm sorry it gave you such a fright. I don't know the exact cause yet, so I'll report it to our technical team today.
role_play: Partner A messages in panic that all their notes vanished after an update. Partner B explains the sign-out cause in plain words, gives one step, and checks the result.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your explanation, then your reply if the customer says "still nothing".
self_check: Did you avoid jargon? · Did you give the cause in one short line? · Did you end with one clear action?

sentence: I'm passing you to Rohan in our payments team, as he can fix the double charge. I've sent him a summary, so you won't need to explain again.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer was charged twice for one order, and only the payments team can reverse a charge, so you must hand the chat over.
recall_cue: You must hand a chat to a specialist. What three things should the customer learn from your handover message?
stress: i'm PASS-ing you to RO-han · in our PAY-ments TEAM · he can FIX the DOUB-le CHARGE · i've SENT him a SUM-ma-ry · you WON'T need to ex-PLAIN a-GAIN
linking: If read aloud: passing_you → "pa-sing-yoo" · sent_him → "sen-tim" · won't_need → "wohn-need"
intonation: If read aloud: steady and confident, falling on "charge" and again on "again"; no rising "is that okay?" tone, because you have already decided.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "charge" begins with a clear "ch" and ends in a soft "j" sound (charj); do not end it with an extra vowel like "char-ja".
customer_emotion: Worried about being bounced around and having to repeat the whole story.
memory_hook: A relay runner hands over the baton with a note taped to it, so the next runner knows the race.
hindi_meaning: मैं आपको हमारी पेमेंट्स टीम के रोहन से जोड़ रहा/रही हूँ, क्योंकि वह डबल चार्ज ठीक कर सकते हैं। मैंने उन्हें एक सारांश भेज दिया है, ताकि आपको दोबारा समझाना न पड़े।
hindi_roman: Main aapko hamari payments team ke Rohan se jod raha/rahi hoon, kyunki vah double charge theek kar sakte hain. Maine unhein ek saaraansh bhej diya hai, taaki aapko dobara samjhaana na pade.
simple_meaning: Rohan from payments will now help you, because he can remove the extra charge. I have already sent him the details, so you do not have to explain it all again.
why_it_works: It says who the customer is going to, why that person is the right one, and that the story has been passed on, so the transfer feels like progress rather than being bounced around.
key_chunk: I'm passing you to ___ in our ___ team, as ___. I've sent ___ a summary.
grammar_pattern: I'm + verb-ing (planned action) · as + reason · so + you won't + verb
grammar_note: "I'm passing you" uses the present continuous for something happening right now.
tone_note: A name, a reason and a summary sound organised and caring. "Transferring you to another department" with no reason sounds like getting rid of the customer.
watch_out: ✗ I will transfer you to other department, please wait. → ✓ I'm passing you to Rohan in our payments team.
dont_say: "This is not my department, transferring you." — it sounds like the agent does not care, and it gives no reason or name.
positive_swap: Instead of "I can't do refunds, you need payments", say "I'm passing you to Rohan in our payments team, as he can fix the double charge."
alt_1: Rohan from our payments team can reverse the extra charge, so I'm connecting you with him now. He already has all the details.
alt_2: I'm bringing in Rohan from payments, who can fix this directly. I've shared our chat with him, so there's nothing to repeat.
