more_formal: I am now transferring you to Rohan in our payments team, who is able to reverse the duplicate charge. I have shared a full summary with him, so you will not need to explain the issue again.
ask_next: Rohan will join in about a minute. Is there anything you'd like me to add to the summary?
replies_you_may_hear: ok thanks · how long will that take? · can't you just do it?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Can't you just do it?" → Agent: "I wish I could. Only the payments team can reverse a charge, and Rohan can do it in this chat, so it's the fastest way."
cultural_note: "Transferring to the concerned team" is common Indian business English; international customers may not know who that is, so name the team and the person.
channel_note: Voice: ask permission, brief the colleague first, then introduce the caller (warm transfer). Email: copy the colleague in and introduce them by name.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it if you can fix the issue yourself; an unneeded transfer adds effort for the customer.
mini_conversation: Customer: I was charged twice for order 77140 | Agent: I'm passing you to Rohan in our payments team, as he can fix the double charge. I've sent him a summary, so you won't need to explain again. | Customer: ok thanks | Agent: Rohan will join in about a minute. Thanks for your patience, Nikhil.
source_rule: Transfer warm: say who and why, brief the colleague, so the customer doesn't repeat themselves.
fill_blank: I'm passing you to Rohan in our payments team, as he can fix the double charge. I've sent him a summary, so you won't need to explain ____.
mcq_question: Which handover message is best when a payments specialist must take over the chat?
mcq_options: A) I am transferring your chat to another department now. Someone will reply to you soon. | B) This is not my department, so I am not able to help you with the double charge today. | C) I'm passing you to Rohan in our payments team, who can fix this. I've sent him the details. | D) Please explain your issue again to the next agent, so that they can help you properly.
mcq_why: C names the person and team, gives the reason and avoids repetition. A tells the customer nothing about who or why; B refuses without a next step; D makes the customer repeat the story.
reorder_task: him / sent / summary / I've / a
reorder_answer: I've sent him a summary
hindi_to_english: Main aapko technical team ke Dev se jod rahi hoon, kyunki woh aapka router theek kar sakte hain. Maine unhein ek summary bhej di hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm passing you to Dev in our technical team, as he can fix your router. I've sent him a summary.
whats_next_customer: how long will that take?
whats_next_reply: Rohan will join in about a minute, and I'll stay in the chat until he does.
role_play: Partner A was charged twice. Partner B decides payments must help, writes the handover message with a name, a reason and a summary, then answers "how long will that take?".
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your handover message and the two-line summary you would send to Rohan.
self_check: Did you name the person and team? · Did you say why they can help? · Did you promise the customer won't repeat themselves?

sentence: To keep your account safe, could you confirm the last four digits of your card? Please don't send the full card number or any one-time passcode.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer wants to change the email on their account, and you need to check they are the account holder before you make changes.
recall_cue: You need to verify a chat customer without putting them at risk. What do you ask for, and what do you warn them never to send?
stress: to KEEP your ac-COUNT SAFE · could you con-FIRM the LAST FOUR DIG-its of your CARD · please DON'T send the FULL card NUM-ber · or any ONE-time PASS-code
linking: If read aloud: keep_your → "kee-pyer" · last_four → "last-four", with a very light t · don't_send → "dohn-send"
intonation: If read aloud: rise on "card?" because it is a yes/no request, then a firm, falling tone on the warning about the passcode.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "last four" has a "-st" cluster before "f"; keep a light "t" (last), not "las". "Digits" is DI-jits, stress on the first syllable.
customer_emotion: Slightly impatient, and possibly unsure why so many checks are needed.
memory_hook: A bank locker: you show your face, not the key. Four digits open the chat; the full number and the code stay in your pocket.
hindi_meaning: आपका अकाउंट सुरक्षित रखने के लिए, क्या आप अपने कार्ड के आख़िरी चार अंक बता सकते हैं? कृपया पूरा कार्ड नंबर या कोई भी ओटीपी न भेजें।
hindi_roman: Aapka account surakshit rakhne ke liye, kya aap apne card ke aakhri chaar ank bata sakte hain? Kripya poora card number ya koi bhi OTP na bhejein.
simple_meaning: For your safety, tell me only the last four numbers on your card. Never type your full card number or a one-time code here.
why_it_works: It says why the check is needed, asks only for what is enough, and warns the customer about what scammers ask for, so the customer feels protected rather than questioned.
key_chunk: To keep your account safe, could you confirm ___?
grammar_pattern: To + base verb (purpose), + could you + base verb …? · Please don't + base verb
grammar_note: "To keep…" at the start gives the purpose before the request, which makes the request feel reasonable.
tone_note: Giving the purpose makes the request feel like protection. "Send your card details for verification" sounds like a scam and teaches customers an unsafe habit.
watch_out: ✗ Please share your card number and OTP for verification. → ✓ Could you confirm the last four digits of your card? Please don't send any one-time passcode.
dont_say: "Share your full card number and the OTP you received." — no genuine agent needs these, and it trains customers to fall for scams.
positive_swap: Instead of "Give me your card details", say "To keep your account safe, could you confirm the last four digits of your card?"
alt_1: For your security, could you tell me the last four digits of the card on your account? Never share the full number or a passcode in chat.
alt_2: Before I change anything, could you confirm the last four digits of your card? We'll never ask for your full card number or a one-time code.
more_formal: To protect your account, could you please confirm the last four digits of the card registered with us? Please do not share your full card number or any one-time passcode.
ask_next: Thank you, that matches. Which new email address would you like on the account?
replies_you_may_hear: 4471 · why do you need that? · I just got a code, do you need it?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I just got a code, do you need it?" → Agent: "No, please keep it to yourself. We'll never ask for a code in chat, and four digits are all I need."
cultural_note: Many Indian customers are used to OTPs for every payment, so they may offer one; tell them clearly not to share it, and use plain "one-time passcode" with international customers.
channel_note: Voice: say "To protect your account" first, slowly. Email: never ask for card details by email; send the customer to a secure sign-in instead.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it if your company verifies through a different method, such as the registered email; ask only what your process requires.
mini_conversation: Customer: I want to change my email | Agent: To keep your account safe, could you confirm the last four digits of your card? Please don't send the full card number or any one-time passcode. | Customer: 4471 | Agent: Thank you, that matches. Could you type the new email address?
source_rule: Verification: state the purpose ("To protect your account…") and ask only for what you need.
fill_blank: ____ keep your account safe, could you confirm the last four digits of your card?
mcq_question: Which verification message is safest in a chat?
mcq_options: A) Please type your full card number and the OTP we have just sent to your phone. | B) Please send us a photo of the front and back of your card so that we can verify you. | C) Could you confirm the last four digits of your card? Please don't send the full number. | D) For security, please confirm your card's expiry date and the three-digit CVV on the back.
mcq_why: C asks only for the last four digits and warns against sharing more. D looks like a normal check but asks for the security code; A and B expose full card details.
reorder_task: account / your / To / safe / keep
reorder_answer: To keep your account safe
hindi_to_english: Aapke account ki suraksha ke liye, apne card ke aakhri chaar ank bataiye. OTP kabhi share mat kijiye.
hindi_to_english_answer: To keep your account safe, could you confirm the last four digits of your card? Please never share a one-time passcode.
whats_next_customer: why do you need that?
whats_next_reply: It lets me check you're the account holder before I change anything, so nobody else can.
role_play: Partner A wants to change their account email and offers their OTP. Partner B asks only for the last four digits, explains why, and stops A from sharing the code.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud the verification message and your reply when the customer offers to send their code.
self_check: Did you give the purpose first? · Did you ask only for the last four digits? · Did you warn against sharing a passcode?

sentence: I'm sorry your last chat didn't go well. I'll pass your feedback to our team lead, and I'll make sure your address is updated right now.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer says the previous agent was rude and did not update their delivery address, and now they want it fixed.
recall_cue: A customer complains about a colleague who served them earlier. How do you respond without blaming or defending that colleague?
stress: i'm SOR-ry your LAST CHAT · DID-n't go WELL · i'll PASS your FEED-back · to our TEAM LEAD · i'll MAKE SURE your ad-DRESS is UP-dat-ed RIGHT NOW
linking: If read aloud: last_chat → "las-chat" · pass_your → "pa-shyer" · right_now → "rai-now"
intonation: If read aloud: low and sincere on the apology, then firmer and falling on "right now" to show action.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "address" is a-DRESS in British English (many Americans say AD-dress for the noun); end on a clean "s" with no extra vowel, and make "feedback" a clear final "k".
customer_emotion: Annoyed and let down, expecting to be ignored again.
memory_hook: One team, one shirt: you don't blame your teammate in front of the fans; you take the ball and score.
hindi_meaning: मुझे खेद है कि आपकी पिछली चैट ठीक नहीं रही। मैं आपका फ़ीडबैक हमारे टीम लीड तक पहुँचाऊँगा/पहुँचाऊँगी, और अभी आपका पता अपडेट करवाता/करवाती हूँ।
hindi_roman: Mujhe khed hai ki aapki pichhli chat theek nahin rahi. Main aapka feedback hamare team lead tak pahunchaunga/pahunchaungi, aur abhi aapka pata update karwata/karwati hoon.
simple_meaning: Sorry the last conversation was bad. I will tell my manager what you said, and I will fix your address now.
why_it_works: It accepts the complaint without blaming the colleague or arguing, shows the feedback goes somewhere real, and fixes the actual problem straight away.
key_chunk: I'm sorry your last ___ didn't go well. I'll pass your feedback to ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm sorry + (that) + past simple negative · I'll make sure + clause
grammar_note: "I'll make sure" is a strong promise that something will happen.
tone_note: Speaking for the company keeps it professional. "He is new" or "That agent was wrong" sounds like gossip and makes the customer doubt the whole team.
watch_out: ✗ Sorry, that agent is new, he doesn't know. → ✓ I'm sorry your last chat didn't go well. I'll pass your feedback to our team lead.
dont_say: "I can't comment on other agents." — it sounds defensive and makes the customer feel the complaint is going nowhere.
positive_swap: Instead of "That wasn't me, I can't comment", say "I'm sorry your last chat didn't go well. I'll pass your feedback to our team lead."
alt_1: Thank you for telling me, and I'm sorry that chat left you frustrated. I'll share this with my team lead and update your address now.
alt_2: That's not the experience we want you to have. I'll report it to our team lead, and I'll update your address myself right now.
more_formal: I am sorry that your previous conversation with us was not satisfactory. I will share your feedback with our team lead and ensure your address is updated immediately.
ask_next: Could you confirm the new address, including the postcode?
replies_you_may_hear: he was so rude · will anything actually happen? · just fix the address
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Will anything actually happen?" → Agent: "I'll send your feedback to our team lead today, and they decide what happens next. What I can do right now is make sure your address is correct."
cultural_note: Defending a colleague ("He is new, sir") can feel loyal, but international customers may hear it as an excuse, so speak for the company instead.
channel_note: Voice: thank the caller for telling you before anything else. Email: acknowledge the complaint in the first line and keep the fix in the same email.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it if the customer is reporting a serious issue such as harassment or fraud by staff; escalate it under your formal process instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: your last agent was rude and didn't even change my address | Agent: I'm sorry your last chat didn't go well. I'll pass your feedback to our team lead, and I'll make sure your address is updated right now. | Customer: 22 Mill Lane, Leeds | Agent: Thank you. That's updated, and your next parcel will go there.
source_rule: Take responsibility for the company (HEARD, often credited to Disney: apologise on its behalf), then act.
fill_blank: I'm sorry your last chat didn't go well. I'll pass your feedback to our team lead, and I'll ____ sure your address is updated right now.
mcq_question: A customer says the previous agent was rude. What is the best reply?
mcq_options: A) He is new, sir, so please excuse him. I am sure that he did not mean to be rude to you today. | B) I am not able to comment on other agents, but I will be happy to help you with your address now. | C) I'm sorry your last chat didn't go well. I'll pass your feedback to our team lead and fix your address. | D) Are you sure he was rude? He may have been following the process, so let me check the chat first.
mcq_why: C accepts the feedback, says where it goes and fixes the problem. A sounds kind but makes excuses for the colleague; B is defensive and D questions the customer.
reorder_task: team / pass / to / your / I'll / our / feedback / lead
reorder_answer: I'll pass your feedback to our team lead
hindi_to_english: Mujhe afsos hai ki pichhli chat achhi nahin rahi. Main yeh baat apne team lead ko bataunga/bataungi aur abhi aapka kaam karta/karti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry your last chat didn't go well. I'll pass this on to my team lead, and I'll sort it out for you now.
whats_next_customer: he was so rude to me
whats_next_reply: I'm really sorry you had that experience. I'll include exactly what you've told me in my feedback, and I'll update your address now.
role_play: Partner A complains that the last agent was rude and didn't update their address. Partner B accepts the feedback without blaming the colleague and fixes the address in the same chat.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your reply to the complaint and your message confirming the new address.
self_check: Did you avoid blaming or defending the colleague? · Did you say where the feedback goes? · Did you fix the real problem?

sentence: I can cancel that for you right away. Before I do, would the Basic plan help? It costs less and keeps all your saved files.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer writes that they want to cancel their cloud storage plan because it has become too expensive; you can see the cheaper Basic plan has room for all their saved files.
recall_cue: A customer wants to cancel because of price. How do you offer one option without blocking or pressuring them?
stress: i CAN CAN-cel that for you RIGHT a-WAY · be-FORE i DO · would the BA-sic PLAN HELP · it COSTS LESS · and KEEPS ALL your SAVED FILES
linking: If read aloud: cancel_that → "kan-sul-that" · right_away → "rai-ta-way" · keeps_all → "keep-sawl"
intonation: If read aloud: a falling, sure tone on "right away", then a light rise on "help?" because it is a genuine yes/no question.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "files" ends in a "z" sound (failz), and "saved" ends in "vd" with the top teeth on the lower lip for v; do not say "sev".
customer_emotion: Decided but slightly guilty, expecting a hard sell.
memory_hook: Hold the exit door open with one hand and point to a cheaper seat with the other: the customer chooses.
hindi_meaning: मैं इसे अभी कैंसल कर सकता/सकती हूँ। उससे पहले, क्या बेसिक प्लान से मदद मिलेगी? वह सस्ता है और आपकी सारी सेव की हुई फ़ाइलें बनी रहती हैं।
hindi_roman: Main ise abhi cancel kar sakta/sakti hoon. Usse pehle, kya Basic plan se madad milegi? Vah sasta hai aur aapki saari save ki hui files bani rehti hain.
simple_meaning: I will cancel if you want. But first, would a cheaper plan that keeps your files work for you?
why_it_works: It says yes to the request first, so the customer does not feel trapped, then offers one option that fixes their real reason (price) and leaves the choice with them.
key_chunk: I can ___ for you right away. Before I do, would ___ help?
grammar_pattern: I can + verb + right away · Before I do, + would + noun + base verb …?
grammar_note: "Before I do" uses "do" to avoid repeating "cancel"; it means "before I cancel".
tone_note: Agreeing first shows respect for the decision. Pushing several offers, or asking "Why do you want to leave?" again and again, feels like pressure.
watch_out: ✗ Sir, why you want to cancel? You will lose all benefits. → ✓ I can cancel that for you right away. Before I do, would the Basic plan help?
dont_say: "Are you sure? You will lose everything." — it uses fear instead of a real option, and many customers leave angrier.
positive_swap: Instead of "You will lose all your files if you cancel", say "Would the Basic plan help? It costs less and keeps all your saved files."
alt_1: Of course, I can cancel it now. One quick option first: the Basic plan is cheaper and keeps your files. Would that suit you?
alt_2: Happy to cancel today. If price is the main reason, the Basic plan might help, as it keeps your files for less. Shall I tell you more, or go ahead?
more_formal: I can certainly cancel your plan today. Before I proceed, may I mention that the Basic plan costs less and retains all your saved files?
ask_next: Would you like me to switch you to Basic, or shall I go ahead with the cancellation?
replies_you_may_hear: how much is Basic? · no thanks, just cancel · ok tell me more
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why are you trying to sell me something?" → Agent: "That's fair, and I'm sorry if it felt that way. I mentioned it only because you said price was the problem. Shall I go ahead and cancel now?"
cultural_note: Some sales-trained agents repeat the offer several times; international customers may find that pushy, so offer once and then respect the answer.
channel_note: Voice: pause after the question and let the customer answer. Email: confirm the cancellation and mention the option in one short line.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it when the customer is leaving because of a serious failure you caused; apologise and fix that first. Never say it "keeps all your saved files" before you have checked that it is true.
mini_conversation: Customer: I want to cancel, it's too expensive | Agent: I can cancel that for you right away. Before I do, would the Basic plan help? It costs less and keeps all your saved files. | Customer: no, just cancel please | Agent: Of course. I've cancelled your plan, and you'll keep access until 30 November.
source_rule: Lead with what you can do and keep effort low; offer one option, then respect the choice.
fill_blank: I can cancel that for you right away. ____ I do, would the Basic plan help?
mcq_question: A customer wants to cancel because of price. Which reply is best?
mcq_options: A) Are you sure? You will lose all your saved files and every benefit of your plan today. | B) Before I cancel, may I ask why you want to leave us? Your answer will help us to improve. | C) Cancellations cannot be done in chat, so please call our helpline on a weekday morning. | D) I can cancel that for you right away. Before I do, would the Basic plan help? It costs less.
mcq_why: D agrees first, then offers one useful option. B looks caring but delays the customer and feels like pressure; A uses fear and C blocks them.
reorder_task: right / that / cancel / I / away / can
reorder_answer: I can cancel that right away
hindi_to_english: Main abhi cancel kar sakti hoon. Usse pehle, kya sasta plan aapke kaam aayega?
hindi_to_english_answer: I can cancel that for you right away. Before I do, would a cheaper plan help?
whats_next_customer: how much is Basic?
whats_next_reply: It's half the price of your current plan, and all your files stay where they are. Would you like to switch?
role_play: Partner A wants to cancel a storage plan because of cost. Partner B agrees, offers the Basic plan once, and then cancels politely when Partner A says no.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud the cancellation reply and your answer when the customer says "no, just cancel".
self_check: Did you agree to cancel first? · Did you offer only one option? · Did you respect a "no" straight away?

sentence: You're right, and the mistake was ours: we used your old address. I'm sorry. I've already sent a replacement to your new one, free of charge.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer's parcel went to her old flat, even though she updated her address before ordering; you have checked the order history, can see the error was ours, and have already dispatched a free replacement to her new address.
recall_cue: The company clearly made the error. How do you admit it in chat in a way that is honest, short and already fixed?
stress: you're RIGHT · the mis-TAKE was OURS · we USED your OLD ad-DRESS · i'm SOR-ry · i've al-READ-y SENT a re-PLACE-ment to your NEW one · FREE of CHARGE
linking: If read aloud: mistake_was_ours → "mis-tay-kwaz-ours" · sent_a → "sen-ta" · free_of → "free-yuv"
intonation: If read aloud: firm fall on "ours", a short pause, a soft "I'm sorry", then a confident fall on "free of charge".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "ours" rhymes with "hours" and ends in "z"; "old" needs a clear final "d" — do not say "ol".
customer_emotion: Annoyed and ready to argue that it was not her fault.
memory_hook: Own it, say sorry, show the fix: three quick taps, like stamping "PAID" on a bill.
hindi_meaning: आप सही हैं, गलती हमारी थी: हमने आपका पुराना पता इस्तेमाल किया। माफ़ कीजिए। मैंने आपके नए पते पर मुफ़्त रिप्लेसमेंट पहले ही भेज दिया है।
hindi_roman: Aap sahi hain, galti hamari thi: humne aapka purana pata istemaal kiya. Maaf kijiye. Maine aapke naye pate par muft replacement pehle hi bhej diya hai.
simple_meaning: You did nothing wrong; we made the error. Sorry. A new one is already on its way to your new address, and you pay nothing.
why_it_works: It admits responsibility in plain words before the customer has to argue, apologises once, and shows the repair is already done. Lewicki's 2016 apology study ranked accepting responsibility and offering repair as the two most important parts.
key_chunk: You're right, and the mistake was ours: ___. I've already ___.
grammar_pattern: You're right + and + the mistake was ours + colon + past simple · I've already + past participle
grammar_note: "I've already sent" (present perfect + already) shows the fix is done, not just promised.
tone_note: Clear ownership ends the argument before it starts. "There may have been some issue at our end" sounds evasive and keeps the customer fighting.
watch_out: ✗ There was some issue at our end, sorry for it. → ✓ The mistake was ours: we used your old address.
dont_say: "It seems the system took the old address." — it blames the system and avoids saying "we".
positive_swap: Instead of "The system picked the old address", say "You're right, and the mistake was ours: we used your old address."
alt_1: That was our error, not yours: we shipped to your old address. I'm sorry. A replacement is already on its way to your new one, at no cost.
alt_2: You're absolutely right, we got the address wrong. I'm sorry about that. I've already sent a free replacement to your new address.
more_formal: You are quite right, and the error was ours: your order was sent to your previous address. Please accept my apologies. A replacement has already been dispatched to your new address at no charge.
ask_next: Would you like me to send the tracking link here, so you can follow the replacement?
replies_you_may_hear: thank you for admitting it · what about the parcel at my old flat? · when will it arrive?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "What about the parcel at my old flat?" → Agent: "You don't need to do anything with it. I'll ask the courier today to collect it, at no cost to you."
cultural_note: Agents trained to avoid admitting fault may write "some issue from our end"; international customers usually trust a plain "the mistake was ours" more.
channel_note: Voice: say "I'm sorry" slowly and sincerely, not quickly at the end. Email: put the admission and the fix in the first two lines.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it before you have checked what happened; admit a mistake only when you know it was the company's.
mini_conversation: Customer: my order went to my OLD address even though I changed it | Agent: You're right, and the mistake was ours: we used your old address. I'm sorry. I've already sent a replacement to your new one, free of charge. | Customer: oh ok, thank you | Agent: It should arrive on Thursday. I'll send the tracking link here now.
source_rule: Apologise specifically, accept responsibility, then offer repair (Lewicki et al., 2016).
fill_blank: You're right, and the mistake was ____: we used your old address.
mcq_question: The company sent an order to the wrong address. Which message admits the error best?
mcq_options: A) The mistake was ours: we used your old address. I'm sorry. I've already sent a replacement. | B) There may have been some issue at our end with your address, and we are looking into it. | C) The system picked up your old address by mistake, so the parcel went to the wrong flat. | D) Did you update the address correctly? Please check your account settings and try again.
mcq_why: A accepts responsibility, apologises and shows the repair. C sounds factual but blames the system; B is vague and D suggests the customer is at fault.
reorder_task: was / right / and / You're / mistake / ours / the
reorder_answer: You're right and the mistake was ours
hindi_to_english: Aap sahi hain, galti hamari thi. Maaf kijiye. Maine naya order pehle hi free mein bhej diya hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: You're right, and the mistake was ours. I'm sorry. I've already sent you a new order, free of charge.
whats_next_customer: can you make sure this doesn't happen again?
whats_next_reply: I've checked, and your new address is now the only one saved on your account, so your next order will go there.
role_play: Partner A's parcel went to their old address after they changed it. Partner B admits the company's mistake in one message, apologises once, and confirms the free replacement.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud the admission message and your reply to "what about the parcel at my old flat?".
self_check: Did you say "the mistake was ours" clearly? · Did you apologise only once? · Did you show the fix is already done?

sentence: I know today hasn't been easy, Mark. Your refund is confirmed for Friday, and I'll message you here if anything changes. Thanks for staying with me.
speaker: Agent
situation: After a long, tense chat about a faulty laptop, the refund is now approved, but the customer is still cold and short with you.
recall_cue: An angry chat is resolved but the customer is still upset. How do you close without sounding cheerful or scripted?
stress: i KNOW to-DAY HAS-n't been EA-sy · your RE-fund is con-FIRMED for FRI-day · i'll MES-sage you HERE · if AN-y-thing CHAN-ges · THANKS for STAY-ing with me
linking: If read aloud: hasn't_been → "haz-n-bin" · message_you → "mes-ij-yoo" · staying_with_me → "stay-ing-with-mee"
intonation: If read aloud: low and warm on the first sentence, steady and clear on "Friday", and a gentle fall on "staying with me". Avoid a bright, sing-song "Have a nice day!".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "Thanks" and "with" need a soft "th" made with the tongue between the teeth, not a "t" (tanks, wit).
customer_emotion: Drained and still a bit angry, though relieved the refund is coming.
memory_hook: Close the door gently, not with a bang: name the hard day, repeat the promise, leave the light on.
hindi_meaning: मैं जानता/जानती हूँ कि आज का दिन आसान नहीं रहा, मार्क। आपका रिफ़ंड शुक्रवार के लिए पक्का है, और कुछ भी बदला तो मैं आपको यहीं मैसेज करूँगा/करूँगी। मेरे साथ बने रहने के लिए धन्यवाद।
hindi_roman: Main jaanta/jaanti hoon ki aaj ka din aasaan nahin raha, Mark. Aapka refund Shukravaar ke liye pakka hai, aur kuchh bhi badla to main aapko yahin message karunga/karungi. Mere saath bane rehne ke liye dhanyavaad.
simple_meaning: I understand this was a hard day for you. Your refund is confirmed for Friday. I will tell you here if anything changes. Thank you for staying with me.
why_it_works: It recognises the customer's feeling instead of pretending all is well, repeats the one fact that matters (the refund date), and leaves a clear next step, so the chat ends on trust rather than tension.
key_chunk: I know today hasn't been easy. Your ___ is confirmed for ___, and I'll ___ if anything changes.
grammar_pattern: Present perfect negative (hasn't been) · is confirmed for + day · I'll + verb + if + present simple
grammar_note: "If anything changes" uses the present simple after "if", even though it is about the future.
tone_note: A quiet, specific close fits the mood. A cheerful "Have a wonderful day! 😊" after an angry chat feels like the agent was not listening.
watch_out: ✗ Is there anything else? Have a nice day! 😊 → ✓ I know today hasn't been easy. Your refund is confirmed for Friday.
dont_say: "Glad I could help! Please rate our chat 5 stars!" — it ignores how the customer feels and sounds like you care only about the score.
positive_swap: Instead of "Sorry for the inconvenience, have a nice day", say "I know today hasn't been easy. Your refund is confirmed for Friday, and I'll message you here if anything changes."
alt_1: I'm sorry today has been so stressful, Mark. The refund is due to reach you on Friday, and I'll update you here if that changes.
alt_2: Thank you for your patience through all this, Mark. Your refund is booked for Friday, and I'll keep an eye on it for you.
more_formal: I appreciate that today has been difficult, Mr Evans. Your refund is confirmed for Friday, and I will contact you if anything changes. Thank you for your patience.
ask_next: Is there anything about the refund you'd like me to check before you go?
replies_you_may_hear: ok. thanks · it shouldn't have taken this long · fine, bye
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "It shouldn't have taken this long." → Agent: "You're right, and I'm sorry it did. I've added a note so our team can see where the delay happened."
cultural_note: Many agents end every chat with "Sorry for the inconvenience, have a nice day"; international customers may hear it as copy-paste, especially after a tense chat.
channel_note: Voice: say it slowly and let the caller say goodbye first. Email: repeat the refund date in the subject line, too.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it if the issue is not resolved yet; then close with the next step and time, not a confirmed result.
mini_conversation: Customer: fine. is that it? | Agent: I know today hasn't been easy, Mark. Your refund is confirmed for Friday, and I'll message you here if anything changes. Thanks for staying with me. | Customer: ok. bye | Agent: Goodbye, Mark. Take care.
source_rule: Close by summarising the next step; return the goodbye; no emoji with upset customers.
fill_blank: I know today ____ been easy, Mark.
mcq_question: An angry chat has just been resolved, but the customer is still upset. Which close fits best?
mcq_options: A) I know today hasn't been easy. Your refund is confirmed for Friday, and I'll message you here if it changes. | B) Glad I could help, Mark! Your refund is confirmed for Friday, so now you can relax and have an awesome day! 😊 | C) Sorry for the inconvenience caused to you. Your refund has been processed and will be credited in due course. | D) Is there anything else I can help you with today? If not, please take a moment to rate this chat.
mcq_why: A recognises the feeling and repeats the key fact and next step. B is friendly but too cheerful for an upset customer; C and D are scripted and ignore the mood.
reorder_task: hasn't / today / I / easy / been / know
reorder_answer: I know today hasn't been easy
hindi_to_english: Main jaanti hoon aaj ka din mushkil raha. Aapka refund Shukravaar ke liye pakka ho gaya hai. Saath bane rehne ke liye shukriya.
hindi_to_english_answer: I know today hasn't been easy. Your refund is confirmed for Friday. Thanks for staying with me.
whats_next_customer: ok. bye then
whats_next_reply: Goodbye, Mark. Take care, and I'll be in touch if anything changes.
role_play: Partner A has spent an hour in a tense chat about a faulty laptop; the refund is now approved. Partner B writes a calm closing message and returns Partner A's short goodbye.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your closing message and your reply to "it shouldn't have taken this long".
self_check: Did you avoid emoji and cheerful filler? · Did you repeat the key date? · Did you say what happens if anything changes?

sentence: Hi Laura, I'm following up on yesterday's outage. Everything is working again now. Could you check your dashboard and let me know if anything still looks wrong?
speaker: Agent
situation: Laura reported that her online shop dashboard was down during yesterday's service outage, and you are messaging her the next morning.
recall_cue: The service was down yesterday and is now fixed. What does a good follow-up message tell the customer and ask them to do?
stress: hi LAU-ra · i'm FOL-low-ing UP on YES-ter-day's OUT-age · EV-ery-thing is WORK-ing a-GAIN · could you CHECK your DASH-board · if AN-y-thing STILL looks WRONG
linking: If read aloud: following_up → "fol-oh-wing-up" · check_your → "chek-yer" · let_me_know → "let-mee-noh" (very light "t")
intonation: If read aloud: friendly lift on "Hi Laura", a confident fall on "working again now", and a rise on "wrong?" because it is a yes/no request.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "working" and "wrong" start with a rounded-lip w, not v. "Outage" is OW-tij, stress on the first part.
customer_emotion: Still a little anxious and unsure if she lost any sales or data.
memory_hook: Like a doctor who phones the day after: "The fever's gone. How do you feel today?"
hindi_meaning: हाय लॉरा, मैं कल के आउटेज के बारे में फ़ॉलो-अप कर रहा/रही हूँ। अब सब कुछ फिर से चल रहा है। क्या आप अपना डैशबोर्ड देखकर बता सकती हैं कि कहीं कुछ अब भी गलत तो नहीं दिख रहा?
hindi_roman: Hi Laura, main kal ke outage ke baare mein follow-up kar raha/rahi hoon. Ab sab kuchh phir se chal raha hai. Kya aap apna dashboard dekhkar bata sakti hain ki kahin kuchh ab bhi galat to nahin dikh raha?
simple_meaning: I'm writing about yesterday's problem. The service works again. Please look at your dashboard and tell me if anything is still wrong.
why_it_works: The customer did not have to chase you. It says why you are writing, gives the good news first, and asks her to confirm, so any leftover problem is found early.
key_chunk: I'm following up on ___. Could you check ___ and let me know if ___?
grammar_pattern: I'm following up on + noun · Could you + verb + and + let me know + if + clause?
grammar_note: "Follow up on" means you are writing again about something from before; "on" is needed.
tone_note: A short, friendly follow-up shows care. "Please confirm the issue is resolved so we can close your ticket" sounds like you care more about closing the ticket than about her.
watch_out: ✗ I am following up for the outage of yesterday. → ✓ I'm following up on yesterday's outage.
dont_say: "Please confirm closure of your ticket." — it puts the ticket first and the customer second.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please confirm we can close the ticket", say "Could you check your dashboard and let me know if anything still looks wrong?"
alt_1: Hi Laura, just checking in after yesterday's outage. Everything's back up now. Is your dashboard looking normal?
alt_2: Good morning, Laura. Yesterday's outage is fixed, and I wanted to make sure your shop is running smoothly. Does everything look right on your side?
more_formal: Dear Laura, I am writing to follow up on yesterday's service outage. All systems are now working normally. Could you please check your dashboard and let me know if anything still appears incorrect?
ask_next: Thanks for checking. If you see any orders missing from yesterday, send me the order numbers and I'll look into them.
replies_you_may_hear: all good now, thanks · two orders are missing · what caused it?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "What caused it? I lost sales." → Agent: "I'm sorry it hit your shop. I don't want to guess at the cause, so I'll ask our engineers and write to you with what they find by 5 pm today."
cultural_note: Some agents write "Hope you are doing well" before every follow-up; that is fine, but international customers often prefer the reason for writing in the first line.
channel_note: Voice: a short call works for key accounts. Email: use a subject like "Follow-up: yesterday's outage" so it is not mistaken for a new issue.
when_not_to_use: Do not send it if the outage is not fully fixed; send a status update with the next time instead.
mini_conversation: Agent: Hi Laura, I'm following up on yesterday's outage. Everything is working again now. Could you check your dashboard and let me know if anything still looks wrong? | Customer: looks ok but 2 orders missing | Agent: Thanks for telling me. Could you send me the two order numbers? | Customer: 30512 and 30518 | Agent: Thank you. I'll check them and update you within the hour.
source_rule: Follow up proactively; say it is a follow-up, give the status, and give one clear next step.
fill_blank: Hi Laura, I'm following ____ on yesterday's outage.
mcq_question: The service outage is fixed. Which follow-up message is best?
mcq_options: A) Hi Laura, please confirm that you are happy for us to close your ticket about yesterday's outage today. | B) Hi Laura, I'm following up on yesterday's outage. Everything is working again. Could you check your dashboard? | C) Hope you are doing well. Yesterday's outage is done and dusted, so I will close the matter on my side. | D) We regret the inconvenience caused yesterday. Thank you for your understanding and patience in this matter.
mcq_why: B gives the reason, the status and one clear request. D is polite but says nothing useful; A puts the ticket first, and C is casual and vague.
reorder_task: following / I'm / outage / up / yesterday's / on
reorder_answer: I'm following up on yesterday's outage
hindi_to_english: Kal ke outage ke baare mein follow-up kar rahi hoon. Ab sab theek chal raha hai. Kuchh galat dikhe to bataiye.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm following up on yesterday's outage. Everything is working again now. Please let me know if anything still looks wrong.
whats_next_customer: two orders are missing
whats_next_reply: Thanks for checking. Could you send me the order numbers? I'll look into them straight away.
role_play: Partner B writes to Partner A, a shop owner, the morning after an outage. Partner A reports two missing orders, and Partner B asks for the numbers and gives a time.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your follow-up message and your reply when the customer reports missing orders.
self_check: Did you say why you are writing in the first line? · Did you give the current status? · Did you ask one clear question?

sentence: There's no fix yet, but your case stays with me. Our engineers are testing a solution, and I'll message you by 3 pm tomorrow with an update.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer's video calls keep dropping because of a known bug, the engineers have not fixed it yet, and the customer asks what happens now.
recall_cue: You can't solve the customer's problem today. How do you show ownership and give them something certain?
stress: there's NO FIX YET · but your CASE STAYS with ME · our en-gi-NEERS are TEST-ing a so-LU-tion · i'll MES-sage you by THREE P-M to-MOR-row
linking: If read aloud: there's_no → "theirz-noh" · stays_with_me → "stay-zwith-mee" · message_you → "mes-ij-yoo"
intonation: If read aloud: honest and level on "no fix yet", then firmer on "stays with me", and a clear, slower fall on "by 3 pm tomorrow".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "engineers" is en-ji-NEERS with stress on the last part, not EN-gi-neers; "There's" starts with a soft voiced "th".
customer_emotion: Frustrated and worried they will be forgotten once the chat ends.
memory_hook: Like a hospital nurse: "The doctor hasn't decided yet, but I'm your nurse, and I'll be back at three."
hindi_meaning: अभी तक कोई समाधान नहीं है, लेकिन आपका केस मेरे पास ही रहेगा। हमारे इंजीनियर एक हल टेस्ट कर रहे हैं, और मैं कल दोपहर 3 बजे तक आपको अपडेट भेजूँगा/भेजूँगी।
hindi_roman: Abhi tak koi samaadhaan nahin hai, lekin aapka case mere paas hi rahega. Hamare engineer ek hal test kar rahe hain, aur main kal dopahar 3 baje tak aapko update bhejunga/bhejungi.
simple_meaning: We haven't fixed it yet, but I am responsible for your case. The engineers are trying a fix, and I will write to you by 3 pm tomorrow.
why_it_works: It is honest that there is no fix, but it gives the customer something certain: one named owner and a time for the next update, which they can hold you to.
key_chunk: There's no ___ yet, but ___. I'll message you by ___ with an update.
grammar_pattern: There's no + noun + yet · I'll + verb + by + time
grammar_note: "By 3 pm" means "at or before 3 pm"; it is a deadline, not an exact time.
tone_note: A specific time sounds trustworthy. "We'll try to fix it soon, hopefully" sounds like nobody is responsible and nothing will happen.
watch_out: ✗ I will update you when there is some progress. → ✓ I'll message you by 3 pm tomorrow with an update.
dont_say: "Hopefully it will be fixed soon." — it gives no time and no owner, so the customer has nothing to rely on.
positive_swap: Instead of "We'll try to fix it ASAP", say "Our engineers are testing a solution, and I'll message you by 3 pm tomorrow with an update."
alt_1: I don't have a fix for you yet, but I'm keeping your case. I'll update you by 3 pm tomorrow, whatever the engineers find.
alt_2: The engineers are still working on this, so there's no fix today. I'm your contact for it, and you'll hear from me by 3 pm tomorrow.
more_formal: Unfortunately, a fix is not yet available. I will remain responsible for your case and will update you by 3 pm tomorrow on the engineers' progress.
ask_next: In the meantime, joining calls from the browser instead of the app should keep them stable. Would you like the steps?
replies_you_may_hear: so I just wait? · what if it's not fixed by then? · ok, thanks for being honest
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "What if it's not fixed by then?" → Agent: "I'll still message you at 3 pm with what the engineers know and the next update time. You won't be left waiting without news."
cultural_note: "At the earliest" and "ASAP" are common in Indian business English; international customers may read them as vague. Give a clock time and a day.
channel_note: Voice: repeat the time slowly and offer to call back. Email: put the update time in the subject line, too.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it if you won't be on shift to send the update; name the colleague who will, or give the team's contact instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: so when will my calls stop dropping? | Agent: There's no fix yet, but your case stays with me. Our engineers are testing a solution, and I'll message you by 3 pm tomorrow with an update. | Customer: so I just wait? | Agent: Not quite. Using the browser instead of the app should keep your calls stable until then.
source_rule: Use "I will" plus a time instead of "we'll try" or "hopefully soon"; give the next step.
fill_blank: There's no fix yet, but your case stays ____ me.
mcq_question: There is no fix for the customer's bug yet. Which message sets expectations best?
mcq_options: A) There's no fix yet, but your case stays with me. I'll message you by 3 pm tomorrow with an update. | B) We will do our best to resolve this as soon as we possibly can. Thank you very much for your patience. | C) Hopefully the engineers will have it fixed soon, and we will let you know as soon as they have done so. | D) It's with the tech team now and out of my hands, so please check back with us later today or tomorrow.
mcq_why: A is honest, names an owner and gives a time. B sounds committed, but "as soon as we possibly can" is not a time; C and D leave the customer with nothing certain.
reorder_task: stays / case / with / Your / me
reorder_answer: Your case stays with me
hindi_to_english: Abhi fix nahin hai, lekin yeh case main hi dekhunga. Kal 3 baje tak main aapko update dunga.
hindi_to_english_answer: There's no fix yet, but I'm keeping your case. I'll update you by 3 pm tomorrow.
whats_next_customer: so I just wait?
whats_next_reply: Not quite. Using the browser instead of the app should keep calls stable until the fix is ready.
role_play: Partner A's video calls keep dropping and asks when it will be fixed. Partner B says honestly there is no fix yet, takes ownership, gives a time, and offers a workaround.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud the ownership message and your reply to "what if it's not fixed by then?".
self_check: Did you say honestly that there is no fix yet? · Did you give a clock time and a day? · Did you show who owns the case?

sentence: Room upgrades are arranged by the hotel itself, so they can help you fastest. Here's their front desk number: +91 832 555 0147. Your booking reference is HT-5821.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer who booked a hotel through [Company]'s travel app asks you to upgrade her room, which only the hotel can do.
recall_cue: A customer asks you for something only another business can do. How do you redirect them without making them feel dismissed?
stress: ROOM UP-grades are ar-RANGED · by the ho-TEL it-SELF · they can HELP you FAST-est · here's their FRONT DESK NUM-ber · your BOOK-ing REF-er-ence
linking: If read aloud: arranged_by → "a-raynj-bai" · help_you → "hel-pyoo" · front_desk → "frun-desk"
intonation: If read aloud: helpful and steady, falling on "fastest"; slow down for the number and the reference so they are clear.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud: "hotel" is ho-TEL with stress on the second syllable, and "fastest" has two "st" clusters — say both clearly, not "fas-tes".
customer_emotion: Hopeful, and a little annoyed at being sent somewhere else.
memory_hook: A good receptionist doesn't say "not my job"; she walks you to the right door and hands you the key.
hindi_meaning: रूम अपग्रेड होटल ख़ुद करता है, इसलिए वही आपकी सबसे जल्दी मदद कर सकते हैं। यह उनके फ़्रंट डेस्क का नंबर है: +91 832 555 0147। आपका बुकिंग रेफ़रेंस HT-5821 है।
hindi_roman: Room upgrade hotel khud karta hai, isliye wahi aapki sabse jaldi madad kar sakte hain. Yeh unke front desk ka number hai: +91 832 555 0147. Aapka booking reference HT-5821 hai.
simple_meaning: Only the hotel can change your room, so contact them directly. Here is their phone number and your booking code.
why_it_works: It explains who can help and why that is faster, then hands over everything the customer needs, so the redirect saves effort instead of feeling like a brush-off.
key_chunk: ___ are arranged by ___, so they can help you fastest. Here's ___.
grammar_pattern: Noun + are + past participle + by + noun (passive) · so + they can + verb
grammar_note: The passive "are arranged by the hotel" puts the focus on the upgrade, not on what you cannot do.
tone_note: Giving the reason and the contact details feels helpful. "That's not our department" or "We don't handle that" sounds like you don't care.
watch_out: ✗ We don't do upgrades, you call hotel yourself. → ✓ Room upgrades are arranged by the hotel itself, so they can help you fastest.
dont_say: "That's not our department, please contact the hotel." — it refuses without a reason and leaves the customer to find the details.
positive_swap: Instead of "We can't do upgrades", say "Room upgrades are arranged by the hotel itself, so they can help you fastest."
alt_1: The hotel handles upgrades directly, so they're the quickest people to ask. Their front desk number is +91 832 555 0147, and your reference is HT-5821.
alt_2: Upgrades are up to the hotel, so I'd contact them first. Here's their number: +91 832 555 0147. Quote your booking reference HT-5821 and they'll find you straight away.
more_formal: Room upgrades are managed directly by the hotel, so they will be able to assist you most quickly. Their front desk can be reached on +91 832 555 0147, and your booking reference is HT-5821.
ask_next: If the upgrade changes your price, let me know and I'll update your booking on our side.
replies_you_may_hear: can't you call them for me? · ok, thanks · I booked with you, not them
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I booked with you, not them." → Agent: "That's fair, and I'm still here for anything about your booking. The hotel controls which rooms are free, so they can confirm an upgrade on the spot."
cultural_note: "Not in our scope" is common in Indian business English; international customers may hear it as a refusal to help. Say who can help and give the details.
channel_note: Voice: offer to transfer or conference the hotel in if your system allows it. Email: put the contact details on separate lines so they are easy to copy.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it if [Company] can request the upgrade itself; never redirect a customer when you could help directly.
mini_conversation: Customer: can you upgrade my room to a sea view? | Agent: Room upgrades are arranged by the hotel itself, so they can help you fastest. Here's their front desk number: +91 832 555 0147. Your booking reference is HT-5821. | Customer: can't you call them for me? | Agent: I'm not able to request upgrades, but if the price changes, I'll update your booking on our side straight away.
source_rule: Lead with what is possible; give the reason in plain words, then an alternative.
fill_blank: Room upgrades are arranged ____ the hotel itself, so they can help you fastest.
mcq_question: A customer asks you to upgrade a hotel room, but only the hotel can do it. Which reply is best?
mcq_options: A) That's not our department, I'm afraid. You will need to sort out any room upgrade with the hotel yourself. | B) Room upgrades are arranged by the hotel, so they can help you fastest. Their front desk number is +91 832 555 0147. | C) Please contact the hotel directly regarding your request, as they will be able to assist you with it today. | D) We don't do upgrades, sorry. It's a hotel matter, so you will have to ask them yourself when you arrive.
mcq_why: B explains who can help and why, and gives the number. C sounds polite but gives nothing to act on; A and D just refuse.
reorder_task: help / They / you / can / fastest
reorder_answer: They can help you fastest
hindi_to_english: Yeh kaam aapka bank karta hai, isliye wahi jaldi madad kar sakte hain. Main aapko payment reference bhej deti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: Your bank handles this, so they can help you fastest. I'll send you the payment reference to give them.
whats_next_customer: what if the hotel says no?
whats_next_reply: Then your booking stays exactly as it is, and the price doesn't change. If you'd like, I can check which nearby hotels have sea-view rooms.
role_play: Partner A asks the travel-app agent for a sea-view upgrade. Partner B explains that the hotel arranges upgrades, gives the number and reference, and answers "I booked with you, not them".
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud the redirect message and your reply to "I booked with you, not them".
self_check: Did you say who can help and why? · Did you give the contact details and reference? · Did you avoid "not our department"?

sentence: I want a refund NOW
speaker: Customer
situation: Halfway through a chat about a late delivery, the customer suddenly types this, with "NOW" in capital letters.
recall_cue: A customer writes one word in capital letters at the end of a demand. What does that tell you, and what must your reply include?
linking: If read aloud: want_a → "won-ta" · a_refund → "uh-REE-fund"
intonation: If read aloud: hard and loud, with heavy stress on "NOW"; the capitals mean shouting.
indian_pron_tip: If you say "refund" in your reply, the noun is stressed on the first part: REE-fund. The verb is re-FUND ("we'll re-FUND you").
customer_emotion: Out of patience, feeling ignored, and wanting control back.
memory_hook: Capital letters are a raised voice on a screen: answer the volume with calm, and the demand with a clear yes, no or when.
hindi_meaning: मुझे अभी रिफ़ंड चाहिए।
hindi_roman: Mujhe abhi refund chahiye.
simple_meaning: Give me my money back immediately. The capital letters show the customer is shouting because they are angry.
why_it_works: The customer feels the chat is going nowhere. They need a direct answer: whether you can refund, what you are doing this minute, and when the money will arrive — not more questions or a script.
key_chunk: I want a ___ NOW = I want it immediately, and I'm angry
grammar_pattern: I want + a + noun + NOW (capitals = shouting in writing)
grammar_note: Capitals on one word add strong stress, like raising your voice on that word.
tone_note: Reply with calm, plain words and a clear action. Telling the customer not to use capitals, or copying their tone, makes the chat worse.
watch_out: ✗ Sir, please don't use capital letters. → ✓ I understand you want this settled now. I can start the refund straight away.
dont_say: "Refunds take 7–10 working days as per policy." — it ignores the feeling, hides behind a rule and says nothing about what you are doing now.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please wait, refund process takes time", say "I can start your refund right now. It should reach your card within 5 working days."
alt_1: just give me my money back
alt_2: refund me right NOW
more_formal: I would like a full refund immediately, please.
ask_next: I understand you want this settled now. I've checked your order, and I can refund the full amount today. It should reach your card within 5 working days. Shall I go ahead?
replies_you_may_hear: yes do it · 5 days?? I want it today · why couldn't you say that before
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "5 days?? I want it today." → Agent: "I'm sending it today. Your bank then takes up to 5 working days to show it, and I'll email you the refund confirmation now so you have proof."
cultural_note: Capital letters read as shouting to every English reader, Indian or international. The customer is not being "rude" on purpose; they feel unheard.
channel_note: Voice: the caller will raise their voice; lower yours and slow down. Email: subject lines like "REFUND NOW!!!" need a reply within hours, with a clear action.
when_not_to_use: Do not reply with a refund promise if the order is not eligible; then say clearly what you can do instead and by when.
mini_conversation: Customer: I want a refund NOW | Agent: I understand you want this settled now. I've checked your order, and I can refund the full amount today. It should reach your card within 5 working days. Shall I go ahead? | Customer: yes | Agent: Done. Your refund reference is RF-3097, and I've emailed you the confirmation.
source_rule: If the customer sounds urgent, reply briefly and at once; empathy line, then action and a time.
fill_blank: I've checked your order, and I can refund the full amount today. Shall I go ____?
mcq_question: What does the customer most likely mean by writing "NOW" in capitals?
mcq_options: A) They pressed the caps lock key by mistake while typing quickly | B) They are adding emphasis, but they are calm and happy to wait a little | C) They are asking you to check the delivery time for the late parcel | D) They are shouting because they feel ignored and want action at once
mcq_why: Capitals in chat show shouting and strong feeling. A is tempting because people do mistype, but one word in capitals at the end of a demand is deliberate; B and C ignore the demand.
reorder_task: refund / I / today / can / you
reorder_answer: I can refund you today
hindi_to_english: Main samajh sakti hoon ki aap yeh abhi suljhana chahte hain. Main aaj hi aapka refund kar sakti hoon. Kya main aage badhoon?
hindi_to_english_answer: I understand you want this settled now. I can refund you today. Shall I go ahead?
whats_next_customer: why couldn't you say that before
whats_next_reply: I'm sorry it took this long. I wanted to check your order first, and the refund is now on its way.
role_play: Partner A types "I want a refund NOW" after a late delivery. Partner B replies calmly with a clear yes, what happens today and when the money arrives, then handles "5 days??".
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your first reply to "I want a refund NOW" and your answer to "5 days?? I want it today".
self_check: Did you avoid commenting on the capital letters? · Did you say clearly what you can do today? · Did you give a time for the money?

sentence: this is a joke
speaker: Customer
situation: You have just told a customer that their repair will take another two weeks, and they reply with this; your system shows a loan device can be sent for long repairs.
recall_cue: A customer replies to bad news with a short sarcastic line. Is it really about humour, and what do they want from you?
linking: If read aloud: this_is_a → "thi-si-za" · a_joke → "uh-johk"
intonation: If read aloud: flat and falling, slow and tired; it is disgust, not laughter.
indian_pron_tip: If you read it aloud, "joke" has a long "oh" sound (johk), not a short "jok"; "this" starts with a soft "th", not "dis".
customer_emotion: Disappointed and insulted, feeling the company does not take them seriously.
memory_hook: Nobody is laughing: "this is a joke" means "this is so bad it can't be serious".
hindi_meaning: यह तो मज़ाक है। (मतलब: यह बिल्कुल बेकार और बेतुका है।)
hindi_roman: Yeh to mazaak hai. (Matlab: yeh bilkul bekaar aur betuka hai.)
simple_meaning: This is ridiculous and unacceptable. The customer is not joking; they mean the service is so bad it feels unreal.
why_it_works: The customer feels let down and not taken seriously. They need you to agree that the wait is too long, without arguing, and then to offer something concrete: a faster option, a loan item or a firm date.
key_chunk: this is a joke = this is unacceptable / ridiculous
grammar_pattern: This + is + a + joke (sarcasm: says the opposite of serious)
grammar_note: Sarcasm uses words that sound light to show strong annoyance; read it as a complaint.
tone_note: Treat it as a serious complaint. Replying with a laugh, "😊", or "It's not a joke, sir" misses the point and sounds mocking.
watch_out: ✗ No sir, it is not a joke, it is our process. → ✓ I understand, two more weeks is a long time. Here's what I can do.
dont_say: "Sorry, but this is our standard repair time." — it defends the process and ignores the feeling.
positive_swap: Instead of "That is the standard time", say "You're right, two more weeks is a long wait. Here's what I can do to help."
alt_1: are you kidding me
alt_2: unbelievable, are you serious?
more_formal: I find this completely unacceptable.
ask_next: You're right, two more weeks is a long wait. What I can do is send you a loan device tomorrow, so you're not left without one. Would that help?
replies_you_may_hear: yes, that would help · I don't want a loan, I want mine back · why does it take so long?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why does it take so long?" → Agent: "The part has to come from the manufacturer. I'll check its delivery date today and message you with it by 5 pm, and again the moment your device is fixed."
cultural_note: Customers in many English-speaking countries use sarcasm in complaints, and it is easy to read it literally when English is not your first language. "This is a joke" is almost never about humour.
channel_note: Voice: you will hear a flat, tired tone; slow down and lower your voice. Email: it may appear as "Is this some kind of joke?" — answer the complaint, not the question.
when_not_to_use: Do not read it as a complaint if the customer adds "lol" after a real joke in a friendly chat; check the context.
mini_conversation: Customer: this is a joke | Agent: You're right, two more weeks is a long wait. What I can do is send you a loan device tomorrow, so you're not left without one. Would that help? | Customer: yes ok | Agent: Done. It will arrive by 1 pm tomorrow, and I'll send the tracking link here.
source_rule: Empathy line, then action; lead with what you can do, never defend the process alone.
fill_blank: You're right, two more weeks is a long ____ (starts with w). What I can do is send you a loan device tomorrow.
mcq_question: After hearing about a two-week delay, a customer writes "this is a joke". What do they mean?
mcq_options: A) They found your message funny and are laughing about it with you | B) They are making a friendly joke and expect you to joke back now | C) They are pleased but surprised that the repair takes two weeks | D) They think the delay is unacceptable and feel let down by it
mcq_why: It is sarcasm for "this is unacceptable". A and B take the words literally, and C ignores the bad news; the context of a two-week delay shows strong annoyance.
reorder_task: do / what / I / Here's / can
reorder_answer: Here's what I can do
hindi_to_english: Aap sahi hain, do hafte bahut lamba intezaar hai. Main yeh kar sakti hoon: kal aapko ek loan device bhej deti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: You're right, two weeks is a long wait. Here's what I can do: I'll send you a loan device tomorrow.
whats_next_customer: I don't want a loan, I want mine back
whats_next_reply: I understand, and your own device is still our priority. The loan is only so you're not left without one, and I'll message you the day yours is ready.
role_play: Partner B tells Partner A their repair needs two more weeks. Partner A replies "this is a joke". Partner B agrees the wait is long and offers a loan device.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your reply to "this is a joke" and your answer to "why does it take so long?".
self_check: Did you treat it as a complaint, not humour? · Did you agree without arguing? · Did you offer something concrete?

sentence: your bot was useless
speaker: Customer
situation: A customer is passed to you after ten minutes with the automated chatbot, which kept sending the same help article.
recall_cue: A customer reaches a human after a chatbot failed them. What are they really feeling, and what should you avoid making them do?
linking: If read aloud: bot_was → "bot-wuz" · was_useless → "wuz-YOOS-lus"
intonation: If read aloud: flat, annoyed, falling on "useless".
indian_pron_tip: If you read it aloud, "was" starts with a rounded-lip w (not v) and ends in a "z" sound; "useless" is YOOS-lus, stress on the first part.
customer_emotion: Fed up after wasted time and afraid they must start all over again.
memory_hook: The customer has already climbed one wrong staircase: don't send them back to the bottom.
hindi_meaning: आपका बॉट बिल्कुल बेकार था।
hindi_roman: Aapka bot bilkul bekaar tha.
simple_meaning: The automatic chat did not help me at all. I wasted time, and I want a real person to fix it.
why_it_works: The customer is tired of repeating themselves and fears starting again. They need a real person who has read what they already typed, agrees without excuses, and moves straight to the problem.
key_chunk: your bot was useless = the automated help didn't solve my problem
grammar_pattern: Your + noun + was + adjective (past: the bad experience is over)
grammar_note: "Was" shows the bot conversation is finished; now they expect something different.
tone_note: Agree briefly and act. Defending the bot ("It is very helpful for most customers") or asking them to explain everything again feels like a second failure.
watch_out: ✗ Our bot helps many customers, please try it again, sir. → ✓ I'm sorry it didn't help. I can see what you wrote, so let's fix it now.
dont_say: "Please explain your issue again." — it ignores what the customer already typed and repeats the bot's failure.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please tell me your issue from the start", say "I can see what you told the bot, so you won't need to repeat it."
alt_1: the chatbot was no help at all
alt_2: finally a human. that bot kept sending me one link
more_formal: The automated assistant was unable to help me with my issue.
ask_next: I'm sorry it didn't help. I can see you're trying to change your delivery date, so let's do that now. Which day suits you?
replies_you_may_hear: thank god a real person · I've explained it 3 times already · ok, Thursday
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I've explained it 3 times already." → Agent: "I know, and I'm sorry. I've read the whole conversation, so you won't need to explain again. I'm changing the date now."
cultural_note: Replies such as "Please tell your issue" can be heard in Indian-English support chats; after a bot failure, international customers may find them abrupt, so show that you have already read their messages.
channel_note: Voice: "Your automated system was useless" after an IVR menu; same response, keep it short. Email: reply to the issue, not the tool.
when_not_to_use: Do not apologise for the bot at length if the customer only mentioned it in passing; one short line, then fix the issue.
mini_conversation: Customer: your bot was useless | Agent: I'm sorry it didn't help. I can see you're trying to change your delivery date, so let's do that now. Which day suits you? | Customer: thursday | Agent: Done. Your parcel will now arrive on Thursday.
source_rule: Reduce customer effort: read the history so the customer never has to repeat themselves (CEB/Gartner effort research).
fill_blank: I'm sorry it didn't help. I can see you're trying ____ change your delivery date.
mcq_question: A customer writes "your bot was useless". What is the best first reply?
mcq_options: A) Our bot has helped many customers, so it should work for you if you try it again. | B) Please explain your issue from the beginning so that I can understand everything properly. | C) Please use the chat bot again; it will guide you step by step through the same process. | D) I'm sorry it didn't help. I can see you want to change your delivery date, so let's do that now.
mcq_why: D apologises briefly and uses what the customer already typed. B seems thorough, but it makes them repeat everything; A defends the tool and C sends them back.
reorder_task: date / change / I / your / trying / see / to / can / you're / delivery
reorder_answer: I can see you're trying to change your delivery date
hindi_to_english: Mujhe afsos hai ki bot se madad nahin mili. Main dekh sakti hoon aapko address badalna hai, chaliye abhi badal dete hain.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry the bot didn't help. I can see you want to change your address, so let's do that now.
whats_next_customer: thank god a real person
whats_next_reply: I'm here now, and I'm sorry it kept sending you one link over and over. I've read your messages, so we can carry on from where you stopped.
role_play: Partner A reaches a human after a chatbot kept sending the same link. Partner B reads the history, apologises in one line and solves the request without asking A to repeat it.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your first reply to "your bot was useless" and your answer to "I've explained it 3 times already".
self_check: Did you avoid defending the bot? · Did you use what the customer already wrote? · Did you move to the fix in your first reply?

sentence: I'm reporting this
speaker: Customer
situation: After a dispute about a deposit that was not returned, the customer writes this and stops replying for a moment.
recall_cue: A customer threatens to report the company. What is behind the threat, and how do you respond without getting defensive?
linking: If read aloud: I'm_reporting → "aim-ri-POR-ting" · reporting_this → "ri-POR-ting-this"
intonation: If read aloud: cold and final, falling on "this".
indian_pron_tip: If you read it aloud, "reporting" is ri-POR-ting with stress on the middle, and "this" needs a soft voiced "th", not "dis".
customer_emotion: Feeling powerless and unfairly treated, looking for someone with more power to step in.
memory_hook: A threat is a flare sent up for help: answer the flare, not the smoke.
hindi_meaning: मैं इसकी शिकायत करने जा रहा/रही हूँ।
hindi_roman: Main iski shikaayat karne ja raha/rahi hoon.
simple_meaning: I am going to complain about this to someone more powerful, such as a regulator, a consumer forum or social media.
why_it_works: The customer feels nobody is listening and wants power back. They need to hear that they have the right to complain, that you are escalating it yourself, and one more chance to fix the real problem.
key_chunk: I'm reporting this = I'm going to complain to a higher authority
grammar_pattern: I'm + verb-ing (present continuous for a decided future plan)
grammar_note: The present continuous here means the customer has already decided to do it.
tone_note: Stay respectful and do not argue or threaten back. "Do whatever you want" or "That won't change anything" makes the customer certain to report it.
watch_out: ✗ Sir, you can report, it will not change anything. → ✓ You have every right to raise it. I'd also like to escalate it myself now.
dont_say: "That is your choice." — it sounds cold and dismissive, and it gives the customer no reason to stay.
positive_swap: Instead of "You can complain if you want", say "You have every right to raise this. I'd like to escalate it to my manager myself right now."
alt_1: I'm going to report you
alt_2: I'll be taking this to the consumer forum
more_formal: I intend to make a formal complaint about this.
ask_next: You have every right to raise this. I'd also like to escalate your deposit case to my manager now, and I'll send you our formal complaint link. Would that help?
replies_you_may_hear: yes, escalate it · I've already filed it · it won't help
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "It won't help." → Agent: "I understand why you feel that way. I've escalated it with a note asking for a reply by tomorrow at noon, and I'll message you here when I hear back."
cultural_note: Replies such as "Please don't report this, sir" can sound like a plea or a pressure tactic to international customers; accept their right to complain and focus on fixing the cause.
channel_note: Voice: the caller may say "I'll be reporting you"; slow down and do not raise your voice. Email: reply with the formal complaints route and your escalation in writing.
when_not_to_use: Do not treat it as a threat to you personally and stop helping; and do not make promises outside your authority just to stop the report.
mini_conversation: Customer: I'm reporting this | Agent: You have every right to raise this. I'd also like to escalate your deposit case to my manager now, and I'll send you our formal complaint link. Would that help? | Customer: fine, escalate it | Agent: Done. Your case number is CM-4410. I've asked for a reply by noon tomorrow, and I'll message you here either way.
source_rule: Escalate when needed; stay respectful, take ownership and give a clear next step and time.
fill_blank: You ____ every right to raise this. I'd also like to escalate it to my manager now.
mcq_question: A customer writes "I'm reporting this". Which reply is best?
mcq_options: A) You have every right to raise this. I'd like to escalate it to my manager now, if that helps. | B) That is your choice, and you are free to report it. Our decision on the deposit will stay the same. | C) Please don't report this, sir. I will try my best to help you and I will do everything I can. | D) Reporting this will not change our decision, so I would advise you to accept the position today.
mcq_why: A respects the customer's right and offers real action. C sounds polite but begs and gives nothing; B is cold and D sounds like a challenge.
reorder_task: right / raise / every / You / have / this / to
reorder_answer: You have every right to raise this
hindi_to_english: Aapko iski shikaayat karne ka poora haq hai. Main khud bhi ise abhi apne manager ko escalate karna chahti hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: You have every right to raise this. I'd also like to escalate it to my manager myself now.
whats_next_customer: I've already filed it
whats_next_reply: That's completely your right. I'll still escalate your deposit case today, so my manager can look at it alongside your report.
role_play: Partner A has not got a deposit back and writes "I'm reporting this". Partner B accepts their right to complain, escalates, gives a case number and a time.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your reply to "I'm reporting this" and your answer to "it won't help".
self_check: Did you accept the customer's right to complain? · Did you offer to escalate yourself? · Did you give a case number or a time?

sentence: ok fine whatever
speaker: Customer
situation: You have offered a partial credit instead of the full refund the customer wanted, and they reply with this.
recall_cue: At the end of a chat, a customer answers your offer with three flat words. Are they happy, and how should you close?
linking: If read aloud: ok_fine → "oh-kay-fain" · fine_whatever → "fain-wot-EV-er"
intonation: If read aloud: flat, low and falling on every word; tired, not agreeing.
indian_pron_tip: If you read it aloud, "whatever" starts with a rounded-lip w (wot-EV-er), not "vot-ever"; the stress is on "EV".
customer_emotion: Disappointed and tired, accepting the offer without being satisfied.
memory_hook: "Fine whatever" is a door left half open: don't slam it with "Great!"; leave a light on.
hindi_meaning: ठीक है, जो भी हो।
hindi_roman: Theek hai, jo bhi ho.
simple_meaning: I'll accept it, but I'm not happy. I've given up arguing.
why_it_works: The customer is not satisfied, only tired. They need you to notice that, without arguing again, to confirm clearly what happens next, and to leave a way back if they change their mind.
key_chunk: fine whatever = I accept, but I'm not happy
grammar_pattern: ok + fine + whatever (flat words; no full sentence shows low energy)
grammar_note: Very short replies with no capital or full stop often show low mood, not agreement.
tone_note: Reply with a short, sincere close and one clear fact. A bright "Great, glad I could help! 😊" sounds like you missed the customer's mood.
watch_out: ✗ Great! Glad I could help! 😊 → ✓ I know it isn't what you hoped for. The £20 credit is on your account now.
dont_say: "Glad I could help! Please rate our chat." — it treats an unhappy customer as satisfied and asks for a score at the worst moment.
positive_swap: Instead of "Great, so the issue is resolved", say "I know it isn't what you hoped for. The credit is on your account now, and you can message us any time."
alt_1: fine, if you say so
alt_2: forget it, whatever
more_formal: Very well, I'll accept that.
ask_next: I know it isn't what you hoped for. The £20 credit is on your account now, and if anything else comes up, just message us here.
replies_you_may_hear: ok · yeah thanks · it's still not fair
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "it's still not fair" → Agent: "I understand, and I'm sorry I couldn't do more. If you'd like a manager to review it, I can pass it on today."
cultural_note: In English, "fine" can mean "I accept, but I am not happy"; if English is your second language, it is easy to read it as a real yes. Look at the flat, short words around it.
channel_note: Voice: you will hear a long sigh or a flat "fine"; lower your energy to match and close gently. Email: rarely appears; customers may simply stop replying.
when_not_to_use: Do not read it as unhappy if it comes after a friendly chat where the customer is just choosing between two equal options.
mini_conversation: Customer: ok fine whatever | Agent: I know it isn't what you hoped for. The £20 credit is on your account now, and if anything else comes up, just message us here. | Customer: ok | Agent: Thank you for your time today, Ben. Take care.
source_rule: Ask whether the issue is resolved rather than assuming it; on an unresolved close, give options and next steps (SQM Group).
fill_blank: The £20 credit is on your account now, and if anything else comes ____, just message us here.
mcq_question: After you offer a partial credit, the customer writes "ok fine whatever". What does this most likely mean?
mcq_options: A) They are pleased with the offer and are ready to close the chat happily | B) They did not read the offer and want you to repeat it for them again | C) They are asking you a question about how to use the credit offered today | D) They accept the offer, but they are unhappy and tired of arguing today
mcq_why: "Fine whatever" means reluctant acceptance. A is tempting because "fine" can mean "good", but here the flat tone shows disappointment.
reorder_task: hoped / it / for / isn't / what / you / I / know
reorder_answer: I know it isn't what you hoped for
hindi_to_english: Mujhe pata hai ki yeh aapki ummeed ke mutaabik nahin hai. £20 ka credit ab aapke account mein aa gaya hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: I know it isn't what you hoped for. The £20 credit is on your account now.
whats_next_customer: yeah thanks anyway
whats_next_reply: You're welcome, Ben. If you change your mind or anything else comes up, just message us here.
role_play: Partner B offers Partner A a £20 credit instead of a full refund. Partner A replies "ok fine whatever". Partner B closes sincerely, confirms the credit and leaves a way back.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your reply to "ok fine whatever" and your answer if the customer adds "it's still not fair".
self_check: Did you notice the customer is not happy? · Did you avoid a cheerful close or emoji? · Did you leave a way back?

sentence: why should I trust you?
speaker: Customer
situation: The customer was promised an engineer visit twice last week and nobody came, and now you are promising a fix.
recall_cue: A customer who was let down before asks why they should believe you. What earns trust in your reply: words or proof?
linking: If read aloud: should_I → "shu-dai" · trust_you → "trus-choo"
intonation: If read aloud: a falling wh- question, slow and bitter; it is a challenge, not a real request for information.
indian_pron_tip: If you read it aloud, "trust" ends in a "-st" cluster; keep the final "t" (trust, not "trus"). "Why" starts with rounded lips, not a v sound.
customer_emotion: Let down and suspicious after broken promises, afraid of being fooled again.
memory_hook: Trust is a receipt, not a speech: show the customer something they can check.
hindi_meaning: मैं आप पर भरोसा क्यों करूँ?
