hindi_roman: Main aap par bharosa kyon karoon?
simple_meaning: You (the company) broke your promises before. Why should I believe this new promise?
why_it_works: The customer has been let down and does not believe words any more. They need you to admit the broken promise, then give proof they can check: an action already done, a reference number, a time — and then keep it.
key_chunk: why should I trust you? = you've let me down before; prove it this time
grammar_pattern: Why + should + I + base verb + you? (a challenge, not a real question)
grammar_note: "Should" here asks for a reason; the customer expects you to show, not tell.
tone_note: Admit the past failure and show proof. "Trust me, sir" or "I assure you 100%" sounds empty to someone who was let down twice.
watch_out: ✗ Trust me, this time it will be done 100%. → ✓ You've every reason to doubt us. I've already booked the engineer for Tuesday at 10 am, and your reference is EN-2287.
dont_say: "I assure you, this time it will definitely happen." — it asks for trust without giving any proof.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please trust me", say "You've every reason to doubt us. Here's what I've already done, and here's the reference so you can check."
alt_1: how do I know you won't forget me too?
alt_2: you said that last time
more_formal: Given what has happened, I'm not sure I can rely on what you're telling me.
ask_next: You've every reason to doubt us after two missed visits. I've already booked the engineer for Tuesday at 10 am, reference EN-2287, and the confirmation is in your inbox now.
replies_you_may_hear: ok, I see the email · we'll see · and if nobody comes again?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "And if nobody comes again?" → Agent: "Then message me here with that reference. I've added my name to the booking, and I'll check at 10:15 on Tuesday that the engineer has arrived."
cultural_note: "Trust me" and "I assure you" are common reassurances in Indian service English; international customers who were let down usually trust a checkable reference more than a promise.
channel_note: Voice: say it slowly, admit the missed visits first, then read the reference clearly. Email: attach or forward the confirmation in the same message.
when_not_to_use: Do not promise a time or action you cannot control (for example a Tuesday check if you will be off shift); give only proof you can actually show.
mini_conversation: Customer: why should I trust you? | Agent: You've every reason to doubt us after two missed visits. I've already booked the engineer for Tuesday at 10 am, reference EN-2287, and the confirmation is in your inbox now. | Customer: ok, I see the email | Agent: Thank you. I'll check on Tuesday at 10:15 that the engineer has arrived.
source_rule: Ownership: replace vague promises with a clear time, a reference number and the next step.
fill_blank: You've every reason to doubt ____ (the company, not just you) after two missed visits.
mcq_question: A customer who was let down twice writes "why should I trust you?". Which reply earns trust best?
mcq_options: A) You've every reason to doubt us. I've already booked the engineer for Tuesday at 10 am, reference EN-2287. | B) Trust me, sir, this time it will be done properly. I personally guarantee that nobody will let you down. | C) I assure you that we are a reliable company, and our customers have trusted us for many years now. | D) I am not the agent who booked you before, so I cannot say why the visits were missed last week.
mcq_why: A admits the failure and gives checkable proof. C sounds professional but is only a claim; B asks for blind trust and D shifts the blame.
reorder_task: doubt / reason / You've / every / us / to
reorder_answer: You've every reason to doubt us
hindi_to_english: Aapke paas hum par shak karne ki poori wajah hai. Maine engineer pehle hi book kar diya hai, aur aapka reference number EN-2287 hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: You've every reason to doubt us. I've already booked the engineer, and your reference number is EN-2287.
whats_next_customer: and if nobody comes again?
whats_next_reply: Then message me here with the reference. I'll check on Tuesday at 10:15 that the engineer has arrived.
role_play: Partner A was promised two engineer visits that never happened and writes "why should I trust you?". Partner B admits the failure and gives proof: a booking, a reference and a check-in time.
record_task: Record yourself reading aloud your reply to "why should I trust you?" and your answer to "and if nobody comes again?".
self_check: Did you admit the past failure? · Did you give proof the customer can check? · Did you avoid "trust me" and "I assure you"?

sentence: Update on your refund request – Ticket #55102
speaker: Agent
situation: You are sending the first update on a customer's refund, and your helpdesk lets you write the subject line of the email.
recall_cue: Your email is about a refund and has a ticket number. What short subject tells the customer exactly what is inside?
linking: If read aloud: update_on → "up-day-ton" · refund_request → "ree-fun-dri-kwest"
intonation: If read aloud: a subject line is a label, so read it flat and falling, with a small pause before the ticket number.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "update" is UP-date with stress on the first part, and the final "t" in "request" and "ticket" should be clear, not dropped.
customer_emotion: Waiting for money back and checking the inbox for news.
memory_hook: A subject line is the label on a box: the customer should know what is inside without opening the lid.
hindi_meaning: आपकी रिफ़ंड रिक्वेस्ट पर अपडेट – टिकट #55102
hindi_roman: Aapki refund request par update – ticket #55102
simple_meaning: This email tells you the latest news about the money you asked to get back.
why_it_works: The customer sees the topic and the ticket number before opening the email, so they can find it again and know it is not spam or a new problem.
key_chunk: Update on your ___ – Ticket #___
grammar_pattern: Noun (Update) + on + your + noun phrase + – + Ticket + number
grammar_note: Subject lines are short labels, so they skip "This is" and usually have no full stop.
tone_note: A specific, calm label sounds professional. A subject like "URGENT!!!" or "Important information" sounds like spam and can worry the customer.
watch_out: ✗ Regarding your query → ✓ Update on your refund request – Ticket #55102
dont_say: "Important information" — it says nothing about the content and looks like spam or a scam email.
positive_swap: Instead of "Your complaint", write "Update on your refund request – Ticket #55102".
alt_1: Your refund for order 62408 – Ticket #55102
alt_2: Refund update for order 62408 (Ticket #55102)
more_formal: Update regarding your refund request – Ticket #55102
ask_next: Hi Daniel, I have an update on your refund for order 62408.
replies_you_may_hear: Thanks, when will I get the money? · Is this about my old order? · Got it, thank you.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why do you keep changing the subject line? I can't find your emails." → Agent: "I'm sorry the emails were hard to find. I'll keep the same subject line from now on so all our emails stay together."
cultural_note: Many Indian office emails use "Regarding your query" or "Reg: complaint". International customers expect a specific topic plus the ticket number.
channel_note: Voice and chat: no subject line; say the topic in the first sentence instead. Email: if you reply in the customer's thread, keep their subject and the "Re:".
when_not_to_use: Do not change the subject when replying inside an existing thread; keep the customer's subject so the emails stay together.
mini_conversation: Customer: I asked for a refund last week. | Agent: Subject: Update on your refund request – Ticket #55102. Hi Daniel, your refund is approved. | Customer: Great, when will I see it? | Agent: It should reach your card within five working days.
source_rule: Email subject: specific, short and with the ticket number; keep it when replying.
fill_blank: Update on your refund request – ____ (starts with T) #55102
mcq_question: You are writing the first update on a customer's refund. Which subject line is best?
mcq_options: A) Important information on your account – Ticket #55102 | B) Update on your refund request – Ticket #55102 | C) Reg: your refund query – see details below | D) URGENT – PLEASE READ – Refund Ticket #55102
mcq_why: B names the topic and the ticket number in a calm label. A has a ticket number but does not say what the email is about, C has no ticket number and uses an office abbreviation, and D is in capital letters, which looks like spam.
reorder_task: refund / Update / Ticket / your / on / request / 55102
reorder_answer: Update on your refund request – Ticket #55102
hindi_to_english: Subject line likhiye: aapke exchange request par update, ticket 60417.
hindi_to_english_answer: Update on your exchange request – Ticket #60417
whats_next_customer: Thanks for the update. When will the money reach my card?
whats_next_reply: Your refund was sent today, and it should reach your card within five working days.
role_play: Partner A is a customer who asked for a refund on order 62408. Partner B writes three possible subject lines for the update email, and A chooses the clearest one and says why.
record_task: Write a subject line for an email updating a customer about a replacement order, Ticket #60233, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Does the subject name the topic in a few clear words? · Did you include the ticket number? · Did you avoid ALL CAPS, "Reg:" and "Important"?

sentence: Hi Daniel, this is Meera from the [Company] support team.
speaker: Agent
situation: You are starting your first reply to a customer called Daniel Brooks, who signed his email with his first name.
recall_cue: How do you open an email to a customer who signed off with his first name, and introduce yourself in one line?
linking: If read aloud: this_is → "thi-siz" · support_team → "su-por-team"
intonation: If read aloud: a short pause after "Daniel", then a friendly, falling tone at the end.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "this" starts with a soft "th" (tongue lightly between the teeth), not "dis"; "support" has the stress on PORT.
customer_emotion: Hoping a real person has read the email.
memory_hook: Use the name the customer gave you, like a shopkeeper who remembers a regular and says hello by name.
hindi_meaning: नमस्ते डैनियल, मैं [Company] की सपोर्ट टीम से मीरा हूँ।
hindi_roman: Namaste Daniel, main [Company] ki support team se Meera hoon.
simple_meaning: Hello Daniel, my name is Meera and I work in the support team.
why_it_works: Using the customer's name shows a person read the email, and giving your own name tells the customer who to reply to.
key_chunk: Hi ___, this is ___ from ___.
grammar_pattern: Hi + first name + , + this is + your name + from + team
grammar_note: In emails we write "this is Meera", not "I am Meera speaking".
tone_note: "Hi" plus a first name is friendly and normal in modern support. "Dear Customer" sounds like a machine, and "Respected Sir" sounds old-fashioned to many readers.
watch_out: ✗ Dear Customer, I am Meera speaking from support. → ✓ Hi Daniel, this is Meera from the [Company] support team.
dont_say: "Dear Customer," — it shows nobody looked at the customer's name and feels like a mass mailing.
positive_swap: Instead of "Dear Customer", write "Hi Daniel, this is Meera from the [Company] support team."
alt_1: Hello Daniel, I'm Meera from the [Company] support team.
alt_2: Hi Daniel, Meera here from [Company] support.
more_formal: Dear Mr Brooks, my name is Meera and I work in the [Company] customer support team.
ask_next: Thank you for writing to us about your order.
replies_you_may_hear: Hi Meera, thanks for getting back to me. · Hello, are you a real person? · Hi, I've been waiting for a reply.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Is this an automatic reply?" → Agent: "No, I'm Meera and I've read your email myself. I'm looking into your order now."
cultural_note: Many Indian emails start with "Respected Sir" or "Dear Sir/Madam". International customers usually expect their name; use "Hi" plus first name if they signed that way, or "Dear Mr/Ms" plus surname if they wrote formally.
channel_note: Voice: "Thank you for calling [Company], this is Meera." Chat: "Hi Daniel, I'm Meera." Email: greeting and your name in the first line, then a blank line before the message.
when_not_to_use: Do not use "Hi" plus first name when the customer wrote formally and signed with a title and surname; use "Dear Mr Brooks" instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: Hello, my blender stopped working. Thanks, Daniel | Agent: Hi Daniel, this is Meera from the [Company] support team. I'm sorry your blender stopped working. | Customer: Hi Meera, can you replace it? | Agent: I'll check your warranty now and email you the next step by 3 pm tomorrow.
source_rule: Greet by name, not "Dear customer"; use a conversational voice.
fill_blank: Hi Daniel, ____ is Meera from the [Company] support team.
mcq_question: The customer signed his email "Daniel". Which opening is best?
mcq_options: A) Dear Customer, I am Meera speaking from the support desk. | B) Respected Sir, this is Meera from the [Company] support team. | C) Hi Daniel, this is Meera from the [Company] support team. | D) Hello Mr Daniel, this is Meera from the [Company] support team.
mcq_why: C uses his name as he signed it and introduces you. D is tempting, but "Mr" goes with a surname (Mr Brooks), not a first name. A ignores his name and sounds like a mass mailing, and B uses "Respected Sir", which is polite in India but international customers may not expect it.
reorder_task: is / from / Hi / support / Meera / the / this / Company / team / Daniel
reorder_answer: Hi Daniel, this is Meera from the [Company] support team.
hindi_to_english: Customer Priya ko greet kijiye aur bataiye ki aap Rahul hain, [Company] support se.
hindi_to_english_answer: Hi Priya, this is Rahul from the [Company] support team.
whats_next_customer: Hi Meera, thanks. Did you find my order?
whats_next_reply: Yes, I found it. Your order 51736 is with the courier and is due to arrive tomorrow.
role_play: Partner A writes a short email about a broken kettle and signs it "Sarah Jones". Partner B writes two openings, one friendly and one formal, and A says which fits her email better.
record_task: Write the greeting and first line of a reply to a customer who signed her email "Anita Kapoor", and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you use the customer's name as they wrote it? · Did you give your own name? · Did you avoid "Dear Customer", and "Respected Sir", which international customers may not expect?

sentence: Thank you for writing to us about your missing parcel.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer has emailed to say a parcel marked as delivered never reached them, and you are starting your reply.
recall_cue: The customer took time to tell you about a problem. What do you say first, and how do you show you read their email?
linking: If read aloud: thank_you → "thang-kyoo" · about_your → "a-bou-chor"
intonation: If read aloud: steady and warm, falling at "parcel" with no rush.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "thank" starts with a soft "th" (tongue between the teeth), not "tank"; "parcel" is PAR-cel, not par-SEL.
customer_emotion: Annoyed and worried the parcel is lost.
memory_hook: Thank the customer and name their problem, like a doctor who repeats your symptom so you know they listened.
hindi_meaning: अपने गुम हुए पार्सल के बारे में हमें लिखने के लिए धन्यवाद।
hindi_roman: Apne gum hue parcel ke baare mein hamein likhne ke liye dhanyavaad.
simple_meaning: Thanks for telling us that your parcel has not arrived.
why_it_works: Thanking the customer makes them feel heard, and naming the exact problem shows you read their email instead of sending a template.
key_chunk: Thank you for writing to us about ___.
grammar_pattern: Thank you + for + verb-ing + about + noun
grammar_note: After "Thank you for" use the -ing form: "for writing", not "for write".
tone_note: Thanking plus naming the problem sounds personal. "Thank you for your query" alone sounds like a template and may annoy an upset customer.
watch_out: ✗ Thank you for write to us. → ✓ Thank you for writing to us about your missing parcel.
dont_say: "Your query has been noted." — it sounds cold and robotic, and says nothing about the customer's problem.
positive_swap: Instead of "Your query has been noted", write "Thank you for writing to us about your missing parcel."
alt_1: Thanks for letting us know that your parcel has not arrived.
alt_2: Thank you for contacting us about your missing parcel.
more_formal: Thank you for your email regarding the parcel that has not reached you.
ask_next: I'm sorry it hasn't arrived. I have already asked the courier to trace it.
replies_you_may_hear: Thanks, any news? · I just want my parcel. · It says delivered but I don't have it.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I don't need thanks, I need my parcel." → Agent: "You're right, and I'm sorry you are still waiting. The courier is tracing it now, and I'll email you by 4 pm with an update."
cultural_note: Indian office emails often begin "This is with reference to your mail". International customers expect a short thank-you and the problem in plain words.
channel_note: Voice: "Thanks for calling about your parcel." Chat: "Thanks for reaching out about your parcel." Email: one line, then the action.
when_not_to_use: Do not start with a thank-you to a very angry customer whose second complaint was ignored; apologise first.
mini_conversation: Customer: My parcel says delivered, but it isn't here. | Agent: Thank you for writing to us about your missing parcel. I'm sorry it hasn't arrived. | Customer: What will you do? | Agent: I've asked the courier to trace it, and I'll update you by 4 pm today.
source_rule: Thank the customer, name the issue, then give one clear next step.
fill_blank: Thank you for ____ (write) to us about your missing parcel.
mcq_question: A customer emails about a missing parcel. Which first line is best?
mcq_options: A) Your query has been noted and will be looked into. | B) Thank you for writing to us about your missing parcel. | C) This is with reference to your mail about the parcel. | D) Thank you for your query. We will look into it soon.
mcq_why: B thanks the customer and names the exact problem. D thanks but could be sent to anyone, C is a common Indian office opening that international customers may not expect, and it does not thank, and A is a cold office phrase.
reorder_task: writing / about / Thank / us / missing / you / to / parcel / for / your
reorder_answer: Thank you for writing to us about your missing parcel.
hindi_to_english: Customer ko damaged phone ke baare mein likhne ke liye thanks kahiye.
hindi_to_english_answer: Thank you for writing to us about your damaged phone.
whats_next_customer: So where is my parcel?
whats_next_reply: I'm checking the courier's last scan myself right now. I'll email you by 4 pm today with what I find.
role_play: Partner A writes an email saying a parcel marked delivered is missing. Partner B writes the first two lines of the reply: a thank-you that names the problem, then the action taken.
record_task: Write the first two lines of a reply to a customer whose shoes arrived in the wrong size, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you use "for" plus an -ing word? · Did you name the customer's exact problem? · Did you follow with an action?

sentence: We have received your email, and I will send you a full answer by 5 pm tomorrow.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer has asked a question that needs a check with the billing team, so you confirm you got it and say when they will hear back.
recall_cue: You cannot answer fully today. What do you tell the customer so they stop worrying their email was lost?
linking: If read aloud: received_your → "ri-SEEV-jer" (d + y join into a "j" sound) · send_you → "sen-joo" · full_answer → "fu-lan-ser"
intonation: If read aloud: a small pause after "email", then a clear, falling tone on "tomorrow" to sound sure.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, say the "v" in "received" with your top teeth on your lower lip (vest, not west), and keep the final "d" in "received" and "send": ri-SEEVD, two syllables.
customer_emotion: Unsure whether anyone has read the email.
memory_hook: Like a courier receipt: you show the parcel has arrived, and you write the delivery time on it.
hindi_meaning: हमें आपका ईमेल मिल गया है, और मैं कल शाम 5 बजे तक आपको पूरा जवाब भेजूँगा/भेजूँगी।
hindi_roman: Hamein aapka email mil gaya hai, aur main kal shaam 5 baje tak aapko poora jawaab bhejunga/bhejungi.
simple_meaning: We got your email, and you will get a complete reply from me before 5 pm tomorrow.
why_it_works: It tells the customer the email is not lost and gives a real time, so they do not need to write again or call to chase.
key_chunk: I will send you ___ by ___.
grammar_pattern: We have + past participle · I will + base verb + by + time
grammar_note: "Have received" shows it has just happened; "will send" is your promise for the future.
tone_note: "I will" plus a time sounds confident and responsible. "We will try to revert soon" sounds vague and uses a word international customers may not expect.
watch_out: ✗ We have received your email and will reply you soon. → ✓ We have received your email, and I will send you a full answer by 5 pm tomorrow.
dont_say: "We will get back to you shortly." — "shortly" is not a time, so the customer cannot plan and will probably chase you.
positive_swap: Instead of "We will try to reply soon", write "I will send you a full answer by 5 pm tomorrow."
alt_1: Thanks for your email. I'm checking this with our billing team and will reply by 5 pm tomorrow.
alt_2: I've received your message, and you'll have a full reply from me by tomorrow at 5 pm.
more_formal: This is to confirm that we have received your email. I will send you a complete response by 5 pm tomorrow.
ask_next: If you have a copy of the invoice, please attach it to your reply so I can check it faster.
replies_you_may_hear: OK, thanks for letting me know. · Can't you answer today? · Fine, but please don't forget.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why can't you answer today?" → Agent: "I know you would like an answer today. I need our billing team to check two charges so that my answer is correct. I will email you by 5 pm tomorrow, and sooner if they finish early."
cultural_note: "We will revert" is common in Indian office email; Oxford lists "revert" meaning "reply" as Indian English. International customers expect "reply" or "get back to you".
channel_note: Voice: "I'll call you back by 5 pm tomorrow." Chat: "I'll email you the full answer by 5 pm tomorrow." Email: one line near the top.
when_not_to_use: Do not send a holding reply when you can answer the whole question now; just answer it.
mini_conversation: Customer: Why was I charged twice? | Agent: We have received your email, and I will send you a full answer by 5 pm tomorrow. | Customer: OK, please don't forget. | Agent: I won't. I'll check both charges with our billing team today.
source_rule: Use "I will" plus a time instead of "we'll try" or "soon".
fill_blank: We have received your email, and I will send you a full answer ____ 5 pm tomorrow at the latest.
mcq_question: You need one day to check a billing question. Which holding reply is best?
mcq_options: A) Thank you for your email. We will revert back to you with an answer very soon. | B) Your email has been forwarded to the billing team and is under process. | C) We have received your email, and I will send you a full answer by 5 pm tomorrow. | D) We have received your email, and someone from our team will contact you shortly.
mcq_why: C confirms the email arrived and gives a real time. A, B and D give no time ("very soon", "under process", "shortly"), and A also uses "revert back" and B "under process", which international readers may not expect.
reorder_task: send / I / full / will / answer / you / a
reorder_answer: I will send you a full answer.
hindi_to_english: Customer ko bataiye ki email mil gaya hai aur aap Monday dopahar 12 baje tak jawaab denge.
hindi_to_english_answer: We have received your email, and I will reply by 12 noon on Monday.
whats_next_customer: OK. Do you need anything else from me?
whats_next_reply: Yes, please could you send a screenshot of the two charges on your bank statement? You can hide your account number.
role_play: Partner A emails about being charged twice. Partner B writes a holding reply that confirms the email arrived, explains the check in one line and gives a real time.
record_task: Write a two-line holding reply to a customer whose warranty question needs a check with the product team, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you confirm you received the email? · Did you give a real day and time? · Did you use "I will" instead of "we will try"?

sentence: To find your order quickly, could you send me the order number? It starts with ORD.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer has emailed about a late delivery but did not include an order number, and they have several orders with you.
recall_cue: The customer forgot a detail you need to find their purchase. How do you ask for it and help them find it?
linking: If read aloud: could_you → "cud-joo" · send_me → "sen-me" · starts_with → "star-tswith"
intonation: If read aloud: rise on "order number?" because it is a yes/no question, then fall on "ORD".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "order" is OR-der. For the "d", touch the ridge just behind your top teeth with the tip of your tongue; do not curl the tongue back, as in the Hindi ड.
customer_emotion: A little impatient because they expected you to know already.
memory_hook: The order number is the key to the customer's locker; ask for the key and tell them which pocket it is in.
hindi_meaning: आपका ऑर्डर जल्दी ढूँढने के लिए, क्या आप मुझे ऑर्डर नंबर भेज सकते हैं? यह ORD से शुरू होता है।
hindi_roman: Aapka order jaldi dhoondhne ke liye, kya aap mujhe order number bhej sakte hain? Yeh ORD se shuru hota hai.
simple_meaning: Please send me your order number so I can find your order fast; it begins with the letters ORD.
why_it_works: It gives the reason first, so the request does not feel like a test, and tells the customer how to recognise the number.
key_chunk: To ___, could you send me ___?
grammar_pattern: To + base verb (reason) + , + could you + base verb + object?
grammar_note: "To find" at the start gives the reason; "could you" makes the request polite.
tone_note: Giving a reason and a hint sounds helpful. "Provide order number" or "May I know your order ID" sounds like a form.
watch_out: ✗ Please provide order no. for further process. → ✓ To find your order quickly, could you send me the order number? It starts with ORD.
dont_say: "Order number is mandatory to process your request." — it sounds like a rule and blames the customer.
positive_swap: Instead of "Provide your order ID", write "To find your order quickly, could you send me the order number?"
alt_1: Could you reply with your order number? You'll find it in your confirmation email.
alt_2: So I can check your delivery, could you send me the order number that begins with ORD?
more_formal: So that I can locate your order, could you please send me the order number? It begins with the letters ORD.
ask_next: Thank you. I can see order ORD-48213 and I'm checking the delivery now.
replies_you_may_hear: It's ORD-48213. · I can't find the email. · Can't you search by my email address?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Can't you just use my email address?" → Agent: "I can see three orders on your email address. The order number tells me which one is late, so I can fix the right one."
cultural_note: "May I know your order ID?" is common in Indian scripts and is grammatical. International customers more often hear "Could you send me…?" or "Could I have…?".
channel_note: Voice: "Could I have your order number, please?" Chat: "Could you type your order number here?" Email: give the reason and where to find it, to avoid another round of emails.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask for the order number if it is already in the customer's email or subject line; read carefully first.
mini_conversation: Customer: My delivery is late again. | Agent: I'm sorry your delivery is late again. To find your order quickly, could you send me the order number? It starts with ORD. | Customer: It's ORD-48213. | Agent: Thank you. I'm checking it now.
source_rule: Verification: say the purpose and ask only for what you need.
fill_blank: ____ find your order quickly, could you send me the order number? It starts with ORD.
mcq_question: A customer with three orders writes "My delivery is late." What is the best reply?
mcq_options: A) The order number is mandatory to process your request, so please send it. | B) To find your order quickly, could you send me the order number? It starts with ORD. | C) We cannot look into your delivery without further details from your side. | D) To confirm it is you, please send your full name, address, date of birth and phone number.
mcq_why: B gives a reason, asks for one thing and says how to find it. D gives a reason too, but asks for far more than you need. A and C sound like rules and give the customer no help.
reorder_task: send / number / you / me / Could / the / order
reorder_answer: Could you send me the order number?
hindi_to_english: Customer se poochhiye ki kya woh ticket number bhej sakte hain, taaki aap complaint jaldi dhoondh saken.
hindi_to_english_answer: To find your complaint quickly, could you send me the ticket number?
whats_next_customer: I can't find the confirmation email.
whats_next_reply: That's fine. Could you tell me the date you ordered and the item name? I'll search for it that way.
role_play: Partner A emails "Where is my delivery?" with no details. Partner B writes a reply that asks for the order number with a reason and a hint; then A says they cannot find it, and B offers another way.
record_task: Write a reply asking a customer for their ticket number, with a reason and a hint where to find it, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you give a reason first? · Did you ask for only one thing? · Did you tell the customer where to find it?

sentence: Could you attach a photo of the damaged item to your reply?
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer writes that their new lamp arrived broken, and you need to see the damage before you arrange a replacement.
recall_cue: You need to see the damage before you can send a new item. What do you ask the customer to add to their next email?
linking: If read aloud: attach_a → "a-ta-cha" · damaged_item → "dam-ij-dye-tem"
intonation: If read aloud: rise at the end on "reply?" because it is a yes/no request.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "photo" is FOH-toh with a long "oh". Start with "f", with your top teeth on your lower lip (fan, not pan), not a breathy "p"; "damaged" ends in a clear "d".
customer_emotion: Disappointed and wanting a quick replacement.
memory_hook: A photo is worth a thousand words, so ask for one picture instead of ten emails describing the crack.
hindi_meaning: क्या आप अपने जवाब में क्षतिग्रस्त सामान की एक फ़ोटो लगा सकते हैं?
hindi_roman: Kya aap apne jawaab mein kshatigrast saamaan ki ek photo laga sakte hain?
simple_meaning: Please add a picture of the broken item when you write back.
why_it_works: It asks for one clear thing in a polite question, so the customer knows exactly what to do and you avoid more emails.
key_chunk: Could you attach ___ to your reply?
grammar_pattern: Could + you + attach + object + to + your reply?
grammar_note: We "attach" a file "to" an email; we do not "attach with" it.
tone_note: A question sounds like a request. "Send photo" or "You have to send proof" sounds like the customer is not trusted.
watch_out: ✗ Could you attach photo of damaged item to your reply? → ✓ Could you attach a photo of the damaged item to your reply?
dont_say: "Send proof of damage." — "proof" sounds like you think the customer may be lying.
positive_swap: Instead of "You have to send proof", write "Could you attach a photo of the damaged item to your reply?"
alt_1: Please could you send a photo of the broken lamp with your reply?
alt_2: Could you reply with a photo that shows the damage?
more_formal: Would you be able to attach a photograph of the damaged item when you reply?
ask_next: A photo of the box and the label would also help, if you still have them.
replies_you_may_hear: Sure, here it is. · I threw the box away. · How do I attach a photo?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why do you need a photo? Don't you believe me?" → Agent: "I do believe you, and I'm sorry it arrived broken. The photo goes to our courier so they can fix the packing problem, and it lets me send your replacement today."
cultural_note: Indian English often says "snap" for a photo and "the same" for the item. International customers say "photo" or "picture" and expect you to name the thing.
channel_note: Voice: "Could you email us a photo of the damage?" Chat: "Could you upload a photo here using the clip icon?" Email: ask for it as an attachment to the reply.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask for a photo when the damage is already clear from the courier report or the customer already sent one.
mini_conversation: Customer: My lamp arrived broken. | Agent: I'm sorry your lamp arrived broken. Could you attach a photo of the damaged item to your reply? | Customer: Here it is. | Agent: Thank you. I've booked a replacement lamp for you today.
source_rule: Ask a clear question and give one clear next step.
fill_blank: Could you attach a photo of the damaged item ____ (starts with t) your reply?
mcq_question: You need to see a broken item before replacing it. Which request is best?
mcq_options: A) Send proof of the damage today so that we can process your claim. | B) Kindly send the snap of the same so that we can look into the matter. | C) Could you attach a photo of the damaged item to your reply? | D) You have to send photos of the lamp, or we cannot arrange a replacement.
mcq_why: C is polite and clear. B is a common Indian-English habit that international customers may find unclear ("snap", "the same"), and A and D sound like you distrust the customer.
reorder_task: photo / Could / attach / you / a
reorder_answer: Could you attach a photo?
hindi_to_english: Customer se kahiye ki apne jawaab mein error message ka screenshot attach karein.
hindi_to_english_answer: Could you attach a screenshot of the error message to your reply?
whats_next_customer: I'm on my phone. How do I attach it?
whats_next_reply: In most email apps, tap the paperclip icon, choose the photo and press send.
role_play: Partner A emails that a dinner plate arrived cracked. Partner B asks for a photo politely; A asks why it is needed, and B explains the reason calmly.
record_task: Write a two-line reply asking a customer for a screenshot of an error message, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you ask with "Could you"? · Did you name the exact thing to photograph? · Did you avoid "proof" (it sounds like distrust) and "the same" (international customers may not expect it)?

sentence: I'm sorry your headphones arrived two days late. I have refunded the delivery charge to your card.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer paid for fast delivery, but their headphones arrived two days after the promised date.
recall_cue: The delivery was late and the customer paid extra for speed. How do you say sorry for the exact problem and fix something?
stress: i'm-SOR-ry · your-HEAD-phones · a-RIVED · two-DAYS-LATE · i-have-re-FUND-ed · the-de-LIV-er-y-CHARGE
linking: If read aloud: arrived_two → "a-rive-too" · refunded_the → "ri-fun-di-the"
intonation: If read aloud: low and sincere on the first sentence, then a clear, steady tone for the action.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, say the "v" in "delivery" with top teeth on the lower lip (vest, not west); "arrived" ends in a clear "d".
customer_emotion: Let down and feeling they paid for nothing.
memory_hook: A real apology has two hands: one says sorry for the exact thing, the other gives something back.
hindi_meaning: मुझे खेद है कि आपके हेडफ़ोन दो दिन देर से पहुँचे। मैंने डिलीवरी चार्ज आपके कार्ड में वापस कर दिया है।
hindi_roman: Mujhe khed hai ki aapke headphone do din der se pahunche. Maine delivery charge aapke card mein wapas kar diya hai.
simple_meaning: I apologise that your headphones came two days late, and I have given back the money you paid for delivery.
why_it_works: It names the exact problem, so the customer knows you understood, and shows an action already done instead of only words.
key_chunk: I'm sorry your ___. I have ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm sorry + (that) + subject + past verb · I have + past participle
grammar_note: Use "I'm sorry" plus what happened; "I have refunded" shows the action is already done.
tone_note: A specific apology plus a fix sounds sincere. "Sorry for the inconvenience caused" sounds copied and does not say what went wrong.
watch_out: ✗ Sorry for the inconvenience caused. → ✓ I'm sorry your headphones arrived two days late. I have refunded the delivery charge to your card.
dont_say: "We regret the inconvenience caused." — it is a stock phrase that does not name the problem or take responsibility.
positive_swap: Instead of "Sorry for the inconvenience", write "I'm sorry your headphones arrived two days late."
alt_1: I apologise that your headphones were two days late. I've refunded your delivery charge.
alt_2: I'm sorry we missed the delivery date for your headphones. I've refunded the delivery charge, and it should reach your card within five working days.
more_formal: Please accept my apologies for the two-day delay in delivering your headphones. I have refunded the delivery charge to your card.
ask_next: You do not need to do anything. The refund should show on your card within five working days.
replies_you_may_hear: Thank you, that's fair. · It's not just the money, I needed them for a trip. · Will this happen again?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I needed them for my trip. A refund doesn't fix that." → Agent: "You're right, and I'm sorry it spoiled your plans. I've also added a note to your account so our team checks your next delivery closely."
cultural_note: "Sorry for the inconvenience caused" is very common in Indian support templates. International customers often read it as a copy-paste line; name the problem instead.
channel_note: Voice: say it slowly, then pause for the customer. Chat: split into two short messages. Email: put it near the top, after the greeting.
when_not_to_use: Do not apologise for a delay before you have checked it really was late; first confirm the facts.
mini_conversation: Customer: I paid for fast delivery and my headphones came two days late. | Agent: I'm sorry your headphones arrived two days late. I have refunded the delivery charge to your card. | Customer: Thanks. When will I see it? | Agent: It should reach your card within five working days.
source_rule: Apologise specifically, take responsibility, then offer a fix.
fill_blank: I'm sorry your headphones arrived two days late. I ____ refunded the delivery charge to your card.
mcq_question: A customer paid for fast delivery, but their headphones arrived two days late. Which apology is best?
mcq_options: A) We are sorry for the inconvenience caused to you by the delay in delivering your order. | B) I'm sorry, but delays can happen with couriers, and this one was outside our control. | C) I'm sorry your headphones arrived two days late. I have refunded the delivery charge to your card. | D) We regret any inconvenience this may have caused and thank you for your patience and understanding.
mcq_why: C names the problem and fixes something. A and D are stock phrases that do not say what went wrong or what you did, and B makes an excuse instead of taking responsibility.
reorder_task: headphones / sorry / late / I'm / arrived / your
reorder_answer: I'm sorry your headphones arrived late.
hindi_to_english: Customer se maafi maangiye ki unka phone charger galat bheja gaya, aur bataiye ki sahi charger aaj bhej diya hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry we sent you the wrong charger. I have sent the right one today.
whats_next_customer: Will this happen again next time?
whats_next_reply: I have reported this delay to our delivery team today. If your next order is late, reply to this email and I will look into it myself.
role_play: Partner A emails that a birthday cake arrived a day late. Partner B writes a specific apology and one action already taken; A pushes back once, and B answers calmly.
record_task: Write a two-sentence apology to a customer who received the wrong colour of shirt, including one action you have taken, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you name the exact problem? · Did you use "I", not only "we"? · Did you include an action already done?

sentence: Good news: your account is unlocked, and you can log in again now.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer was locked out after too many wrong passwords, and you have just reset the account.
recall_cue: The problem is solved. How do you tell the customer in one line, and what can they do now?
linking: If read aloud: account_is → "a-coun-tis" · log_in → "lo-gin" · unlocked_and → "un-lock-tand"
intonation: If read aloud: bright, rising energy on "Good news", then a clear fall on "now".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "unlocked" ends in a "t" sound (un-LOKT), not "un-lock-ed" with an extra syllable.
customer_emotion: Frustrated at being locked out and relieved to hear news.
memory_hook: Lead with the good news like opening the door first, then tell them they can walk in.
hindi_meaning: अच्छी ख़बर: आपका अकाउंट अनलॉक हो गया है, और अब आप फिर से लॉग इन कर सकते हैं।
hindi_roman: Achchhi khabar: aapka account unlock ho gaya hai, aur ab aap phir se log in kar sakte hain.
simple_meaning: Your account works again, and you can sign in right now.
why_it_works: The customer reads the result in the first line and knows exactly what to do next, without searching through the email.
key_chunk: Good news: your ___ is ___, and you can ___ now.
grammar_pattern: Good news + : + subject + is + adjective + , and + you can + base verb
grammar_note: "Unlocked" here is an adjective that describes the account now.
tone_note: Starting with the result sounds confident and kind. "Your issue has been resolved from our end" sounds stiff and does not tell the customer what to do.
watch_out: ✗ Good news: your account is unlock, and you can login again now. → ✓ Good news: your account is unlocked, and you can log in again now.
dont_say: "The issue has been resolved at our end." — it is vague, and "at our end" hints the problem may still exist at the customer's end.
positive_swap: Instead of "Issue resolved from our end", write "Good news: your account is unlocked, and you can log in again now."
alt_1: Your account is working again, so you can sign in now.
alt_2: I've unlocked your account, and you can log in straight away.
more_formal: I am pleased to confirm that your account has been unlocked, and you can now log in as usual.
ask_next: If you still see an error when you log in, reply to this email and I'll check it right away.
replies_you_may_hear: Great, it works, thanks! · I still can't log in. · Do I need a new password?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "It still doesn't work." → Agent: "I'm sorry it still isn't working. Could you send me a screenshot of the message you see? I'll check it straight away."
cultural_note: "Resolved from our end" is a common Indian support phrase. International customers prefer the actual result in plain words and what they can do now.
channel_note: Voice: "Good news, your account is unlocked. Could you try logging in now while I'm on the line?" Chat: same short line, then wait for them to try. Email: put it in the first line.
when_not_to_use: Do not say an issue is fixed before you have tested it or before the change has gone through.
mini_conversation: Customer: I'm locked out of my account. | Agent: Good news: your account is unlocked, and you can log in again now. | Customer: It works, thank you. | Agent: You're welcome. Is there anything else I can help with?
source_rule: Give one clear next step in plain words.
fill_blank: Good ____: your account is unlocked, and you can log in again now.
mcq_question: You have fixed a customer's locked account. Which line is best to start the email?
mcq_options: A) Your issue has been resolved from our end, so please check and confirm. | B) Good news: your account is unlocked, and you can log in again now. | C) The needful has been done on your account, and the ticket is now closed. | D) Please check and confirm if you are now able to access your account.
mcq_why: B gives the result and the next step. A sounds professional but vague, and "from our end" can sound like the problem may still be on the customer's side. C is fine in Indian office English, but international customers may not expect "the needful", and it does not say what was done, and D leaves the customer to find out the result alone.
reorder_task: you / account / is / unlocked / and / your / can / now / log / in
reorder_answer: Your account is unlocked, and you can log in now.
hindi_to_english: Customer ko bataiye ki unka password reset ho gaya hai aur woh ab login kar sakte hain.
hindi_to_english_answer: Good news: your password has been reset, and you can log in now.
whats_next_customer: Do I need to change my password?
whats_next_reply: Your current password works again. If you would like a new one, go to Settings, then Security, after you log in.
role_play: Partner A emails that their gift card does not work. Partner B writes the "fixed" email: the good news first, then what A can do now, then a line in case it still fails.
record_task: Write a two-line email telling a customer that their delivery address is now corrected, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did the result come in the first line? · Did you say what the customer can do now? · Did you say what was fixed, not just "resolved from our end"?

sentence: Next, our courier will collect the parcel from your address on Friday between 10 am and 2 pm.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer is returning a faulty toaster, and you have booked a pickup for them.
recall_cue: The return is booked. What does the customer need to know about what happens next, and when?
stress: NEXT · our-COUR-i-er-will-col-LECT · the-PAR-cel · on-FRI-day · be-TWEEN-TEN-ay-EM · and-TWO-pee-EM
linking: If read aloud: collect_the → "co-lec-the" · parcel_from → "par-sel-from"
intonation: If read aloud: pause after "Next", then slow down for the day and time so they are clear.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "courier" is KOO-ri-er; keep the "t" at the end of "collect" clear, not "collec".
customer_emotion: Wants the return to be easy and not to waste a day at home.
memory_hook: Next step equals who, what, when: courier, parcel, Friday 10 to 2.
hindi_meaning: अगला कदम: हमारा कूरियर शुक्रवार सुबह 10 से दोपहर 2 बजे के बीच आपके पते से पार्सल ले जाएगा।
hindi_roman: Agla kadam: hamara courier shukravaar subah 10 se dopahar 2 baje ke beech aapke pate se parcel le jayega.
simple_meaning: On Friday, between 10 in the morning and 2 in the afternoon, a delivery person will come to pick up the box.
why_it_works: It tells the customer who will come, what they will take and when, so the customer can plan and does not need to ask again.
key_chunk: Next, ___ will ___ on ___ between ___ and ___.
grammar_pattern: Next + , + subject + will + base verb + on + day + between + time + and + time
grammar_note: Use "on" for days and "between … and …" for a time window.
tone_note: Exact facts sound reliable. "Our team will contact you for pickup" leaves the customer waiting and guessing.
watch_out: ✗ Pickup will be done on Friday in between 10 to 2. → ✓ Next, our courier will collect the parcel from your address on Friday between 10 am and 2 pm.
dont_say: "Pickup will happen in 3-5 days." — a wide range with no day makes the customer stay home and wait.
positive_swap: Instead of "Our team will contact you shortly", write "Next, our courier will collect the parcel on Friday between 10 am and 2 pm."
alt_1: Our courier will pick up the parcel from your home on Friday, between 10 am and 2 pm.
alt_2: The next step is a pickup from your address this Friday, any time from 10 am to 2 pm.
more_formal: As the next step, our courier will collect the parcel from your address on Friday between 10:00 am and 2:00 pm.
ask_next: Please pack the toaster in its box and have it ready by the door before 10 am on Friday.
replies_you_may_hear: Friday is fine. · I'm not home on Friday. · Do I need to print anything?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I work on Friday. Can't they come on Saturday?" → Agent: "Of course. I can see a free slot on Saturday between 9 am and 1 pm. Shall I book that for you?"
cultural_note: "In between 10 to 2" is common in Indian English. International customers expect "between 10 am and 2 pm" or "from 10 am to 2 pm".
channel_note: Voice: say the time slowly and repeat it. Chat: put the day and time on their own line. Email: put the next step in bold or as a numbered step.
when_not_to_use: Do not give a day and time before the courier has confirmed the booking.
mini_conversation: Customer: How do I return the toaster? | Agent: Next, our courier will collect the parcel from your address on Friday between 10 am and 2 pm. | Customer: Do I need to print a label? | Agent: No, the courier will bring one.
source_rule: Give one clear next step; number the steps if there are several.
fill_blank: Next, our courier will collect the parcel from your address on Friday ____ 10 am and 2 pm.
mcq_question: Which line best explains the next step for a return?
mcq_options: A) Your return is booked, and our courier will pick up the parcel within the next few working days. | B) Your return is booked. Our team will contact you shortly to confirm the day and time of the pickup. | C) Next, our courier will collect the parcel from your address on Friday between 10 am and 2 pm. | D) Your return is booked for Friday, and the courier will call you before arriving to collect the parcel.
mcq_why: C says who, what and when, with a time window. A and B give no day or time, and D gives the day but not the time, so the customer cannot plan.
reorder_task: will / Friday / collect / courier / on / Our / parcel / the
reorder_answer: Our courier will collect the parcel on Friday.
hindi_to_english: Customer ko bataiye ki technician Tuesday ko subah 9 se 12 ke beech aayega.
hindi_to_english_answer: Next, our technician will visit you on Tuesday between 9 am and 12 noon.
whats_next_customer: Do I need to be at home?
whats_next_reply: Yes, or someone else can hand over the parcel for you.
role_play: Partner A wants to return a pair of shoes. Partner B writes the next step with who, what, day and time; A asks to change the day, and B offers another slot.
record_task: Write a one-line next step telling a customer when a technician will visit, with the day and a time window, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you say who will come? · Did you give a day and a time window? · Did you use "between … and …" correctly?

sentence: If you have any other questions, just reply to this email and I'll be happy to help.
speaker: Agent
situation: You have answered a customer's question about their warranty, and you are writing the last line before your sign-off.
recall_cue: The email is almost finished. How do you invite the customer to write again without sounding like a template?
linking: If read aloud: have_any → "ha-ven-ee" · reply_to → "ri-ply-tuh" · I'll_be → "ail-bee"
intonation: If read aloud: a small pause after "questions", then a warm, falling tone on "help".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "other" has a soft "th" (tongue between the teeth), not "ud-der"; "questions" ends in a clear "nz".
customer_emotion: Satisfied and ready to finish.
memory_hook: Leave the door open: a closing line is like a shopkeeper saying "come back any time".
hindi_meaning: अगर आपके कोई और सवाल हैं, तो बस इस ईमेल का जवाब दें, मुझे मदद करके ख़ुशी होगी।
hindi_roman: Agar aapke koi aur sawaal hain, to bas is email ka jawaab dein, mujhe madad karke khushi hogi.
simple_meaning: Write back to this email if you want to ask anything else; I am glad to help.
why_it_works: It tells the customer exactly how to get more help (reply to this email) and sounds personal because of "I'll".
key_chunk: If you have any other ___, just ___.
grammar_pattern: If + you + have + noun + , + imperative + and + I'll + be + adjective + to + verb
grammar_note: In an "if" sentence, use the present ("have") in the first part and "I'll" in the second.
tone_note: "Just reply" makes it easy and friendly. "Please feel free to revert in case of any further queries" sounds stiff to international readers.
watch_out: ✗ If you will have any other questions, just reply to this email. → ✓ If you have any other questions, just reply to this email and I'll be happy to help.
dont_say: "Please do not reply to this email." on a support reply — it shuts the door when the customer may still need help.
positive_swap: Instead of "Feel free to revert for further queries", write "If you have any other questions, just reply to this email."
alt_1: If anything else comes up, just reply here and I'll help.
alt_2: Do let me know if you have any other questions; I'm happy to help.
more_formal: Should you have any further questions, please reply to this email and I will be glad to assist.
ask_next: Kind regards, Meera Nair, [Company]
replies_you_may_hear: Thanks, that's all. · Actually, one more thing… · Great, thank you for your help.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I replied last time and nobody answered." → Agent: "I'm sorry nobody answered your last email. This email comes straight to me, and I'll reply within one working day."
cultural_note: "Feel free to revert" is a common Indian sign-off line; Oxford marks "revert" meaning "reply" as Indian English, so international customers may not expect it.
channel_note: Voice: "Is there anything else I can help you with today?" Chat: "Anything else I can help with?" Email: invite a reply, since the customer cannot answer you live.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it on an email where the problem is still open; give the next step and a date instead.
mini_conversation: Customer: Thanks for explaining the warranty. | Agent: You're welcome. If you have any other questions, just reply to this email and I'll be happy to help. | Customer: Actually, does it cover the battery? | Agent: Yes, the battery is covered for one year.
source_rule: Close by checking the issue is resolved; don't invite "anything else" on an unresolved issue.
fill_blank: If you ____ any other questions, just reply to this email and I'll be happy to help.
mcq_question: You solved the customer's problem. Which closing line is best?
mcq_options: A) If you have any other questions, just reply to this email and I'll be happy to help. | B) Your ticket is now closed, so please do not reply to this email, as it is not monitored. | C) Thank you for contacting us. Feel free to revert in case of any further queries. | D) Your issue is marked as resolved and the ticket has been closed from our end.
mcq_why: A is warm and tells the customer how to get more help. B shuts the door and D only reports a status. C is polite in Indian office English, but "revert" may not be expected by international readers.
reorder_task: reply / email / to / just / this
reorder_answer: Just reply to this email.
hindi_to_english: Customer ko bataiye ki agar koi aur sawaal ho to woh is email ka jawaab de sakte hain.
hindi_to_english_answer: If you have any other questions, just reply to this email.
whats_next_customer: Thanks, that's everything.
whats_next_reply: You're welcome, Daniel. Enjoy your new speaker.
role_play: Partner A asks by email how long their warranty lasts. Partner B answers in two lines and ends with an inviting closing line; A replies with one more question, and B answers it.
record_task: Write the last two lines of an email to a customer whose refund is complete: a closing line and a sign-off. Send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Is the problem really solved? · Did you say how to get more help? · Did you write "reply" rather than "revert", which international customers may not expect?

sentence: Best regards, Meera, Customer Support, [Company]
speaker: Agent
situation: You are ending a reply to a customer and need a short, professional sign-off with your name and team.
recall_cue: What two or three words do you write before your name at the end of a support email, and what comes after your name?
linking: If read aloud: best_regards → "bes-ri-gardz" · customer_support → "cus-tum-er-suh-port"
intonation: If read aloud: a sign-off is not read in a call; if you read it, keep it flat and falling.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, keep the "t" in "best" before "regards" light but present, and end "regards" with a "dz" sound, not "rigard".
customer_emotion: Finishing the email and wanting to know who helped them.
memory_hook: A sign-off is your name badge at the door: a warm word, your name, your team.
hindi_meaning: शुभकामनाओं सहित, मीरा, ग्राहक सहायता, [Company]
hindi_roman: Shubhkaamnaon sahit, Meera, grahak sahayata, [Company]
simple_meaning: A polite goodbye, then the writer's name, team and company.
why_it_works: A real name makes the customer feel a person helped them and tells them who to ask for next time; the team and company make it easy to trust.
key_chunk: Best regards, ___, ___, [Company]
grammar_pattern: Closing phrase + , + first name + , + team + , + company
grammar_note: Only the first word of the closing gets a capital: "Best regards", not "Best Regards".
tone_note: "Best regards" is safe for almost every customer. "Thanks and regards" with no name, or "Yours faithfully", sounds old-fashioned or cold.
watch_out: ✗ Best Regards, Customer Support → ✓ Best regards, Meera, Customer Support, [Company]
dont_say: "Regards, Team [Company]" with no name — the customer does not know who helped them and cannot ask for you again.
positive_swap: Instead of "Thanks & Regards, Support Team", write "Best regards, Meera, Customer Support, [Company]".
alt_1: Kind regards, Meera, Customer Support, [Company]
alt_2: Thanks, Meera, [Company] Support
more_formal: Yours sincerely, Meera Nair, Customer Support Team, [Company]
ask_next: Ticket #55931 · Reply to this email to continue the conversation.
replies_you_may_hear: Thanks, Meera. · Hi Meera, I have one more question. · Can I ask for you next time?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Can I speak to you directly next time?" → Agent: "Just reply to this email and it will come to me. If I'm away, a colleague will see our full conversation."
cultural_note: "Thanks & Regards" is very common in Indian office email. International customers are used to "Best regards" or "Kind regards" plus a real first name; a Zendesk analysis (quoted secondhand) found "Best regards" did better than some other closings, but the reasons are unclear, so treat that as weak evidence.
channel_note: Voice: "Thank you for calling. Have a good day." Chat: "Thanks for chatting with us, Daniel." Email: sign-off, name, team, company, on separate lines.
when_not_to_use: Do not use a cheerful "Cheers!" when writing to a customer who has just complained or lost money.
mini_conversation: Customer: Thanks for sorting out my refund. | Agent: You're welcome. Best regards, Meera, Customer Support, [Company] | Customer: Thank you, Meera. | Agent: It was a pleasure, Daniel. Have a good week.
source_rule: Sign off warmly with your own name; "Best regards" is a safe choice.
fill_blank: Best ____ (starts with r), Meera, Customer Support, [Company]
mcq_question: Which sign-off is best for a support email to an international customer?
mcq_options: A) Thanks & Regards, Support Team, [Company] | B) Best regards, Meera, Customer Support, [Company] | C) Yours obediently, Executive, Customer Care, [Company] | D) Cheers!!! Meera, Customer Support, [Company]
mcq_why: B is warm, professional and gives a real name and team. A is common in Indian offices, but it has no name, so the customer does not know who helped. C is old-fashioned and also has no name, and D is too casual for a support email.
reorder_task: Support / Customer / regards / Meera / Best
reorder_answer: Best regards, Meera, Customer Support
hindi_to_english: Email ka sign-off likhiye: Kind regards, naam Arjun, team Billing Team, aur company [Company].
hindi_to_english_answer: Kind regards, Arjun, Billing Team, [Company]
whats_next_customer: Thanks, Meera, you were very helpful.
whats_next_reply: Thank you, Daniel, that's kind of you. I'm glad I could help.
role_play: Partner A shows three sign-offs used in their office. Partner B rewrites each one with a closing phrase, a real first name, a team and [Company].
record_task: Write a full sign-off for yourself (closing phrase, your first name, your team and [Company]) and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you use a real first name? · Did you write "regards" with a small "r"? · Did you avoid "Thanks & Regards" with no name?

sentence: I'm just following up on my email from Monday. Do you still need help with your refund?
speaker: Agent
situation: You asked a customer on Monday to choose how they want their refund (on the original card or as store credit), and it is now Thursday with no reply.
recall_cue: The customer has gone quiet for three days. How do you remind them politely without sounding like you are chasing?
linking: If read aloud: following_up → "fol-oh-in-gup" · still_need → "stil-need" · help_with → "hel-pwith"
intonation: If read aloud: friendly and light on the first sentence, then rise on "refund?" because it is a yes/no question.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, keep the final "d" in "need" and "refund" clear; "Monday" is MUN-day, not MON-day with an "o" as in "on".
customer_emotion: Busy or forgetful, not necessarily unhappy.
memory_hook: A follow-up is a light knock on the door, not a loud bang.
hindi_meaning: मैं बस सोमवार वाले अपने ईमेल के बारे में याद दिला रहा/रही हूँ। क्या आपको अभी भी रिफ़ंड के लिए मदद चाहिए?
hindi_roman: Main bas Somvaar waale apne email ke baare mein yaad dila raha/rahi hoon. Kya aapko abhi bhi refund ke liye madad chahiye?
simple_meaning: I wrote to you on Monday; I want to check if you still need help getting your money back.
why_it_works: It reminds the customer which email you mean and asks an easy yes/no question, so it is simple to answer and does not sound like blame.
key_chunk: I'm just following up on ___. Do you still need help with ___?
grammar_pattern: I'm + just + verb-ing + on + noun · Do + you + still + need + noun?
grammar_note: "Following up on" means writing again about something you sent before.
tone_note: "Just" and the question make it gentle. "You have not replied to our email" sounds like you are blaming the customer.
watch_out: ✗ I am just follow up on my email from Monday. → ✓ I'm just following up on my email from Monday. Do you still need help with your refund?
dont_say: "As you have not responded, we are closing your ticket." — it sounds like a punishment and may lose a customer who was simply busy.
positive_swap: Instead of "You have not replied yet", write "I'm just following up on my email from Monday."
alt_1: I wanted to check in about my email on Monday. Can I still help with your refund?
alt_2: Following up on Monday's email: are you still waiting for your refund?
more_formal: I am writing to follow up on my email of Monday. Please let me know whether you still need assistance with your refund.
ask_next: If so, please reply with "card" or "store credit" and I'll process the refund the same day.
replies_you_may_hear: Sorry, I was travelling. · Yes, please send it to my card. · No, it's sorted now, thanks.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Stop emailing me, I'm busy." → Agent: "Of course, I'm sorry for the extra emails. I'll keep your request open for 14 days, so you can reply whenever it suits you."
cultural_note: "Gentle reminder" is common in Indian office email and can sound pushy to some international readers. A light "just following up" plus a question feels friendlier.
channel_note: Voice: "I'm calling about the email I sent on Monday." Chat: "Are you still there, Daniel?" Email: keep the same subject line with "Follow-up" so the customer sees it is not new.
when_not_to_use: Do not send a follow-up the next morning; give the customer a fair time to reply first.
mini_conversation: Customer: (no reply for three days) | Agent: I'm just following up on my email from Monday. Do you still need help with your refund? | Customer: Sorry, I was away. Yes, please. | Agent: Thank you for replying. Would you like the refund on your original card or as store credit?
source_rule: Follow-ups: say it is a follow-up (in the subject too) so it is not read as a new issue.
fill_blank: I'm just ____ up on my email from Monday. Do you still need help with your refund?
mcq_question: A customer has not replied for three days. Which follow-up is best?
mcq_options: A) I'm just following up on my email from Monday. Do you still need help with your refund? | B) You have not replied to our email from Monday, so please reply with the details we asked for. | C) Gentle reminder: please reply at the earliest, as we are still waiting for your response. | D) As we have not heard from you since Monday, your ticket will be closed today unless you reply.
mcq_why: A says which email and asks an easy question. B blames the customer, C is polite in Indian office English but can feel pushy, and D sounds like a threat.
reorder_task: following / just / I'm / up / my / on / email
reorder_answer: I'm just following up on my email.
hindi_to_english: Customer ko yaad dilaiye ki aapne Tuesday ko email bheja tha, aur poochhiye ki kya unhe abhi bhi exchange chahiye.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm just following up on my email from Tuesday. Do you still need help with your exchange?
whats_next_customer: Sorry, I was away. What did you need?
whats_next_reply: That's fine, thank you for replying. I need to know if you would like the refund on your original card or as store credit.
role_play: Partner A asked for a refund but did not reply when Partner B asked how to send the money. Partner B writes a polite follow-up; A replies late and apologises, and B answers warmly.
record_task: Write a follow-up email to a customer who has not replied for four days about a size exchange, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you say which earlier email you mean? · Did you ask an easy yes/no question? · Did you avoid blaming the customer?

sentence: I've attached your invoice for order 48213 as a PDF.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer asked for a copy of their invoice for an office claim, and you are sending it.
recall_cue: You are sending a document with your email. How do you tell the customer what is attached, without old-fashioned office phrases?
linking: If read aloud: I've_attached → "ai-va-tacht" · invoice_for → "in-voy-sfor"
intonation: If read aloud: steady, falling at "PDF", with the numbers read in pairs or one by one.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "attached" ends in "cht" (one syllable at the end: a-TACHT), not "a-tach-ed"; "invoice" has a clear "v", top teeth on the lower lip.
customer_emotion: Needs the document quickly for a claim.
memory_hook: Name the attachment like a gift tag: say what is inside the box, not "the same".
hindi_meaning: आपके ऑर्डर 48213 का इनवॉइस मैंने PDF के रूप में अटैच कर दिया है।
hindi_roman: Aapke order 48213 ka invoice maine PDF ke roop mein attach kar diya hai.
simple_meaning: Your bill for order 48213 is added to this email as a PDF file.
why_it_works: It names the document, the order and the format, so the customer knows what to look for and does not miss the attachment.
key_chunk: I've attached your ___ as a ___.
grammar_pattern: I've (I have) + attached + your + noun + for + noun + as + a + format
grammar_note: "I've attached" (present perfect) tells the customer the file is already in this email.
tone_note: A short, plain sentence sounds modern and clear. "Please find the same attached herewith" sounds old-fashioned and does not say what "the same" is.
watch_out: ✗ I have attach your invoice for order 48213 in PDF. → ✓ I've attached your invoice for order 48213 as a PDF.
dont_say: "PFA." — many customers do not know this abbreviation, and it looks rushed.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please find the same attached", write "I've attached your invoice for order 48213 as a PDF."
alt_1: Your invoice for order 48213 is attached as a PDF.
alt_2: I've added the PDF invoice for order 48213 to this email.
more_formal: Please find attached your invoice for order 48213 in PDF format.
ask_next: If you need the invoice in your company's name, just reply with the company name and address.
replies_you_may_hear: Thanks, got it. · I can't open the file. · Can you add my company name?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "There's no attachment!" → Agent: "I'm sorry, it didn't come through. I've attached it again now; it's called Invoice-48213.pdf."
cultural_note: "PFA" and "Please find the same attached" are common in Indian office email. International customers expect you to name the document in a normal sentence.
channel_note: Voice: "I'll email you the invoice now as a PDF." Chat: "I've uploaded your invoice here as a PDF." Email: name the file and attach it before you press send.
when_not_to_use: Do not write this line until the file is really attached; check before you send, or the customer has to write again.
mini_conversation: Customer: Could you send me my invoice? | Agent: Of course. I've attached your invoice for order 48213 as a PDF. | Customer: Thanks, I can open it. | Agent: Great. Just reply if you need anything else.
source_rule: Name the thing instead of "the same"; use plain words.
fill_blank: I've attached your invoice for order 48213 ____ (starts with a) a PDF.
mcq_question: You are sending an invoice. Which sentence is best for an international customer?
mcq_options: A) I've attached your invoice for order 48213 as a PDF. | B) PFA the invoice for order 48213, kindly acknowledge receipt. | C) Please find the same attached herewith, as requested. | D) Invoice attachment is there in this mail, please check.
mcq_why: A names the document, order and format. B uses an abbreviation many customers do not know, plus "kindly", which international customers may not expect, C is a habit from Indian office email where "the same" does not tell the reader what is attached, and D sounds abrupt.
reorder_task: PDF / your / as / attached / invoice / I've / a
reorder_answer: I've attached your invoice as a PDF.
hindi_to_english: Customer ko bataiye ki aapne unka warranty card PDF mein attach kiya hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: I've attached your warranty card as a PDF.
whats_next_customer: Can you put my company name on it?
whats_next_reply: Yes. Please reply with your company name and address, and I'll send a new invoice today.
role_play: Partner A asks by email for a delivery receipt and a warranty card. Partner B writes the reply naming both attachments; A says one file will not open, and B resends it.
record_task: Write a one-line email telling a customer you have attached their return label, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you name the document and the order? · Did you avoid "the same" and "PFA", which international customers may not expect? · Did you check the file was really attached?

sentence: Thanks for your email. Our team is offline right now, and we will reply by 11 am on the next working day.
speaker: Agent
situation: You are writing the automatic reply that customers receive when they email outside support hours.
recall_cue: Nobody is at work when the customer writes. What should the automatic reply promise, and when?
stress: THANKS-for-your-EE-mail · our-TEAM-is-OFF-line · RIGHT-NOW · we-will-re-PLY · by-e-LEV-en-ay-EM · on-the-NEXT-WORK-ing-DAY
linking: If read aloud: thanks_for → "thank-sfor" · team_is → "tee-miz" · next_working → "nex-working"
intonation: If read aloud: calm and steady, with a clear fall on "working day".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "working" starts with a "w": round your lips, no teeth on the lip, so it does not sound like "vorking".
customer_emotion: Hoping for help and unsure if anyone will see the email.
memory_hook: An auto-reply is a note on a closed shop door: "Back tomorrow at 9", not just "Closed".
hindi_meaning: आपके ईमेल के लिए धन्यवाद। हमारी टीम अभी ऑफ़लाइन है, और हम अगले कार्य दिवस सुबह 11 बजे तक जवाब देंगे।
hindi_roman: Aapke email ke liye dhanyavaad. Hamari team abhi offline hai, aur hum agle kaarya divas subah 11 baje tak jawaab denge.
simple_meaning: We got your email, but nobody is working now; you will get an answer before 11 in the morning on our next work day.
why_it_works: It confirms the email arrived, explains the silence and gives a real time, so the customer does not send the same email again.
key_chunk: Our team is ___ right now, and we will reply by ___.
grammar_pattern: Our team + is + adjective + right now · we will + base verb + by + time
grammar_note: "By 11 am" means "at 11 am or before".
tone_note: A clear time sounds trustworthy. "Your mail will be attended in due course" sounds old-fashioned and gives no time.
watch_out: ✗ Your mail will be attended at the earliest. → ✓ Thanks for your email. Our team is offline right now, and we will reply by 11 am on the next working day.
dont_say: "We are closed." alone — it gives no time and makes the customer think the email is lost.
positive_swap: Instead of "We will revert at the earliest", write "We will reply by 11 am on the next working day."
alt_1: Thanks for writing to us. We're away right now and will answer by 11 am on our next working day.
alt_2: We've got your email. Our support team is back at 9 am on the next working day and will reply by 11 am.
more_formal: Thank you for your email. Our support team is currently unavailable, and we will respond by 11:00 am on the next working day.
ask_next: If your order has not shipped yet, you can still cancel it in your account under My Orders.
replies_you_may_hear: OK, thanks. · It's urgent, is there a phone number? · Will someone really reply?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "It's urgent and I can't wait until tomorrow." → Agent (next morning): "Good morning, Daniel. I'm sorry you had to wait. I'm checking your order now, and I will email you within the hour."
cultural_note: "At the earliest" and "will be attended" are common in Indian office English. International customers expect a plain sentence with a clear time.
channel_note: Voice: a recorded message gives the opening hours. Chat: "We're offline now; leave a message and we'll email you by 11 am." Email: the auto-reply goes out at once.
when_not_to_use: Do not promise "by 11 am" in an auto-reply if your team cannot really meet that time on busy days.
mini_conversation: Customer: (emails at 10 pm) My order is wrong. | Agent: (auto-reply) Thanks for your email. Our team is offline right now, and we will reply by 11 am on the next working day. | Customer: (next day) Any update? | Agent: Good morning, Daniel. I'm sorry your order was wrong; I've arranged a replacement.
source_rule: Use "I will"/"we will" plus a real time instead of "soon".
fill_blank: Our team is offline right now, and we will reply ____ 11 am on the next working day at the latest.
mcq_question: Which line is best for an out-of-hours automatic reply?
mcq_options: A) Thanks for your email. We are closed at the moment, so please contact us again during office hours. | B) Thank you for contacting us. Your mail will be attended at the earliest by the concerned team. | C) This is an automated message. Do not reply to this email, as this mailbox is not monitored by us. | D) Thanks for your email. Our team is offline right now, and we will reply by 11 am on the next working day.
mcq_why: D confirms the email arrived and gives a real time. A gives no time and sends the customer away, B sounds polite in Indian office English but "at the earliest" is not a time, and C shuts the door.
reorder_task: is / right / team / now / Our / offline
reorder_answer: Our team is offline right now.
hindi_to_english: Auto-reply likhiye: email ke liye dhanyavaad, hamari team abhi offline hai aur Monday dopahar 12 baje tak jawaab denge.
hindi_to_english_answer: Thanks for your email. Our team is offline right now, and we will reply by 12 noon on Monday.
whats_next_customer: It's urgent. Is there a phone number?
whats_next_reply: Our phone line opens at 9 am, and the number is on our Contact Us page. You can also cancel an order yourself under My Orders.
role_play: Partner A is a manager. Partner B writes an out-of-hours auto-reply with a clear time and one self-help tip; A checks it for a real time and plain words.
record_task: Write a two-line out-of-hours auto-reply for a weekend, saying when the team will reply, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you confirm the email arrived? · Did you give a real time? · Did you avoid "at the earliest" and "will be attended"?

sentence: I am writing to complain about my late delivery.
speaker: Customer
situation: This is the first line of a new email from a customer whose order arrived a week late.
recall_cue: An email starts with a formal "complain" line. What does the customer want you to understand, and what do you write first?
linking: If read aloud: writing_to → "wri-ting-tuh" · about_my → "a-bou-my"
intonation: If read aloud: firm and falling; it is a formal statement, not a question.
indian_pron_tip: If you read the customer's line aloud, "complain" is com-PLAIN with stress on the second part, and "delivery" has a clear "v" (teeth on lip).
customer_emotion: Annoyed and wanting the company to take them seriously.
memory_hook: "Complain" is a red flag at the top of the email: read everything carefully and apologise for the exact problem.
hindi_meaning: मैं अपनी देर से आई डिलीवरी के बारे में शिकायत करने के लिए लिख रहा/रही हूँ।
hindi_roman: Main apni der se aayi delivery ke baare mein shikaayat karne ke liye likh raha/rahi hoon.
simple_meaning: I am unhappy because my order came late, and I want you to know.
why_it_works: The customer chose a formal, official line to show this is serious. They want an apology, an explanation and often something to make up for it, not a template.
key_chunk: I am writing to complain about ___.
grammar_pattern: I am writing + to + verb + about + noun
grammar_note: "I am writing to…" is a fixed formal opening that gives the reason for the email.
tone_note: The customer is formal, so reply in a calm, respectful tone. A cheerful "Hi there!" or a smiley would sound like you are not taking it seriously.
watch_out: ✗ Thank you for your feedback! 😊 → ✓ I'm sorry your delivery was late, and thank you for telling us.
dont_say: "We have noted your feedback." — a complaint is not feedback, and this line sounds like nothing will happen.
positive_swap: Instead of "Thank you for your valuable feedback", write "I'm sorry your delivery was a week late."
alt_1: I want to make a complaint about my delivery.
alt_2: I'm very unhappy that my order arrived late.
more_formal: I wish to make a formal complaint regarding the late delivery of my order.
ask_next: I'm sorry your delivery was a week late. I've checked your order, and here is what happened.
