key_chunk: As ___, we can't ___. I understand ___, but I can offer you ___.
grammar_pattern: As + reason clause, + we can't + verb + now. · I understand + (that) clause, + but + I can offer you + noun, or + noun + if + condition
grammar_note: "As" here means "because"; it introduces the reason before the decision.
tone_note: Putting the reason first and the options last leaves the customer with something to say yes to. "This is not possible as per our policy" sounds like a wall.
watch_out: ✗ As per policy, return is not possible. → ✓ As the 30-day return period ended on 2 May, we can't accept a return now.
dont_say: "Unfortunately, we cannot help you with this request." — it closes the conversation and offers nothing.
positive_swap: Instead of "We cannot accept your return", write "What I can offer you is full store credit, or a free repair if the machine has a fault."
alt_1: The return period closed on 2 May, so a refund is no longer available. I know you were hoping to return the machine, but I can arrange full store credit, or a free repair if it has a fault.
alt_2: Because the machine was delivered more than 30 days ago, we can't take it back. I'm sorry this is not the news you wanted, but we can give you store credit, or repair it free of charge if it has a fault.
more_formal: As the 30-day return period ended on 2 May, we are unable to accept a return. I appreciate that this is not the outcome you had hoped for; however, I would be glad to offer full store credit or, if the machine is faulty, a free repair.
ask_next: Please let me know which option you prefer, and I will set it up within one working day.
replies_you_may_hear: Fine, I'll take the store credit. · It was faulty from day one, so the return window should not apply. · I want to speak to a manager.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "It was faulty from the start, so the return period is irrelevant." → Agent: "Thank you for telling me. If the machine has a fault, the warranty covers it, so I can book a free repair or replacement. Could you describe what happens when you switch it on?"
cultural_note: "As per policy, it is not possible" is common in Indian service writing. International customers may read it as hiding behind rules; they expect the actual reason and an alternative.
channel_note: Voice: say the empathy line slowly and pause before the options. Chat: send the reason and the options as two short messages. Email: put the options on two separate lines.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this before you know why the customer wants to return the item; if the machine is faulty, check the warranty first, because a fault is usually a repair or replacement case.
mini_conversation: Customer: I'd like to return the coffee machine I bought in March. | Agent: As the 30-day return period ended on 2 May, we can't accept a return now. I understand this isn't the answer you were hoping for, but I can offer you full store credit, or a free repair if the machine has a fault. | Customer: Store credit is fine. | Agent: Thank you. I will add the credit to your account today and email you a confirmation by 5 pm.
source_rule: Saying no by email: reason, then empathy, then an alternative, then a follow-up; never a bare "No". Don't hide behind "policy" (derived advice).
fill_blank: As the 30-day return period ended on 2 May, we can't accept a return now. I understand this isn't the answer you were hoping for, ____ I can offer you full store credit, or a free repair if the machine has a fault.
mcq_question: A customer asks to return an item after the return window has closed. Which reply follows best practice?
mcq_options: A) Under our returns policy, items cannot be returned after 30 days, so I am afraid this is not possible. | B) I'm sorry, but we cannot accept returns after 30 days, so I am unable to help with this request. | C) The return period ended on 2 May, so we can't take it back. I can offer store credit or a free repair. | D) Please contact the manufacturer about this, as we are not able to take back items after the return period.
mcq_why: C gives the reason and two alternatives. A is tempting because it sounds official, but it hides behind "policy" and offers nothing. B says no with no alternative, and D passes the customer on.
reorder_task: repair / you / can / free / I / a / offer
reorder_answer: I can offer you a free repair.
hindi_to_english: Exchange ka samay khatam ho gaya hai, lekin main aapko store credit de sakta hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: The exchange period has ended, but I can offer you store credit instead.
whats_next_customer: Can you make an exception just this once?
whats_next_reply: I understand why you are asking, but I'm not able to approve a return after 30 days. What I can do is add the store credit today, or book a free repair this week if the machine has a fault.
role_play: Partner A asks by email to return shoes 45 days after delivery. Partner B writes a reply that gives the reason, shows empathy and offers two alternatives.
record_task: Write a three-sentence email declining a late return of a jacket, offering two alternatives, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you give a real reason, not just "policy"? · Did you offer at least one alternative? · Did your email end on what you can do, not on "no"?

sentence: I'm sorry we charged your card three times for a single order; that was our mistake. I have refunded the two extra payments of $129 today, and I will email you the bank reference by 5 pm.
speaker: Agent
situation: A system error charged a customer three times for one order, and you are writing to apologise and confirm what has been done.
recall_cue: Your company made a serious billing error. How do you own the mistake in a few words and show that the fix is already done?
stress: i'm-SOR-ry · we-CHARGED-your-CARD · THREE-TIMES · for-a-SIN-gle-OR-der · that-was-our-mis-TAKE · i-have-re-FUND-ed · the-TWO-EX-tra-PAY-ments · of-a-HUN-dred-and-TWEN-ty-NINE-DOL-lars · to-DAY · and-i-will-E-mail-you · the-BANK-REF-er-ence · by-FIVE-P-M
linking: If read aloud: charged_your → "charj-jor" · that_was → "that-wuz" · email_you → "ee-may-lyoo"
intonation: If read aloud: low and serious on "our mistake", a clear pause after it, then a steadier, confident tone on "refunded" and a firm fall on "5 pm".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, say "charged" with a clear final "d" sound joined to the "j" ("charjd"), and "mistake" as mi-STAKE with stress on the second part, not MIS-take.
customer_emotion: Alarmed and angry about money taken without permission.
memory_hook: Three charges, three moves: say SORRY, say OUR MISTAKE, say what is already REFUNDED, like three coins going back into a wallet.
hindi_meaning: मुझे खेद है कि हमने एक ही ऑर्डर के लिए आपके कार्ड से तीन बार पैसे काटे; यह हमारी ग़लती थी। मैंने आज $129 के दो अतिरिक्त भुगतान वापस कर दिए हैं, और शाम 5 बजे तक आपको बैंक रेफ़रेंस ईमेल कर दूँगा/दूँगी।
hindi_roman: Mujhe khed hai ki humne ek hi order ke liye aapke card se teen baar paise kaate; yeh hamari galti thi. Maine aaj $129 ke do atirikt bhugtaan wapas kar diye hain, aur shaam 5 baje tak aapko bank reference email kar doonga/doongi.
simple_meaning: We took your money three times by mistake. It was our fault. I have sent back the two extra payments today, and I will send you proof by 5 pm.
why_it_works: It says clearly whose fault it was, which matters most in an apology, and pairs it with a repair already made and a time for proof. The customer does not have to chase anything.
key_chunk: I'm sorry we ___; that was our mistake. I have ___, and I will ___ by ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm sorry (that) + we + past simple; that was our mistake. · I have + past participle + today · I will + verb + by + time
grammar_note: "That was our mistake" is a short, complete sentence that takes responsibility without excuses.
tone_note: The short, plain sentences sound sincere. Long explanations about "technical issues" before the apology sound like excuses and make the customer angrier.
watch_out: ✗ Due to some technical issue, your card was charged three times. → ✓ I'm sorry we charged your card three times for a single order; that was our mistake.
dont_say: "This was due to a technical glitch at our end." — it blames the system, not the company, and sounds like an excuse.
positive_swap: Instead of "The error occurred due to a system issue", write "That was our mistake, and I have refunded the extra payments today."
alt_1: I'm very sorry: we charged you three times for one order, and that should never have happened. I have refunded both extra payments of $129 today.
alt_2: Charging you three times for one order was our error, and I apologise. I have refunded the two extra payments, and I will send you the bank reference by 5 pm today.
more_formal: Please accept my sincere apology for charging your card three times for a single order; the error was entirely ours. I have refunded the two additional payments of $129 today and will email you the bank reference by 5 pm.
ask_next: If your bank has charged you any fees because of this, please send me the statement, and I will ask our billing team to refund them and reply to you by Friday.
replies_you_may_hear: When will I actually see the money? · My account went overdrawn because of this. · Thank you for being honest about it.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "My account went overdrawn because of you." → Agent: "I'm sorry our mistake left your account overdrawn. Please send me the bank statement showing the fee, and I will ask our billing team to refund it. I will email you their answer by Friday."
cultural_note: "Thrice" and "got debited" are common in Indian English. International customers may find "thrice" old-fashioned and "got debited" vague; "three times" and "we charged" are clearer.
channel_note: Voice: say the apology first, slowly, before any detail. Chat: send the apology and the refund as two short messages. Email: put the refund amount and the time for proof on separate lines.
when_not_to_use: Do not say "that was our mistake" before you have checked the facts; if the bank caused the extra charges, apologise for the worry and explain what you found.
mini_conversation: Customer: You have charged me three times! | Agent: I'm sorry we charged your card three times for a single order; that was our mistake. I have refunded the two extra payments of $129 today, and I will email you the bank reference by 5 pm. | Customer: How long until I see it? | Agent: Banks usually show it within a few working days; the reference will help your bank trace it.
source_rule: Apologise specifically and take responsibility, then offer repair; responsibility ranked most important (Lewicki et al., 2016).
fill_blank: I'm sorry we charged your card three times for a single order; that was our mistake. I have ____ (refund) the two extra payments of $129 today.
mcq_question: Your company charged a customer three times. Which sentence takes responsibility best?
mcq_options: A) The error occurred because of a technical issue in our payment system, which is now being fixed. | B) I apologise for the error on our side and for any inconvenience this may have caused you. | C) That was our mistake, and I have refunded the two extra payments to your card today. | D) We are very sorry this happened, and our system has been updated so it will not happen again.
mcq_why: C owns the error and shows the repair already made. A is tempting because it explains the cause, but it blames a "technical issue" instead of taking responsibility; B and D apologise but show no repair.
reorder_task: card / we / three / I'm / sorry / times / charged / your
reorder_answer: I'm sorry we charged your card three times.
hindi_to_english: Humne aapko galat bill bheja; yeh hamari galti thi. Maine sahi bill aaj bhej diya hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: We sent you the wrong bill, and that was our mistake. I have sent the correct bill today.
whats_next_customer: How do I know this won't happen again?
whats_next_reply: I have asked our billing team to find the cause, and I will email you their findings by Thursday. If you see any further charge before then, reply to me and I will look at it the same day.
role_play: Partner A is a customer charged twice for a hotel booking. Partner B writes an apology email that takes responsibility, names the refund already made and gives a time for proof.
record_task: Write a short apology email for sending a customer the wrong invoice twice, including the fix and a time, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you say clearly that it was your company's mistake? · Did you name an action already taken? · Did you give a time for the next update?

sentence: As an apology for the delay, I have added a $20 credit to your account, which you can use on any future order.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer's order arrived nine days late after several broken promises, the problem is now solved, and you are allowed to offer a small goodwill credit.
recall_cue: The problem is fixed, but the customer waited far too long. How do you offer a small extra gesture without making it sound like a bribe?
stress: as-an-a-POL-o-gy · for-the-de-LAY · i-have-AD-ded · a-TWEN-ty-DOL-lar-CRED-it · to-your-ac-COUNT · which-you-can-USE · on-an-y-FU-ture-OR-der
linking: If read aloud: added_a → "ad-di-da" · credit_to → "cred-i-too" · use_on → "yoo-zon"
intonation: If read aloud: warm and falling on "delay", then a gentle steady tone through "account", and a soft fall on "future order"; no rise, because this is a gift, not a question.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "apology" is a-POL-o-gy with stress on the second part, and "future" is FEW-cher, not "fu-tyoor"; keep the "t" in "credit" light, tongue behind the top teeth.
customer_emotion: Relieved the problem is over but still annoyed about the wait.
memory_hook: A small gift tag tied to the apology: the tag says what it is for, how much, and when to use it.
hindi_meaning: देरी के लिए माफ़ी के तौर पर, मैंने आपके खाते में $20 का क्रेडिट जोड़ दिया है, जिसे आप अपने किसी भी अगले ऑर्डर पर इस्तेमाल कर सकते हैं।
hindi_roman: Deri ke liye maafi ke taur par, maine aapke account mein $20 ka credit jod diya hai, jise aap apne kisi bhi agle order par istemaal kar sakte hain.
simple_meaning: Because we made you wait, I have given you $20 to spend with us next time.
why_it_works: It links the gesture clearly to the delay, so it reads as part of the apology, not a trick. It is already done and tells the customer exactly how to use it, so there is nothing to claim or chase.
key_chunk: As an apology for ___, I have added ___ to your account.
grammar_pattern: As an apology for + noun, + I have + past participle + … + which you can + verb …
grammar_note: "Which you can use…" adds information about the credit without starting a new sentence.
tone_note: Saying "as an apology" makes it sincere. "As a special one-time exception" sounds like a favour the customer should be grateful for, which can annoy them.
watch_out: ✗ As apology of the delay, I have added 20$ credit in your account. → ✓ As an apology for the delay, I have added a $20 credit to your account.
dont_say: "As a one-time exception, management has approved compensation." — it sounds grudging and makes the gesture about the company, not the customer.
positive_swap: Instead of "This is a one-time exception", write "As an apology for the delay, I have added a $20 credit to your account."
alt_1: To say sorry for the long wait, I have added a $20 credit to your account for your next order.
alt_2: I have also added a $20 credit to your account as an apology for the delay; it will be applied automatically at checkout.
more_formal: As a gesture of apology for the delay, I have applied a $20 credit to your account, which you are welcome to use on any future order.
ask_next: The credit is already visible under "My account"; please reply if you cannot see it.
replies_you_may_hear: Thank you, that is kind. · I'd rather have a refund than credit. · Does the credit expire?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I don't want credit; I want money back." → Agent: "I understand. I will check today whether the $20 can go back to your original card instead, and I will email you the answer by 5 pm."
cultural_note: Indian-English emails often say "please use the same" or "kindly avail the offer". International customers may not expect these phrases; name the credit and say how to use it.
channel_note: Voice: say it warmly and confirm the customer heard the amount. Chat: one short message, then a check that it shows in their account. Email: put the amount and how to use it on one clear line.
when_not_to_use: Do not offer a credit before the main problem is fixed; it can feel like you are trying to buy the customer's silence.
mini_conversation: Customer: My order finally arrived, nine days late. | Agent: I'm sorry your order arrived nine days late. As an apology for the delay, I have added a $20 credit to your account, which you can use on any future order. | Customer: Does it expire? | Agent: It is valid for 12 months, and I have sent the details to your email.
source_rule: Apology plus repair: an offer of repair ranked second only to taking responsibility (Lewicki et al., 2016).
fill_blank: As an apology ____ the delay, I have added a $20 credit to your account, which you can use on any future order.
mcq_question: Which sentence offers a goodwill credit in the most sincere way?
mcq_options: A) As a one-time exception, management has approved a $20 credit for your account. | B) As an apology for the delay, I have added a $20 credit to your account today. | C) We have credited $20 to your account, and we hope you will order from us again soon. | D) You can claim a $20 credit for the delay by replying to this email with your order number.
mcq_why: B links the credit to the delay and says it is already done. A is tempting because it sounds official, but "one-time exception" makes the credit sound like a favour; C sells instead of apologising, and D makes the customer do the work.
reorder_task: account / added / to / your / credit / have / a / I
reorder_answer: I have added a credit to your account.
hindi_to_english: Der se delivery ke liye maafi ke taur par maine aapke account mein $15 ka credit jod diya hai.
hindi_to_english_answer: As an apology for the late delivery, I have added a $15 credit to your account.
whats_next_customer: Can I use it on sale items?
whats_next_reply: Yes, you can use it on any item, including sale items, and it applies automatically at checkout.
role_play: Partner A's furniture delivery was a week late after two missed slots. Partner B writes an email that apologises for the delay and offers a credit, saying how to use it.
record_task: Write two sentences offering a goodwill credit to a customer whose repair took three weeks, and send them as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you link the gesture to the specific delay? · Did you say it is already done? · Did you explain how the customer can use it?

sentence: Thank you for your email. I have passed your case to our customer relations team, and Priya Shah from that team will contact you directly by Wednesday.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer's email says they will take legal action if their insurance claim is not paid, and you must reply calmly without arguing or giving legal opinions; the customer relations team has assigned Priya Shah, who can contact the customer by Wednesday.
recall_cue: An email mentions lawyers and court. What do you do with the case, who contacts the customer next, and when?
stress: THANK-you · for-your-E-mail · i've-PASSED-your-CASE · CUS-tom-er-re-LA-tions-TEAM · PRI-ya-SHAH · con-TACT-you · di-RECT-ly · by-WEDNES-day
linking: If read aloud: passed_your → "pas-chor" · contact_you → "kon-tak-choo" · to_our → "too-wow-er"
intonation: If read aloud: level and calm throughout, with no rising tones; pause after "email", and finish with a clear fall on "Wednesday" so the date sounds certain.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "Wednesday" is "WENZ-day" (the first "d" is silent), and "relations" begins with a light "r", not a rolled one; "passed" ends in a "t" sound ("past").
customer_emotion: Angry, distrustful and trying to force a response.
memory_hook: A relay baton: you do not run the legal race yourself, you pass the baton to the right runner and say when they will arrive.
hindi_meaning: आपके ईमेल के लिए धन्यवाद। मैंने आपका मामला हमारी कस्टमर रिलेशन्स टीम को भेज दिया है, और उस टीम की प्रिया शाह बुधवार तक आपसे सीधे संपर्क करेंगी।
hindi_roman: Aapke email ke liye dhanyavaad. Maine aapka maamla hamari customer relations team ko bhej diya hai, aur us team ki Priya Shah budhvaar tak aapse seedhe sampark karengi.
simple_meaning: Thanks for writing. A special team now has your case, and a named person from it will contact you by Wednesday.
why_it_works: It neither argues with the threat nor ignores it. It shows the case has gone to the right people, gives a real name and a day, and keeps the tone level so nothing in the reply can make things worse.
key_chunk: I have passed your case to ___, and ___ will contact you by ___.
grammar_pattern: I have + passed + object + to + team, + and + name + will + verb + by + day
grammar_note: "Will contact you by Wednesday" means "on or before Wednesday", so it is a promise with a limit.
tone_note: No emotion, no defence and no legal words sounds professional. Lines like "Threats will not help you" or "You are free to go to court" sound hostile and can be quoted against the company.
watch_out: ✗ Your matter has been forwarded to concerned team, they will contact you soon. → ✓ I have passed your case to our customer relations team, and Priya Shah will contact you directly by Wednesday.
dont_say: "There is no need to threaten us." — it judges the customer and turns a complaint into a fight.
positive_swap: Instead of "We cannot discuss legal matters", write "I have passed your case to our customer relations team, who will contact you directly by Wednesday."
alt_1: Thank you for letting us know how serious this is for you. Your case is now with our customer relations team, and Priya Shah will email you by Wednesday.
alt_2: I have shared your email and case history with our customer relations team. Priya Shah will be your contact and will be in touch by Wednesday.
more_formal: Thank you for your email. I have referred your case to our customer relations team, and Priya Shah, who will manage it from now on, will contact you directly by Wednesday.
ask_next: In the meantime, if you have any documents you would like Priya to see, please reply to this email and I will pass them on today.
replies_you_may_hear: Why can't you deal with it yourself? · Wednesday is too late. · Fine, but I expect a proper answer this time.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Wednesday is too late; my lawyer is waiting." → Agent: "I understand the urgency. I have asked Priya to contact you as early as possible, and I will confirm by tomorrow afternoon whether she can reply sooner."
cultural_note: Indian service emails often say "forwarded to the concerned team, they will revert". International customers may not expect "revert" for "reply", and "the concerned team" sounds faceless; a named person and a day build trust.
channel_note: Voice: stay calm, do not argue, and say you will pass it on. Chat: say you are passing it to a specialist team and give the day. Email: keep it short; every word may be shown to a lawyer.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this if your company has its own required wording for legal threats; follow that wording and your team lead's instructions.
mini_conversation: Customer: If my claim is not paid, my lawyer will be in touch. | Agent: Thank you for your email. I have passed your case to our customer relations team, and Priya Shah from that team will contact you directly by Wednesday. | Customer: Why not you? | Agent: Priya's team handles cases like yours and can make decisions that I cannot, so she is the best person to help.
source_rule: Escalate with a named owner and a clear time; replace vague promises with the next step and a deadline.
fill_blank: I have ____ (pass) your case to our customer relations team, and Priya Shah from that team will contact you directly by Wednesday.
mcq_question: A customer threatens legal action by email. Which reply is the safest and most professional?
mcq_options: A) I understand you are upset, but there is no need to mention lawyers or courts in an email like this. | B) You are free to take legal action, but it will not make your claim go through any faster than this. | C) I have passed your case to our customer relations team, and Priya Shah will contact you by Wednesday. | D) Your matter has been forwarded to the concerned team, who will get back to you as soon as possible.
mcq_why: C names the team, a person and a day without arguing. D is tempting because it is polite, but it is vague and gives no name or time. A and B argue with the customer.
reorder_task: by / will / Wednesday / Priya / you / contact
reorder_answer: Priya will contact you by Wednesday.
hindi_to_english: Maine aapka case hamari senior team ko bhej diya hai; Rahul Mehta Friday tak aapko call karenge.
hindi_to_english_answer: I have passed your case to our senior team, and Rahul Mehta will call you by Friday.
whats_next_customer: I want written confirmation that my complaint is on record.
whats_next_reply: Your complaint is recorded under reference CR-4518, and this email is your written confirmation.
role_play: Partner A writes an email saying they will "see the company in court" over a lost parcel. Partner B replies without arguing, names the team and person taking over, and gives a day.
record_task: Write a three-sentence reply to an email that threatens legal action over a refused refund, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you avoid arguing with or judging the customer? · Did you name a person or team and a day? · Did you avoid giving any legal opinion?

sentence: I saw your post about the missed installation, and I'm sorry it took a public message to get our attention. I'm now handling your case personally, and an engineer is booked for Saturday morning.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer posted on social media that their broadband installation was missed twice, the social team asked you to follow up privately by email, and you have booked an engineer for Saturday morning.
recall_cue: A customer complained in public and you are now writing privately. What do you admit about how they had to reach you, and what do you take over?
stress: i-SAW-your-POST · a-bout-the-MISSED-in-stal-LA-tion · and-i'm-SOR-ry · it-TOOK-a-PUB-lic-MES-sage · to-GET-our-at-TEN-tion · i'm-now-HAN-dling · your-CASE · PER-son-al-ly · and-an-en-gi-NEER · is-BOOKED · for-SAT-ur-day-MORN-ing
linking: If read aloud: saw_your → "saw-yor" · missed_installation → "mis-tin-stuh-LAY-shun" · get_our → "ge-tower"
intonation: If read aloud: sincere and falling on "attention", pause, then a confident, steady tone on "personally", and a clear fall on "Saturday morning".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "engineer" is en-ji-NEER with stress on the last part, not EN-gi-neer; "missed" ends in a "t" sound ("mist"), and "installation" has stress on LA.
customer_emotion: Frustrated, ignored, and testing whether the company will act now.
memory_hook: The spotlight is on: step out of the crowd, admit they had to shout, and hand them your own name and a date.
hindi_meaning: मैंने इंस्टॉलेशन छूटने के बारे में आपकी पोस्ट देखी, और मुझे खेद है कि हमारा ध्यान खींचने के लिए आपको पब्लिक में मैसेज लिखना पड़ा। अब मैं ख़ुद आपका मामला देख रहा/रही हूँ, और शनिवार सुबह के लिए इंजीनियर बुक है।
hindi_roman: Maine installation chhootne ke baare mein aapki post dekhi, aur mujhe khed hai ki hamara dhyaan kheenchne ke liye aapko public mein message likhna pada. Ab main khud aapka maamla dekh raha/rahi hoon, aur shanivaar subah ke liye engineer book hai.
simple_meaning: I read what you posted. I'm sorry you had to complain in public before we noticed. I'm now looking after your case myself, and an engineer will come on Saturday morning.
why_it_works: It admits the real failure, that the customer had to go public to be heard, instead of pretending all is normal. Then it gives a single owner and a booked date, which is what moves a public complaint into a private fix.
key_chunk: I'm sorry it took ___ to ___. I'm now handling your case personally, and ___.
grammar_pattern: I'm sorry (that) + it took + noun + to + verb · I'm now + -ing + personally
grammar_note: "It took a public message to get our attention" means "only a public message made us notice".
tone_note: Owning the failure sounds human. Asking the customer to "delete the post" or "please DM us for faster resolution" sounds as if the company cares about its image, not the problem.
watch_out: ✗ Sorry for the inconvenience, we will look into it soon. → ✓ I'm now handling your case personally, and an engineer is booked for Saturday morning.
dont_say: "Could you please take down the post now that we are in touch?" — it puts the company's image before the customer's problem.
positive_swap: Instead of "We noticed your negative post", write "I saw your post about the missed installation, and I'm sorry it took a public message to get our attention."
alt_1: Thank you for raising this, even though you should not have had to do it publicly. I am now your one point of contact, and an engineer is confirmed for Saturday morning.
alt_2: I have read your post and your earlier emails, and I'm sorry we let you down twice. I have booked an engineer for Saturday morning and will check with you on Saturday afternoon that everything works.
more_formal: I have seen your post regarding the missed installation, and I apologise that it took a public message to bring this to our attention. I am now managing your case personally, and an engineer has been booked for Saturday morning.
ask_next: Could you confirm that someone will be at home between 9 am and 12 noon on Saturday?
replies_you_may_hear: Why did it take a public post? · Saturday works, but I've heard that before. · I'll update my post if it actually happens.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I've heard promises before." → Agent: "That is fair. I will call you on Friday evening to confirm the engineer's name and arrival window, and you can reply to me directly at any time."
cultural_note: Some Indian support replies to public posts say "Request you to share details over DM, we will look into the same." International customers may not expect "the same" for the problem; they want the problem named and an owner.
channel_note: Voice: call if possible; a human voice repairs trust faster. Chat: move to a private chat and give your name. Email: one short paragraph with your name, the date and a direct reply address.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this if you have not actually booked the fix yet; promising a date you have not confirmed will lead to a second public post.
mini_conversation: Customer: (on social media) Second missed installation. Nobody answers. | Agent: (by email) I saw your post about the missed installation, and I'm sorry it took a public message to get our attention. I'm now handling your case personally, and an engineer is booked for Saturday morning. | Customer: What time? | Agent: Between 9 am and 12 noon. I will call you on Friday to confirm the engineer's name.
source_rule: Take ownership: "I'll personally follow up… by 4 pm tomorrow"; give a clear timeline and next step, not vague promises.
fill_blank: I'm now ____ (handle) your case personally, and an engineer is booked for Saturday morning.
mcq_question: A customer complained publicly about a missed installation. Which private email line is best?
mcq_options: A) Thank you for your message. Now that we are in touch, could you please take down your post about us? | B) We are sorry for any inconvenience caused, and your complaint has been forwarded to our installations team. | C) I'm sorry it took a public message to get our attention. I'm now handling your case personally. | D) We have seen your comments about us online and would like to resolve this issue as soon as possible.
mcq_why: C admits the failure and takes ownership. A is tempting because the team may want the post gone, but asking for it puts the brand before the customer. B and D give no owner and no date.
reorder_task: handling / I'm / personally / case / your / now
reorder_answer: I'm now handling your case personally.
hindi_to_english: Mujhe khed hai ki aapko public mein likhna pada; ab main khud aapka case dekh raha/rahi hoon.
hindi_to_english_answer: I'm sorry you had to raise this publicly. I'm now handling your case personally.
whats_next_customer: Will the engineer actually turn up this time?
whats_next_reply: That is a fair question after two missed visits. I will confirm the engineer's name and time with you on Friday, and if anything changes I will call you before 8 am on Saturday.
role_play: Partner A posted publicly that a refund promised three times never arrived. Partner B writes the private follow-up email: admits the failure, takes ownership and gives a date.
record_task: Write a private email to a customer who complained publicly about a delayed delivery, taking ownership and giving one booked action, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you admit the customer had to go public to be heard? · Did you name yourself as the owner? · Did you avoid asking them to delete the post?

sentence: Your app was still connecting to our old server, which is why it kept logging you out. To fix it: 1) sign out, 2) delete the app, 3) install it again and sign in.
speaker: Agent
situation: After a technical investigation, you found why a customer's banking app logs them out every few minutes, and you must explain the cause and the fix to a non-technical customer.
recall_cue: The cause is technical and the customer is not. How do you give the reason in one plain sentence and the fix as short numbered steps?
stress: your-APP · was-STILL-con-NECT-ing · to-our-OLD-SER-ver · which-is-WHY · it-KEPT-LOG-ging-you-OUT · to-FIX-it · SIGN-OUT · de-LETE-the-APP · in-STALL-it-a-GAIN · and-SIGN-IN
linking: If read aloud: which_is → "wi-chiz" · logging_you_out → "log-ging-yoo-WOUT" · install_it_again → "in-STAL-lit-uh-GEN"
intonation: If read aloud: a falling tone at the end of the cause, then read each numbered step as a short separate unit with a small pause and a slight rise until the last step, which falls.
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "server" has a "v" sound: top teeth touch the lower lip, not rounded lips as for "w"; and "kept" keeps both final sounds, "p" and "t", not "kep".
customer_emotion: Fed up and a little anxious about losing access to their money.
memory_hook: A short map with three numbered stops: one line saying why the road was blocked, then stop 1, stop 2, stop 3.
hindi_meaning: आपका ऐप अब भी हमारे पुराने सर्वर से जुड़ रहा था, इसी वजह से वह आपको बार-बार लॉग आउट कर रहा था। ठीक करने के लिए: 1) साइन आउट करें, 2) ऐप डिलीट करें, 3) उसे दोबारा इंस्टॉल करके साइन इन करें।
hindi_roman: Aapka app ab bhi hamare purane server se jud raha tha, isi wajah se woh aapko baar-baar log out kar raha tha. Theek karne ke liye: 1) sign out karein, 2) app delete karein, 3) use dobara install karke sign in karein.
simple_meaning: The app was talking to an old computer of ours, so it kept signing you out. Sign out, remove the app, put it back and sign in again.
why_it_works: One plain sentence explains the cause without jargon like "cache" or "token", so the customer trusts the fix. Numbered steps are easy to follow on a phone and reduce follow-up questions.
grammar_pattern: Past continuous (was connecting) + , which is why + past simple · imperative steps (sign out, delete, install)
grammar_note: "Which is why" links a cause to its result in one sentence.
tone_note: Plain words show respect for a non-expert. "Please clear the cache and re-authenticate your session token" sounds like a test of the customer's knowledge.
watch_out: ✗ You have to clear cache and install again the app. → ✓ To fix it: 1) sign out, 2) delete the app, 3) install it again and sign in.
dont_say: "The issue is due to legacy endpoint token invalidation." — the customer cannot act on words they do not know.
positive_swap: Instead of "You have to reinstall the app", write "To fix it: 1) sign out, 2) delete the app, 3) install it again and sign in."
alt_1: The logouts happened because your app was still linked to our old server. Three quick steps will fix it: sign out, delete the app, then install it again and sign in.
alt_2: We found the cause: your app was using our old server. Please sign out, delete the app, and install it again; when you sign in, it will connect to the new server.
more_formal: Our investigation found that your app was still connecting to a server we have retired, which caused the repeated logouts. To resolve this, please: 1) sign out, 2) delete the app, and 3) reinstall it and sign in.
ask_next: Once you have signed in again, could you reply to let me know whether you stay logged in?
replies_you_may_hear: Will I lose my saved payees? · Done, it seems to work now. · I'm not sure how to delete an app.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why should I do the work? It's your fault." → Agent: "You're right that the cause was on our side, and I'm sorry. These steps take about two minutes, and if you prefer, I can call you and go through them together."
cultural_note: "Kindly do the needful" is common in Indian technical emails. International customers may not expect it, because it does not say what to do; name each action as a numbered step.
channel_note: Voice: give one step at a time and wait for "done". Chat: send each step as a separate short message. Email: number the steps, one per line.
when_not_to_use: Do not give numbered self-fix steps to a customer who has said they are not comfortable with technology; offer to call and guide them.
mini_conversation: Customer: Your app logs me out every five minutes! | Agent: Your app was still connecting to our old server, which is why it kept logging you out. To fix it: 1) sign out, 2) delete the app, 3) install it again and sign in. | Customer: Will I lose my data? | Agent: No, your accounts and payees are stored with us, so they will be there when you sign in.
source_rule: Email body: plain words, number multi-step instructions, and one clear next step (ICMI plain language).
fill_blank: Your app was still connecting to our old server, w____ is why it kept logging you out.
mcq_question: Which explanation of a technical fix is best for a non-technical customer?
mcq_options: A) The app was using our old server; to fix it, sign out, delete the app and install it again. | B) The logouts are caused by an expired session token, so please clear your cache and sign in again. | C) We are aware of a backend issue with the login service, and our engineers are working on it now. | D) This is a known issue, so you have to delete the app and install it again before you can log in.
mcq_why: A gives a plain cause and clear steps. B is tempting because it is technically correct, but most customers do not know what a cache or token is. C gives no steps, and D sounds like an order.
reorder_task: logging / it / kept / why / is / you / which / out
reorder_answer: which is why it kept logging you out
hindi_to_english: Printer purane driver ki wajah se band ho raha tha; naya driver install kariye aur printer restart kariye.
hindi_to_english_answer: The printer was stopping because of an old driver. To fix it: 1) install the new driver, 2) restart the printer.
whats_next_customer: It still logs me out after I did all three steps.
whats_next_reply: I'm sorry that did not fix it, and thank you for trying. I have asked our technical team to reset your account from our side today, and I will email you by 4 pm once it is done.
role_play: Partner A's smart TV app keeps freezing because of an old version. Partner B writes an email explaining the cause in one plain sentence and the fix in three numbered steps.
record_task: Write an email explaining in plain words why a customer's emails are not syncing, with a three-step numbered fix, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you explain the cause without jargon? · Did you number the steps? · Did each step start with a clear action verb?

sentence: Here is where things stand: the refund for your headphones has been processed, but our warehouse team is still tracing the missing charger. I will update you on the charger by Friday.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer raised two problems in one order; one is solved and one is still open, and you need to report both honestly in one email.
recall_cue: One part of the problem is solved and one is not. How do you report both clearly without making the whole case sound finished?
stress: HERE-is-WHERE-things-STAND · the-RE-fund · for-your-HEAD-phones · has-been-PRO-cessed · but-our-WARE-house-TEAM · is-still-TRAY-sing · the-MISS-ing-CHAR-ger · i-will-up-DATE-you · on-the-CHAR-ger · by-FRI-day
linking: If read aloud: here_is → "hee-riz" · update_you → "up-DAY-choo" · you_on → "yoo-won"
intonation: If read aloud: a slight pause after "stand", a falling, satisfied tone on "processed", a lower, serious tone after "but", and a firm fall on "Friday".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "things" starts with "th" (tongue between the teeth), not "tings"; "processed" ends with "st" ("PRO-sest"), keeping both final sounds.
customer_emotion: Pleased about the refund but worried the rest will be forgotten.
memory_hook: A two-column scoreboard: DONE on the left, STILL OPEN on the right, with a date written under the open column.
hindi_meaning: अभी की स्थिति यह है: आपके हेडफ़ोन का रिफ़ंड प्रोसेस हो चुका है, लेकिन हमारी वेयरहाउस टीम अभी भी खोए हुए चार्जर को ढूँढ रही है। मैं चार्जर के बारे में शुक्रवार तक आपको अपडेट दूँगा/दूँगी।
hindi_roman: Abhi ki sthiti yeh hai: aapke headphones ka refund process ho chuka hai, lekin hamari warehouse team abhi bhi khoye hue charger ko dhoondh rahi hai. Main charger ke baare mein shukravaar tak aapko update doonga/doongi.
simple_meaning: Your money for the headphones is on its way back. We are still looking for the charger. I will tell you more by Friday.
why_it_works: It separates what is done from what is not, so the customer does not think the whole case is closed. The open part has an owner and a date, which stops the customer from chasing.
key_chunk: Here is where things stand: ___ has been ___, but ___ is still ___. I will update you on ___ by ___.
grammar_pattern: Present perfect passive (has been processed) for done · present continuous (is still tracing) for not done · I will + verb + by + day
grammar_note: "Has been processed" means it is finished; "is still tracing" means the work is going on now.
tone_note: Clear, balanced reporting sounds trustworthy. "Your issue has been resolved" when part of it is still open sounds dishonest and leads to angrier emails later.
watch_out: ✗ Your issue is resolved, only charger is pending. → ✓ The refund for your headphones has been processed, but our warehouse team is still tracing the missing charger.
dont_say: "Your complaint is resolved." — when only half is fixed, it is not true and the customer will reopen the case angrier.
positive_swap: Instead of "The charger is not found yet", write "Our warehouse team is still tracing the missing charger, and I will update you by Friday."
alt_1: Here is an update on both parts of your request. The headphones refund is complete; the missing charger is still being traced, and I will write to you about it by Friday.
alt_2: Good news first: your headphones refund has gone through. Our warehouse team is still looking for the missing charger, and you will hear from me by Friday.
more_formal: I would like to update you on both matters. The refund for your headphones has now been processed; however, our warehouse team is still tracing the missing charger, and I will provide an update on this by Friday.
ask_next: If the charger cannot be found by Friday, would you prefer a replacement or a refund for it?
replies_you_may_hear: Thanks, I can see the refund. · Why is the charger taking so long? · Just send me a new charger instead.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Just send a new one; I don't care about tracing it." → Agent: "Of course. I have ordered a new charger for you today, and I will email you the tracking number by tomorrow."
cultural_note: Indian-English updates often say "the matter is under process". International customers may not expect this phrase; it does not say who is doing what or when it will finish.
channel_note: Voice: say "two updates" first, then each one. Chat: one message for the done part, one for the open part. Email: you can use two short lines, "Done:" and "Still open:".
when_not_to_use: Do not use this to close a ticket; if part of the issue is still open, the ticket should stay open too.
mini_conversation: Customer: Any news on my refund and the missing charger? | Agent: Here is where things stand: the refund for your headphones has been processed, but our warehouse team is still tracing the missing charger. I will update you on the charger by Friday. | Customer: And if it is lost? | Agent: Then on Friday I will offer you a new charger at no cost or a refund, whichever you prefer.
source_rule: Be specific about what will happen and when: a clear timeline, a reference and the next step.
fill_blank: The refund for your headphones has been ____ (process), but our warehouse team is still tracing the missing charger.
mcq_question: One part of a customer's problem is fixed and one is not. Which update is best?
mcq_options: A) Your issue has been resolved, and we will contact you again only if anything else comes up. | B) The refund is complete, and the charger is being handled by our warehouse team at the moment. | C) We are working on both parts of your case and will update you as soon as we have any news. | D) The refund is done, but the charger is still being traced; I will update you by Friday.
mcq_why: D separates the done part from the open part and gives a date. A is tempting because it sounds positive, but it is not true when the charger is still missing. B and C give no date for the open part.
reorder_task: by / update / will / I / Friday / you
reorder_answer: I will update you by Friday.
hindi_to_english: Aapka refund ho gaya hai, lekin replacement abhi tak dispatch nahin hua; main kal tak update doonga/doongi.
hindi_to_english_answer: Your refund has been processed, but the replacement has not been dispatched yet. I will update you by tomorrow.
whats_next_customer: So is my case closed now?
whats_next_reply: Not yet. I will keep it open until the charger question is settled, and I will write to you by Friday either way.
role_play: Partner A ordered a sofa and cushions; the sofa was refunded but the cushions are still missing. Partner B writes an update that reports both parts and gives a date.
record_task: Write an email update in which a damaged phone has been replaced but the case is still waiting for a refund of the delivery fee, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you clearly say what is done? · Did you clearly say what is still open? · Did you give a date for the open part?

sentence: I need to correct something I told you yesterday: your warranty covers the screen for 12 months, not 24. I'm sorry I gave you the wrong figure, and the repair you booked is still covered.
speaker: Agent
situation: You told a customer yesterday that their screen warranty lasts 24 months, but you have checked and it is 12, so you must correct it in writing.
recall_cue: You gave a customer wrong information yesterday. How do you correct it at once, own the error and reassure them about what still stands?
stress: i-NEED-to-cor-RECT · SOME-thing · i-TOLD-you-YES-ter-day · your-WAR-ran-ty · COV-ers-the-SCREEN · for-TWELVE-MONTHS · NOT-TWEN-ty-FOUR · i'm-SOR-ry · i-GAVE-you-the-WRONG-FIG-ure · and-the-re-PAIR · you-BOOKED · is-STILL-COV-ered
linking: If read aloud: need_to → "nee-tuh" · told_you → "tol-joo" · gave_you → "gay-vyoo"
intonation: If read aloud: steady and direct up to the colon, a short pause, strong contrastive stress on "twelve" and "not twenty-four", then a softer, reassuring fall on "still covered".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "months" ends in "nths": say the "th" and the "s" ("munths"), not "munts"; "warranty" is WOR-ran-ty with the "w" made with rounded lips, not teeth on lip.
customer_emotion: Surprised, possibly suspicious, and worried about what else was wrong.
memory_hook: A red pen on yesterday's note: cross out 24, write 12, and draw a tick next to the repair that still stands.
hindi_meaning: मैंने आपको कल जो बताया था, उसमें सुधार करना है: आपकी वारंटी स्क्रीन को 24 नहीं, 12 महीने तक कवर करती है। ग़लत आँकड़ा बताने के लिए मुझे खेद है, और आपने जो रिपेयर बुक किया है वह अब भी कवर है।
hindi_roman: Maine aapko kal jo bataya tha, usmein sudhaar karna hai: aapki warranty screen ko 24 nahin, 12 mahine tak cover karti hai. Galat aankda batane ke liye mujhe khed hai, aur aapne jo repair book kiya hai woh ab bhi cover hai.
simple_meaning: I gave you a wrong number yesterday. The screen warranty is one year, not two. Sorry for that. Your booked repair is still covered by the warranty.
why_it_works: It corrects the mistake in the first sentence instead of hiding it in the middle, and it owns the error with "I told you". It then removes the customer's biggest worry by confirming what has not changed.
key_chunk: I need to correct something I told you ___: ___, not ___.
grammar_pattern: I need to + verb · something (that) I told you + time · X, not Y (contrast)
grammar_note: "X, not Y" is a short way to replace a wrong fact with the right one.
tone_note: Correcting quickly and plainly builds trust. Writing "There was some miscommunication" hides who made the mistake and sounds evasive.
watch_out: ✗ Please note there was some miscommunication regarding the warranty period. → ✓ I need to correct something I told you yesterday: your warranty covers the screen for 12 months, not 24.
dont_say: "There seems to have been a misunderstanding on your part." — it blames the customer for your error.
positive_swap: Instead of "The information given earlier was wrong", write "I need to correct something I told you yesterday."
alt_1: I'm writing to correct my email from yesterday: the screen warranty is 12 months, not 24. I'm sorry for the mistake; your booked repair is not affected.
alt_2: I gave you the wrong warranty period yesterday, and I apologise. It is 12 months for the screen, and your repair on Monday is still covered.
more_formal: I must correct the information I gave you yesterday: your warranty covers the screen for 12 months, not 24. I apologise for giving you the wrong figure; your booked repair remains fully covered.
ask_next: If you made any decision based on the 24 months I mentioned, please tell me and I will check your options and reply by tomorrow.
replies_you_may_hear: Thanks for being honest. · So what else did you get wrong? · I only bought the extended cover because of what you said.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "I bought extra cover because you said 24 months." → Agent: "I understand, and I'm sorry my mistake led you to buy it. I will ask for that cover to be cancelled and refunded in full, and I will confirm by tomorrow."
cultural_note: Indian-English emails sometimes say "please ignore the previous mail" without saying what was wrong. International customers may not expect this; state the correct fact and own the mistake.
channel_note: Voice: say "I need to correct something" first, slowly, so the caller listens. Chat: one short message with the right fact. Email: put the corrected fact in the first line, and in bold if your tool allows.
when_not_to_use: Do not send this until you have checked the correct figure yourself; a second wrong number is worse than a short delay.
mini_conversation: Customer: Thanks for confirming the two-year screen warranty. | Agent: I need to correct something I told you yesterday: your warranty covers the screen for 12 months, not 24. I'm sorry I gave you the wrong figure, and the repair you booked is still covered. | Customer: OK, at least the repair is fine. | Agent: Yes, it is confirmed for Monday at no cost.
source_rule: Apologise specifically and take responsibility, then confirm what you will do (Lewicki et al., 2016).
fill_blank: I need to correct something I told you yesterday: your warranty covers the screen for 12 months, ____ 24.
mcq_question: You gave a customer the wrong warranty period yesterday. Which sentence starts the correction best?
mcq_options: A) I need to correct something I told you yesterday: your screen warranty is 12 months, not 24. | B) Please ignore my previous email, as it contained some incorrect information about your warranty. | C) There was some miscommunication yesterday about your warranty, and I would like to clarify it. | D) Our records show that your screen warranty is 12 months, so the earlier figure does not apply.
mcq_why: A owns the mistake and gives the correct fact. C is tempting because it sounds soft, but it hides who made the error. B and D change the fact without owning the mistake.
reorder_task: told / to / correct / you / I / something / need / I
reorder_answer: I need to correct something I told you.
hindi_to_english: Maine aapko kal jo bataya tha, use sahi karna hai: aapki delivery Tuesday ko nahin, Thursday ko hogi.
hindi_to_english_answer: I need to correct something I told you yesterday: your delivery is on Thursday, not Tuesday.
whats_next_customer: How do I know the 12 months is right?
whats_next_reply: That is a fair question. I have attached the warranty page for your model, and the screen cover is on page 2.
role_play: Partner A was told a refund would take three days, but it takes ten. Partner B writes an email that corrects the information, apologises and confirms what still stands.
record_task: Write an email correcting a delivery date you gave a customer by mistake, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did the correct fact appear in your first sentence? · Did you say "I" told you, not "there was a miscommunication"? · Did you confirm what has not changed?

sentence: To sum up: your two accounts have been merged, the duplicate charge has been refunded, and your new plan starts on 1 June. As everything is now sorted, I'll close this ticket, but you can reopen it at any time by replying to this email.
speaker: Agent
situation: After a two-week email thread with several problems, everything is now fixed and you are writing the final email to close the ticket.
recall_cue: A long thread is finally finished. How do you list what was done, check it is all settled and tell the customer how to come back?
stress: to-SUM-UP · your-TWO-ac-COUNTS · have-been-MERGED · the-DU-pli-cate-CHARGE · has-been-re-FUND-ed · and-your-NEW-PLAN · STARTS-on-the-FIRST-of-JUNE · as-EV-ry-thing-is-now-SOR-ted · i'll-CLOSE-this-TICK-et · but-you-can-re-O-pen-it · at-an-y-TIME · by-re-PLY-ing · to-this-E-mail
linking: If read aloud: sum_up → "suh-mup" · accounts_have → "a-COUNT-sav" · reopen_it → "ree-oh-pe-nit"
intonation: If read aloud: a short pause after "sum up", a slight rise on each of the first two items and a fall on "1 June", then a friendly, falling tone on "replying to this email".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "merged" ends in "rjd" said together ("murjd"), not "mer-ged"; "accounts" keeps the final "nts", not "accoun".
customer_emotion: Tired of the long thread and relieved it might be over.
memory_hook: A receipt at the end of shopping: each item listed, a total line saying "done", and a note that returns are welcome.
hindi_meaning: संक्षेप में: आपके दोनों खाते मर्ज कर दिए गए हैं, दोहरा चार्ज वापस कर दिया गया है, और आपका नया प्लान 1 जून से शुरू होगा। अब सब कुछ ठीक हो गया है, इसलिए मैं यह टिकट बंद कर रहा/रही हूँ, लेकिन आप इस ईमेल का जवाब देकर इसे कभी भी फिर से खोल सकते हैं।
hindi_roman: Sankshep mein: aapke dono account merge kar diye gaye hain, dohra charge wapas kar diya gaya hai, aur aapka naya plan 1 June se shuru hoga. Ab sab kuch theek ho gaya hai, isliye main yeh ticket band kar raha/rahi hoon, lekin aap is email ka jawaab dekar ise kabhi bhi phir se khol sakte hain.
simple_meaning: Here is everything we did. It is all finished, so I am closing your case, but just reply if you need us again.
why_it_works: Listing each outcome lets the customer check nothing was missed after a long thread. Saying how to reopen the ticket makes closing it feel safe, not like being dismissed.
key_chunk: To sum up: ___, ___, and ___. As everything is now sorted, I'll close this ticket, but ___.
grammar_pattern: To sum up: + list of present perfect passives (have been merged, has been refunded) · As + reason, + I'll + verb, + but + you can + verb
grammar_note: "Has been refunded" (present perfect passive) says the job is done without repeating "I did" each time.
tone_note: A clear summary sounds professional and caring. "Closing this ticket as no further action is required" sounds cold and as if the company wants to get rid of the customer.
watch_out: ✗ As discussed, all issues are resolved, hence closing the ticket. → ✓ To sum up: your two accounts have been merged, the duplicate charge has been refunded, and your new plan starts on 1 June.
dont_say: "We are closing this ticket as no further action is required from our end." — it sounds cold and gives no way back.
positive_swap: Instead of "This ticket will be closed", write "As everything is now sorted, I'll close this ticket, but you can reopen it at any time by replying to this email."
alt_1: Here is a quick summary: your accounts are merged, the extra charge is refunded, and your new plan begins on 1 June. I'll close the ticket now; just reply to this email if anything else comes up.
alt_2: Everything we discussed is now done: accounts merged, duplicate charge refunded, new plan from 1 June. I'm closing this ticket, and a reply to this email will reopen it.
more_formal: To summarise, your two accounts have been merged, the duplicate charge has been refunded, and your new plan will begin on 1 June. As all matters are now resolved, I will close this ticket; however, you may reopen it at any time by replying to this email.
ask_next: Thank you for your patience over the past two weeks, and I hope the new plan works well for you.
replies_you_may_hear: Thanks, that all looks right. · Wait, I still haven't received the refund. · Can I keep your name for next time?
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "The refund still isn't in my account." → Agent: "Thank you for telling me. I will keep the ticket open, check the refund with our payments team today, and send you the bank reference by tomorrow."
cultural_note: Indian-English closing emails often use "hence closing the ticket" or "thanks and regards". International customers may not expect "hence"; a plain summary and "I'll close this ticket" sound friendlier.
channel_note: Voice: summarise aloud, then ask whether everything is resolved before closing. Chat: send the summary as a short list, then ask "Is everything sorted on your side?". Email: use the summary line, or a short list if there are more than three items.
when_not_to_use: Do not send this if any item is still open; use a partial-update email instead and keep the ticket open.
mini_conversation: Customer: I think that's everything now. | Agent: To sum up: your two accounts have been merged, the duplicate charge has been refunded, and your new plan starts on 1 June. As everything is now sorted, I'll close this ticket, but you can reopen it at any time by replying to this email. | Customer: Great, thanks for sticking with it. | Agent: You're welcome. Thank you for your patience over the past two weeks.
source_rule: Close by summarising the outcomes and next steps; check the issue is resolved before closing.
fill_blank: To sum up: your two accounts have been merged, the duplicate charge has been ____ (refund), and your new plan starts on 1 June.
mcq_question: You are closing a long email thread where every issue is now fixed. Which closing is best?
mcq_options: A) To sum up: accounts merged, charge refunded, new plan from 1 June. Reply to this email to reopen the ticket. | B) As all of your issues are now resolved, this ticket is closed and no further action is required from our end. | C) Your accounts, refund and new plan are all dealt with. Thank you for contacting us, and have a good day. | D) Thank you for your patience over the past two weeks. Is there anything else I can help you with today?
mcq_why: A lists every outcome and gives a way back. D is tempting because it is polite, but at the end of a long thread the customer needs a summary, not an open question. B sounds cold, and C gives no way back.
reorder_task: email / replying / reopen / you / to / it / can / by / this
reorder_answer: You can reopen it by replying to this email.
hindi_to_english: Sankshep mein: aapka address update ho gaya hai aur naya card bhej diya gaya hai. Main yeh ticket ab band kar raha/rahi hoon, lekin aap is email ka jawaab dekar ise phir se khol sakte hain.
hindi_to_english_answer: To sum up: your address has been updated and your new card has been sent. I'll close this ticket now, but you can reply to this email to reopen it.
whats_next_customer: Thanks. Can I contact you directly if something goes wrong?
whats_next_reply: Yes. Reply to this email and the ticket will reopen with the full history, so you will not need to explain everything again.
role_play: Partner A has had a three-week thread about a broken fridge: a repair, a refund of the call-out fee and a new warranty. Partner B writes the closing email with a summary.
record_task: Write a closing email that summarises three things fixed on a customer's broadband account and tells them how to reopen the ticket, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you list every outcome? · Did you check that nothing is still open? · Did you tell the customer how to reopen the ticket?

sentence: If you feel we have put things right, we would be grateful for a short review. If something still isn't right, please reply to this email so I can fix it.
speaker: Agent
situation: A difficult case has just been resolved after a complaint, and you want to ask for a review without pressuring a customer who was recently upset.
recall_cue: A recently upset customer is now happy. How do you ask for a review without pressure, and what do you offer if they are still not happy?
stress: if-you-FEEL · we-have-PUT-things-RIGHT · we-would-be-GRATE-ful · for-a-SHORT-re-VIEW · if-SOME-thing · STILL-ISN'T-RIGHT · please-re-PLY-to-this-E-mail · so-i-can-FIX-it
linking: If read aloud: if_you → "i-fyoo" · so_I → "soh-wy" · fix_it → "fik-sit"
intonation: If read aloud: a gentle rise on "put things right", a soft fall on "review", a short pause, then a warm, steady tone on "reply to this email".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "review" has a "v" sound: top teeth touch the lower lip ("ri-VYOO"), not "ri-wyoo"; and "grateful" is GRATE-ful, two syllables, with a clear "t".
customer_emotion: Satisfied now, but still remembering the earlier frustration.
memory_hook: A door with two handles: one says "review us", the other says "tell me what is wrong", and the customer chooses.
hindi_meaning: अगर आपको लगता है कि हमने चीज़ें ठीक कर दी हैं, तो एक छोटा रिव्यू देने पर हम आभारी होंगे। अगर अब भी कुछ ठीक नहीं है, तो कृपया इस ईमेल का जवाब दें ताकि मैं उसे ठीक कर सकूँ।
hindi_roman: Agar aapko lagta hai ki humne cheezein theek kar di hain, to ek chhota review dene par hum aabhaari honge. Agar ab bhi kuch theek nahin hai, to kripya is email ka jawaab dein taaki main use theek kar sakoon.
simple_meaning: If you are happy with how we fixed this, please write a short review. If not, reply to this email and I will fix it.
why_it_works: The "if you feel" condition leaves the choice with the customer, so it does not sound like pressure. Offering a route for problems shows you care more about fixing things than about the score.
key_chunk: If you feel ___, we would be grateful for ___. If ___, please ___ so I can ___.
grammar_pattern: If + present simple, + we would be grateful for + noun · If + present simple, + please + verb + so (that) + I can + verb
grammar_note: "We would be grateful for" is a polite, indirect way to ask for something.
tone_note: The conditional makes the request modest. "Please give us 5 stars" sounds like pressure, and it can feel insulting to a customer who has just had a bad experience.
watch_out: ✗ Please give 5-star rating for my service, it is very important to me. → ✓ If you feel we have put things right, we would be grateful for a short review.
dont_say: "Please rate us 5 stars, it helps my performance." — it pressures the customer and makes the review about the agent.
positive_swap: Instead of "Contact me before you post anything", write "If something still isn't right, please reply to this email so I can fix it."
alt_1: If you are happy with how this was handled, a short review would mean a lot to our team. If not, please tell me what is still wrong.
alt_2: When you have a moment, and only if you feel we put things right, we would welcome a short review. I'm also here if anything still needs fixing.
more_formal: Should you feel that we have resolved matters to your satisfaction, we would be grateful for a brief review. If anything remains unresolved, please reply to me directly so that I can address it.
ask_next: Thank you again for your patience while we sorted this out.
replies_you_may_hear: Sure, happy to. · I'll think about it. · Honestly, the delay still annoys me.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Honestly, the delay still annoys me." → Agent: "That is completely fair, and thank you for telling me. Please do not feel any need to leave a review; is there anything I can still do about the delay?"
cultural_note: Indian-English requests often say "kindly give your valuable feedback" or "kindly rate 5 stars". International customers may not expect this; a soft, optional request sounds more sincere.
channel_note: Voice: ask lightly at the very end, only if the caller is clearly happy. Chat: one short line after the customer says thanks. Email: put the review request after the summary, never in the subject line.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask for a review when the customer is still upset or the issue is only partly fixed.
mini_conversation: Customer: Thanks, the new phone works perfectly. | Agent: I'm glad to hear it. If you feel we have put things right, we would be grateful for a short review. If something still isn't right, please reply to this email so I can fix it. | Customer: Happy to leave one. | Agent: Thank you, and enjoy the new phone.
source_rule: Close only after checking the issue is resolved; do not ask closing questions on an unresolved case.
fill_blank: If you feel we have put things right, we would be grateful ____ a short review.
mcq_question: A customer whose complaint was just fixed seems happy. Which review request is best?
mcq_options: A) If you have a moment, please give us 5 stars, because good ratings are very important to our team. | B) Please take two minutes to rate us today; your review helps me reach my monthly target. | C) Now that the problem is fixed, we expect you to complete the review form sent to your email. | D) If you feel we have put things right, we would be grateful for a short review of our service.
mcq_why: D leaves the choice to the customer and is modest. A is tempting because it is polite in form, but asking for a set score is pressure. B makes it about your target, and C is an order.
reorder_task: grateful / a / We / for / would / review / short / be
reorder_answer: We would be grateful for a short review.
hindi_to_english: Agar aap hamari service se khush hain, to ek chhota review dene par hum aabhaari honge.
hindi_to_english_answer: If you are happy with our service, we would be grateful for a short review.
whats_next_customer: Where do I leave the review?
whats_next_reply: I will send you the review link in a separate email today. You can use it whenever suits you.
role_play: Partner A's damaged sofa was replaced after a complaint and they are now happy. Partner B writes the final email with a sensitive review request and a route for any remaining problem.
record_task: Write two sentences asking a customer for a review after a resolved complaint, with a route for any remaining problem, and send them as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you make the review optional? · Did you avoid asking for a specific star rating? · Did you offer a way to report a remaining problem?

sentence: I can see why you are angry: you were promised a callback twice, and we did not call. I'm sorry. I will call you myself at 11 am tomorrow, or at another time that suits you better.
speaker: Agent
situation: A customer has sent an angry email in capital letters because two promised callbacks never happened, and you are replying.
recall_cue: The customer is furious because a promise was broken twice. How do you name the reason for the anger, apologise briefly, and make a promise you will personally keep?
stress: i-can-SEE-WHY · you-are-AN-gry · you-were-PROM-ised · a-CALL-back-TWICE · and-we-did-not-CALL · i'm-SOR-ry · i-will-CALL-you-my-SELF · at-e-LEV-en-A-M · to-MOR-row · or-at-a-NUTH-er-TIME · that-SUITS-you-BET-ter
linking: If read aloud: promised_a → "PROM-is-ta" · call_you → "caw-lyoo" · at_another → "a-ta-NUTH-er"
intonation: If read aloud: low and steady, not rising, on "angry"; pause before "I'm sorry" and say it simply; then a firm, falling tone on "tomorrow".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "promised" ends in "st" ("PROM-ist"), not "pro-mi-sed"; "eleven" is i-LEV-en with a "v" (teeth on lip), not "i-lewen".
customer_emotion: Furious, let down and feeling ignored.
memory_hook: A broken promise gets mended with a stronger knot: name the break, say sorry, tie a new promise to your own name and an exact time.
hindi_meaning: मैं समझ सकता/सकती हूँ कि आप नाराज़ क्यों हैं: आपसे दो बार कॉलबैक का वादा किया गया और हमने कॉल नहीं किया। मुझे खेद है। मैं कल सुबह 11 बजे ख़ुद आपको कॉल करूँगा/करूँगी, या किसी और समय जो आपके लिए बेहतर हो।
hindi_roman: Main samajh sakta/sakti hoon ki aap naraaz kyon hain: aapse do baar callback ka vaada kiya gaya aur humne call nahin kiya. Mujhe khed hai. Main kal subah 11 baje khud aapko call karoonga/karoongi, ya kisi aur samay jo aapke liye behtar ho.
simple_meaning: You are right to be angry; we said we would call you two times and we did not. Sorry. I will call you myself tomorrow at 11, or when you like.
why_it_works: It names the exact reason for the anger, which shows the agent has read the email properly. A short apology plus a personal, timed promise answers the real problem: the customer no longer trusts the company's promises.
key_chunk: I can see why you are ___: ___. I'm sorry. I will ___ myself at ___.
grammar_pattern: I can see why + subject + verb · passive past (you were promised) · I will + verb + myself + at + time
grammar_note: "You were promised" (passive) focuses on what happened to the customer, not on who forgot.
tone_note: Naming the feeling and the cause is respectful. "Please calm down" or "There is no need for capital letters" judges the customer and makes them angrier.
watch_out: ✗ Please calm down, we will arrange callback soon. → ✓ I can see why you are angry: you were promised a callback twice, and we did not call.
dont_say: "There is no need to write in capitals." — it criticises the customer's style instead of fixing the broken promise.
positive_swap: Instead of "Please don't be rude", write "I can see why you are angry, and I'm sorry."
alt_1: You have every reason to be angry; we promised to call you twice and did not. I'm sorry. I will call you myself tomorrow at 11 am, unless another time is better for you.
alt_2: I understand your anger, as two promised callbacks never happened. I apologise. I have blocked 11 am tomorrow in my own calendar to call you, or you can suggest another time.
more_formal: I fully understand your frustration: you were promised a callback on two occasions, and neither took place. Please accept my apology. I will telephone you personally at 11 am tomorrow, or at any other time that is more convenient.
ask_next: Is the number ending 4471 still the best one to reach you on?
replies_you_may_hear: Fine, 11 is OK. · Why should I believe you this time? · Don't call, just fix it by email.
if_customer_pushes: Customer: "Why should I believe you this time?" → Agent: "That is fair after what happened. I have put the call in my own calendar, and if anything stops me, I will email you before 11 am."
cultural_note: "Please calm down" or "Please cooperate" can appear in Indian service replies to angry emails. International customers may not expect this; it reads as blaming them, so name the feeling and act instead.
channel_note: Voice: let the caller finish, then say this slowly. Chat: send the empathy line and the promise as two messages. Email: reply within the same working day if you can, and keep it short.
when_not_to_use: Do not promise a personal callback if you will not be on shift at that time; offer a time you can actually keep.
mini_conversation: Customer: NOBODY HAS CALLED ME. TWICE! | Agent: I can see why you are angry: you were promised a callback twice, and we did not call. I'm sorry. I will call you myself at 11 am tomorrow, or at another time that suits you better. | Customer: 11 is fine. Don't forget. | Agent: I won't. I have put it in my calendar, and I will call the number ending 4471.
source_rule: Never say "calm down"; name the feeling, then act with "I will" plus a time.
fill_blank: I can see why you are angry: you were ____ (promise) a callback twice, and we did not call.
mcq_question: An angry customer was promised two callbacks that never happened. Which reply is best?
mcq_options: A) I can see why you are angry, and I'm sorry. I will call you myself at 11 am tomorrow. | B) Please calm down, as I want to help you. A senior colleague will call you back as soon as possible. | C) I understand that you are upset, but there is no need to write in capital letters in an email. | D) We are sorry for the delay in calling you. Our team is very busy, so delays can sometimes happen.
mcq_why: A names the feeling, apologises and gives a personal, timed promise. B is tempting because it promises a call, but "calm down" usually makes people angrier, and "soon" is vague. C criticises the customer's capitals, and D makes excuses.
reorder_task: why / angry / are / I / you / see / can
reorder_answer: I can see why you are angry.
hindi_to_english: Main samajh sakta/sakti hoon ki aap pareshaan kyon hain. Main kal subah 10 baje khud aapko call karoonga/karoongi.
hindi_to_english_answer: I can see why you are upset. I will call you myself at 10 am tomorrow.
whats_next_customer: And what if you don't call either?
whats_next_reply: I will call. If anything stops me, I will email you before 11 am with a new time, and you can reply to me directly.
role_play: Partner A writes an angry email because a technician missed two visits. Partner B replies: names the reason for the anger, apologises briefly and makes a personal, timed promise.
record_task: Write a reply to an angry email about two missed delivery slots, naming the feeling and making one timed promise, and send it as text or a photo for audit.
self_check: Did you name the reason for the anger? · Did you avoid "calm down" or any comment on the customer's tone? · Did you make a promise with your name and an exact time?

sentence: Thank you for asking for a copy of your personal data. To protect your account, could you reply from the email address registered with us? Once we have confirmed it is you, I will start the request and tell you when to expect the file.
speaker: Agent
situation: An email arrives from an unknown address asking for a copy of all the personal data your company holds about an account, and you must check identity before sharing anything.
recall_cue: Someone asks for all their personal data from an address you do not recognise. What reason do you give, what one thing do you ask for, and what happens next?
stress: THANK-you · for-ASK-ing · for-a-COP-y · of-your-PER-son-al-DA-ta · to-pro-TECT · your-ac-COUNT · could-you-re-PLY · from-the-E-mail-ad-DRESS · REG-is-tered-with-US · once-we-have-con-FIRMED-it-is-YOU · i-will-START-the-re-QUEST · and-TELL-you · when-to-ex-PECT-the-FILE
linking: If read aloud: copy_of → "cop-pee-yuv" · protect_your → "pro-tek-chor" · confirmed_it → "con-fir-mdit"
intonation: If read aloud: a rise on "registered with us?" because it is a yes/no request, a short pause, then a steady fall on "expect the file".
indian_pron_tip: If read aloud, "data" is DAY-ta or DAH-ta with a light alveolar "t" (tongue behind the top teeth), not a heavy retroflex "t"; "protect" keeps the final "ct", not "protec".
customer_emotion: Curious or concerned about privacy, possibly suspicious of the company.
memory_hook: A locked filing cabinet: you show the customer the lock, ask for the one key that fits, then promise to open it.
hindi_meaning: अपने पर्सनल डेटा की कॉपी माँगने के लिए धन्यवाद। आपके अकाउंट की सुरक्षा के लिए, क्या आप हमारे पास रजिस्टर्ड ईमेल एड्रेस से जवाब दे सकते हैं? जब हम पुष्टि कर लेंगे कि यह आप ही हैं, तब मैं रिक्वेस्ट शुरू करूँगा/करूँगी और बताऊँगा/बताऊँगी कि फ़ाइल कब तक मिलेगी।
hindi_roman: Apne personal data ki copy maangne ke liye dhanyavaad. Aapke account ki suraksha ke liye, kya aap hamare paas registered email address se jawaab de sakte hain? Jab hum pushti kar lenge ki yeh aap hi hain, tab main request shuru karoonga/karoongi aur bataoonga/bataoongi ki file kab tak milegi.
simple_meaning: Thanks for asking. To keep your information safe, please write to us from the email address on your account. Then I will start and tell you when the file will come.
why_it_works: It thanks the customer instead of treating the request as a problem, states the purpose of the check, and asks for only one thing. The customer knows what happens next and why.
key_chunk: To protect your account, could you ___? Once we have confirmed ___, I will ___.
grammar_pattern: To + verb (purpose), + could you + verb …? · Once + present perfect, + I will + verb
grammar_note: "Once we have confirmed" means "after we confirm"; the present perfect shows one step must finish before the next.
tone_note: Stating the purpose makes the check feel protective, not suspicious. "We cannot share data with unknown persons" sounds like an accusation.
watch_out: ✗ Please send your Aadhaar, PAN and bank statement for verification. → ✓ To protect your account, could you reply from the email address registered with us?
dont_say: "We cannot share any data with you." — it sounds like a refusal and does not tell the customer how to get what they are entitled to.
positive_swap: Instead of "We need your ID proof before we can do anything", write "To protect your account, could you reply from the email address registered with us?"
alt_1: Thank you for your data request. To keep your information safe, please send your request from the email address on your account, and I will then get it started.
alt_2: We're happy to help with your data request. For security, could you reply from your registered email address? I will confirm the expected date as soon as we have checked it.
